1.subtitle: The Great Indictment
1.intro: Overview. Isaiah begins not with comfort but with a courtroom. God summons heaven and earth as witnesses and places his own people in the dock. The charge is devastating: Israel, whom he raised and nurtured, has rebelled more thoroughly than a dumb animal ignores its owner. Chapter 1 is the book's overture: every major theme sounds here before the symphony begins. The depth of human guilt, the futility of religion without repentance, and the astonishing willingness of God to forgive — all three are stated before chapter 2 begins.

sections.title: The Indictment
sections.commentary:
God opens his case with a comparison that should have been impossible: the ox knows its owner, the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know its God. In the ancient world this was a mark of the deepest stupidity — the dumb animal grasps a relationship that God's covenant people have forgotten. The Reformers identified this as the root form of sin: not first immorality but the failure of the heart to treasure and trust its maker. Every other sin in Isaiah's catalogue grows from this soil.

v. 2 — “Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me.” The word rebelled (pasha) is the language of political revolt — a vassal breaking covenant with his sovereign. What God names first is not a list of sins but the posture behind them: the will turned in defiance against the one who gave it life.

Verses 5–6 paint the consequence as a body covered head to foot in untreated wounds. The damage is total and wilfully unaddressed. This is Isaiah's version of what Paul systematises in Romans 3: sin has corrupted every faculty. Yet verse 9 inserts a grace note that anchors everything: if any survivors remain at all, it is only because the LORD of hosts preserved them. Mercy is the only explanation for a remnant.

sections.title: Religion Without Repentance
sections.commentary:
God does not here condemn the sacrificial system — he instituted it. What he condemns is using religious activity as a substitute for transformed hearts. They were keeping the calendar, attending the feasts, multiplying their offerings — and God calls it an abomination. Why? Because their hands were full of blood (v. 15). The outward form had been severed from inward reality. This is the exact diagnosis Jesus levels at the Pharisees in Matthew 23: meticulous about tithes of mint, careless about justice and mercy.

v. 13 — “Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me.” The word vain (shav) means emptiness, falsehood. The offerings are not wrong in themselves; they are lying — claiming a devotion that does not exist. God would rather have silence than liturgy that misrepresents the heart.

Verse 18 arrives after this severity like sunlight through a storm, and its force depends entirely on what precedes it. “Come now, let us reason together” is a legal summons, not a gentle suggestion. God invites people whose hands are full of blood to stand in his courtroom and discover that his mercy outweighs their guilt. The scarlet and crimson will become snow and wool. R.C. Sproul called this one of the clearest gospel declarations in the Old Testament: total guilt, total cleansing, freely offered.

sections.title: The Faithful City and the Promise of Restoration
sections.commentary:
The lament of verse 21 is a love poem reversed. Jerusalem was made to be the city of God's glory — righteous, just, faithful. She has become a harlot. The image is painful precisely because the relationship was so intimate. God is not merely offended; he is grieved. The silver has become dross, the wine has been watered down.

The refining image of verse 25 is crucial: God will smelt away the dross. Judgment in Isaiah is rarely merely punitive; it is disciplinary and ultimately restorative. Keller draws attention to this pattern throughout the prophets: God uses hard providences to bring his people back to himself, not to destroy them. The silver is still there beneath the dross.

v. 27 — “Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness.” This is the theology of the whole book in miniature. Redemption does not come by overlooking sin but through justice satisfied — which ultimately points forward to the cross, where divine justice and mercy meet in the same act.

keyVerse.quote: “Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.”
keyVerse.note: This verse follows one of the most severe indictments in Scripture — which is precisely what gives it its force. The invitation is extended not to the respectable but to the guilty, not after improvement but before it. The transformation promised is not gradual but total: scarlet to snow, crimson to wool. God does not say ‘reform first, then I will reason with you.’ He says ‘come’ — and the coming is itself an act of grace enabling the response.

1.theology:
Grace and repentance. Chapter 1 holds together two things that feel contradictory: the totality of human guilt (vv. 2–8) and the totality of divine mercy (v. 18). The grace on offer is not the product of Israel's repentance — it is the invitation that makes repentance possible. God does not say “repent and then I will reason with you.” He says “come” first.

True worship. Verses 10–17 raise the question every generation must answer: what does God actually want from his people's worship? The answer is not fewer religious acts but hearts that correspond to the acts. The problem is not ceremony but integrity — form without substance, attendance without adoration.
1.reflection: Isaiah 1 confronts two persistent temptations simultaneously: the temptation to substitute religious activity for genuine heart-worship, and the temptation to despair at the depth of one's own guilt. The chapter exposes both — and verse 18 cuts through both at once. If you have ever thought your sin was too deep or too long-standing for grace, read verse 18 slowly, in the context of everything that precedes it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 1 is the book's overture: God arraigns covenant Israel before the court of heaven. The indictment is total—a people who know God yet act as if they do not. The liturgical system has become a cover for social injustice. Yet the chapter ends not with execution but with an offer: come, let us reason together. Repentance is still possible; refusal is final.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter unfolds the logic of the covenant lawsuit (rib): God as suzerain, Israel as vassal, heaven and earth as witnesses. The theology is Sinaitic—the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy frame Israel's condition. Yet it also anticipates the gospel: the stain that cannot be removed by ceremony is removed by grace. Motyer: ch. 1 is a compressed Isaiah—judgment and hope woven together.
verseByVerse.examples: Every generation produces a church that maintains religious forms while abandoning justice and mercy. Isaiah 1 indicts comfortable Christianity that worships on Sunday while ignoring the widow, the orphan, and the oppressed on Monday.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz'—Isaiah means 'the LORD saves,' a name that encapsulates the book's theology. The term vision (hazon) suggests direct prophetic perception: Isaiah does not merely reason about God but sees him. 'Concerning Judah and Jerusalem'—the book is geographically local but cosmically universal; Jerusalem is the axis around which world history revolves. 'In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah'—a span of roughly 740–700 BC, from national prosperity to near-catastrophe. Oswalt: this historical grounding insists that Isaiah's message is not timeless philosophy but God's word into concrete crisis.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the LORD has spoken: “Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth'—the summons invokes creation as witness to the covenant lawsuit (cf. Deut. 32:1). The entire cosmos is called to observe Israel's unfaithfulness. ‘Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled’—the Hebrew bānim (sons/children) evokes the Exodus calling: Israel is God's firstborn son (Ex. 4:22). To rebel against such a Father is not merely lawbreaking but the betrayal of love. 'The ox knows its owner... but Israel does not know'—the bitter irony: dumb animals recognize their provider; God's covenant people do not. Motyer: the comparison is deliberately humiliating—Israel has fallen below the animal in basic orientation toward its master.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, offspring of evildoers, children who deal corruptly! They have forsaken the LORD, they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged. Why will you still be struck down? Why will you continue to rebel? The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, sinful nation'—the woe particle (hoy) signals lamentation as much as condemnation: God mourns over Israel even as he indicts her. 'Laden with iniquity'—the image is of a burden-bearer crushed under cargo he cannot set down; sin accumulates and weighs. 'They have despised the Holy One of Israel'—Isaiah's signature title for God appears here first. The Holy One is not distant—he has named Israel as his people. To despise him is therefore an intimate act of rejection. 'Why will you still be struck down?'—discipline has not produced repentance; the patient endures surgery but refuses the cure. Oswalt: Israel has reached a pathological state where punishment no longer corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no soundness in it, but bruises and sores and raw wounds; they are not pressed out or bound up or softened with oil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no soundness'—the medical metaphor is total: the whole body politic is afflicted. There is no healthy part from which healing can begin. 'Bruises and sores and raw wounds'—three terms for injuries in different stages of severity, accumulating toward the untreated. 'Not pressed out or bound up or softened with oil'—untreated wounds fester; Israel's wounds go without the remedies available in ancient medicine. Kidner: the nation is not merely sick but neglected—no one has applied the remedies at hand. The metaphor will recur in ch. 53 where the Servant bears these very wounds on behalf of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Your country lies desolate; your cities are burned with fire; in your very presence foreigners devour your land; it is desolate, as overthrown by foreigners. And the daughter of Zion is left like a booth in a vineyard, like a lodge in a cucumber field, like a besieged city. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your country lies desolate; your cities are burned with fire'—the language may reflect Sennacherib's Assyrian campaign (701 BC) which devastated Judah's cities. The vision is of a land stripped bare. 'The daughter of Zion is left like a booth in a vineyard'—a harvest shelter: temporary, fragile, abandoned at season's end. Jerusalem stands alone amid ruin. 'Like a besieged city'—isolation within desolation: enemies without, moral collapse within. Young: the image captures the paradox of election—Jerusalem is still standing, not because of her own strength but because God has not yet finished with her.

verseByVerse.quote: If the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors, we should have been like Sodom, and become like Gomorrah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors'—the word survivors (sarid) points to the doctrine of the remnant, one of Isaiah's great themes. The remnant is not the fruit of Israel's faithfulness but of God's restraint. 'We should have been like Sodom, and become like Gomorrah'—total annihilation is the logical consequence of total apostasy. That Jerusalem still exists is pure grace. Motyer: the survival of even one is miracle; the existence of any is the sign that God's purposes for his people have not been abandoned. Paul cites this verse in Romans 9:29 to ground his theology of sovereign grace.

verseByVerse.quote: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah! What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” says the LORD; “I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed beasts; I do not delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of goats. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You rulers of Sodom... you people of Gomorrah'—the shock is deliberate: Jerusalem's leaders are Sodom's rulers. The city of David has become the city of judgment. God does not address them as his people but as the paradigm of wickedness. 'What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?'—the rhetorical question is devastating: God, who instituted sacrifice, now disclaims it. This is not an abolition of the cult but a refusal of cult divorced from covenant ethics. Motyer: sacrifice without obedience is not incomplete worship—it is an offense. The system has been inverted: the forms remain but the substance has been evacuated.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come to appear before me, who has required of you this trampling of my courts? Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me. New moon and Sabbath and the calling of convocations— I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who has required of you this trampling of my courts?'—God disowns the very worship he commanded. The worshippers attend the temple but it is trampling, not reverence: their feet crush the sacred space because their lives crush the poor. 'Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination'—the strongest language in the vocabulary of holiness applied to the prescribed offerings. 'I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly'—a compressed paradox: the Hebrew tolerance of twin opposites in one sentence captures the moral contradiction. Oswalt: God cannot simultaneously be a God of justice and accept worship from those who practice injustice—the two cancel.

verseByVerse.quote: Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates; they have become a burden to me; I am weary of bearing them. When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My soul hates'—the language of personal antipathy, not mere theological disapproval. God's emotional response to hypocritical worship is loathing. 'I am weary of bearing them'—the festivals that were to be Israel's delight have become God's burden. The irony is total: Israel's religion fatigues the God it claims to honor. 'When you spread out your hands... I will hide my eyes'—the posture of prayer (hands extended) meets the turned face of God. The worshipper performs; God looks away. 'Your hands are full of blood'—the hands spread out in prayer are the same hands that have done violence to the poor and weak. The liturgy cannot cleanse what the life has stained.

verseByVerse.quote: Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes; cease to do evil, learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean'—not ritual ablution but moral cleansing. The imperatives are stacked: wash, make clean, remove, cease, learn, seek, correct, bring, plead—nine commands of urgent repentance. 'Remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes'—the deeds are visible to God even when concealed from human courts. 'Seek justice, correct oppression'—the Hebrew for correct (ashshiru) means either to straighten or to restrain: either reform the oppressor or check his power. 'Bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause'—the two most vulnerable classes in ancient society. Keller: the test of authentic religion has always been care for the vulnerable; you cannot worship the Father while ignoring his children in need.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool. If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Come, now, let us reason together'—after the scorching indictment, an astonishing invitation. God the plaintiff invites the defendant into dialogue. The forensic language becomes pastoral: God wants not execution but reconciliation. 'Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow'—scarlet and crimson were the most permanent dyes of the ancient world; no washing could remove them. Yet God promises transformation that only he can accomplish. Motyer: the grammar is declarative not conditional—God declares what he will do, not merely what might happen if conditions are met. 'If you are willing and obedient'—faith expressed in readiness to receive and walk accordingly.

verseByVerse.quote: but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword; for the mouth of the LORD has spoken. How the faithful city has become a whore, she who was full of justice! Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword'—the alternative to grace is judgment. The covenant offers two paths: blessing for obedience, curse for rebellion (Deut. 28). 'For the mouth of the LORD has spoken'—the divine imprimatur seals both the offer and the threat. 'How the faithful city has become a whore'—the lament (ekhah) echoes the opening of Lamentations; this is grief, not merely condemnation. Harlotry is Isaiah's metaphor for covenant infidelity (cf. Hosea, Jeremiah): Jerusalem was married to the LORD and has played the adulteress. 'Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers'—the contrast measures the depth of the fall from what she was to what she has become.

verseByVerse.quote: Your silver has become dross, your best wine mixed with water. Your princes are rebels and companions of thieves. Everyone loves a bribe and runs after gifts. They do not bring justice to the fatherless, and the widow's cause does not come to them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your silver has become dross'—the metallurgical image: what appeared valuable is revealed as worthless base metal. The city's leadership, its currency, its covenantal substance—all adulterated. 'Your best wine mixed with water'—diluted for deceptive profit; what is sold as pure wine is a watered-down product. 'Your princes are rebels and companions of thieves'—the leaders who should uphold the covenant are in league with its violators. 'Everyone loves a bribe'—the justice system is purchasable; the poor cannot afford access to their own courts. Oswalt: when leaders are corrupt, the entire social fabric unravels; visible injustice in the courts is the symptom of invisible spiritual collapse.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, declares: “Ah, I will get relief from my enemies and avenge myself on my foes. I will turn my hand against you and will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord GOD of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel'—the triple divine title accumulates weight; this is God in his full sovereignty acting. 'I will get relief from my enemies'—God's own people have become his adversaries. The paradox is devastating: the covenant partner is now the opponent. 'I will smelt away your dross as with lye'—the metallurgical image returns: God as refiner, Judah as ore. The smelting is painful (judgment) but purposive (purification). Lye (alkali) intensifies the refining process. Motyer: God's wrath against his people is not a contradiction of his love but its instrument—he will not leave them as they are.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city.” Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will restore your judges as at the first'—the goal of the smelting is restoration, not annihilation. The Davidic ideal: leaders who embody justice. 'Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city'—the name reverses the lament of v. 21. What Jerusalem has ceased to be, she shall become. This is eschatological hope grounded in divine determination. 'Zion shall be redeemed by justice'—the redemption is not despite justice but through it: God's own righteous character is the ground and means of Zion's salvation. Calvin: this points beyond any historical restoration to the final renewal of the city of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But rebels and sinners shall be broken together, and those who forsake the LORD shall be consumed. For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Rebels and sinners shall be broken together'—the sorting is decisive: within the one people there are those who repent (v. 27) and those who rebel. Both exist together in the present; at the end they are separated by divine judgment. 'They shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired'—the oaks are sacred trees associated with Canaanite fertility worship (cf. Hos. 4:13). Israel's syncretism—mixing Yahweh worship with Canaanite religious sites—will be exposed as the shameful thing it always was. 'The gardens that you have chosen'—not vegetable gardens but cultic gardens, sites of pagan ritual. The objects of desire will become sources of shame.

verseByVerse.quote: For you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water. And the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together, with none to quench them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like an oak whose leaf withers'—the irony is complete: Israel worshipped at oaks; now she becomes a withered oak. The object of false trust becomes the image of judgment. 'Like a garden without water'—the garden without irrigation in the Near Eastern climate dies quickly; without the LORD who is the water of life, Israel withers. 'The strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together'—the mighty man and his achievements become fuel for his own destruction. Self-generated strength produces self-generated judgment. Oswalt: the chapter ends with the terrifying image of irreversible combustion—judgment that cannot be quenched because the material itself is the fuel.

2.subtitle: The Mountain of the LORD and the Day Against Pride
2.intro: Overview. Chapter 2 holds two visions in dramatic tension: the glorious future when all nations stream to Zion to learn God's ways (vv. 1–5), and the coming day when God levels everything proud and lofty (vv. 6–22). The chapter's governing refrain — the LORD alone will be exalted in that day — appears twice, staking out the theological conviction that drives everything: history is moving toward the exclusive exaltation of God, and everything that sets itself up in his place will be brought low before that day arrives.

sections.title: The Mountain of the LORD
sections.commentary:
The vision of verses 2–4 is one of the great eschatological passages of the Old Testament. In the latter days, the mountain of God's house will be established as the highest of mountains — not a geographical claim but a theological one: God's authority will be visibly supreme over every competing claim to human allegiance. Nations will not be forced to Zion; they will flow to it, drawn by the gravity of what is there.

v. 4 — “They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore.” The famous image is not naive pacifism but the consequence of a prior transformation: when all disputes are settled at God's throne, weapons of war become instruments of harvest. Peace is not achieved by disarmament; it comes from the reign of the Prince of Peace.

Verse 5 is the pivot from vision to application: “O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD.” The vision of the future is not meant to be admired from a distance; it is meant to change how God's people live now. Begg often notes this structure in the prophets: grand theology always lands in a personal call. The light is coming — so walk in it today.

sections.title: The Day of the LORD Against Pride
sections.commentary:
The contrast with the vision of verses 1–5 could not be sharper. There, nations stream up to God; here, people scramble down into caves to hide from him. The difference is entirely a matter of whether his appearing is welcomed or feared — and that depends on whether one has received his grace or resisted it.

The catalogue of verses 12–16 is deliberately comprehensive: cedars, oaks, mountains, towers, fortified walls, ships. Everything humanity builds its confidence upon has a day against it. God is not threatened by these things; he simply outranks them. Sproul called this one of the most important texts for understanding the holiness of God: the refrain the LORD alone will be exalted is the governing principle of all history.

v. 22 — “Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?” The most bracing command in the chapter. Cease putting ultimate confidence in human beings, however gifted or powerful. Even the greatest human leader is a creature dependent on the next breath. The only safe foundation is the one who will still be standing when the cedars have fallen.

keyVerse.quote: “The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.”
keyVerse.note: This phrase appears twice in the chapter (vv. 11 and 17), functioning as a refrain. Isaiah is not predicting that God will eventually win after a close contest. He is declaring that the exaltation of the LORD is the fixed destination of all history — and every human attempt at self-exaltation is moving against the tide of the universe.

2.theology:
The Day of the LORD. This concept — a decisive intervention of God to judge evil and establish his kingdom — runs throughout the prophets and into the New Testament. In Isaiah 2 it has a double edge: terror for the proud (vv. 10–22) and glory for those who stream to Zion (vv. 2–4). The same event produces both outcomes, depending entirely on whether one is under God's judgment or his grace.

Idolatry as pride. The idols of verses 8 and 20 are not simply bad religion; they are an expression of the deeper sin named in verse 22: the elevation of the human above the divine. Idolatry is pride in concrete form — the decision to trust the work of one's own hands rather than the God who made the hands.
2.reflection: The two halves of chapter 2 speak to the same reality from two angles. The vision of the nations streaming to Zion is meant to produce longing and hope. The vision of the day against pride is meant to produce sober self-examination. The question the chapter leaves ringing: where are you placing your confidence — in the things that will be brought low, or in the LORD who alone will be exalted?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. <sup>2</sup>It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, <sup>3</sup>and many peoples shall come, and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths." <sup>10</sup>Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty. <sup>11</sup>The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. <sup>12</sup>For the LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up— and it shall be brought low; <sup>13</sup>against all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up; and against all the oaks of Bashan; <sup>14</sup>against all the lofty mountains, and against all the uplifted hills; <sup>15</sup>against every high tower, and against every fortified wall; <sup>16</sup>against all the ships of Tarshish, and against all the beautiful craft. <sup>17</sup>And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. <sup>18</sup>And the idols shall utterly pass away. <sup>19</sup>And people shall enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. <sup>20</sup>In that day mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats, <sup>21</sup>to enter the caverns of the rocks and the clefts of the cliffs, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. <sup>22</sup>Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Mountain of the LORD and the Day of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 2 holds two visions in tension: the exaltation of Zion as the center of the nations (vv. 2–4), and the terror of the Day of the LORD against human pride (vv. 6–22). The chapter begins with the highest hope and descends through a catalog of human arrogance to a call to abandon all false trust. Zion's exaltation is the foundation that makes human pride all the more inexcusable.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology is eschatological: the 'latter days' reach beyond any historical moment to the final resolution of history when all nations stream to the LORD. Yet the Day of the LORD is also the moment when everything human beings have trusted instead of God is revealed as nothing. The two visions together define what true glory is (God's) and what counterfeit glory is (human achievement). Webb: the juxtaposition is the book's permanent challenge—choose the mountain that rises or the pride that falls.
verseByVerse.examples: The church lives between these two visions: already citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, not yet at the consummation. Human culture still erects towers of pride—technology, military power, financial systems. Isaiah 2 calls the church to stop trusting in these and to walk in the light of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw'—the double superscription (cf. 1:1) marks the beginning of a new unit. Seeing the word is prophetic idiom: the prophet perceives divine revelation as vision. 'Concerning Judah and Jerusalem'—the geographical focus continues; the nations will come to Jerusalem (vv. 2–3), and Jerusalem's inhabitants will face the Day of the LORD (vv. 6–21). Motyer: the repetition signals that ch. 2 is not a loose continuation but a fresh divine address on the same subjects.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come, and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.” For out of Zion shall go the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the latter days'—the eschatological horizon: what is described transcends any single historical moment and reaches to the final state of things. 'The mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest'—not geographical elevation but covenantal preeminence. God's dwelling place will be recognized as the ultimate authority. 'All the nations shall flow to it'—the impossible reversal: nations do not go up to Jerusalem now, but will. The flow is voluntary—drawn, not compelled. 'That he may teach us his ways'—the nations come not merely to observe but to learn; the missionary dynamic originates in Zion's magnetism. 'Out of Zion shall go the law'—Torah as light to the nations (cf. 42:6; 49:6). Oswalt: this vision of universal pilgrimage is the telos of all Isaiah's ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore. O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He shall judge between the nations'—the LORD as universal arbiter: all international conflict referred to his court. 'They shall beat their swords into plowshares'—the most famous image of the chapter. The instrument of war is recycled into the instrument of food production: violence transformed into life-sustaining labor. This is not mere disarmament but the transformation of human vocation. 'Neither shall they learn war anymore'—war is a taught skill; when the teacher is gone the skill disappears. 'O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD'—the vision of the nations' future becomes a summons for Israel's present. Webb: if this is where history is going, Israel should already be walking there.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have rejected your people, the house of Jacob, because they are full of things from the east and of fortune-tellers like the Philistines, and they strike hands with the foreigners. Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures; their land is filled with horses, and there is no end to their chariots. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You have rejected your people'—God's rejection is the consequence of Israel's prior rejection of him: covenant mutual abandonment. 'Full of things from the east'—occult practices and divination imported from Mesopotamia, the source of Israel's cultural infatuation. 'Fortune-tellers like the Philistines'—the irony: Israel was to be distinct from the nations; now she has adopted pagan practices from her historic enemies. 'Their land is filled with silver and gold... horses and chariots'—exactly what Deuteronomy 17:16–17 forbade the king to multiply. Military and economic power have replaced reliance on the LORD. Motyer: the three accumulations (occultism, wealth, military) are three forms of self-sufficiency that crowd out God.

verseByVerse.quote: Their land is filled with idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their own fingers have made. So man is humbled, and each one is brought low— do not forgive them! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Their land is filled with idols'—idolatry completes the triad: occultism, materialism, idolatry. The land promised as God's dwelling is filled with competitors for his throne. 'They bow down to the work of their hands'—the fundamental absurdity of idolatry: the creature worships what it has made. The manufacturer becomes the devotee. 'So man is humbled, and each one is brought low'—worship of the idol degrades the worshipper. To bow before what you made is to become lower than your own creation. 'Do not forgive them'—a jarring petition, possibly the prophet's own voice, marking the point where the time for easy mercy has closed. Oswalt: the petition acknowledges that some rejections become irreversible.

verseByVerse.quote: Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty. The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Enter into the rock and hide in the dust'—the proud who have set themselves up now flee into the earth. The irony: they tried to rise; they end up hiding in the ground. 'From before the terror of the LORD'—the Day of the LORD reveals God's character in its fullness; those who have not known him as Savior will know him as judge, and the experience is terrifying. 'The haughty looks of man shall be brought low'—the Hebrew uses triple repetition of the root for height (rum): lofty man, lofty pride, lofty looks—all brought down. 'The LORD alone will be exalted in that day'—the great leveling: when the Day comes, only one height remains. Calvin: this is not God's defeat of enemies but the reassertion of his rightful glory.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up— and it shall be brought low; against all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up, and against all the oaks of Bashan; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty'—the Day of the LORD is an appointed meeting: God and human pride face to face. The judgment is not capricious but principled: it falls on pride as such. 'Against all the cedars of Lebanon'—the cedar was the symbol of magnificence and power in the ancient world; Solomon imported them for the temple and palace. Here they represent everything humanly impressive. 'And all the oaks of Bashan'—Bashan's oaks were famous for their strength. Motyer: the natural world's most impressive specimens represent human achievement at its most commanding—the judgment sweeps through all categories.

verseByVerse.quote: against all the lofty mountains, and against all the uplifted hills; against every high tower, and against every fortified wall; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Against all the lofty mountains... uplifted hills'—the catalog moves from the organic to the constructed. Mountains and hills are nature's heights; towers and walls are human constructions. Both fall under the same judgment. 'Against every high tower, and against every fortified wall'—military architecture: the tower commanded the field of battle; the wall was the city's security. Both represent the human project of self-protection apart from God. Young: the comprehensive list covers all categories of human reliance—natural beauty, built strength—to show that nothing escapes the Day of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: against all the ships of Tarshish, and against all the beautiful craft. And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Against all the ships of Tarshish'—the great commercial vessels of the Mediterranean, the symbol of international trade and wealth. Tarshish represents the farthest reach of commerce. 'Against all the beautiful craft'—the stately ships. Oswalt: the ships represent international economic power, the ancient world's equivalent of globalized finance. 'The haughtiness of man shall be humbled'—the refrain (cf. vv. 9, 11) drives the point home: the Day's agenda is singular and relentless. Human pride in every form—military, commercial, architectural, natural—must bow. The LORD alone is exalted; all else must find its proper level.

verseByVerse.quote: And the idols shall utterly pass away. And people shall enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'And the idols shall utterly pass away'—the Day disposes of idols definitively. What was worshipped is revealed as nothing and disappears. The Hebrew uses total language: utterly, completely. 'People shall enter the caves of the rocks'—not just hiding but burrowing into the earth: the reversal of the tower-builders. Instead of ascending they descend into caves. 'When he rises to terrify the earth'—God's theophanic appearance is the cause. The earth itself trembles at his arising. Motyer: the sequence is precise—idols vanish, people flee, earth trembles; each stage follows necessarily from God's appearing in his majesty.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats, to enter the caverns of the rocks and the clefts of the cliffs, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold'—the precious metals invested in idolatry are abandoned. The idols that were treasured become burdens to be thrown away as people flee. 'To the moles and to the bats'—creatures of darkness and underground; the idols go to creatures that cannot see them and will not worship them. The final destination of the gods is the animal kingdom. 'From before the terror of the LORD'—the motivation for fleeing is the encounter with God's glory. Childs: the abandonment of idols is not repentance but terror; they are thrown away not because they were wrong but because they are now useless for escape.

verseByVerse.quote: Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath'—the conclusion draws the practical implication from the entire chapter. Human beings are nostrils-and-breath: the same dust that God animated at creation (Gen. 2:7). 'For of what account is he?'—the rhetorical question expects the answer: none. Not nothing in the sense of worthlessness as God's image-bearer, but nothing as a foundation for ultimate trust. Motyer: the call to stop regarding man is the positive side of the Day's message—if God alone is exalted, then man alone must not be trusted. Keller: every generation must learn anew that placing ultimate hope in human leadership, human systems, or human achievement is spiritual folly.

3.subtitle: Judgment on Jerusalem's Leaders
3.intro: Overview. Chapter 3 works out a specific form of divine judgment: the withdrawal of good leadership. When God removes his blessing from a society, one of the earliest signs is the collapse of wise governance — boys become princes, the incompetent are elevated, the social order unravels from the top. The second half of the chapter turns to the women of Zion — not to single them out but because their pride and extravagance are a precise symptom of a society that has turned entirely inward, using wealth as a measure of worth while justice goes unsought.

sections.title: Leadership Stripped Away
sections.commentary:
God's judgment begins not as a foreign invasion but as a withdrawal. Support and supply, warrior and soldier, judge and prophet, elder and counsellor — all are removed. What remains is verse 4: boys as princes, infants as rulers. This is not a judgment on youth but on immaturity and the absence of wisdom that comes from fearing God. Leadership that is reactive, self-serving, and untethered from moral reality is itself a form of divine curse on a nation.

v. 9 — “They proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it.” There is a progression in moral decay: sin is first committed in secret, then tolerated, then normalised, then celebrated. When shamelessness itself becomes a virtue and the hiding instinct is gone, the society has moved beyond self-correction. MacArthur notes this is precisely the trajectory Paul traces in Romans 1.

The legal action of verse 13 — God rising to contend, standing to judge — is the backdrop for everything. The charge against the leaders is specific: you have devoured the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses. Leaders who exploit the vulnerable will give account. The care of the poor appears throughout Isaiah as a mark of genuine covenant faithfulness.

vv. 10–11 — “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them… Woe to the wicked!” Tucked inside a chapter of unrelenting judgment, these two verses function as a pastoral anchor. They do not promise that the righteous will escape the chaos of a collapsing society. They declare ultimate outcomes. The moral universe God made has not been suspended.

sections.title: The Women of Zion
sections.commentary:
The extended passage on the women of Zion is frequently misread as prudishness about fashion. The point is different. Isaiah lists twenty-one items of luxury — anklets, headbands, crescents, perfume boxes, signet rings — painting a picture of a society that has turned its energy and imagination entirely toward self-adornment while the poor are ground down and justice is sold. The problem is not beauty; it is the idolatry of status, the use of wealth as the ultimate measure of worth.

The reversal of verse 24 is devastating in its symmetry: perfume replaced by rottenness, a belt by a rope, well-set hair by baldness, a rich robe by sackcloth, beauty by branding. The chapter ends in silence: “empty, she shall sit on the ground.” The city that adorned herself with finery ends stripped and silent. This is where every idolatrous substitute for God eventually arrives.

keyVerse.quote: “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him.”
keyVerse.note: These two verses in the middle of unrelenting judgment are a reminder that Isaiah's God is not random or arbitrary in his dealings. The moral universe holds. Whatever suffering the righteous endure in a corrupt society, the final word over their lives is well. This is not optimism but eschatological certainty — and it is enough to make perseverance possible.

3.reflection: Chapter 3 is uncomfortable precisely because its diagnoses are recognisable across every generation: bad governance as divine judgment, normalised shamelessness, the powerful exploiting the poor, status-display substituting for character. The pastoral response is not despair but the posture of verses 10–11: keep trusting that it shall be well with the righteous, and keep doing good.

O my people, your guides mislead you and they have swallowed up the course of your paths. <sup>13</sup>The LORD has taken his place to contend; he stands to judge peoples. <sup>14</sup>The LORD will enter into judgment with the elders and princes of his people: "It is you who have devoured the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in your houses. <sup>15</sup>What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor?" declares the Lord GOD of hosts. <sup>16</sup>The LORD said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes, mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet, <sup>17</sup>therefore the Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will lay bare their secret parts. <sup>18</sup>In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; <sup>19</sup>the pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves; <sup>20</sup>the headdresses, the armlets, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets; <sup>21</sup>the signet rings and nose rings; <sup>22</sup>the festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the handbags; <sup>23</sup>the mirrors, the linen garments, the turbans, and the veils. <sup>24</sup>Instead of perfume there will be rottenness; and instead of a belt, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a rich robe, a skirt of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty. <sup>25</sup>Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle. <sup>26</sup>And her gates shall lament and mourn; empty, she shall sit on the ground.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Collapse of Society and the Judgment of Jerusalem's Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 3 describes society unraveling from the top down: God removes competent leadership, chaos replaces order, and the vulnerable are left unprotected. The second half (vv. 16–26) focuses on Jerusalem's wealthy women whose pride epitomizes the city's spiritual condition. Their adornment is elaborate; their judgment will be total.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology is covenantal causation: when a society abandons God, God removes the structures that held it together. Leadership, wisdom, experience, craft—all are gifts that God gives and withdraws. The catalog of women's ornaments (vv. 18–23) is not puritanical aversion to beauty but a theological inventory: everything used to project status will be stripped away. Webb: Isaiah 3 is one of the Bible's most penetrating analyses of social collapse.
verseByVerse.examples: The church must grapple with Isaiah 3's social analysis: leadership failure, the exploitation of the poor by the powerful, and the use of material display to signal value rather than character. The women of Jerusalem used adornment to project worth the city did not have; every generation finds its equivalent form of false display.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the Lord GOD of hosts is taking away from Jerusalem and from Judah support and supply, all support of bread, and all support of water; the mighty man and the soldier, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord GOD of hosts is taking away'—divine subtraction: God removes rather than directly punishes. The removal of good is itself judgment. 'Support and supply'—the Hebrew encompasses everything that sustains social life, both the material (bread, water) and the human (competent leaders). 'All support of bread, and all support of water'—the removal of basic food and water security; famine as covenant curse (Deut. 28:23–24). 'The mighty man and the soldier, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder'—military, judicial, prophetic, and traditional wisdom all removed. Motyer: the list is a sociology of competence; God removes every category of leadership the society depends upon.

verseByVerse.quote: the captain of fifty and the man of rank, the counselor and the skillful magician and the expert in charms. And I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The captain of fifty and the man of rank'—military middle management and social aristocracy both removed. 'The counselor and the skillful magician and the expert in charms'—even the practitioners of occult wisdom (condemned elsewhere) are named because their removal signals total social confusion: there will be no wisdom, legitimate or otherwise. 'I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them'—the ultimate civic degradation. Not merely bad leadership but the absence of adult leadership. Oswalt: this is both literal (Judah's final kings were weak and young) and symbolic—a society that rejects divine wisdom will be governed by immaturity and caprice.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people will oppress one another, every one his fellow and every one his neighbor; the youth will be insolent to the elder, and the despised to the honorable. For a man will take hold of his brother in the house of his father, saying: “You have a cloak; you shall be our leader, and this heap of ruins shall be under your rule.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The people will oppress one another'—social solidarity collapses; the covenant community turns predatory. 'Every one his fellow and every one his neighbor'—the concentric circles of community (family, neighbor, fellow-citizen) all become zones of exploitation. 'The youth will be insolent to the elder'—generational hierarchy inverted: the young show contempt for the wisdom of age. 'You have a cloak; you shall be our leader'—desperate conditions produce absurd leadership criteria: any man with a coat can rule the rubble. The standard for leadership has collapsed to the material minimum. Young: the scene depicts total social desperation where the outward sign of the most basic sufficiency becomes the qualification for authority.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day he will speak out, saying: “I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor cloak; you shall not make me leader of the people.” For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their speech and their deeds are against the LORD, defying his glorious presence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will not be a healer'—the would-be leader refuses. No one wants the position because there is nothing left to govern. 'In my house there is neither bread nor cloak'—the universal destitution: the most basic necessities gone. 'You shall not make me leader of the people'—even compelled leadership is refused when ruin is total. 'For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen'—the prophetic perfect: as certain as if already accomplished. 'Their speech and their deeds are against the LORD'—the root cause of social collapse is theological. Society fell because it defied God in word and deed, not merely structurally. Motyer: the moral and theological are inseparable; social collapse is always downstream of spiritual collapse.

verseByVerse.quote: For the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it. Woe to them! For they have brought evil on themselves. Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The look on their faces bears witness against them'—shamelessness: the face that once blushed at sin now displays it openly. The loss of moral shame is both symptom and accelerant of social collapse. 'They proclaim their sin like Sodom'—Sodom's sin was not only its act but its brazenness; it was the city that demanded its wickedness openly (Gen. 19:9). 'Woe to them! For they have brought evil on themselves'—the woe interprets the judgment: they are not passive victims but active architects of their ruin. 'Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them'—within the judgment there is a sorting. The righteous will eat the fruit of their deeds: the covenant blessings belong to the faithful. Oswalt: the two-way sorting is a constant in Isaiah's theology of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him. My people—infants are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, your guides mislead you and they have swallowed up the course of your paths. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him'—the negative counterpart to v. 10's assurance for the righteous. The lex talionis is covenantal: what the hands deal out returns to the dealer. 'Infants are their oppressors, and women rule over them'—not an insult to women but a description of the total inversion of social order; the structures of competent leadership have so collapsed that those who were not in leadership positions now lead by default. 'Your guides mislead you'—the leaders are actively harmful, not merely incompetent; they do not merely fail to find the path, they direct away from it. Calvin: misleading leaders are worse than absent leaders; they consume the path itself rather than simply leaving it unmarked.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has taken his place to contend; he stands to judge peoples. The LORD will enter into judgment with the elders and princes of his people: “It is you who have devoured the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in your houses. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD has taken his place to contend'—the divine tribunal convenes. God steps forward as plaintiff and judge simultaneously. This is the prophetic rib (lawsuit) pattern at its most direct. 'He stands to judge peoples'—the scope is both Israel specifically (the elders and princes named next) and peoples generally. 'It is you who have devoured the vineyard'—the vineyard is Israel (cf. 5:1–7); the leaders appointed to tend it have consumed it for themselves. 'The spoil of the poor is in your houses'—what the leaders have accumulated is specifically identified as plunder taken from the vulnerable. The houses of the powerful are repositories of injustice. Webb: the judgment is not abstract but specific—God names both the crime and the criminals.

verseByVerse.quote: What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor?” declares the Lord GOD of hosts. The LORD said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes, mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor?'—the rhetorical question demands an answer that cannot be given. Grinding the face is brutal imagery: the face pressed against the grinding stone. The poor are not merely disadvantaged but actively destroyed. 'Declares the Lord GOD of hosts'—the divine title underscores authority. 'The daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks'—the shift from economic injustice to social vanity is not arbitrary: Isaiah sees the pride of the women as the spiritual expression of the same pride that oppressed the poor. 'Mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet'—elaborate movement and ankle jewelry designed to attract attention. Motyer: the women embody the city's defining posture of self-regard.

verseByVerse.quote: the Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will lay bare their secret parts. In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion'—the judgment mirrors the sin: pride in beautiful hair is met with scalp disease or shaving. The body that was the object of elaborate beautification becomes the site of public humiliation. 'The LORD will lay bare their secret parts'—exile's shame: captives were stripped and marched. What was concealed and adorned is exposed. 'In that day the Lord will take away the finery'—the long catalog begins. Every ornament listed in vv. 18–23 represents something that will be removed. Young: the stripping is not mere punishment but revelation—what is underneath the adornment is exposed to the light of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: the pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves; the headdresses, the armlets, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves'—fine jewelry items: pendants hung from ears or neck; bracelets adorned wrists; scarves were decorative fabric. 'The headdresses, the armlets, the sashes'—head coverings of fine fabric, upper-arm ornaments, elaborate belts. 'The perfume boxes'—small containers worn around the neck releasing fragrance; cf. the beloved's perfume in Song of Songs. 'The amulets'—charms worn for protection, often with religious or magical significance. Oswalt: the list's exhaustive detail forces the reader to visualize the totality of what will be stripped; Isaiah is thorough because the judgment will be thorough—nothing retained, nothing spared.

verseByVerse.quote: the signet rings and nose rings; the festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the handbags; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The signet rings and nose rings'—signet rings carried legal identity and authority; nose rings were costly jewelry. Both personal identity (signet) and aesthetic display (nose ring) are removed. 'The festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks'—garments for special occasions, elegant outer garments, everyday cloaks—the full wardrobe is cataloged. 'The handbags'—the satchels or purses carried by women of means. Motyer: the list moves from external jewelry to practical possessions, covering every category of personal adornment and belonging; nothing is exempted from the stripping that divine judgment accomplishes.

verseByVerse.quote: the linen garments, the turbans, and the veils. Instead of perfume there will be rottenness; and instead of a belt, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a rich robe, a skirt of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The linen garments, the turbans, and the veils'—the finest fabrics, elaborate head-wrapping, and face-covering completes the inventory. Every element of dress is accounted for. 'Instead of perfume there will be rottenness'—the scent of death replaces the fragrance of life. 'Instead of a belt, a rope'—the belt that gathered the fine robe replaced by the rope that binds the captive. 'Instead of well-set hair, baldness'—mourning's sign and the mark of the shamed captive. 'Branding instead of beauty'—the slave-mark burned into flesh where ornament once rested. Childs: the sevenfold 'instead of' sequence is a comprehensive reversal—every element of former glory has its precise negative counterpart in judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle. And her gates shall lament and mourn; emptied, she shall sit on the ground. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle'—the women's adornment has been stripped; now the men who were their protectors fall in war. The social structure that supported the women's display collapses militarily. 'Her gates shall lament and mourn'—the city-gate was the center of civic life: justice, commerce, community. When the gate mourns, public life has ended. 'Emptied, she shall sit on the ground'—Jerusalem personified as a widow in the posture of grief: sitting on the ground (the posture of Lamentations). Motyer: the chapter ends with the city as bereft woman—the reversal of Zion the mother and queen. What was proud sits desolate in the dust.

4.subtitle: The Branch of the LORD
4.intro: Overview. Chapter 4 is only six verses — a brief but essential shaft of light after the darkness of chapter 3. Without it, the reader might conclude that Isaiah's God is nothing but a judge. Embedded here is one of the earliest Messianic titles in the book: the Branch of the LORD. The movement is from desolation (v. 1) to beauty and glory (vv. 2–6), from stripping to clothing, from exposure to shelter. What judgment removes, grace restores — and more than restores.

sections.title: Desolation: The Context for Grace
sections.commentary:
Verse 1 connects directly to the closing verses of chapter 3, where the men of Jerusalem have fallen in battle. The image of seven women seeking one man is a picture of demographic collapse — a society so depleted by war that normal social structures have been torn apart. “Seven” carries the sense of completeness; this is not an exceptional case but a widespread condition.

It is important not to skip verse 1 on the way to verse 2. The grace of verse 2 is only felt when the desolation of verse 1 is held in full view. This is how God's comfort consistently works in Scripture: it comes into specific darkness, not over it. The branch grows from devastated ground.

sections.title: The Branch and the Cloud of Glory
sections.commentary:
“In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious.” The Branch (tsemach) is a Messianic title Isaiah introduces here and that later prophets develop richly — Jeremiah calls him “a righteous Branch” who will execute justice (Jer 23:5); Zechariah applies it to the coming king-priest who will build the temple of God (Zech 6:12–13). In Isaiah 4 the Branch appears in the aftermath of judgment as the one in whom beauty and glory are restored — a remarkable contrast with the Servant of chapter 53, who had “no form or majesty that we should look at him.” Both are true: the Branch comes first in hidden glory, then in open magnificence.

v. 3 — “He who is left in Zion… will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem.” The phrase recorded for life is election language. The survivor community is not one that escaped disaster by luck; it is one specifically preserved and specifically cleansed (v. 4). This anticipates the New Testament doctrine of a people chosen by God and kept through every storm.

The closing image of cloud by day and fire by night is explicitly new-exodus language — the divine presence that guided Israel through the wilderness now covering the entire redeemed community. God's presence, once mediated through a portable tent, will shelter the whole people. Revelation 21:3 announces its final form: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.”

keyVerse.quote: “In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: The title “Branch” introduced here is one of the richest Messianic descriptions in the Old Testament. It suggests organic growth — something that grows naturally from existing roots rather than arriving as an alien intrusion. Jesus is not an afterthought to Israel's story; he grows from it, as a branch from a tree. And in him, what was laid waste becomes beautiful again.

4.theology:
The Messianic Branch. Isaiah 4:2 introduces a title that runs through the prophets and reaches its fulfilment in Christ. The Branch theology emphasises continuity (he grows from the root of Israel's history, from the line of David) and transformation (he brings what the tree itself could never produce — holiness, glory, shelter for all who come to him). Matthew's genealogy matters because Jesus is the Branch, traceable to Abraham and David.

Remnant and election. The concept of the preserved remnant — those “recorded for life” — runs throughout Isaiah. It is not earned survival but sovereign preservation. Paul develops this in Romans 9–11: the existence of a faithful remnant within Israel is always a demonstration of grace, never of deserving.
4.reflection: Chapter 4 is the antidote to despair after the severity of chapters 1–3. Judgment is real; the stripping is real. But the Branch of the LORD is also real — and he is coming. The community that will receive him is not the proudest or most impressive, but the survivors: those who have been through the fire and found that God was in it.
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach." <sup>2</sup>In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel. <sup>3</sup>And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem, <sup>4</sup>when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning. <sup>5</sup>Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a canopy. <sup>6</sup>There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Branch of the LORD and the Renewed Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 4 is a hinge: it closes the judgment sequence of ch. 3 (v. 1) and opens the restoration vision that anticipates the book's great themes. The Branch of the LORD (v. 2) is the first messianic title in the book. The chapter ends with a new Exodus: the pillar of cloud and fire returns to cover the redeemed remnant.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology moves from judgment to grace through the remnant. Those who survive the judgment are not survivors by their own merit but the holy remnant that God himself has washed clean. The theophanic cloud and fire recall Sinai and the wilderness: God's presence with his people is the essence of salvation. Motyer: ch. 4 is a compressed eschatological vision—messianic figure, purified remnant, renewed divine presence gathered into six verses.
verseByVerse.examples: The Branch is the first of Isaiah's great messianic titles, developed in 11:1 and picked up by Jeremiah and Zechariah. Every generation of God's people lives by the promise of vv. 2–6: a purified community sheltered by divine presence. The cloud-and-fire imagery is fulfilled in the glory that fills the new temple (Ezek. 43) and in the Lamb who is the temple of the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21–22).

verseByVerse.quote: And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach.” In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Seven women shall take hold of one man'—the aftermath of the war of 3:25: men have fallen; women are desperate for marriage and the social protection of a name. 'We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes'—renouncing the normal marriage claim; they ask only for the name that removes social shame. 'The branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious'—the transition is abrupt and intentional. From the depth of social ruin rises the Branch: the messianic shoot who will be all that Israel was not. Childs: the Branch is both the Davidic scion and a new act of divine creation—he is the LORD's branch, not merely David's. 'The fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors'—the land's abundance restored as sign of spiritual renewal.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem, when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He who is left in Zion... will be called holy'—the remnant's defining characteristic is not survival but holiness. They are not merely the remainder but the consecrated ones. 'Everyone who has been recorded for life'—the divine registry: God keeps the names of the living (cf. Ex. 32:32; Rev. 20:12). Election is personal and permanent. 'When the Lord shall have washed away the filth'—the holiness is not inherent but achieved by divine cleansing. The same Jerusalem whose daughters paraded their adornment will have its filth removed. 'By a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning'—the Spirit as purifying fire. Oswalt: the cleansing is painful (burning) but thorough; the result is holiness, not comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a canopy. There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion... a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night'—the new Exodus: the pillar of cloud and fire that guided and protected Israel in the wilderness (Ex. 13:21–22) returns to cover the restored community. Create (bara) is the word of Genesis 1: this is a new-creation act. 'For over all the glory there will be a canopy'—the glory (kabod) is both God's presence and the community's honor in him. The canopy shelters the glory as the tabernacle sheltered the ark. 'A booth for shade... a refuge and a shelter from the storm'—Webb: the imagery accumulates: shade, refuge, shelter. God's presence is the comprehensive protection of his people in every weather and every condition.

5.subtitle: The Song of the Vineyard and the Six Woes
5.intro: Overview. Chapter 5 is one of Isaiah's most accomplished literary compositions. It opens with a love song that turns into a lawsuit (vv. 1–7), catalogues six specific moral and social sins with the prophetic “Woe” associated with funeral laments (vv. 8–23), and closes with a vision of judgment so swift it leaves no room for delay (vv. 24–30). Jesus knew this chapter intimately; his parable of the tenants in Matthew 21 is a direct retelling of the vineyard song, using the same rhetorical strategy of drawing hearers into passing judgment before they realise they are the ones in the dock.

sections.title: The Song of the Vineyard
sections.commentary:
Isaiah opens as a singer performing a love song about his friend's vineyard. Listeners expect a celebration. As they hear of all the careful preparation — the choice hillside, the clearing of stones, the planted vines, the watchtower, the wine vat — they are drawn into sympathy with the farmer. Then the twist: after all that investment, wild grapes. The farmer invites the audience to judge: “What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it?” Nothing. The failure is entirely the vineyard's. Before the listeners realise it, they have judged themselves.

v. 7 — “He looked for justice (mishpat), but behold, bloodshed (mispach); for righteousness (tsedaqah), but behold, an outcry (tse'aqah).” Isaiah's Hebrew puns are untranslatable but unforgettable. The vineyard produced the exact inverse of what it was planted to yield — not ignorance of God's standard but systematic inversion of it.

sections.title: The Six Woes
sections.commentary:
The six woes cover the sins that most thoroughly unravel a society. The first (v. 8) targets covetous land accumulation — the wealthy systematically displacing small landowners until entire communities are dispossessed. The second (vv. 11–12) targets hedonism without God: feasting, music, and wine consumed as ends in themselves, so that the revellers “do not regard the deeds of the LORD.” It is possible to be surrounded by beauty and culture and remain entirely blind to God.

The fourth woe (v. 20) speaks most directly across every age: Woe to those who call evil good and good evil. This is not simple moral confusion but moral inversion — a systematic relabelling of God's categories. Sproul often observed that the greatest danger to a society is not that it does evil but that it redefines evil as good, thereby removing any vocabulary for repentance. When darkness is called light, people stop looking for the switch.

v. 21 — “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight!” Intellectual pride — the refusal to submit one's judgments to the word of God — is the root from which moral inversion grows. The order of the woes is not accidental: self-wisdom precedes and enables the inversion of moral categories.

sections.title: The Coming Judgment
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends with the sound of an army. The force described in verses 26–29 is terrifyingly efficient: no one tired, no one stumbling, not a sandal strap broken, arrows sharp, bows bent. God does not improvise; he whistles, and they come.

v. 25 — “For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.” This phrase becomes a haunting refrain in chapters 9–10, repeated four times. Each repetition marks another stage of judgment on a people who will not turn back. God's patience is purposeful — and it has a limit.

The chapter closes in darkness — the answer to the unanswered question of verse 4: “What more was there to do?” When every care has been given and the vineyard still produces wild grapes, what remains is night. But Isaiah's book does not end here. The same voice that pronounces this darkness will say in 9:2: “the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.”

keyVerse.quote: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!”
keyVerse.note: This woe does not describe a society that has forgotten God's standards but one that has actively inverted them. The triple parallelism (evil/good, darkness/light, bitter/sweet) emphasises that this is comprehensive and deliberate. Once a culture reaches this stage, self-correction from within is almost impossible — the moral vocabulary needed for repentance has been destroyed. Only a word from outside the system can break through.

5.theology: Covenant and social justice. The woes of Isaiah 5 are not primarily political commentary; they are covenant charges. Israel was called to be a society that embodied God's character — justice for the poor, honest weights, truthful speech. The woes describe what a covenant community looks like when it has abandoned the God of the covenant while keeping its religious forms. Social justice in Isaiah is always the fruit of true worship, never its substitute.
5.reflection: Isaiah 5 asks the question God himself asks of the vineyard: what more could have been done? Everything was provided; nothing more could be given. The chapter is an invitation to honest self-examination — not only about the sins of society, but about the fruit one's own life is bearing for the One who planted it with such care.
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. <sup>2</sup>He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. <sup>3</sup>And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. <sup>4</sup>What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes? <sup>5</sup>And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down. <sup>6</sup>I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. <sup>7</sup>For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting; and he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!
