<sup>8</sup>Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land. <sup>9</sup>The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: "Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant. <sup>10</sup>For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah." <sup>11</sup>Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them! <sup>12</sup>They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands. <sup>13</sup>Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst. <sup>14</sup>Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and the nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down, her revelers and he who exults in her. <sup>15</sup>Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low. <sup>16</sup>But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy in righteousness. <sup>17</sup>Then the lambs shall graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich. <sup>18</sup>Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes, <sup>19</sup>who say: "Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!" <sup>20</sup>Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter! <sup>21</sup>Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight! <sup>22</sup>Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink, <sup>23</sup>who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right! <sup>24</sup>Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. <sup>25</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains quaked; and their corpses were as refuse in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. <sup>26</sup>He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come! <sup>27</sup>None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken; <sup>28</sup>their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind. <sup>29</sup>Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue. <sup>30</sup>They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — The Song of the Vineyard and the Six Woes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 5 opens with one of the most beautiful and devastating parables in the Old Testament: the song of the vineyard. God planted, tended, and hoped for Israel—and received violence instead of justice, a cry instead of righteousness. The parable leads to six woes that catalog Israel's specific sins. The chapter closes with God summoning a foreign army as his instrument of judgment.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology of the vineyard parable is covenantal: God's investment in Israel was total, and his expectation was proportional. The woes target specific sins—economic injustice, hedonism, intellectual pride, moral inversion, self-wisdom, judicial corruption. Together they depict a society that has rejected God in practice while maintaining religious form. The invading army at the chapter's end is not random history but divine summons. Motyer: the parable is the book's signature for Israel's inexcusable failure.
verseByVerse.examples: The vineyard parable was Jesus' template for his own parable of the tenants (Matt. 21:33–46). Every generation of God's people is the vineyard—loved, tended, expected to bear fruit. The six woes provide a diagnostic tool for any age: wherever wealth insulates from justice, where pleasure crowds out God, where good is called evil, Isaiah's indictment applies with full force.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard'—the parable opens as a love song, drawing the audience in before the devastating turn. The beloved is the LORD; the vineyard is Israel (v. 7). 'On a very fertile hill'—the best possible location: the investment began with ideal conditions. 'He dug it and cleared it of stones and planted it with choice vines'—the divine labor is exhaustive: preparation, cultivation, planting with the finest stock. 'He built a watchtower... hewed out a wine vat'—infrastructure for protection and harvest. Every reasonable preparation was made. 'He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes'—the punch line. Wild grapes (be'ushim) are the opposite of the choice fruit expected. Motyer: the shock is total—perfect conditions, perfect care, perfect failure.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Judge between me and my vineyard'—God invites the audience to be the jury. The listeners are asked to adjudicate before they realize they are the defendants. 'What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it?'—the defense of God's conduct: the jury is asked to find a single omission, a single neglect. There is none. The failure lies entirely with the vineyard. 'Why did it yield wild grapes?'—the question hangs unanswered. Oswalt: the rhetorical power of the parable is that it moves the audience to condemn themselves before the prophet identifies them as the condemned. Jesus' use of the same technique (Matt. 21:41) shows he learned from Isaiah's master stroke.

verseByVerse.quote: And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down. I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured'—the hedge protected the vineyard from wild animals; its removal exposes to depredation. 'I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down'—the double dismantling of protection: hedge and wall, the two layers of defense. 'I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed'—abandonment: the withholding of labor that sustained the vineyard. Without pruning the vine goes wild; without hoeing the soil becomes unworkable. 'I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it'—God controls the rain (Elijah's great demonstration, 1 Kings 17–18). The withholding of rain is covenant curse (Deut. 28:24). Motyer: God's judgment is expressed as withdrawal—he stops doing what he was doing on their behalf.

verseByVerse.quote: For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting; and he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel'—the parable's interpretation, given explicitly. Israel is the vineyard; Judah is the pleasant planting (the favored part). 'He looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed'—the Hebrew wordplay is devastating: mishpat (justice) and mishpakh (bloodshed); tsedaqah (righteousness) and tse'aqah (outcry/cry of distress). The sounds are alike; the meanings opposite. God expected the one and got the other. Oswalt: the paronomasia makes the point unforgettable—the distance between what was expected and what was delivered is audible. Calvin: the outcry of the oppressed rises to heaven as the indictment of the oppressor.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land. The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: “Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field'—the first woe targets the consolidation of land by the wealthy. Deuteronomy's jubilee provisions were designed to prevent exactly this: every fifty years, land returned to its original family. The land-grabbers have evicted or ignored jubilee. 'Until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone'—the bitter end of monopoly: the land-owner has eliminated all neighbors. He has what he wanted but at the cost of community. 'Many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant'—the judgment matches the sin. The houses accumulated will stand empty. Motyer: the irony is precise—they gathered to possess; they will possess empty buildings in a depopulated land.

verseByVerse.quote: For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah.” Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath'—catastrophic agricultural failure: a bath was about six gallons; ten acres producing six gallons is near-total crop failure. 'A homer of seed shall yield but an ephah'—a homer is about six bushels; an ephah is one-tenth. Ten percent return on seed planted is covenant curse (Deut. 28:38). The land will revolt against the injustice done to it. 'Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink'—the second woe: the hedonists who organize their entire day around alcohol. Rising early for drink means the whole day is consumed. 'As wine inflames them'—passion for alcohol replaces passion for God. Young: the woe targets not occasional enjoyment but the ordering of life around intoxication as its governing purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands. Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts'—a full musical ensemble: the instruments of celebration. There is nothing wrong with music or feasting; the condemnation follows. 'But they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands'—the sin is not the pleasure but the ignorance it produces. Feasting with no regard for the one who gives the feast. History unfolds around them—God is at work—but they cannot see it because their eyes are fixed on their cups. 'Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge'—the exile follows the blindness. Knowledge (da'at) in Isaiah is covenantal knowledge: knowing God and living accordingly. Childs: ignorance of God is not merely intellectual deficit but practical apostasy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and the nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down, her revelers and he who exults in her. Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure'—Sheol personified as a monster with expanding appetite, devouring the population of Jerusalem. The imagery is vivid: death opens its jaw wide enough to swallow a city. 'The nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down'—all classes, the high and the many: no one is exempt. The very categories of distinction in life are abolished in Sheol. 'Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low'—the refrain from ch. 2:9, 11, 17 returns. Human pride brought down by divine majesty: the Day of the LORD runs through the woes as their culmination. Oswalt: Sheol here is the historical experience of mass death in judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy One of Israel shows himself holy in righteousness. Then shall the lambs graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy One of Israel shows himself holy in righteousness'—the great reversal: as human pride goes down, God's glory goes up. His judgment is not arbitrary but the expression of his holy character. Justice and righteousness are the two pillars of the Davidic throne (9:7; cf. Ps. 89:14); when they are violated, God reasserts them in judgment. 'Then shall the lambs graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich'—the pastoral aftermath: what the wealthy hoarded for themselves becomes common grazing ground. The ruins of the mansion feed the wanderer's flock. Motyer: the reversal is precise—the accumulated wealth is dissipated into the commons.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes, and who say: “Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes'—the third woe: sin is not stumbled into but deliberately hauled in, with increasing effort (cords to cart ropes). The metaphor suggests both the labor of sin and its progressive weight: what begins as a cord becomes a rope. 'Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it'—mocking provocation: daring God to act. The scoffers do not merely doubt God's judgment; they challenge it openly. 'Let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near'—sarcasm directed at the prophet's warnings. Oswalt: this is practical atheism with a religious vocabulary; they invoke the Holy One while daring him to appear.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter! Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to those who call evil good and good evil'—the fourth woe: moral inversion, the systematic reversal of the categories of ethics. This is not merely confusion but deliberate relabeling: calling the wicked righteous and the righteous wicked. 'Who put darkness for light and light for darkness'—epistemological blindness masquerading as insight. The compass is inverted; the moral map is upside down. 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes'—the fifth woe follows directly: self-wisdom. The person who reverses good and evil does so because he trusts his own judgment over God's. Childs: the two woes are connected—moral inversion flows from epistemological pride. Keller: when we stop anchoring morality in God's character, we inevitably invert it according to our own preferences.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink, who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink'—the sixth woe returns to hedonism but adds a further dimension: the courage and skill invested in drinking should be invested in justice. 'Heroes' and 'valiant men' are military terms; Israel's warriors have redirected their valor to the wine bowl. 'Who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right'—the corruption of the justice system: the scales of justice tipped by money. The poor cannot buy acquittal; the rich cannot be condemned. Motyer: those who are brave only at the banquet have no courage left for the hard work of justice. Calvin: bribery in the courts is violence done to God himself, who is the protector of the innocent.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains quaked; and their corpses were as refuse in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As the tongue of fire devours the stubble'—the agricultural images give way to fire. Stubble and dry grass burn completely and quickly; so Israel's accumulated sin is consumed in judgment. 'Their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust'—the plant dies from the inside (root) and the outside (blossom); total organic failure. 'They have rejected the law of the LORD... and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel'—the double root of all the woes: rejection and contempt. 'His anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still'—the terrifying refrain that recurs in ch. 9: the judgment is not finished. Oswalt: the outstretched hand is the hand of discipline that has not yet accomplished its purifying purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come! None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth'—God summons the military power of distant nations as easily as a beekeeper whistles for bees (cf. 7:18). The army does not come by chance or historical accident but by divine summons. 'Quickly, speedily they come'—the army's response is immediate and total. There is no delay between the divine signal and the national response. 'None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps'—superhuman readiness: the army God summons is perfectly conditioned. 'Not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken'—military readiness in detail: equipment intact, no negligence. Motyer: the catalog of their readiness emphasizes that God's instrument of judgment arrives in perfect condition for its appointed task.

verseByVerse.quote: their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind. Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent'—offensive weapons ready for immediate use; no preparation time needed. 'Their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind'—hardness and speed: flint hoofs do not chip; whirlwind wheels cannot be stopped. The army is both durable and fast. 'Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar'—the lion's roar is the announcement of attack; once the lion roars over its prey, the prey is taken. 'They carry it off, and none can rescue'—the finality of the seizure. No human power can intervene between this army and its divinely appointed prey. Oswalt: the description builds to the terrifying inevitability of God's judgment when it is finally and fully released.

verseByVerse.quote: They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like the growling of the sea'—the sea's roar is elemental and unstoppable; the army's sound is natural force. 'If one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress'—in every direction, judgment. There is no safe quarter, no place to flee. The cosmic imagery (darkness) has returned: the chapter that began with God's vineyard ends with darkness covering the land. 'The light is darkened by its clouds'—even the light is obscured: total deprivation of hope. Motyer: the chapter ends where the book will later arrive at its darkest moments—darkness covering the land until the great light of ch. 9 rises. The structural arc of the book is already visible in the ending of ch. 5.

50.subtitle: The Servant’s Obedience
50.intro: Overview. Chapter 50 contains the third Servant Song (vv. 4–9), one of four passages in Isaiah 40–55 where an unnamed figure — identified by the New Testament as Jesus — speaks in the first person about his calling and suffering. The Song is framed by two passages that give it context: God’s unanswered questions about Israel’s unfaithfulness (vv. 1–3), and a closing challenge about two ways of responding to darkness (vv. 10–11). What emerges is a portrait of the Servant as the one who models everything Israel failed to be — attentive where she was deaf, obedient where she was rebellious, trusting where she was self-reliant.

sections.title: The LORD’s Unanswered Questions
sections.commentary:
God opens the chapter with two rhetorical questions addressed to the exiles: Where is the divorce certificate that proves I sent Israel away? Who is the creditor to whom I sold you? The expected answer to both is: there is none. God did not issue a divorce; Israel walked out. He sold no one; the people sold themselves through their own sins. The point is carefully chosen. A divorced wife has been formally and permanently sent away. A sold slave can still be redeemed. By framing the exile in terms of debt rather than divorce, God is already hinting that the door back is open.

Verses 2–3 reverse the direction: it was not God who was absent, but the people. He came and called; no one answered. This failure of response — God speaking, Israel not listening — is one of the defining patterns of Isaiah. It makes the Servant’s posture in the next section all the more striking. Where the nation turned a deaf ear, the Servant wakes each morning to listen.

v. 2 — “Why, when I came, was there no one? When I called, was there no one to answer?” The same lament echoes at the end of the book (65:12; 66:4). The tragedy is not divine absence but human unresponsiveness. The one who made the sea and dried it up was more than capable of acting; what he found was a people who had stopped listening.

sections.title: The Third Servant Song — Morning by Morning
sections.commentary:
The Servant speaks. His opening self-description is not of power or authority but of being taught. God has given him the tongue of those who are taught — a disciple’s tongue — so that he knows how to speak a sustaining word to the weary. Before the Servant can minister to the exhausted, he must first receive. Before he speaks, he listens. This pattern — formation before deployment, reception before proclamation — runs against every instinct toward self-sufficiency.

v. 4 — “Morning by morning he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” The repetition of morning by morning is deliberate: the daily discipline of attentiveness is what produces the tongue that can sustain the weary. R.C. Sproul noted that the great preachers are always, first, the great listeners.

Verses 5–6 move from formation to suffering. The Servant did not rebel, did not turn back — and was beaten, had his beard pulled, was spat on. The specificity should stop the reader: Isaiah is not describing symbolic suffering but physical particulars that Matthew 26:67 and 27:30 record as history. The Gospel writers noted these details as events; Isaiah named them as prophecy seven centuries earlier.

The section closes with confidence: “The Lord GOD helps me — therefore I have set my face like a flint.” Luke 9:51 uses this exact language of Jesus turning toward Jerusalem. The courtroom image of verses 8–9 becomes in Paul’s hands the cry of Romans 8:33: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?”

sections.title: Two Ways of Walking in Darkness
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends by placing two kinds of people before two different futures. The first fears the LORD, obeys the Servant’s voice, and yet walks in darkness — no light, no felt assurance, no visible sign that trust is warranted. To this person God gives a single instruction: trust, and rely on your God. The second person lights their own fire, surrounding themselves with their own sparks — the refusal to wait on God producing its own alternative. The verdict is blunt: you shall lie down in torment. The fires kindled for comfort become the fire they inhabit.

v. 10 — “Let him trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God.” This is the practical application of everything the Servant demonstrated. He walked toward suffering with his face set like flint — not because he could see the outcome, but because he knew who held it. The same confidence is now extended to all who follow in his way.

keyVerse.quote: “But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.”
keyVerse.note: The confidence here is entirely derivative — it flows from God’s help, not the Servant’s constitution. Luke 9:51 applies “set his face” directly to Jesus heading to Jerusalem, and the deliberateness is the point: he is not swept toward the cross by events but walks toward it with resolution, grounded in the certainty that the Father is with him.

50.reflection: The Servant’s day begins with listening before speaking, receiving before giving. This is not merely a spiritual discipline — it is the source of the sustaining word he is able to offer the weary. Where are you most tempted to speak, teach, or act before you have first sat quietly to receive? And where in your life are you lighting your own fire rather than waiting in the dark for God’s?
50.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. <sup>2</sup>Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst. <sup>3</sup>I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering." <sup>4</sup>The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. <sup>5</sup>The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. <sup>6</sup>I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting. <sup>7</sup>But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame. <sup>8</sup>He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. <sup>9</sup>Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up. <sup>10</sup>Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God. <sup>11</sup>Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Third Servant Song: The Taught Tongue and the Set Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third servant song (vv.4-9) presents the servant as a model disciple — awakened morning by morning to receive God's word and taught to sustain the weary. He offers his back to those who beat him, his cheeks to those who pull his beard, his face to shame and spitting. Yet he does not draw back, because God vindicates him. The chapter ends with a warning to those who kindle their own fires rather than trusting in the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Suffering and vindication: the third servant song introduces the element of rejection and physical suffering for the first time in explicit terms. The servant's posture is deliberate and voluntary: 'I gave my back to those who strike' — not helpless victimhood but chosen suffering in obedience to God. The confidence that sustains this suffering: 'the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced.' Vindication belongs to God, not to the servant's own defense.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer sees the progression across the servant songs: Song 1 (42:1-9) presents the servant's character and mission; Song 2 (49:1-9) reveals his discouragement and enlarged commission; Song 3 (50:4-9) shows his suffering and confident faith; Song 4 (52:13-53:12) narrates the atoning death and exaltation. Each song deepens the portrait toward the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: 'Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. Why, when I came, was there no one? When I called, was there no answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God responds to the implicit charge of abandonment by reversing it: there is no divorce certificate, no bill of sale — God did not send Israel away. Israel's own iniquities sold themselves into exile. The question is my hand shortened? picks up the common complaint that God has lost his power. His answer: he dried up the sea in the first exodus. He can redeem again. Childs: the dialogue format reveals that the exiles are blaming God for the exile, and God gently but firmly redirects the blame to its proper source — Israel's sin — while reasserting his saving power.

verseByVerse.quote: I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering. The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's power over creation (clothing heavens with blackness) transitions to the servant's speech. The servant has the tongue of a disciple (limmudim, those who are taught) — trained to sustain the weary with a single word. Morning by morning — the daily discipline of listening precedes the daily ministry of speaking. Motyer: the servant's ability to sustain others with a word flows from his own sustained attention to God's word. The ministry of encouragement is rooted in the discipline of listening to God before speaking to people.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's response to the opened ear is obedience without retreat: I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. Then the suffering is itemized with stark precision: back beaten, beard pulled out, face disgraced, spit upon. These are not accidental humiliations but deliberate choices — the servant gave himself to these sufferings. Matthew 26:67-68, 27:26-30 describes Jesus enduring exactly these indignities. Young: the servant's suffering is chosen, not merely endured — the willingness of the cross is here in seed form.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame. He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: I have set my face like a flint — absolute determination, immovable resolve, borrowed by Luke 9:51: Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem. The servant's confidence is not self-generated but grounded: the Lord GOD helps me. The courtroom language of v.8 — who will contend? who is my adversary? — anticipates Paul's who shall bring any charge against God's elect? in Romans 8:33-34. Motyer: the servant faces his trial with the confidence that the Judge is on his side — this is the deep structure of Christian assurance.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up. Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The adversaries who try to condemn the servant will wear out like moth-eaten garments — temporary, fragile, destined to disintegrate. The servant's vindication is certain. Then the invitation: whoever fears the LORD and walks in darkness should trust in the name of the LORD. The servant's own path — suffering in darkness, trusting without visible vindication — is the path he commends to all who follow him. Childs: the darkness of v.10 is not ignorance but the darkness of suffering without explanation. In that darkness, trust is the commanded response.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by your own light, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in sorrow. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The warning closes the chapter: those who refuse to trust in the LORD and instead kindle their own fire — provide their own light, manufacture their own salvation — will lie down in sorrow. The self-made fire that guides them leads to bed of grief. Oswalt: human self-sufficiency (lighting one's own torch rather than waiting for God's light) is ultimately self-destructive. The darkness of trust (v.10) is safer than the fire of self-reliance. The image anticipates every form of human wisdom that refuses to depend on God's word and servant.

51.subtitle: Look to the Rock from Which You Were Cut
51.intro: Overview. Chapter 51 is a sustained call to remembrance — look back to Abraham, look back to the exodus, look up to the heavens God made — as the ground for present courage. God’s salvation will last when the heavens vanish; his righteousness endures forever. The chapter ends with the cup of wrath taken from Israel’s lips and placed in the hand of her oppressors.

sections.title: Look to Abraham
sections.commentary:
Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were cut, to the quarry from which you were hewn. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you — when he was but one I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. One man, childless, and from him came a nation. The logic of the call is: if God can do that from one, he can rebuild Zion from its ruins.

v. 6 — “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.” The contrast is between two kinds of permanence. The heavens and earth feel maximally stable — but they are contingent and will pass. God’s salvation is not contingent; it will outlast the cosmos. 2 Pet. 3:10–13 and Rev. 21:1 describe this passing from the outside.

sections.title: The Arm of the LORD
sections.commentary:
Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in the days of old. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who dried up the sea, who made the depths into a road for the redeemed? The appeal to the exodus is not nostalgia but argument: the same arm that acted then can act now.

God promises to comfort Zion and silence the one who taunts. Then the reversal: the cup of staggering — the bowl of God’s wrath that Jerusalem has been drinking — will be taken from her hand and placed in the hand of those who afflicted her. The suffering is not permanent; the oppressors’ temporary power is not the final arrangement.

keyVerse.quote: “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.”
keyVerse.note: The permanence of God’s salvation is grounded in the impermanence of everything else. When even the heavens and earth are revealed as contingent, the one thing that stands is what God has declared. This is not escapism but realism: the most stable-seeming things will pass; the apparently fragile promise will not.

51.reflection: God says: look to Abraham — I called one man and multiplied him. Where in your situation does the evidence look like “only one” or “only remnant”? What would it mean to draw courage from the Abraham-logic: that God specializes in beginnings that look statistically impossible?
51.text: <sup>1</sup>"Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the quarry from which you were dug. <sup>2</sup>Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you; for he was but one when I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. <sup>3</sup>For the LORD comforts Zion; he comforts all her waste places and makes her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of song. <sup>4</sup>Give attention to me, my people, and give ear to me, my nation; for a law will go out from me, and I will set my justice for a light to the peoples. <sup>5</sup>My righteousness draws near, my salvation has gone out, and my arms will judge the peoples; the coastlands hope for me, and for my arm they wait. <sup>6</sup>Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and they who dwell in it will die in like manner; but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed. <sup>7</sup>Listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man, nor be dismayed at their revilings. <sup>8</sup>For the moth will eat them up like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool, but my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to all generations." <sup>9</sup>Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in days of old, the generations of long ago. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? <sup>10</sup>Was it not you who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass over? <sup>11</sup>And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. <sup>12</sup>"I, I am he who comforts you; who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass, <sup>13</sup>and have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth, and you fear continually all the day because of the wrath of the oppressor, when he sets himself to destroy? And where is the wrath of the oppressor? <sup>14</sup>He who is bowed down shall speedily be released; he shall not die and go down to the pit, neither shall his bread be lacking. <sup>15</sup>I am the LORD your God, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar— the LORD of hosts is his name. <sup>16</sup>And I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, establishing the heavens and laying the foundations of the earth, and saying to Zion, 'You are my people.'" <sup>17</sup>Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering. <sup>18</sup>There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne; there is none to take her by the hand among all the sons she has brought up. <sup>19</sup>These two things have happened to you— who will console you?— devastation and destruction, famine and sword; who will comfort you? <sup>20</sup>Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God. <sup>21</sup>Therefore hear this, you who are afflicted, who are drunk, but not with wine: <sup>22</sup>Thus says your Lord, the LORD, your God who pleads the cause of his people: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; <sup>23</sup>and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors, who have said to you, 'Bow down, that we may pass over'; and you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Awake, Awake: the Arm of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three times the chapter calls for awakening — first to Israel (vv.1, 7), then to the arm of the LORD (v.9), then to Jerusalem herself (v.17). God points to Abraham and Sarah as the prototype of fruitfulness from barrenness. His salvation and righteousness are everlasting. The cup of wrath that Jerusalem drank is taken from her hand and given to her tormentors.
verseByVerse.theology: Memory and hope: the call to look to Abraham and Sarah (v.2) grounds hope in precedent — a barren couple became a multitude. Similarly the exiled community, few and scattered, will become many. The arm of the LORD (v.9) is personified as a warrior who slew Rahab and dried the sea. The same arm will lead a new exodus. The cup of divine wrath (vv.17-23) passes from Israel to her oppressors — God's justice works in both directions.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer identifies the three-fold 'awake' (vv.9, 17; 52:1) as structuring the chapter and its sequel. The arm of the LORD that the exiles call upon becomes the suffering arm of the servant (53:1) — the very arm of God's salvation is the servant's sacrificial death. The cup of wrath that Jerusalem drinks becomes the cup the servant drains in her place.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the quarry from which you were dug. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you; for he was but one when I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The exiles who pursue righteousness are called to historical memory. The rock from which Israel was hewn is Abraham — one person, barren wife, no descendants when God called. Yet God blessed and multiplied them into a nation. Oswalt: the precedent of Abraham and Sarah is God's pastoral argument from pattern. If God created a nation from a barren couple, he can restore a nation from a scattered remnant. Faith is always partly retrospective — looking at what God has already done.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD will comfort Zion; he will comfort all her waste places and will make her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of song. Give attention to me, my people, and give ear to me, my nation; for a law will go out from me, and I will set my justice for a light to the peoples. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Comfort transforms the physical landscape — waste becomes Eden, desert becomes garden. The creation language (Eden, garden of the LORD) signals new creation: God is not merely restoring what was but making something that was never before. Joy and song replace mourning and silence. Then the universal note: God's law and justice will be a light to the peoples — reaching beyond Israel's restoration to the world's illumination. Childs: the comfort of Zion is not an end in itself but the first act of the universal restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: My righteousness draws near, my salvation has gone out, and my arms will judge the peoples; the coastlands hope for me, and for my arm they wait. Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and they who dwell in it will die in like manner; but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast between creation's transience and God's eternal salvation: heavens like smoke, earth wearing out like an old garment, its inhabitants dying. But God's salvation is forever; his righteousness will never be dismayed. This is cosmic eschatology — the created order will end, but the redemptive order will not. Jesus echoes this in Matt 24:35: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. Motyer: the permanence of God's salvation makes it the only reliable investment — everything else depreciates to zero.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man, nor be dismayed at their revilings. For the moth will eat them up like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool, but my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to all generations. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The second address — to those who have God's law in their hearts (Jer 31:33, the new covenant). The reproach and reviling of persecutors is temporary: moth and worm consume them, as they do all created things. But God's righteousness and salvation persist to all generations. This is the pastoral logic of the eternal: the temporary opposition of the wicked does not threaten the permanent salvation of God. Young: fear not the reproach of man is addressed to those who feel the weight of being a minority in a hostile culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in days of old, the generations of long ago. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass over? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The community's prayer: Awake, arm of the LORD! — an urgent cry for divine action. The arm is personified as a warrior who defeated Rahab (a chaos-monster, here a name for Egypt) and dried the Red Sea. The exodus is the paradigm act of divine strength. This prayer will be answered in ch53 where the arm of the LORD is revealed — in the servant's suffering. Motyer: the connection between this prayer for the arm and the servant's identity as the arm (53:1) is the structural heart of chs51-53.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. I, I am he who comforts you; who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: V.11 nearly quotes 35:10 — the Highway of Holiness refrain — joining the return of the ransomed with everlasting joy. Then God's self-identification: I, I am he who comforts you. The doubled I is emphatic. And the rebuke: who are you that you are afraid of man who dies? The transience of human oppressors (made like grass) makes fear of them disproportionate. Oswalt: the comfort of God is the antidote to the fear of man. When God fills the foreground, every human threat shrinks to proper size.

verseByVerse.quote: and have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth, and you fear continually all the day because of the wrath of the oppressor, when he sets himself to destroy? And where is the wrath of the oppressor? He who is bowed down shall speedily be released; he shall not die and go down to the pit; neither shall his bread fail. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The diagnosis: you have forgotten the LORD your Maker and therefore fear the oppressor continuously. The forgetfulness is the root; the fear is the fruit. The remedy is not psychological but theological — remember who your God is. The liberator's promise: the bowed-down one shall speedily be released, shall not die, shall not starve. Every specific fear is addressed. Young: the pastoral genius of Isaiah is to address specific anxieties with specific promises grounded in specific truths about God's character.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar — the LORD of hosts is his name. And I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, establishing the heavens and laying the foundation of the earth, and saying to Zion, 'You are my people.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The LORD who stirs up the sea (sovereign over nature's most terrifying force) has put his words in Israel's mouth and covered them with the shadow of his hand. The creator who established heavens and earth claims his people in the simplest covenant formula: You are my people. Childs: the movement from creation (establishing heavens and earth) to covenant (you are my people) is the movement of biblical theology — the Creator becomes the Covenant-Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering. There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne; there is none to take her by the hand among all the sons she has brought up. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The third awakening command — now addressed to Jerusalem herself. She has drunk the cup of divine wrath to the dregs — the exile was no half-measure but the full weight of judgment. And she has been left without help: sons born and raised, yet none to guide or lead. The desolation is complete. But the command wake presupposes recovery — you are called to rise, which means rising is possible. Motyer: the cup of wrath that Jerusalem drinks in judgment is the same cup that the servant will drain in ch53, taking it from her hand.

verseByVerse.quote: These two things have happened to you — who will console you? — devastation and destruction, famine and sword; who will comfort you? Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The two pairs of disaster — devastation and destruction, famine and sword — describe the fall of Jerusalem with graphic simplicity. Sons fainted in the streets like netted antelopes: helpless, trapped, exhausted. Who will comfort you? — the question that will be answered by God himself (40:1, 51:3, 12). The depth of the desolation makes the coming comfort all the more glorious. Young: the lament of vv.17-20 must be heard fully before the promise of vv.21-23 can land with its proper weight.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear this, you who are afflicted, who are drunk, but not with wine: Thus says your Lord, the LORD, your God who pleads the cause of his people: 'Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The reversal begins: the cup of staggering is taken from Jerusalem's hand. God himself has pleaded her cause — the advocate becomes the judge who rules in her favor. Drink no more — the sentence is complete, the judgment exhausted. The same hand that held out the cup of wrath now takes it away. This is the shape of atonement: someone must drain the cup. The servant will do this in ch53. Oswalt: the transfer of the cup from Israel to her oppressors in v.23 is a picture of what the servant accomplishes — the righteous bearing what the guilty deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors, who have said to you, 'Bow down, that we may pass over'; and you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The cup passes to the tormentors who forced prostration — who treated Jerusalem as pavement. The humiliation is precisely reversed: those who walked over God's people will themselves be brought low. The justice is poetic and exact. Motyer: the oppressor's cruelty — using human beings as a road — is itself the measure of their judgment. God does not invent a new punishment; he simply applies the same measure they used. The chapter ends with promise: the cup of wrath has been redirected, and the ransomed will return with singing (v.11).

52.subtitle: How Beautiful Are the Feet
52.intro: Overview. Chapter 52 is a trumpet call to Zion — wake up, get up, shake off the dust, put on your beautiful garments. The exile is ending; the prisoners are being released; the herald is coming. The famous verse about beautiful feet brings the good news of peace, salvation, and the reign of God. The chapter ends with the introduction to the greatest of the Servant Songs: “Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up.”

sections.title: Awake, O Zion
sections.commentary:
Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem. Shake yourself free of the dust; arise, O captive Jerusalem. For the LORD has redeemed Jerusalem. The grounds for the command are the indicative of redemption: the imperative to rise is grounded in the fact of being ransomed.

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.” Paul quotes verse 7 twice (Rom. 10:15; Eph. 6:15) as the description of gospel proclamation. The content of the good news is compressed into three phrases: peace, happiness (welfare), salvation. And the summary: your God reigns. The whole mission of the herald is to announce that God has taken up his kingship.

v. 7 — “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’” The beauty falls on the feet — the most pedestrian part of the body — because it is the one who comes that matters. The message is not beautiful because of how it is packaged but because of what it announces: the end of exile and the beginning of God’s reign.

sections.title: The Servant Introduced
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with the opening lines of the fourth Servant Song: Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted. As many were astonished at him — his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance — so he shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths. The exaltation and the disfigurement belong together. The one who is highest was lowest; the one who astonishes kings was astonishing in his suffering first.

keyVerse.quote: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace… who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’”
keyVerse.note: Paul’s use of this verse in Romans 10:15 extends the herald imagery to every Christian witness. The feet are beautiful not because the herald is but because of what they carry. Every announcement of the gospel is an echo of this verse: “your God reigns” is the irreducible content of Christian proclamation.

52.reflection: Zion is told to shake off the dust and put on beautiful garments — before she sees the full deliverance. The command to rise precedes the visible evidence that rising makes sense. Where in your life is God calling you to rise and dress for freedom before you can yet see the liberation he has promised?

Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised. <sup>6</sup>Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am." <sup>7</sup>How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns." <sup>8</sup>The voice of your watchmen— they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion. <sup>9</sup>Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. <sup>10</sup>The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. <sup>11</sup>Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. <sup>12</sup>For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard. <sup>13</sup>Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted. <sup>14</sup>As many were astonished at you— his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind— <sup>15</sup>so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Beautiful Feet and the Servant Exalted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem is commanded to awaken, shake off the dust, and put on her beautiful garments — the exile is over. The herald's feet on the mountains announce peace and salvation. Watchmen see the LORD's return to Zion. Then the chapter transitions to the opening of the fourth and greatest servant song (vv.13-15): the servant who was marred beyond human recognition will be exalted above kings.
verseByVerse.theology: The gospel announcement and the servant's exaltation: vv.7-10 are the most direct 'good news' announcement in the Old Testament — Paul quotes v.7 in Romans 10:15 as the mandate for gospel preaching. The servant's exaltation in vv.13-15 sets up the suffering of ch53. The pattern is exaltation-suffering-exaltation: the servant will be high and lifted up (v.13), then marred and despised (53:2-3), then exalted and glorified (53:10-12).
verseByVerse.examples: Oswalt notes that vv.13-15 introduce the servant with language borrowed from ch6 — 'high and lifted up' (same Hebrew as 6:1, the throne of God). The servant who suffers in ch53 is introduced with the vocabulary of God's own exaltation. This is one of Isaiah's most profound Christological signals.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean. Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourth awakening command — now Zion is addressed directly. Put on your strength, put on your beautiful garments — dress for celebration, not mourning. Uncircumcised and unclean refers to Babylonian oppressors who profaned the holy city. Zion is to shake off the dust of mourning and humiliation, rise from the ground, loose her own bonds. Motyer: the commands are divine gifts — God does not say try to rise but rise, and the command carries the power of its fulfillment. Gospel imperatives are always enablements.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: 'You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money.' For thus says the Lord GOD: 'My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sale was for nothing (no benefit to God); the redemption is without price (no payment to Babylon). God owes Babylon nothing — he simply reclaims what is his. The historical catalog — Egypt, Assyria, Babylon — places the exile in a pattern of oppression that God repeatedly reverses. Oswalt: every exodus in Israel's history is the same story: oppressors take for nothing; God restores for nothing. The grace is free because the oppressor had no legitimate claim and the Redeemer needs no compensation.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore what have I here, declares the LORD, seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail, declares the LORD, and continually all the day my name is despised. Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's motivation is his name's honor: rulers are wailing, God's name is being despised by the nations. My people shall know my name — the return from exile will be an act of revelation. Here I am — the simplest possible self-disclosure, the same words Jacob heard at Bethel (Gen 28:16). The God who seemed absent will make himself unmistakably present. Young: the exile appeared to deny God's reality and power; the return will vindicate both, restoring honor to the name that was despised.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, 'Your God reigns.' The voice of your watchmen — they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet — the herald's feet, worn and dusty from travel, are beautiful because of what they carry. Paul quotes this in Romans 10:15 to ground the necessity of gospel proclamation: how are they to hear without someone preaching? The message is three-fold: peace, happiness, salvation — all summarized in your God reigns. The watchmen who see the LORD's return break into song. Motyer: the gospel is always essentially this: your God reigns — the sovereignty of God is the foundation of all gospel proclamation.

verseByVerse.quote: Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the ruins sing. Waste places of Jerusalem — the rubble itself is commanded to rejoice. The comfort and redemption of Jerusalem are accomplished facts: perfect tense, done. Then the universal scope: all nations see; all ends of the earth witness. The bared arm — the divine warrior revealing his power — is the arm of the LORD that ch51 prayed for, now revealed. Childs: the salvation that begins with Jerusalem's restoration is visible to every nation and available to every person. This is the gospel's geographic scope.

verseByVerse.quote: Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Depart, depart — the new exodus command. Unlike the first exodus from Egypt (eaten in haste, Passover urgency), this departure is unhurried: not in haste, not in flight. The LORD goes before as pillar of fire; the God of Israel guards the rear. The priestly instructions — carry no unclean thing, purify yourselves — mark this as a sacred procession, not merely a migration. Young: the unhurried quality of the new exodus signals its completeness. The first exodus was an escape; the new exodus is a triumphant procession.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted. As many were astonished at you — his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind — (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The fourth servant song begins. High and lifted up and exalted — the exact language of 6:1, the vision of God enthroned. The servant bears God's own vocabulary of exaltation. But the contrast with v.14 is immediate: that same servant, at some point, will be marred beyond recognition — no longer resembling a human being. Motyer: the servant who is exalted like God is the servant who suffers beyond what humanity can endure. The two conditions bracket ch53 and form the frame of the atonement story.

verseByVerse.quote: so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him, for that which has not been told them they shall see, and that which they have not heard they shall understand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The marred servant will sprinkle many nations — a priestly act, connected to the atonement rituals of Leviticus. Kings will be silenced before him. What was unseen and unheard will be revealed and understood. Paul quotes v.15 in Romans 15:21 as the basis for pioneer mission: going where Christ has not yet been named. Childs: the sprinkling of nations is the global extension of the servant's atoning work — the priestly function performed by one person becomes effective for the whole world.

53.subtitle: The Suffering Servant
53.intro: Overview. Isaiah 53 is the summit of the book and one of the most theologically dense passages in all of Scripture. The fourth Servant Song (52:13–53:12) describes a figure who suffers not for his own sin but for the sins of others — pierced for transgressions, crushed for iniquities, bearing the iniquity of us all. The New Testament identifies the Servant as Jesus Christ, and more of Isaiah 53 is quoted in the New Testament than any other Old Testament passage. The text is written in the past tense, as if the suffering is already accomplished and the speakers are looking back in astonished confession.

sections.title: Who Has Believed Our Report?
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a question that is also a lament: who has believed what he heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? The Servant grew up like a young plant, like a root out of dry ground. He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief — and we hid our faces from him; we esteemed him not.

The confession is extraordinary: we did not see what we were looking at. The arm of the LORD was at work in the one we turned away from. John quotes verse 1 at the end of his account of Jesus’ public ministry (John 12:38) as the explanation for why the crowds did not believe despite the signs. The message was there; the believing was not.

sections.title: Pierced for Our Transgressions
sections.commentary:
The center of the chapter — and perhaps the center of the entire Old Testament. He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.

The substitutionary logic is precise: our transgressions, our iniquities, our peace, our healing — but the piercing and crushing fall on him. Peter quotes verse 24 directly in 1 Pet. 2:24: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.” Paul’s entire theology of the atonement traces back to this passage.

v. 6 — “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” The universality of the straying (“all we”; “every one”) meets the singularity of the bearing (“on him”). The LORD is the agent: he is the one who lays the iniquity. This is not the Servant volunteering for something God did not plan; it is God’s own act of transferring the weight.

sections.title: He Was Silent
sections.commentary:
He was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb led to slaughter, like a sheep before its shearers, he was silent. By oppression and judgment he was taken away. Who considered that he was cut off from the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? They made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death — a detail Matthew records precisely (27:57–60): buried in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea.

The silence is not passive; it is chosen. The Servant of chapter 50 set his face like flint and gave himself voluntarily. The silence before accusers is the same agency as the set face — the Servant is not a victim of the proceedings but the one directing them from within.

sections.title: He Shall See and Be Satisfied
sections.commentary:
Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief. When his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.

v. 11 — “Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied.” This is justification language: the Servant sees the result of his suffering — the many made righteous — and is satisfied. The satisfaction is God’s justice met and the Servant’s joy complete. It is the theological ground of Hebrews 12:2: “for the joy set before him he endured the cross.”

Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors. The chapter ends with the Servant alive, interceding, victorious — resurrection implied in every word.

keyVerse.quote: “But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.”
keyVerse.note: This verse is the clearest statement of penal substitutionary atonement in the entire Bible. The prepositions carry the weight: for our transgressions, for our iniquities. The chastisement (divine judicial punishment) fell on him so that peace could come to us. This is not one theory of the atonement among others — it is the grammar Isaiah uses to describe what God planned.

53.theology: Penal Substitutionary Atonement. Isaiah 53 is the Old Testament’s fullest statement of what the New Testament calls penal substitution: the righteous one bearing the punishment that belonged to the unrighteous. The key elements are all present — the guilt of “all we” (v. 6), the transfer by God himself (“the LORD has laid on him”), the specific categories of piercing for transgressions and crushing for iniquities (v. 5), and the result: peace and healing for those whose iniquity he bore. Reformed theology has consistently held that this is not merely one way of describing the atonement but its structural core — the mechanism by which the justice of God and the mercy of God are both fully expressed in a single act at Calvary. R.C. Sproul called Isaiah 53 the chapter that makes the cross comprehensible.
53.reflection: The chapter opens with a question about believing: “Who has believed what he heard from us?” And it closes with intercession: the Servant makes intercession for the transgressors. You are among the transgressors for whom he intercedes. What difference does it make — practically, emotionally, theologically — to know that the risen Christ is right now interceding for you at the Father’s right hand (Rom. 8:34)?
53.text: <sup>1</sup>Who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? <sup>2</sup>For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. <sup>3</sup>He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. <sup>4</sup>Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. <sup>5</sup>But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. <sup>6</sup>All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned— every one— to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. <sup>7</sup>He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. <sup>8</sup>By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? <sup>9</sup>And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. <sup>10</sup>Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. <sup>11</sup>Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. <sup>12</sup>Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The climax and center of Isaiah, and the single most quoted and applied chapter of the Old Testament in the New Testament. The servant is despised, rejected, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Yet all was not as it appeared: he bore our griefs, carried our sorrows, was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities. Upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace; with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all.
verseByVerse.theology: Substitutionary atonement: Isaiah 53 is the Old Testament foundation for the doctrine of penal substitution. The servant suffers not for his own sin (he had done no violence, nor was there any deceit in his mouth, v.9) but for others'. The transfer of iniquity is explicit: 'the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all' (v.6). The result is peace and healing for the many. The servant's suffering is purposive (v.10 — 'it was the will of the LORD to crush him') and productive (v.11 — 'by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous').
verseByVerse.examples: Every major NT writer quotes Isaiah 53. Matthew 8:17 (he took our infirmities), Luke 22:37 (numbered with transgressors), John 12:38 (who has believed our report?), Acts 8:32-33 (Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch reading this passage), Romans 10:16, 1 Peter 2:22-25 (he bore our sins). Oswalt calls it the 'Calvary of the Old Testament.' Motyer's commentary on this chapter is among the finest theological writing in evangelical scholarship.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The opening is a lament of unbelief: the message has been proclaimed but not believed. John 12:38 quotes this after recording that even after Jesus's miracles, many did not believe — it was to fulfill Isaiah 53:1. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:16 to explain Israel's rejection of the gospel. The arm of the LORD connects to 51:9-10 (the arm that split the sea) and 52:10 (the arm bared before nations) — the arm of salvation is the servant, whose identity as the divine arm is the surprising, unbelievable revelation. Young: unbelief is the primary problem the servant's mission addresses, and it begins with the announcement of his suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we would look at him, and no beauty that we would desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's appearance is the opposite of royal majesty. A young plant from dry ground — fragile, unexpected, not impressive. No form, no majesty, no beauty that would attract attention. Despised, rejected, a man of sorrows — grief is his characteristic atmosphere. Men hide their faces from him. The Incarnation fulfills this: the Son of God came not as a warrior-king but as a Galilean carpenter. Motyer: Isaiah 53:2-3 is the Old Testament theology of the Incarnation — God choosing the humility and hiddenness that the world despises as the form of ultimate revelation.

verseByVerse.quote: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. (ESV)
