verseByVerse.commentary: The great substitutionary declaration. The observer's misreading: they assumed his suffering was divine punishment for his own sin (stricken, smitten by God). The reality: he bore our griefs, carried our sorrows, was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities. Every pronouns is possessive and the object is the collective human sin. With his wounds we are healed — Peter quotes this directly in 1 Pet 2:24. Oswalt: the five-fold repetition of substitutionary prepositions (for, for, upon, with) makes the doctrine unmistakable — the servant's suffering is not his own but ours, and its effect is our healing.

verseByVerse.quote: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: All we like sheep have gone astray — universal, inclusive, without exception. Every one to his own way — the sin of self-direction, the insistence on autonomy. The LORD's response: lay the iniquity of all on one. This is the Day of Atonement logic (Lev 16) — the goat bearing the people's sin. The servant's silence under oppression is both voluntary and fulfilling: the lamb led to slaughter does not protest. Philip quotes v.7-8 to the Ethiopian eunuch as a preview of the gospel (Acts 8:32-35). Childs: the silence of the servant is the silence of one who has chosen to bear rather than resist.

verseByVerse.quote: By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant is cut off from the land of the living — killed. His generation does not comprehend why: stricken for the transgression of my people is the unrecognized truth. The grave detail is strikingly specific: with the wicked and with a rich man. Jesus died between criminals, buried in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb (a rich man). The servant's innocence is then declared: no violence, no deceit. He dies as the innocent for the guilty. Young: this is the foundational claim of atonement — the substitute must be without sin; a sinner cannot atone for other sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The most theologically precise verse in Isaiah: it was the will of the LORD to crush him. The servant's suffering was not accident, not merely the result of human evil, but the Father's plan of redemption. His soul makes an offering for guilt — the Hebrew asham, the guilt offering of Lev 5 — the servant is both priest and sacrifice. The resurrection follows: he will see his offspring, prolong his days, see and be satisfied. Motyer: the guilt offering had to be wholly consumed; the servant's death is complete. But then — see offspring, prolong days. The only way to prolong days after death is resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's reward: a portion with the many, spoil with the strong — the victor's share after battle. The basis: he poured out his soul to death (voluntary, total self-giving), was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37 quotes this of the crucifixion), bore the sin of many, and now makes intercession for transgressors. The risen, exalted servant continues to intercede — this is the heart of Hebrews 7:25 and Romans 8:34. Oswalt: the chapter that begins with rejection and suffering ends with divine reward and intercessory ministry — the full arc of the gospel from Good Friday to the ascension.

6.subtitle: Holy, Holy, Holy — Isaiah's Vision and Call
6.intro: Overview. Chapter 6 is one of the most significant passages in the entire Bible. Isaiah receives a vision of the LORD enthroned in his heavenly temple, surrounded by seraphim who cry the trisagion — “Holy, holy, holy.” The vision undoes him completely; he confesses his uncleanness and is cleansed by a coal from the altar. Then he hears the divine council deliberating and responds with the most famous volunteer in Scripture: “Here am I! Send me.” The commission he is given is deeply strange — he is told to speak words that will harden rather than soften, until the land is devastated. Yet even here, a holy seed remains in the stump.

sections.title: The Vision of the Holy God
sections.commentary:
The vision is anchored in history: “In the year that King Uzziah died.” Uzziah had reigned for fifty-two years — an entire generation of stability. His death was a political crisis. Isaiah receives this vision precisely when human leadership has failed, and what he sees is not a successor king but the King who never vacates his throne. The LORD is “high and lifted up” — the same Hebrew phrase used in 52:13 of the Servant. The temple is full of his train: not his robe but the overflow of his glory, so vast that its hem fills the entire sanctuary.

The seraphim — literally “burning ones” — cover their faces and their feet in the presence of God. They have been in his presence continually; they have never grown used to it. Their worship is not performance but prostration. And what they cry is not “powerful, powerful, powerful” or “glorious, glorious, glorious” but “holy, holy, holy.” Holiness is the attribute of attributes — the one quality of God that receives the threefold emphasis.

v. 3 — “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.” The trisagion — used again in Revelation 4:8 — is the highest form of emphasis available in Hebrew. Not just holy, not doubly holy, but holy beyond all comparison. The holiness proclaimed here is not merely moral purity but ontological otherness: God is categorically unlike anything in creation.

sections.title: Woe Is Me — The Coal from the Altar
sections.commentary:
Isaiah's response to the vision is not “how wonderful” but “woe is me.” He does not say “I am not worthy”; he says “I am undone” — the word means to be destroyed, to come apart. His first concern is the specific failure of his lips: “I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips.” He has just heard lips burning with perfect praise; his own lips have never come close. The comparison is annihilating.

v. 5 — “For my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!” Isaiah does not say he has seen God's back or his shadow. He has seen the King. John 12:41 identifies this vision as a sight of Christ's glory: “Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.” The vision of Isaiah 6 is, in John's reading, a vision of the pre-incarnate Son.

The seraph's response is immediate: a coal from the altar — the place of sacrifice — touched to the lips. “Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.” The cleansing does not come from Isaiah's efforts; it comes from the altar. Atonement is the answer to the problem that holiness exposes. What the vision breaks, the sacrifice repairs.

sections.title: The Call, the Commission, and the Strange Message
sections.commentary:
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” The plural “us” in a divine context has long been read by Christian interpreters as a trace of the trinitarian life — a deliberation within the Godhead. Isaiah's response — “Here am I! Send me” — is not presumption but the overflow of a man who has been cleansed. He could not have said it in verse 5; he can say it in verse 8 because the coal has done its work. Readiness for service follows from, and does not precede, the experience of grace.

The commission is difficult. Isaiah is told to speak so that the people will hear without understanding and see without perceiving, their hearts growing fat and their ears heavy. This is judicial hardening — a sovereign act in which continued rejection of the word results in increasing incapacity to receive it. Jesus quotes this passage in Matthew 13:14–15 to explain his parables. Paul cites it in Acts 28:26–27 to explain Israel's unbelief. The hardening is real, it is just, and it is the consequence of prior rejection.

v. 13 — “The holy seed is its stump.” The chapter ends not in total darkness but with a remnant image. A felled tree still has a stump, and a stump can still produce a shoot. This seed anticipates the Branch of chapter 4, the root of Jesse in chapter 11, and ultimately the one who grows from apparently barren ground in chapter 53.

keyVerse.quote: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”
keyVerse.note: The trisagion is the heart of Isaiah's vision and arguably the heart of the entire book. Every chapter of Isaiah flows from this reality: God is holy, and the earth belongs to him. Judgment is what holiness does when it encounters persistent unrepentance. Comfort is what holiness does when it encounters the broken and contrite. The missionary call of verse 8 is also a response to this: if the whole earth is full of his glory, the whole earth needs to hear about it.

6.theology:
The holiness of God. Isaiah 6 is the definitive Old Testament text on holiness as God's fundamental attribute. Holiness is not primarily about moral purity (though it includes it) but about God's absolute separateness from everything created. He is the only self-existent being; everything else derives its existence from him. This is why the seraphim cover themselves: in the presence of uncreated holiness, the most exalted of created beings are utterly undone.

Atonement and access. The movement of verses 5–7 is the movement of the entire gospel: the vision of holiness produces awareness of guilt; guilt produces the cry of undoing; and in response to that cry, God provides cleansing from the altar. Isaiah does not clean himself up before approaching God; God reaches to him. Access to the holy God is always the result of atonement, never of moral self-improvement.

The Trinity. The plural “us” of verse 8, combined with John 12:41 (identifying the vision as a sight of Christ) and the Spirit's role throughout the prophets, has led the church from its earliest centuries to read Isaiah 6 as a scene in which all three persons are present.
6.reflection: Isaiah's “Here am I! Send me” is often quoted as a model of eagerness for service — but it only makes sense after what precedes it. He is not a volunteer who has assessed the risks and decided to help. He is a ruined man who has been remade by the coal from the altar, and his readiness is the overflow of that experience. True willingness for costly service is always downstream of being undone and restored.
6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. <sup>2</sup>Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew. <sup>3</sup>And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" <sup>4</sup>And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. <sup>5</sup>And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!" <sup>6</sup>Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. <sup>7</sup>And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for." <sup>8</sup>And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me." <sup>9</sup>And he said, "Go, and say to this people: 'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.' <sup>10</sup>Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed." <sup>11</sup>Then I said, "How long, O Lord?" And he said: "Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste, <sup>12</sup>and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land. <sup>13</sup>And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Throne, the Coal, and the Commission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 6 is the prophet's call narrative, placed not at the book's beginning but after five chapters of indictment. The sequence is deliberate: only after hearing what God requires (ch. 1–5) does Isaiah see who God is. The vision is the most concentrated theophany in the Old Testament: the LORD enthroned, worshipped by seraphim whose holiness burns, the prophet undone, cleansed, and commissioned.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology is foundational for the entire book. The Holy One of Israel—Isaiah's signature divine title—is not an abstraction but a reality before which even the seraphim veil their faces. The prophet's confession is the only appropriate response to holiness; the coal that cleanses is the only remedy. The commission to preach to those who will not hear is the mystery at the heart of prophetic ministry—and the mystery at the heart of sovereign grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah 6 has shaped Christian theology at every point: the trisagion became the church's primary liturgical ascription; John 12:41 says Isaiah saw Christ's glory; Paul quotes vv. 9–10 in Romans 11:8 to explain Israel's hardening. The commission to preach in the face of unbelief is the permanent form of prophetic ministry in every age.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the year that King Uzziah died'—740 BC, the year of political transition. Uzziah had reigned fifty-two years; his death marks the end of a long era of stability. At the moment of earthly throne-transition, Isaiah sees the eternal throne. 'I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up'—the vision is of divine sovereignty undisturbed by political change. The earthly throne is vacant; the heavenly throne is occupied. 'The train of his robe filled the temple'—the filling of the temple by divine presence anticipates the dedication of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11) and Ezekiel's temple vision. 'Above him stood the seraphim'—the burning ones (sarap means to burn): angelic beings whose nature is fire in God's presence. Oswalt: the seraphim demonstrate by their posture (veiled face, veiled feet) what holiness requires even of the holiest created beings.

verseByVerse.quote: And one called to another and said: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!” And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts'—the trisagion, the triple ascription, intensifies holiness to the absolute degree. In Hebrew, repetition indicates degree; the triple 'holy' is the superlative of the superlative: God is holy beyond any conceivable measure. 'The whole earth is full of his glory'—the glory that fills the robe (v. 1) fills the whole earth. What the temple contained is cosmic in scope. 'The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice'—the voice of the seraphim, not even God's voice, shakes the temple. Motyer: if the worship of created beings reverberates through the cosmos, what must the presence of the Creator himself do? 'The house was filled with smoke'—theophanic smoke: the cloud of divine presence (Ex. 19:18; Rev. 15:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And I said: “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!” Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe is me! For I am lost'—the only appropriate response to unmediated holiness. The same woe (hoy) used against the wicked in ch. 1–5 Isaiah now pronounces on himself. The vision of God produces self-knowledge: the prophet who proclaimed the people's sins now sees his own. 'I am a man of unclean lips'—lips are the instrument of prophetic speech; the prophet finds the very faculty of his calling to be defiled. 'For my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts'—the reason for the self-condemnation: direct encounter with absolute holiness. Oswalt: the prophet does not say 'I am good but not good enough'—he says he is lost. Holiness does not grade on a curve. 'One of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal'—the remedy comes immediately; grace follows the honest confession without delay.

verseByVerse.quote: And he touched my mouth and said: “Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.” And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am! Send me.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for'—three declarations of cleansing: touched, guilt taken away, sin atoned. The coal from the altar carries the atoning power of the sacrificial system: the altar is the place where sin meets fire and is consumed. 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?'—the divine council: God's rhetorical question, not a desperate search, but an invitation into purpose. 'For us'—the plural hints at the divine complexity that later revelation will identify as Trinitarian (cf. Gen. 1:26; John 12:41). 'Here I am! Send me'—the response of the cleansed prophet: immediate, total, unqualified. Motyer: the commission follows the cleansing; only the man whose lips have been touched by holy fire can bear the holy word to a resistant people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, “Go, and say to this people: ‘Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.’ Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive'—the most disturbing commission in prophecy: Isaiah is sent not to produce repentance but to harden. The paradox: faithful preaching accelerates the judgment rather than preventing it. 'Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes'—the prophet's preaching is the instrument of judicial hardening: God uses the word that should save to judge those who refuse to receive it. 'Lest they see... and turn and be healed'—the purpose clause reveals what is being withheld: healing through seeing, hearing, and understanding. Childs: this is not arbitrary exclusion but the logic of covenant rejection—those who persistently refuse the offer of grace find the offer withdrawn. Jesus quotes this text six times in the Gospels; Paul cites it in Romans 11 and Acts 28.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, “How long, O Lord?” And he said: “Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste, and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'How long, O Lord?'—the prophet's question reveals that even the bearer of the hardening commission finds it painful. The duration of judicial hardening is asked in the spirit of lament, not cynicism. 'Until cities lie waste without inhabitant'—the answer is terrifying: the hardening continues until the land is depopulated. The commission is not temporary or corrective but extends through the full course of judgment. 'The LORD removes people far away'—exile: the covenant curse of dispossession and removal from the land (Deut. 28:64). 'The forsaken places are many in the midst of the land'—the reversal of God's original gift: a land filled with his people becomes a land emptied of them. Motyer: the hardening is the consequence of persistent rejection taken to its logical end.

verseByVerse.quote: And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled.” The holy seed is its stump. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again'—even the remnant will face fire; the judgment is not satisfied with partial purification. The decimation of decimation: a tenth of a tenth. 'Like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled'—the tree is cut down, but the stump persists. Total destruction is not the final word. 'The holy seed is its stump'—the last two words of the chapter (in Hebrew, the holy seed) are the pivot of the entire commission. The hardening, the desolation, the burning—all of it moves toward the stump, and in the stump is the holy seed. Oswalt: the judgment is not terminal but seminal. The tree falls; the stump sprouts. Webb: the holy seed is the remnant that will become the Branch of 4:2—the shoot from the stump of Jesse (11:1). The book's hope begins here, in the charred remnant of the burning.

7.subtitle: The Sign of Immanuel
7.intro: Overview. Chapter 7 is set during the Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 734–732 BC), when the kingdoms of Syria and northern Israel formed an alliance against Judah. King Ahaz of Jerusalem, faced with this threat, is leaning toward appealing to Assyria rather than trusting God. Isaiah is sent with a message of reassurance — and with a call to faith that Ahaz refuses. The sign God offers in response to that refusal is one of the most contested and theologically significant prophecies in the Old Testament: a young woman will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel. Matthew 1:23 identifies the ultimate fulfilment of this sign as the virgin birth of Jesus.

sections.title: Fear Not — Stand Firm in Faith
sections.commentary:
The political situation is desperate. The armies of Syria and Ephraim are marching toward Jerusalem, and “the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (v. 2). Isaiah is sent with his son Shear-jashub — whose name means “a remnant shall return” — to meet the king at the Fuller's Field. The child's presence is itself a message: even if judgment comes, a remnant will remain.

God's assessment of the threat is deliberately deflating: Syria and Ephraim are “two smoldering stumps of firebrands” (v. 4). They were once dangerous fires; now they are dying embers. The scheme to replace Ahaz with a puppet king will not succeed. Isaiah's word is categorical: “It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass.”

v. 9 — “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.” The Hebrew is a wordplay on the root aman (to be firm, to trust — the root of “amen”). The stability of Ahaz's kingdom depends not on Assyrian military aid but on whether his faith rests on the word of God. Trust is not a religious extra but the basis of all true security.

sections.title: The Sign of Immanuel
sections.commentary:
God offers Ahaz a sign — anything, from the depths to the heights of heaven. Ahaz refuses, cloaking his unbelief in the language of piety: “I will not put the LORD to the test.” Isaiah's response is one of the most exasperated sentences in all the prophets: “Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?” Ahaz is not being devout; he is hiding. He has already decided to trust Assyria, and a sign from God would complicate that decision.

v. 14 — “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.” The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age — always a virgin in its Old Testament usage. The Greek Septuagint translates it with parthenos, the unambiguous word for virgin, and Matthew 1:23 quotes the LXX in applying the verse to Jesus. A near fulfilment existed in Isaiah's day; the ultimate fulfilment — the one the near event pointed toward — is the birth of Christ.

The name “Immanuel” — God with us — is the theological centre of the sign. God is not dealing with his people from a safe distance. He will enter their situation personally. This is what the incarnation fulfils in a way no near-term birth could: in Jesus, God is literally, bodily, materially with us.

sections.title: The Razor from Assyria
sections.commentary: The chapter closes with a series of oracles describing what the Assyrian alliance Ahaz has chosen will actually produce. God will whistle for Egypt and Assyria, and the very power Ahaz is relying on for deliverance will be the instrument of devastation. The image of the hired razor shaving everything off — head, beard, legs — is one of profound humiliation. Ahaz thought he was hiring Assyria; Isaiah tells him God is hiring Assyria — and the target is not just the enemies but Judah itself. Faith deferred always costs more than the thing it was trying to avoid.

keyVerse.quote: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”
keyVerse.note: The sign is given not to Ahaz but despite Ahaz — it is addressed to “the house of David” (v. 13), the dynasty that will eventually produce the one the sign points to. Matthew's use of this verse is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of what the near event was designed to foreshadow: a birth that is genuinely miraculous, a child who is genuinely God-with-us, in a way that no ordinary birth in Isaiah's day could be.

7.theology:
Dual fulfilment of prophecy. Isaiah 7:14 is the clearest example in Scripture of a prophecy with both a near and an ultimate fulfilment. The near sign existed in Isaiah's own day; the ultimate sign is the birth of Christ. Prophecy in this model is like a shadow cast by an object in front of a light — the shadow tells you something real about the shape of the object, but the object is greater than the shadow.

The incarnation as answer to fear. The context of Isaiah 7 is terror — a shaking king, a threatened city. God's response is not a battle plan but a name: Immanuel. The answer to human fear in the face of overwhelming circumstances is always the same in Scripture: God with us. This is what the incarnation means in Matthew 1 — not a new religious idea but the arrival, in person, of the one Isaiah promised to the frightened house of David.
7.reflection: Ahaz's refusal of a sign is a portrait of a peculiarly religious form of unbelief: using the language of reverence to avoid the demand of trust. It is possible to be scrupulously religious while refusing to actually rely on God. The question Isaiah's chapter asks is the same one it asked Ahaz: where is your security actually resting — on the word of God, or on the alliance you have quietly arranged?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it. <sup>2</sup>When the house of David was told, "Syria is in league with Ephraim," the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind. <sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Isaiah, "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. <sup>4</sup>And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah. <sup>5</sup>Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying, <sup>6</sup>"Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it," <sup>7</sup>thus says the Lord GOD: It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass. <sup>8</sup>For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people. <sup>9</sup>And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'" <sup>10</sup>Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz: <sup>11</sup>"Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven." <sup>12</sup>But Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test." <sup>13</sup>And he said, "Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? <sup>14</sup>Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. <sup>15</sup>He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. <sup>16</sup>For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted. <sup>17</sup>The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah— the king of Assyria." <sup>18</sup>In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. <sup>19</sup>And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures. <sup>20</sup>In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River— with the king of Assyria— the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also. <sup>21</sup>In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep, <sup>22</sup>and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey. <sup>23</sup>In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns. <sup>24</sup>With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns. <sup>25</sup>And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Ahaz, the Immanuel Sign, and the Assyrian Shadow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 7 is one of the most theologically dense chapters in the book. The historical crisis is Ahaz's refusal to trust God against the Syro-Ephraimite coalition (735 BC); his faithlessness provokes the Immanuel sign—one of the Bible's greatest messianic promises. The sign is immediately dark: the child's birth will mark the time before Assyria devastates the land. History and eschatology interlock.
verseByVerse.examples: Matthew 1:23 cites Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus from the virgin Mary. The New Testament does not merely spiritualize the text: the same theological logic applies—when the house of David is in crisis, God himself comes to be with his people. Every generation that faces threats to the covenant community can draw on the Immanuel promise.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it. When the house of David was told, “Syria is in league with Ephraim,” the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the days of Ahaz'—the historical setting is the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 735–732 BC. Two of Judah's neighbors—Syria (Rezin) and the northern kingdom Israel (Pekah)—have formed an alliance and marched against Jerusalem to depose Ahaz and install a puppet king. 'But could not yet mount an attack against it'—the parenthetical qualification is theological: God's restraint is already operating before Isaiah even speaks. 'Syria is in league with Ephraim'—the message of geopolitical alliance. 'The heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind'—the simile is vivid: not merely anxiety but total trembling. Oswalt: the king's fear is understandable but culpable—he is shaking before a threat that God has already limited.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Isaiah, “Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Go out to meet Ahaz'—the divine initiative: God sends Isaiah to the king at the very place where Ahaz is likely inspecting Jerusalem's water supply in preparation for siege. 'You and Shear-jashub your son'—Shear-jashub means 'a remnant shall return': Isaiah's son is a walking sermon, a living sign. His presence embodies hope even in crisis. 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear'—four imperatives of faith offered against the trembling described in v. 2. 'These two smoldering stumps of firebrands'—the dismissive image: Rezin and Pekah, who seem so fearsome, are merely smoldering stubs, not blazing torches. Their fire is nearly spent. Motyer: God's perspective on what terrifies us is the perspective we need to borrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying, “Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it,” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you'—the political plan is named: the coalition aims to topple the Davidic dynasty and replace Ahaz with a compliant non-Davidic figure (the son of Tabeel). 'Let us go up against Judah and terrify it'—the word terrify (bulah) appears; the enemies plan to paralyze Judah with fear before they even arrive militarily. 'Set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it'—the Davidic line is the target: a non-Davidic king installed in Jerusalem would sever the covenant line. Young: the attack is ultimately not against Ahaz personally but against the promises God made to David (2 Sam. 7).

verseByVerse.quote: therefore thus says the Lord GOD: “'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass. For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass'—the divine verdict is categorical and immediate: the plot will fail. The Lord GOD decrees against the coalition before it has moved. 'For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin'—a series of reductions: Syria's head is merely a city; the city's head is merely a man. The great threat is reduced to human scale. 'Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people'—the longer-range prophecy: the northern kingdom has sixty-five years at most. This is fulfilled in the Assyrian deportation of 722 BC and subsequent repopulation. Childs: God answers the immediate threat with a word that reaches beyond it to the larger historical horizon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah'—the reduction continues: Israel's head is merely a city; the city's head is merely a man, and a man whose patronymic is used rather than his name (Pekah)—a subtle slight. 'If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all'—the Hebrew wordplay is untranslatable: ta'aminu (be firm in faith) and te'amenu (be firm/stand). Faith and stability use the same root. Oswalt: the point is not merely a play on words but a theological reality—trust in God is the only foundation that holds when political structures shake. Motyer: Ahaz's trembling (v. 2) is precisely the symptom of faithlessness; the cure is faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz: “Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ask a sign of the LORD your God'—an extraordinary invitation. God offers Ahaz a sign of his own choosing, unrestricted in scope: as deep as Sheol (the lowest conceivable place) or as high as heaven (the highest). The offer is lavish, the grace extravagant. 'Let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven'—the comprehensiveness of the offer underscores that Ahaz's faith-failure will not be due to insufficient evidence. God is willing to perform any confirming sign. Motyer: God does not demand blind faith from Ahaz but offers him every confirmation available. The refusal that follows is therefore without excuse—Ahaz has rejected not a demanding God but a generous one.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test.” And he said, “Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test'—Ahaz cites Deuteronomy 6:16 as his reason for refusing. The piety is false: his refusal is not devotion but policy. He has already sent to Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:7); asking God for a sign would complicate his Assyrian alliance. He refuses not because he fears God but because he trusts Assyria. 'Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?'—Isaiah's stinging rebuke. The prophet speaks not of your God (as God spoke: 'your God') but my God—Ahaz has forfeited the relationship. Webb: false humility before God is one of the subtlest and most damaging forms of unbelief.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign'—despite Ahaz's refusal, God gives the sign. The sign is not for Ahaz alone but for the house of David and, through them, for the world. 'The virgin shall conceive and bear a son'—the Hebrew almah means young woman of marriageable age, typically unmarried; the LXX translates parthenos (virgin), which Matthew 1:23 follows. The sign transcends its immediate historical referent. 'And shall call his name Immanuel'—God with us: the name is the theological center of the entire passage and of Isaiah's theology. The sign is not primarily a calendar marker but a covenantal declaration: God will not abandon his people. 'He shall eat curds and honey'—in the near term, the land's devastation (v. 22) will reduce even this child to the food of subsistence. Oswalt: the sign reaches from the immediate crisis to the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted. The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah—the king of Assyria. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted'—the near-term timetable: the Syro-Ephraimite coalition will collapse within a child's early years. This was fulfilled when Assyria destroyed Damascus (732 BC) and Samaria (722 BC). 'The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people... the king of Assyria'—the dark irony: Ahaz fled to Assyria for help, and Assyria will become the instrument of Judah's devastation. The ally becomes the threat. Young: Ahaz's faithlessness trades the threat of two smoldering stumps for the devastation of an imperial power.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria'—the divine summons of military power, as in 5:26. Flies (Egypt) and bees (Assyria) are both swarming, stinging, unavoidable. God whistles; they come instantly. 'They will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks'—the swarming imagery: every terrain feature of Judah is covered. There is nowhere in the land free from the presence of the invaders. Motyer: the land Ahaz hoped to protect by his Assyrian policy becomes the land covered by the very power he courted.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River—with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also. In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River'—the razor is hired: Assyria is God's contracted tool. 'The River' is the Euphrates—Assyria's heartland. 'The head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also'—total shaving: in ancient Near Eastern culture, the beard was a man's dignity; removing it was maximum humiliation. The land will be stripped bare as a man shaved of all hair. 'In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep'—the reduction of agricultural life: instead of herds and flocks, one cow and two sheep. Childs: the once-prosperous land of Israel, flowing with milk and honey in the covenantal sense, is reduced to the subsistence level of a refugee economy.

verseByVerse.quote: and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey. In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds'—the few animals left produce disproportionate milk because there are so few people remaining to consume it. The abundance is the abundance of desolation: more food per person because so many people are gone. 'Everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey'—the sign of Immanuel (v. 15) is here connected to the reality of devastation: the child eating curds and honey is not prosperity but subsistence amid ruin. 'Every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns'—the vineyard of ch. 5 returns: the cultivated land reverts to wilderness. Oswalt: the vineyard parable reaches its historical fulfillment in these verses.

verseByVerse.quote: With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns. And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'With bow and arrows a man will come there'—the cultivated land becomes hunting ground. Bows and arrows are for game, not harvest; the land has reverted to the wild. 'All the land will be briers and thorns'—the double curse from vv. 22–23 continues and intensifies: the agricultural landscape is gone. 'The hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns'—even the terraced hillsides of Judah, which required enormous labor to maintain, are abandoned. 'They will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread'—pasture land instead of vineyard: the highest agricultural use (viticulture) replaced by the lowest (open grazing). Motyer: the judgment systematically reverses Judah's careful cultivation of the promised land.

8.subtitle: Fear God Alone
8.intro: Overview. Chapter 8 continues directly from chapter 7, moving through the immediate fulfilment of the Immanuel sign in the birth of Isaiah's second son, to the announcement that Assyria will overwhelm the land like a flood, to a searching call to fear God rather than the conspiracies and crises that are making everyone else afraid. The chapter ends in darkness — those who have rejected the word of God have no light — but Isaiah and his children stand within that darkness as living signs of God's purposes.

sections.title: Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz and the Flood of Assyria
sections.commentary:
Isaiah's second son is given a name that means “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil” — a prophecy in a name. Before the child is old enough to say “my father” or “my mother,” the wealth of Damascus and Samaria will be carried off by Assyria. The sign is specific and dated: this is not vague prophecy but a named child whose growth will mark the timeline of fulfilment.

The image of the waters of Shiloah (v. 6) — the gentle stream through Jerusalem — being rejected in favour of the mighty Euphrates is one of Isaiah's most powerful metaphors. Judah has despised the quiet provision of God and longed for the impressive power of Assyria. The consequence is that the great river will come — but it will not stop at the border. It will rise “up to the neck,” leaving only the head above water. The very power chosen as a solution becomes the flooding problem.

v. 10 — “Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us.” The chapter places Immanuel here as a battle cry — not just a name but a declaration that all the plotting of the nations runs up against the fact of God's presence. Every alliance that does not account for God is building on nothing.

sections.title: Fear the LORD of Hosts
sections.commentary:
The LORD speaks directly to Isaiah and calls him out of the prevailing culture of fear: “Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread.” The nation is in a panic over Syria and Ephraim. God's word to Isaiah is: their fear is misplaced. Calibrate your dread to the right object.

v. 13 — “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honour as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” Fear of God is not offered here as a competitor to wisdom or courage but as their source. The person who fears God properly will not be paralysed by the fear of circumstances, because they understand that the one who controls all circumstances is also the one who is for them. Peter quotes this verse in 1 Peter 3:14–15, applying it to Christians facing persecution.

The closing verses are stark. Those who do not speak according to the law and testimony — the word of God — have no light in them. In the darkness that follows the rejection of God's word, people will look to the dead and find no answer. Isaiah and his children stand as signs and portents — living testimonies that God has spoken, even when the word is not welcomed.

keyVerse.quote: “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honour as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.”
keyVerse.note: This verse reorients what fear is for. Fear is not to be eliminated but redirected. The person who fears the right thing — the LORD of hosts — will be freed from the paralysing fear of everything else. Peter's use of this text in 1 Peter 3 makes the application explicit: in a hostile world, the answer to anxiety about circumstances is not stoic courage but a heart that is occupied with the holiness of God.

8.reflection: The chapter diagnoses a failure that is both common and hard to see in oneself: calibrating one's fear to the wrong object. The people of Judah were afraid of the right threats by the wrong standard — afraid of Syria when they should have been afraid of the God who governs Syria. The question the chapter asks directly: what is it in your own situation that is producing your deepest anxiety, and is that fear proportioned to the reality of who God is?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to me, "Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters, 'Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.'" <sup>2</sup>And I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, to attest for me. <sup>3</sup>And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, "Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz; <sup>4</sup>for before the boy knows how to cry 'My father' or 'My mother,' the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria." <sup>5</sup>The LORD spoke to me again: <sup>6</sup>"Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah, <sup>7</sup>therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory. And it will rise over all its channels and go over all its banks, <sup>8</sup>and it will sweep on into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck, and its outspread wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Immanuel." <sup>9</sup>Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered; give ear, all you far countries; strap on your armor and be shattered; strap on your armor and be shattered. <sup>10</sup>Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us. <sup>11</sup>For the LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying: <sup>12</sup>"Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. <sup>13</sup>But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. <sup>14</sup>And he will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, a trap and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. <sup>15</sup>And many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken." <sup>16</sup>Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples. <sup>17</sup>I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and I will hope in him. <sup>18</sup>Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel from the LORD of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. <sup>19</sup>And when they say to you, "Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter," should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? <sup>20</sup>To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn. <sup>21</sup>They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry. And when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. <sup>22</sup>And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish. And they will be thrust into thick darkness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz and the Darkness Before Dawn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 8 continues the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. God commands Isaiah to inscribe a name—Maher-shalal-hash-baz ('swift is the plunder, speedy is the prey')—as a prophetic witness. Isaiah's son by the prophetess bears this name as a living sign. The chapter then turns to the choice facing Israel: the gentle waters of Shiloah (trust in God) or the overwhelming flood of Assyria (the consequence of faithlessness). The chapter ends with instructions to the prophet's disciples: bind the testimony, wait for God, and refuse the spirit of divination.
verseByVerse.examples: The pattern of the faithful remnant preserving God's word in a hostile culture is the permanent pattern of the church in any age of apostasy. Isaiah's instructions to 'bind the testimony, seal the teaching among my disciples' (v. 16) describe the ministry of every faithful pastor, parent, and teacher who preserves the word for the next generation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, “Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters, 'Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.' And I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, to attest for me.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters'—the prophecy is inscribed publicly, in ordinary script that anyone can read. The word must be datable and verifiable. 'Maher-shalal-hash-baz'—the name means swift is the plunder, speedy is the prey: a prophecy of military conquest compressed into a name. The name-as-prophecy is characteristic of Isaiah's sign-children. 'I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah'—two named witnesses provide legal verification; when the prophecy is fulfilled, the witnesses can confirm it was given beforehand. Oswalt: the prophetic word is not private oracle but public record—God's word is given in history and verified by history.

verseByVerse.quote: And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, “Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz; for before the boy knows how to cry 'My father' or 'My mother,' the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son'—Isaiah's wife is called the prophetess, either because she is a prophet herself or as the wife of a prophet. The son born is the living enactment of the written tablet: name becomes flesh. 'Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz'—the name confirmed at birth. 'Before the boy knows how to cry “My father” or “My mother”'—within two years at most: the earliest words a child learns. 'The riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria'—Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC; the timeline is precise. Motyer: the sign-child makes the prophetic word embodied and time-stamped—it cannot be claimed later as coincidence.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to me again: “Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The waters of Shiloah that flow gently'—Shiloah (later Siloam) was Jerusalem's primary water source: a small, gentle stream running from the Gihon spring. Its gentleness is the gentleness of trust in God—quiet, unpretentious, life-giving. 'This people has refused the waters of Shiloah'—the covenant community has rejected the quiet provision of God. 'And rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah'—instead of rejoicing in God's protection, they rejoice in the foreign alliance. Childs: the people's rejoicing in Rezin and Pekah probably refers to the northern tribes who welcomed the Syro-Ephraimite coalition as liberation from the Davidic house. The rejected water is God's gentle rule; the preferred alternative is foreign military power.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory. And it will rise over all its channels and go over all its banks, and it will sweep into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck, and its outspread wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Immanuel.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many'—the River is the Euphrates: the Nile of Mesopotamia, a massive flood-force. What was refused (Shiloah's gentle stream) is replaced by what is terrifying (the Euphrates in flood). 'It will sweep into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck'—the flood reaches up to the neck: threatening drowning but not yet drowning. The land survives—barely. 'O Immanuel'—the address to Immanuel stops the flood imagery cold. The land is his land: 'your land.' Because it is Immanuel's land, the flood cannot finally overwhelm it. Motyer: the address to Immanuel is the theological key to the entire passage—the limit on Assyria's devastation is God-with-us.

verseByVerse.quote: Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered; give ear, all you far countries; strap on your armor and be shattered; strap on your armor and be shattered. Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered'—the defiant summons to the nations: try your worst; you will be shattered. The triple repetition of breaking (hattu, hatu, hatu) is a taunt: all the nations' preparations will end in the same result. 'Strap on your armor and be shattered'—the armor is real; the shattering is certain. Military preparation cannot overcome divine opposition. 'Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand'—the plans of the nations are dissolved by God's will. 'For God is with us'—the translation of Immanuel closes the taunt: the reason no coalition can succeed is the presence of God with his people. Oswalt: the battle cry of the remnant is not their strength but God's name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying: “Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me'—the intensity of prophetic reception: the hand of the LORD is the overwhelming pressure of divine communication (cf. Ezek. 1:3; 3:22). 'Warned me not to walk in the way of this people'—the prophet is called out of his culture's anxieties. The people's responses—conspiracy-fear, dread—are not Isaiah's responses. 'Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy'—the political paranoia of the court: every alliance is seen as conspiracy, every foreign contact as treason. Isaiah is to refuse this framework. Childs: the prophet must resist the pressure of public opinion, which tends to see every crisis through the lens of the prevailing fear.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, a trap and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread'—the reorientation of fear: not the Syro-Ephraimite coalition, not Assyria, but the LORD. To fear God is to cease fearing everything else—not because everything else is harmless but because the LORD transcends every earthly threat. 'He will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling'—the same God is both refuge (sanctuary) and danger (stumbling stone), depending on where one stands relative to faith. For those who trust, he is the sanctuary; for those who refuse, he is the stone they trip over. Motyer: this verse is quoted in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8 as fulfilled in Christ—he is both cornerstone and stumbling stone.

verseByVerse.quote: And many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken.“ Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken'—the consequence of rejecting God as sanctuary: he becomes the trap. The nation that refuses its refuge finds its very refusal has set the snare. 'Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples'—the command to preserve the prophetic word within the faithful remnant. When the nation rejects the word, it is entrusted to disciples who will guard and transmit it. Young: this is the origin of the prophetic scroll tradition—the word that the nation rejects is preserved by those who receive it. It anticipates the entire canonical function of the written prophetic word across generations.

verseByVerse.quote: I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and I will hope in him. Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel from the LORD of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob'—the prophet's personal confession of faith in a time of divine hiddenness. God's face is hidden from the nation; Isaiah waits anyway. This is the faith of the remnant: trusting God when evidence of his presence is withheld. 'I will hope in him'—hope directed not at circumstances but at God himself. 'I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel'—Isaiah's family is itself a prophetic text: Shear-jashub (a remnant shall return), Maher-shalal-hash-baz (swift is the plunder), and Immanuel (through the mother). Their names map the entire theological landscape of the crisis. Motyer: the prophet's household is a miniature of the faithful remnant within apostate Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they say to you, “Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter,” should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter'—the alternative to prophetic faith: consulting the dead through spirit mediums. The description chirp and mutter captures the technique of spirit-communication, which produced animal-like sounds. 'Should not a people inquire of their God?'—the rhetorical reversal: why would the living God's people consult the dead? 'Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?'—the absurdity of necromancy exposed: the dead have no access to life's answers. 'To the teaching and to the testimony!'—the twofold foundation: Torah (teaching) and the prophetic word (testimony) are the only reliable guides. 'If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn'—no light whatsoever. Webb: the criterion for all wisdom is the written word of God.

verseByVerse.quote: They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry. And when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish. And they will be thrust into thick darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry'—the consequences of rejecting the word: not illumination but starvation. The people who refused God's light now wander in famine. 'When they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God'—hunger produces rage; rage produces blasphemy. The people curse the only one who could have helped them. 'And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish'—in every direction they look—upward (v. 21) and earthward—there is only darkness. 'And they will be thrust into thick darkness'—the final word of the chapter is darkness. It is the darkness before the great light of ch. 9:2. Childs: the structure is deliberate: the book descends into darkness so that the light can be appreciated as what it truly is.

9.subtitle: A Great Light — The Child Born to Us
9.intro: Overview. Chapter 9 moves from the darkness at the end of chapter 8 to one of the most luminous promises in all of Scripture. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. What follows is simultaneously poetic, political, and theological: a child has been born, a son has been given, and the government will rest on his shoulders. The four names given to this child constitute the most compressed Christology in the Old Testament. Chapter 9 is the prophetic foundation for every proclamation that points beyond the manger to the throne.

sections.title: A Great Light in the Darkness
sections.commentary:
Isaiah begins by specifying the geography of the promise: Zebulun and Naphtali, the northern territories — the very regions most thoroughly overrun by Assyria. These were the first to fall and the last anyone would expect to be glorified. Yet it is precisely these “Galilee of the nations” regions that will first see the great light. Matthew 4:13–16 quotes this passage to explain why Jesus based his ministry in Capernaum and Galilee rather than Jerusalem — the light goes first to the most forgotten places.

v. 3 — “You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the plunder.” The images are harvest and victory — abundance and vindication arriving simultaneously. The joy is not muted or tentative; it is the full-throated celebration of people who had long lived under oppression and now find it lifted.

sections.title: For Unto Us a Child Is Born
sections.commentary:
“For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder.” The construction is deliberate: the child is born (humanity) but the son is given (the gift comes from above). Both the human birth and the divine sending are stated. And the government — all authority, all rule — rests on this single shoulder. This is not a constitutional monarchy; this is the absolute and righteous reign of the one to whom all authority belongs.

The four names are given as a compound title — a unified description of who this child is:

v. 6 — The four names. Wonderful Counsellor: not a counsellor who is wonderful but one whose counsel is itself a wonder, beyond ordinary human wisdom. Mighty God (El Gibbor): the second name is unambiguous — this child is called God. Not godlike, not divine in some reduced sense, but El. Everlasting Father: the eternal source and sustainer of his people's life. Prince of Peace: the one in whom all the shalom Isaiah has described as history's goal actually arrives.

Verse 7 closes with a promise as comprehensive as it is unconditional: “Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.” This kingdom will not peak and decline. It will not be subject to the cycles of rise and fall that mark every human empire. The “zeal of the LORD of hosts” will perform it. The guarantee is not human faithfulness but divine zeal.

keyVerse.quote: “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
keyVerse.note: The name Mighty God (El Gibbor) is the same phrase used of God himself in Isaiah 10:21. Isaiah is not hedging when he calls this coming child God; he is asserting it. The full weight of orthodox Christology — the genuine divinity of the Son — has its Old Testament foundation here. Matthew, Luke, and John each draw on Isaiah 9 in their portraits of Jesus.

9.theology:
The person of Christ. The four names of Isaiah 9:6 have been central to the church's reflection on who Jesus is since the earliest centuries. The name Mighty God grounds the assertions of John 1:1 and Philippians 2:6 — that Jesus is not merely a great teacher but God himself. The child who is born is simultaneously the Son who is given: the human birth and the divine mission are two aspects of a single event.

The Kingdom of God. “The government shall be upon his shoulder” points to the political dimension of Christ's lordship that is often underemphasised. Jesus does not merely save individual souls; he rules a kingdom. The “increase of his government” with “no end” describes an expansion already underway — every person who comes under the reign of the Prince of Peace is a new territory in which the kingdom advances.
9.reflection: Isaiah 9 was written to people living in the specific darkness of Assyrian occupation. The promise of a child born to them was addressed to their situation, not over it. Whatever darkness you are living in, the promise is the same: “the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.” The question is not whether the light has come — it has — but whether you are facing it.
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. <sup>2</sup>The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone. <sup>3</sup>You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil. <sup>4</sup>For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian. <sup>5</sup>For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire. <sup>6</sup>For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. <sup>7</sup>Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. <sup>8</sup>The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel; <sup>9</sup>and all the people will know, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart: <sup>10</sup>"The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place." <sup>11</sup>But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. <sup>12</sup>The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. <sup>13</sup>The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts. <sup>14</sup>So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day— <sup>15</sup>the elder and honored man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail; <sup>16</sup>for those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up. <sup>17</sup>Therefore the Lord does not rejoice over their young men, and has no compassion on their fatherless and widows; for everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. <sup>18</sup>For wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns; it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke. <sup>19</sup>Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts the land is scorched, and the people are like fuel for the fire; no one spares another. <sup>20</sup>They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied; each devours the flesh of his own arm, <sup>21</sup>Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh; together they are against Judah. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Great Light and the Outstretched Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 9 opens with one of the Bible's most luminous passages—the prophecy of the child whose government shall have no end—then pivots to a devastating sequence of covenant judgments against the northern kingdom. The contrast is stark and intentional: the chapter holds the highest hope and the deepest warning side by side.
verseByVerse.examples: The New Testament applies 9:1–2 to the ministry of Jesus in Galilee (Matt. 4:15–16) and 9:6–7 to his birth and eternal kingship. The fourfold divine name has been the church's treasure for two millennia. The outstretched-hand refrain (vv. 12, 17, 21) is a sobering reminder that judgment can intensify even as the promised king approaches.

verseByVerse.quote: But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish. In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But there will be no gloom for her who was in anguish'—the chapter opens as a reversal of ch. 8's darkness (8:22). The 'but' (ki) is the pivot of the entire book's movement from judgment to salvation. 'The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali'—the northern territories, the first conquered by Assyria (734 BC, Tiglath-pileser III). They bore contempt first; they will receive glory first. 'The way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations'—the geographical description Matthew 4:15 cites as fulfilled in Jesus' ministry in Galilee. The first region to suffer will be the first to see the great light. Motyer: the logic of grace reverses the logic of judgment—the most desolate become the first recipients of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone. You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light'—the prophetic perfect: so certain is the salvation that it is spoken as accomplished. Walking in darkness is the condition of those without God's word (8:20); seeing the great light is the condition of those to whom it comes. 'Those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness'—the Hebrew tsalmaveth (shadow of death) intensifies: not merely dark but death-dark. 'You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy'—the joy is covenantal: the people grow not merely in number but in gladness before God. 'As with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil'—two images of abundant joy: harvest-joy (labor's fruit) and victory-joy (war's spoil). Oswalt: the joy is proportional to the preceding darkness; great suffering precedes great gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, and the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian. For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, and the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian'—the liberation from oppression is compared to Gideon's defeat of Midian (Judges 7): miraculous, disproportionate, entirely God's doing. The three instruments of oppression (yoke, staff, rod) are all broken. 'Every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire'—a comprehensive disarmament: the paraphernalia of war consigned to the fire. Young: the burning of military equipment signals the permanent end of war—not merely a ceasefire but the removal of war's instruments, which will no longer be needed. This is the fulfillment of 2:4 (swords into plowshares).

verseByVerse.quote: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For to us a child is born, to us a son is given'—the double announcement: born (human, historical entry) and given (divine gift, not merely natural). The child is both from us (incarnate) and for us (given). 'The government shall be upon his shoulder'—the shoulder that bears the government is the same shoulders that bore the cross; the throne he occupies is the throne won through suffering. 'Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace'—four throne-names, each a divine attribute applied to the child. Mighty God (El Gibbor) is unambiguously divine in Hebrew usage. 'Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end'—eschatological kingship: not a dynasty that ends but a reign that expands without limit. 'The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this'—not human effort or political strategy but divine passion. Motyer: the promise rests entirely on God's own determination to accomplish it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel; and all the people will know it—Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria—who say in pride and in arrogance of heart: (ESV)
