verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord has sent a word against Jacob, and it will fall on Israel'—the pivot from vision to oracle of judgment. The same divine word that announces the child-king now falls against Jacob (a name for the northern kingdom in its election-failing). 'It will fall on Israel'—the word is ballistic: sent and landing. 'And all the people will know it'—not the announcement of salvation but the announcement of judgment. 'Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who say in pride and in arrogance of heart'—pride is the key: the nation that should be humbled by Assyrian pressure has responded with defiance. Oswalt: the fundamental sin is always the same—the pride that refuses to acknowledge God's hand in history.

verseByVerse.quote: “The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place.” But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stones'—the defiant response to partial judgment: instead of repentance, the nation plans to rebuild bigger and better. Bricks are mud and straw (cheap); dressed stones are quarried and hewn (expensive). The damage is met with upgraded construction. 'The sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place'—the same logic: the common sycamore-fig replaced by the aristocratic cedar. The nation responds to discipline with escalation rather than submission. 'But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him'—God's response to the defiant rebuilding is to activate more adversaries. The nation's plan to outbuild the damage will be overwhelmed by new attacks. Motyer: pride turns divine discipline into divine escalation.

verseByVerse.quote: The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. For the people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth'—enemies on two fronts. The east-west double attack was the ancient form of strategic encirclement. 'For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still'—the refrain that will echo through vv. 17 and 21: the judgment is not finished because the purpose of the judgment (repentance) has not been achieved. 'For the people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts'—the diagnostic: discipline without repentance. The wound should produce the turning; it has produced only defiance. Webb: the outstretched hand is both the hand of judgment and the hand reaching for a response that never comes.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day— the elder and honored man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day'—comprehensive judgment in a single act: all levels of society removed simultaneously. Head and tail, palm and reed—the proud and the humble, the lofty and the low. 'The elder and honored man is the head'—the elder represents traditional authority and social honor: wisdom and experience that should guide the nation. 'And the prophet who teaches lies is the tail'—the false prophet brings up the rear, the most dangerous leader because he speaks in God's name while leading astray. Young: the society is destroyed from the top (false elders) and the bottom (false prophets)—all guidance is corrupted.

verseByVerse.quote: for those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up. Therefore the Lord does not rejoice over their young men, and has no compassion on their fatherless and widows; for everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up'—the tragic complicity: leaders and followers go down together. The guides are culpable; the guided are complicit. 'The Lord does not rejoice over their young men'—normally the death of the young is deeply mourned; now God does not rejoice (the understatement for 'has no compassion'). The corruption is so comprehensive that even the vulnerable (fatherless, widows) receive no compassion—because they too are ungodly. 'For everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly'—the total depravity of a society that has fully rejected God. 'His anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still'—the second repetition of the refrain: judgment intensifies because nothing has changed.

verseByVerse.quote: For wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns; it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke. Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts the land is scorched, and the people are like fuel for the fire; no one spares his brother. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns'—wickedness as self-consuming fire: sin destroys the social fabric it inhabits. The fire feeds on the dry tinder of a society already stripped of living faithfulness. 'It kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke'—the fire escalates: from scrub (briers) to forest (thickets). Social wickedness spreads and intensifies. 'The people are like fuel for the fire'—the individuals who constitute the society become the fuel that feeds the judgment. 'No one spares his brother'—the most intimate social bond (brotherhood) dissolves; the fire of wickedness destroys even family solidarity. Childs: the social dissolution is the visible sign of the spiritual fire consuming the covenant community.

verseByVerse.quote: They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied; each devours the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh; together they are against Judah. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied'—the insatiable appetite of a society consuming itself. Every direction of consumption leaves still hungry: the appetite of wickedness is never filled. 'Each devours the flesh of his own arm'—the extreme image: self-cannibalism. The body politic devours itself. 'Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh'—the two halves of the northern kingdom are at war with each other. This was historically true in the period of Israelite civil war that preceded Assyria's conquest. 'Together they are against Judah'—despite internal civil war, they unite only in hostility to the south. 'His anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still'—the third and final repetition of the refrain in this unit. Oswalt: the outstretched hand is both inexhaustible judgment and unaccepted offer.

10.subtitle: Woe to Unjust Laws — Assyria the Rod of God
10.intro: Overview. Chapter 10 operates on two levels simultaneously. The first is immediate and political: God will use Assyria as his instrument of judgment against Israel, but Assyria's own arrogance means it will then be judged in turn. The second level is theological and universal: how does God govern history through the free actions of wicked human agents? The chapter offers no evasion of this question. God is sovereign over the nations; the nations are morally responsible for their own actions; both are fully true.

sections.title: Woe to Unjust Legislators
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens by continuing the woes of chapter 5. Woe to those who write laws designed to deprive the poor of their rights and make widows and orphans their plunder. This is not random corruption but systemic oppression built into the structure of society — laws crafted to protect the powerful by exploiting the vulnerable.

v. 3 — “What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar?” The day of reckoning cannot be legislated away. The same legal skill used to construct unjust systems is entirely useless when the God who is not subject to human law arrives. Wealth and legal ingenuity have never yet survived a divine audit.

sections.title: Assyria: The Rod of God's Anger
sections.commentary:
“Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!” God calls Assyria his rod — his instrument. The world's most powerful empire is a staff in the hand of the LORD, directed against Israel to punish her for her sins. Assyria does not know this (v. 7: “But he does not so intend”); the Assyrian king acts out of pure imperial ambition. Yet God is sovereign over the outcome.

The boast of the Assyrian king in verses 8–11 is magnificent in its arrogance: my commanders are all kings; I have taken city after city; shall Jerusalem not fare the same as Samaria? What the king does not perceive is that he is not the one swinging the axe — he is the axe. Axes do not take credit for the work of the carpenter.

vv. 15–16 — “Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it?” The image deflates the imperial self-understanding in a single question. Human power, however impressive, is always instrumental — always in the hand of a larger power. Assyria's failure was not incompetence; it was the assumption that its success was self-generated.

Assyria's judgment is therefore just: not for doing what God used it to do, but for the pride and cruelty with which it did it. God holds nations morally accountable even when he is sovereignly directing their actions. Both human responsibility and divine sovereignty are fully true at the same time.

sections.title: The Remnant Returns — Do Not Fear Assyria
sections.commentary:
In that day, the remnant of Israel will lean no longer on the one who struck them but on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. This is the conversion Isaiah has been calling for throughout: not a military solution but a theological one. Stop leaning on human empires and lean on God.

v. 20 — “In that day the remnant of Israel… will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.” The phrase in truth (or in faithfulness) distinguishes genuine trust from the religious performance Isaiah has already condemned. The remnant's reliance on God will not be ceremonial. It will be real.

The chapter closes with Assyria's army described as a great forest being cut down. And from Israel's devastated stump, a shoot will grow (11:1). The cutting down that looks like the end is, for God's people, the preparation for new growth.

keyVerse.quote: “Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!”
keyVerse.note: God is not reacting to Assyria's power by co-opting it; he is directing it. The world's dominant military superpower is a tool in the hand of the LORD. This does not make Assyria innocent — verses 12–19 make clear they will be judged for their pride. But it does make God sovereign over the most frightening human powers of every age.

10.theology: Divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Isaiah 10 raises the hardest question in theology with complete directness: how can God sovereignly direct the actions of wicked human agents and still hold those agents morally responsible for what they do? Isaiah does not resolve the tension but asserts both sides of it. God planned it; Assyria chose it; God will judge Assyria for it. Paul addresses the same tension in Romans 9 and offers the same response: the clay does not question the potter. The mystery is real, but its resolution lies in the character of the God who is both sovereign and just.
10.reflection: The two temptations this chapter addresses are the same ones Israel faced: leaning on the overwhelming power that threatens you, and despairing when that power seems unstoppable. God's word to the remnant (v. 24) is simply “do not be afraid.” The basis for that courage is not a better military assessment but a theological one: the LORD of hosts has a purpose, and no human empire is the last word in any situation. What is the ‘Assyria’ in your own life — the overwhelming power you are tempted either to appease or to despair before?
