verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — The Woe of Assyria and the Promise of the Remnant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 10 completes the outstretched-hand sequence with a woe against unjust Judean legislators, then turns to address Assyria itself. God used Assyria as his instrument of judgment, but Assyria exceeded its mandate by claiming credit for what God was doing through it. The instrument is judged by the one who wielded it. The chapter ends with the promise of a remnant and a vivid description of Assyria's advance—and its reversal.
verseByVerse.examples: The theology of Assyria-as-instrument applies to every human power God uses in history: nations, individuals, institutions. God's use of them does not excuse their sin; his judgment of them does not negate his purpose. The church must hold both together: God is sovereign over history, and human agents are accountable for their actions within it.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression, to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right, that widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees'—the woe falls on Judean legislators who use legal mechanisms to institutionalize injustice. This is not random crime but systemic oppression codified into law. 'The writers who keep writing oppression'—the scribes and administrators who give the decrees their legal form. The legal system itself becomes the instrument of injustice. 'To turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of their right'—the specific mechanism: legal maneuvering that denies the poor access to their own rights. 'That widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey'—the most vulnerable become prey: the legislative predators feast on those who cannot defend themselves. Calvin: when the law protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable, it has become a weapon of wickedness.

verseByVerse.quote: What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth? Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners or fall among the slain. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar?'—the day of punishment (yom pekuddah) is the day of divine reckoning. The ruin 'from afar' is Assyria, the distant instrument of judgment. 'To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth?'—the two things the unjust have trusted (powerful connections and accumulated wealth) will both fail. There is nowhere to hide and nowhere to deposit the goods taken from the poor. 'Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners or fall among the slain'—two destinies: captivity or death. 'For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still'—the refrain continues from ch. 9: the judgment is still unfinished. Motyer: the fourth repetition of the refrain; the divine patience is also divine persistence.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger'—the woe-particle (hoy) now falls on Assyria, a non-covenant nation. God addresses it directly as his instrument. The rod is God's rod: the one who swings it is God, not Assyria. 'The staff in their hands is my fury'—Assyria's military power is not its own but God's redirected fury against Israel. 'Against a godless nation I send him'—Israel is called godless (khanef): having forfeited its covenant character. Assyria is the appropriate instrument against a nation that has become like the nations. 'To take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets'—the mandate is specific: conquest and pillage within God's purposes. Oswalt: the distinction between God's purpose and Assyria's action is the key to understanding this chapter—same events, different interpretations.

verseByVerse.quote: But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few. For he says: “Are not my commanders all kings? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think'—the crucial distinction: Assyria's intention and God's intention are different. Assyria is God's instrument but not God's servant; it acts within God's plan without sharing God's purpose. 'It is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few'—Assyria's real intention is imperial expansion without limit, not the limited punitive mission God assigned. 'Are not my commanders all kings?'—Assyria's boast: the vassals and commanders of Assyria outrank other nations' kings. The imperial hierarchy dazzles Assyria with its own power. Young: the boast reveals the nature of the sin—pride in military organization, treating conquest as inherently glorious rather than as morally accountable action.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus? As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?'—Assyria's catalog of conquered cities: each comparison equates a new conquest with a previous one. The logic is imperial momentum: every city falls; Jerusalem will be the same. 'As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria'—the theological claim: if Assyria defeated nations with greater idol-power, it can certainly defeat Judah. Assyria measures divine protection by the quality of local idols. Childs: the boast is fundamentally confused about the nature of the God who protects Jerusalem—he is not a local deity but the LORD of hosts who controls Assyria itself.

verseByVerse.quote: shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?“ When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?'—Assyria lumps Judah's God with Samaria's idols: the fundamental blasphemy. The LORD of hosts is equated with carved images—which is the blindness of total pride. 'When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem'—God will use Assyria for his appointed purpose; then he will lay it aside. The instrument serves until the work is done, not indefinitely. 'He will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria'—the punishment is specifically of the speech: the boasting, the comparison of the LORD to idols, the self-exaltation. Motyer: God assigns Assyria its task; Assyria exceeds the assignment; God then holds Assyria accountable for the excess.

verseByVerse.quote: For he says: “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding; I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures; like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones. My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples; and as one gathers eggs that have been forsaken, so I have gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom'—Assyria's double self-attribution: military strength and personal wisdom. Both are false claims: the strength is God's rod; the wisdom is God's mandate. 'I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures'—the actions Assyria claims as its own achievements are precisely what God commissioned it to do. 'Like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones'—the bull is a symbol of irresistible power. 'My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples'—the plundering is easy, effortless, like gathering eggs from an abandoned nest. 'There was none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped'—total passivity of the conquered: no resistance. Oswalt: Assyria's boast is the boast of an axe claiming to be the woodsman.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? As if a rod should wield him who lifts it, or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood! Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it?'—the reductio ad absurdum of Assyrian pride: the tool claims credit from the craftsman. The axe boasting over the woodsman is the image of the absurdity of a nation boasting against the God who wielded it. 'As if a rod should wield him who lifts it'—the reversal: the rod commanding the hand. 'Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors'—God's judgment on Assyria: not military defeat at first but disease sent among the warriors. 'Under his glory a burning will be kindled'—the glory (military pride) becomes the fuel for the fire of judgment. Motyer: the glory that should have been attributed to God will be the glory that is consumed by judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The light of Israel will become a fire, and his Holy One a flame, and it will burn and devour his thorns and briers in one day. The glory of his forest and of his fruitful land the LORD will destroy, both soul and body, and it will be as when a sick man wastes away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The light of Israel will become a fire, and his Holy One a flame'—the same divine presence that is salvation (light) to Israel is destruction (fire) to Assyria. The Holy One of Israel is not merely Israel's protector but the active judge of those who oppose his purposes. 'It will burn and devour his thorns and briers in one day'—the speed is divine: Assyria's vast military apparatus consumed in a single day. The imagery of thorns and briers (also used in ch. 5 and 7 for Judah's desolation) now applies to Assyria. 'The glory of his forest and of his fruitful land the LORD will destroy, both soul and body'—the forest is Assyria's imperial might; soul and body means completely, without remainder. 'It will be as when a sick man wastes away'—the wasting sickness of v. 16 reaches its end: total debilitation. Childs: the destruction anticipates the miraculous defeat of Sennacherib (37:36) where 185,000 Assyrian soldiers die in one night.

verseByVerse.quote: The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down. In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down'—the vast Assyrian army reduced to a number a child can count and record. The irony: Assyria's commanders boasted that all their generals outranked other nations' kings (v. 8); now a child can write their names. 'In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them'—the lesson of history learned: after Assyria's fall, Israel will stop seeking security in the very power that oppressed it. 'But will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth'—the theological goal of all the judgment: a people that trusts God rather than human military power. Oswalt: the whole sequence of discipline and deliverance aims at this—the reorientation of Israel's trust.

verseByVerse.quote: A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God'—Shear-jashub's name (Isaiah's son, 7:3) is now interpreted: the return of the remnant is both physical (from exile) and spiritual (to God). 'The mighty God'—El Gibbor: the same divine name applied to the child of 9:6. The remnant returns to the child who was given, the Wonderful Counselor who is Mighty God. 'For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return'—the Abraham-promise (Gen. 22:17) is not nullified but refined: the sand-multitude is not the heir; the faithful remnant is. 'Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness'—the destruction is just, abundant, purposive. Paul cites this verse in Romans 9:27 to explain the remnant-principle in his own generation.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord GOD of hosts will make a full end, as decreed, in the midst of all the earth. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD of hosts: “O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian; he strikes you with the rod and lifts up his staff against you as the Egyptians did. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord GOD of hosts will make a full end, as decreed, in the midst of all the earth'—the judgment on Assyria is not arbitrary but decreed; it will be carried out fully, publicly, on the world stage. 'O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian'—direct pastoral address to the remnant community. In the midst of the account of Assyrian terror, God calls his people not to fear. 'He strikes you with the rod and lifts up his staff against you as the Egyptians did'—the comparison is intentional: just as Egypt struck Israel but then was judged, so Assyria strikes but will be judged. The Exodus-pattern recurs. Motyer: God is saying: I have been through this before with your ancestors; I know how this ends.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction. And the LORD of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. And his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction'—the reversal is imminent from God's perspective. The divine fury that has been directed against Israel through Assyria will now be turned against Assyria itself. 'The LORD of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb'—Oreb was a Midianite prince killed by Gideon's forces (Judg. 7:25): another miraculous victory requiring no large army. 'His staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt'—the Mosaic typology is explicit: the same staff that divided the Red Sea will be raised against Assyria. Young: the accumulated weight of the Exodus and Gideon typologies assures the remnant that God's pattern of deliverance is reliable.

verseByVerse.quote: And in that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke will be broken because of the fat. He came to Aiath; he passed through Migron; at Michmash he stored his supplies; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke will be broken because of the fat'—the liberation from Assyrian oppression: the burden and yoke (the instruments of servitude) removed. 'Because of the fat'—probably because the neck has grown too large for the yoke: the nation has been strengthened beyond the capacity of Assyrian control. 'He came to Aiath; he passed through Migron; at Michmash he stored his supplies'—the march of Assyria toward Jerusalem is described with precise geographical detail, creating dramatic tension. Each place-name is a step closer to the city. Childs: the geographic specificity is not mere historical reporting but literary art—the reader feels the advance with each name.

verseByVerse.quote: they crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodged for the night; Ramah trembled; Gibeah of Saul fled away. Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodged for the night'—Geba is only six miles northeast of Jerusalem; the army is close. 'Ramah trembled; Gibeah of Saul fled away'—the trembling spreads: towns that remember Saul's former glory now flee in panic. 'Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth!'—the prophet addresses the towns in the path of the advance. Each is called to cry out, give attention, or simply named with pathos ('poor Anathoth'). Anathoth is Jeremiah's hometown; the prophet will later experience the bitterness of these towns' betrayal. Young: the vivid detail makes the advance real and the subsequent deliverance all the more miraculous.

verseByVerse.quote: Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety. This very day he will halt at Nob, shaking his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety'—the panic spreads to more villages; none can stand before the Assyrian advance. 'This very day he will halt at Nob, shaking his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem'—Nob is the last high ground before Jerusalem: the army is visible from the city, close enough to shake its fist. The gesture of defiance (shaking the fist) is maximum contempt. But this is the limit: 'this very day he will halt.' The advance stops at Nob—not because Assyria chose to stop but because God's decree has set the boundary. Motyer: the halt at Nob is the moment where divine sovereignty becomes visible in the narrative; the fist raised against Zion is the last act before judgment falls.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low. He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power'—the divine woodsman returns (cf. v. 15: the axe and the woodsman). Now God himself takes the axe to Assyria, the forest. 'The great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low'—the same vocabulary of human pride from ch. 2 (high, lofty) applied to Assyria's final fall. 'He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One'—Lebanon's cedar forests were the supreme symbol of imperial pride. The Majestic One (ha-addir) fells even Lebanon. The chapter ends at the stump: the proud tree of Assyrian empire hewn down. Oswalt: the stump prepares the way for ch. 11's shoot from the stump of Jesse—out of one fall comes new life.

11.subtitle: The Root of Jesse and the Peaceable Kingdom
11.intro: Overview. Chapter 11 is the great Messianic vision that follows the cutting down of the forest in chapter 10. From the stump of Jesse — the royal house reduced to near-extinction — a shoot will grow. The chapter describes the character of the coming king (vv. 1–5), the transformed creation over which he will reign (vv. 6–9), and the worldwide gathering of his people (vv. 10–16). It is one of the most complete portraits of the Messiah in all of Isaiah, and the New Testament draws on it repeatedly.

sections.title: The Shoot from the Stump of Jesse
sections.commentary:
The image of a shoot from the stump of Jesse is a study in divine reversals. The forest of chapter 10 is being cut down — mighty Assyria, and with it every human power that has set itself up against God. But from the stump that most people would consider finished, a shoot emerges. Jesse was David's father; by naming Jesse rather than David, Isaiah is reaching back past the royal dynasty to its humble root. The Messiah does not arrive at the height of the monarchy's glory but from its most reduced state.

v. 2 — “And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.” The six-fold description of the Spirit's work — wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear of the LORD — is the basis for the traditional Christian doctrine of the seven gifts of the Spirit (the LXX adds “piety” to the six). This is the equipment the Branch needs for his reign. At Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descends on him — the fulfillment of this verse (Matt 3:16).

Verses 3–5 describe a king who does not judge by appearances or rumours but by righteousness and faithfulness — whose verdicts are accurate because they are based on God's reality rather than human perception. The poor and meek will be vindicated; the wicked will be struck down. This is the justice the unjust legislators of chapter 10 refused to exercise — and that the Branch will establish forever.

sections.title: The Peaceable Kingdom
sections.commentary:
The famous images of wolf and lamb, leopard and goat, lion and calf lying down together have been debated as literal or metaphorical for centuries. What is not debatable is their intent: they describe the comprehensive transformation of creation under the reign of the Messiah. The predator-prey relationship — one of the most basic features of fallen nature — will be reversed. The wolf will not merely tolerate the lamb; they will share the same space.

The key to understanding the vision is verse 9: “They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.” The peace of the kingdom flows from the knowledge of God flooding the earth. Creation is transformed from within by the spread of the knowledge of its Creator. This is why Paul's vision of the redeemed creation in Romans 8 — creation “groaning” as it waits for the revelation of the sons of God — draws on exactly this imagery.

v. 9 — “The earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.” Habakkuk 2:14 quotes this verse almost exactly. It is the ultimate missionary vision: not a few scattered souls who know God, but the whole earth saturated with his knowledge as completely and universally as the sea covers the ocean floor.

sections.title: The Worldwide Gathering
sections.commentary:
“In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples — of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious.” Paul quotes verse 10 in Romans 15:12 as the foundation for his Gentile mission: the root of Jesse standing as a banner for the nations is the gospel going to the ends of the earth. What Isaiah saw as a future hope, Paul is enacting as present mission.

The gathering of the dispersed of Israel from the four corners of the earth (vv. 11–12) is both a near promise of return from exile and an ultimate promise of eschatological gathering that the exile only partially fulfils. The new exodus described in verses 15–16 — a highway for the remnant, the sea dried up — deliberately echoes the original Exodus. God's great redemptive acts follow a pattern: the original establishes the template; the later ones fulfil and surpass it.

keyVerse.quote: “And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The Spirit's resting on the Messiah is not temporary or intermittent but permanent — he rests on him. At Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descends and remains (John 1:32–33). The full range of Spirit-gifts needed for the Messiah's work — wisdom to teach, counsel to govern, might to deliver, knowledge and fear of God to judge rightly — are all present in him simultaneously and without measure (John 3:34).

11.theology:
The Messiah and the Spirit. Isaiah 11 is one of the foundational texts for the New Testament's understanding of the relationship between the Spirit and the Son. The Spirit does not supplement the Son's deity; he equips the Son's humanity for his mission. This is why Luke's Gospel emphasises the Spirit's activity throughout Jesus' ministry — at his conception, baptism, temptation, and first sermon (Luke 4:18, quoting Isaiah 61). The Spirit-filled Messiah is the model for all Spirit-filled ministry.

New creation. The peaceable kingdom of verses 6–9 is the Old Testament's most vivid description of what Scripture elsewhere calls the new creation. It is not simply a return to Eden but a transformation of the created order under the reign of the righteous King. This is why Revelation 21–22 draws on imagery from both Genesis and Isaiah: the new creation is both recovery and transcendence.
11.reflection: The shoot from Jesse's stump grows from a situation that looks finished. The dynasty is reduced; the forest has been cut down; the stump is all that remains. If you are in a season that feels like a stump — where what you had hoped for seems to have been cut off — Isaiah 11 is written for you. God's most significant growth often comes from the most apparently finished starting points.
11.text: <sup>1</sup>There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit. <sup>2</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. <sup>3</sup>And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, <sup>4</sup>but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked. <sup>5</sup>Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins. <sup>6</sup>The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them. <sup>7</sup>The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. <sup>8</sup>The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. <sup>9</sup>They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. <sup>10</sup>In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples— of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious. <sup>11</sup>In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea. <sup>12</sup>He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. <sup>13</sup>The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim. <sup>14</sup>But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines to the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them. <sup>15</sup>And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals. <sup>16</sup>And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Shoot from Jesse and the Peaceable Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 11 is among the most beloved chapters in the entire Old Testament: the messianic king described in terms of the Spirit's fullness, the justice of his rule, and the radical peace of his kingdom. The chapter moves from the Shoot (v. 1) to the Spirit (v. 2) to the reign of justice (vv. 3–5) to the peaceable kingdom (vv. 6–9) to the second Exodus (vv. 10–16).
verseByVerse.examples: The New Testament applies 11:1 to Jesus as the Branch (Matt. 2:23; Rev. 5:5) and 11:10 to the universal Gentile mission (Rom. 15:12). The peaceable kingdom has sustained the church's eschatological hope for two millennia. Every Lord's Day is a foretaste of the kingdom where the knowledge of the LORD covers the earth as the waters cover the sea.

verseByVerse.quote: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit. And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse'—the stump of ch. 6:13 and the felled forest of ch. 10:33–34 produce the unexpected shoot. Not from the reigning dynasty (David) but from its root (Jesse): a new beginning from a humbled starting point. The shoot is the Branch of 4:2 and the child of 9:6. 'And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him'—the Spirit descending and remaining: not a temporary empowering but a permanent anointing. The verb rest (nuakh) suggests settled, dwelling presence. 'The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD'—the sixfold description (seven with 'the Spirit of the LORD') became the basis for the seven gifts of the Spirit. Motyer: the Spirit's fullness on the Messiah contrasts with the Spirit's absence from Ahaz and the leaders of ch. 3.

verseByVerse.quote: And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'His delight shall be in the fear of the LORD'—the king finds pleasure in exactly what Israel's leaders rejected: the fear of God. The foundation of wise governance is delight in submission to God. 'He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear'—he transcends appearance and hearsay: his judgment penetrates to reality. This is the justice Ahaz and the rulers of ch. 3 could not render because they were bribed. 'With righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek'—the king's court is perfectly calibrated for the vulnerable: the poor and meek receive exactly what earlier courts denied them. 'He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth'—his word is his weapon; he needs no army. Oswalt: this is Psalm 72 brought to its fulfillment—the king who actually achieves what every covenant king was anointed to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins. The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins'—clothing as character: the belt (the foundational garment, holding everything else together) is righteousness and faithfulness. The king is not merely dressed in justice but bound by it—it is constitutive of who he is. 'The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat'—the radical peace of the new creation: predator-prey relationships transformed. This is not allegory; it is the theological symbol of a creation restored to its Edenic harmony under the righteous king. 'And a little child shall lead them'—the child motif returns (cf. 9:6; 11:8): the vulnerability of childhood is now the mode of leadership. Motyer: the child leading the wolf and the lamb is the reversal of the child hiding from the weapons of ch. 7.

verseByVerse.quote: The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together'—the domesticated and the wild share peacefully. The predator has been transformed, not merely restrained: it grazes alongside the prey. 'The lion shall eat straw like the ox'—the apex predator becomes an herbivore. The change is not behavioral accommodation but ontological transformation under the king's reign. 'The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den'—the most lethal reptiles become harmless to the most vulnerable humans. Young: the child-cobra pairing deliberately reverses Genesis 3:15—the seed that was to be struck by the serpent now plays safely over its den, because the curse has been reversed by the righteous king.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples—of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain'—the holy mountain (Zion) extends its peace to the whole earth. What was promised for the mountain (2:2–4) is here universalized: no hurting, no destroying, anywhere. 'For the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea'—the telos of the peaceable kingdom is covenantal knowledge. Waters covering the sea: a complete, total, seamless filling. No spot uncovered. The knowledge of the LORD (da'at YHWH) is not merely information but the intimate knowing that changes life. 'The root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples'—the root-of-Jesse becomes a signal (nes, a banner) for all nations, not just Israel. The nations inquire of him. Paul cites v. 10 in Romans 15:12 as the mandate for Gentile mission. Webb: the cosmic vision of vv. 6–9 is grounded in the person of the root of Jesse.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea. He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant'—the first recovery was the Exodus from Egypt; the second is the new Exodus from every direction of exile. 'From Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea'—the eight regions cover the compass: east (Assyria, Elam, Shinar), west (coastlands), north (Hamath), south (Egypt, Pathros, Cush). The dispersed are gathered from everywhere. 'He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth'—the second Exodus is universal: both houses, all four corners. Motyer: the new Exodus is more comprehensive than the first because the scattering has been more comprehensive than Egypt's bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim. But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off'—the internal division of the covenant people healed. The Syro-Ephraimite crisis of ch. 7 (where the northern kingdom attacked the southern) will be definitively reversed. 'Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim'—mutual reconciliation: neither the jealousy from the north nor the harassment from the south. The two halves of Israel restored to unity. 'But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east'—united, the two halves act against the historic enemies: Philistines, Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites. Childs: the internal unity produces external effectiveness; division had been the source of Israel's vulnerability to all these nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals. And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River'—the new Exodus requires new miracles: the Sea of Egypt (the Gulf of Suez) dried up; the Euphrates (the River) struck into seven fords. The supernatural geography of the first Exodus is replicated for the second. 'And he will lead people across in sandals'—the ease of the crossing: sandals rather than bare feet suggests comfort and dignity. 'And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant'—what was the path of exile (the route to Assyrian deportation) becomes the route of return. The highway of the LORD runs from Assyria home. 'As there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt'—the Exodus-typology closes the chapter: the second Exodus will be recognized as the pattern set by the first, now accomplished on a universal scale.

12.subtitle: A Song of Salvation
12.intro: Overview. Chapter 12 is a short hymn of praise — only six verses — that brings the first major section of Isaiah (chapters 1–12) to a doxological close. After eleven chapters of judgment, warning, and Messianic promise, the redeemed community breaks into song. The language draws on the Exodus (v. 2 quotes from the Song of Moses in Exodus 15) and looks forward to the gathering described at the end of chapter 11. This is what the people of God sound like when they have arrived at where God was always taking them.

sections.title: I Will Trust and Not Be Afraid
sections.commentary:
“You will say in that day: I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me.” The opening verse acknowledges that God's anger was real and deserved, and that his turning of it away is an act of pure grace. The song does not begin with innocence but with the acknowledgment of guilt forgiven. This is authentic praise: it knows what it has been forgiven from.

v. 2 — “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.” This is almost a direct quotation from the Song of Moses (Exod 15:2). Isaiah's redeemed community sings the same song as those who crossed the Red Sea — because they have experienced the same salvation. The new exodus has the same Redeemer.

Verse 3 — “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” — is the verse Jesus quotes in John 7:37–38 at the Feast of Tabernacles: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” The wells of salvation are not a future reality to be waited for; in Christ, they are open now.

sections.title: Make Known His Deeds Among the Peoples
sections.commentary: The second half of the hymn turns outward. Salvation received becomes mission declared: “Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted.” The redeemed community does not keep its salvation private. The glad shouting of verse 6 — “for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel” — echoes back to the trisagion of chapter 6, but now from the lips of the forgiven rather than the seraphim. The same holiness that undid Isaiah now becomes the ground of the community's joy. This is the arc of the entire gospel: the holy God who should destroy the sinner instead saves him, and the sinner worships.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.”
keyVerse.note: The word translated salvation is Yeshua — the same name as Jesus. “God is my Yeshua” is, in retrospect, a name as much as a statement. The song that brings the first section of Isaiah to a close is a song about the one who will bring all of God's purposes to their close.

12.reflection: Chapter 12 ends the first major section of Isaiah at the highest point imaginable: the redeemed community singing with joy, drawing from wells of salvation, declaring God's name among the nations. This is the destination God has been aiming at through all eleven chapters of judgment and promise. Whatever stage of the journey you are on, this is where it ends.
12.text: <sup>1</sup>You will say in that day: "I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. <sup>2</sup>Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation." <sup>3</sup>With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. <sup>4</sup>And you will say in that day: "Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted. <sup>5</sup>Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth. <sup>6</sup>Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Song of the Redeemed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 12 is the psalmic conclusion to the first major movement of the book (ch. 1–12). It is a brief, radiant song of thanksgiving placed in the mouth of the redeemed community after the events described in ch. 11. The song has two stanzas (vv. 1–3 and vv. 4–6), each beginning with 'you will say in that day.' It is the liturgy of the second Exodus.
verseByVerse.examples: The church sings ch. 12 every time it gathers for worship: drawing water from the wells of salvation (v. 3), proclaiming the LORD's name among the nations (v. 4), shouting and singing for joy because the Holy One of Israel dwells in its midst (v. 6). The eschatological song anticipated here is the new song of the Lamb in Revelation 15.

verseByVerse.quote: You will say in that day: “I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me'—the thanksgiving is grounded in the experience of both anger and grace. The anger was real (ch. 1–10); its turning is grace (ch. 11). The word comfort (nakham) will become a major theme of ch. 40–55: Isaiah's great comfort chapters are anticipated here. 'Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid'—the new Exodus song echoes Moses (Ex. 15:2; cf. Ps. 118:14). The three things required of faith—trust, fearlessness, gratitude—are all summoned. 'The LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation'—Motyer: salvation is not merely a past event (he saved me) but a present reality (he has become my salvation): God is the salvation, not merely its vehicle.

verseByVerse.quote: With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. And you will say in that day: “Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation'—the wells of salvation: God himself is the source (cf. Jer. 2:13, 17:13). Drawing water with joy is the image of unhurried, abundant access to God's provision. The wells do not run dry; joy is the condition of drawing. 'Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name'—the second stanza begins with mission: the redeemed are to make known what God has done. 'Make known his deeds among the peoples'—the witness is universal: the nations are the audience. The salvation accomplished through the root of Jesse (11:10) is now proclaimed. 'Proclaim that his name is exalted'—the goal of proclamation is the exaltation of the divine name, not the reputation of Israel. Webb: the community that has experienced salvation becomes the missionary community that announces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth. Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously'—the verb sing praises (zamru) is the root of the Psalter's musical language. The praise is not generic but specific: 'for he has done gloriously.' The acts of salvation are the content of the song. 'Let this be made known in all the earth'—the proclamation of ch. 11's gathering and 12:4's witness culminates: the whole earth is the intended audience. 'Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion'—Zion's inhabitants are the chorus of the new creation. Shouting and singing together: volume and melody, the full register of gladness. 'For great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel'—the chapter ends and the entire first movement of Isaiah (ch. 1–12) ends with the signature title. The Holy One, whose holiness undid the prophet (ch. 6), now dwells in the midst of the redeemed community. Motyer: the great circle of the book's first movement is complete—from the arraignment of ch. 1 to the song of ch. 12, from Israel weary of God to Zion exulting in him.

13.subtitle: The Oracle Against Babylon
13.intro: Overview. Chapters 13–23 contain a series of oracles against the nations, beginning with Babylon. This is significant: Isaiah is prophesying the fall of Babylon more than a century before Babylon became a dominant power, and roughly two centuries before Cyrus of Persia conquered it in 539 BC. The oracle against Babylon serves a dual purpose — it announces specific historical judgment on a specific empire, and it uses that judgment as a lens through which to see the ultimate Day of the LORD against all that opposes God.

sections.title: Muster the Troops — The Day of the LORD Against Babylon
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with a battle summons: a banner raised, troops mustered, the gates of the nobles thrown open. But this is no ordinary war council — these are “my consecrated ones” and “my mighty warriors” (v. 3). God is the one assembling the army; the coming destruction of Babylon is his project. The language quickly escalates beyond any single historical event into the cosmic register of the Day of the LORD.

vv. 9–10 — “Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.” The cosmic darkness language — stars dimmed, sun darkened — recurs in the New Testament as a description of the last day (Matt 24:29; Rev 6:12–13). Isaiah's oracle against Babylon becomes a template for every ultimate divine judgment.

The pride of verse 11 is the specific charge: “I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant.” Babylon's sin is not merely military aggression but the arrogance of a power that has forgotten it is answerable to anyone. This is the sin of every empire, including the last.

sections.title: Babylon Fallen — Like Sodom and Gomorrah
sections.commentary: God will stir up the Medes against Babylon (v. 17) — a specific prophecy of the Persian-Median coalition that overthrew Babylon in 539 BC, fulfilled precisely. The description of abandoned Babylon in verses 19–22 — never inhabited, never settled, no Arab pitching his tent there, owls nesting, jackals lying down, ostriches dancing — uses exactly the imagery that Revelation 18 employs for the fall of the final Babylon. The historical fall of Babylon in the 6th century BC is a down-payment on the ultimate fall of everything that Babylon represents.

keyVerse.quote: “I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless.”
keyVerse.note: The oracle against one specific historical empire has this universal horizon: “I will punish the world.” Babylon is the instance; the world's arrogance is the charge. Every empire that mistakes its power for permanence is, in Isaiah's vision, standing where Babylon stood — and heading where Babylon went.

13.reflection: The oracles against the nations in Isaiah 13–23 are not comfortable reading, but they answer an urgent question: does God see what the nations are doing? Is there accountability beyond the reach of any earthly court? The answer of this chapter is unambiguous. The pomp of the arrogant has an expiry date set by God himself.
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. <sup>2</sup>On a bare mountain raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. <sup>3</sup>I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones. <sup>4</sup>The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle. <sup>5</sup>They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land. <sup>6</sup>Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! <sup>7</sup>Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. <sup>8</sup>They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame. <sup>9</sup>Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. <sup>10</sup>For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light. <sup>11</sup>I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless. <sup>12</sup>I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir. <sup>13</sup>Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger. <sup>14</sup>And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. <sup>15</sup>Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword. <sup>16</sup>Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished. <sup>17</sup>Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold. <sup>18</sup>Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children. <sup>19</sup>And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. <sup>20</sup>It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there. <sup>21</sup>But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. <sup>22</sup>Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 13 opens the great section of oracles against the nations (ch. 13–23). The placement of Babylon first is theologically significant: Babylon is both the historical power that will destroy Jerusalem and the symbolic epitome of all anti-God empire. The chapter describes the Day of the LORD against Babylon in cosmic terms—stars darkened, heavens trembling—that reach beyond the historical fall of Babylon (539 BC, Cyrus) to the final dissolution of every empire that opposes God.
verseByVerse.examples: Revelation 17–18 uses Isaiah 13 and 47 as the template for the fall of 'Babylon the great'—every human empire that makes itself ultimate. The church reads Isaiah 13 as the promise that no earthly power can permanently prevail against God's purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. On a bare mountain raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The oracle concerning Babylon'—the Hebrew massa (burden/oracle) signals a weighty prophetic word, often of judgment. Isaiah is writing in the 8th century BC, over a century before Babylon's fall; the prophecy's long reach demonstrates the reality of divine foreknowledge. 'Which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw'—the prophetic authorship is asserted; the book's integrity demands it. 'On a bare mountain raise a signal'—the signal-flag summons the troops of divine judgment. Motyer: the oracle opens with military mobilization, but the army being summoned is God's. The bare mountain makes the signal visible for maximum distance—God's call to judgment is unmistakable.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty warriors, my proudly exulting ones, to execute my anger. The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I myself have commanded my consecrated ones'—God is the commander-in-chief; the armies gathered are his consecrated ones (meqoddoshai), set apart for this holy purpose. The language of priestly consecration applied to military service underscores the sacred character of divine judgment. 'My proudly exulting ones'—the warriors exult in God's cause, not their own. 'The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude'—the noise of gathering armies on the horizon; the cosmic scale of the mustering makes it sound like the whole world is moving. 'The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle'—the decisive statement: the source of this army is the LORD of hosts himself. Oswalt: the same divine name (LORD of hosts) that governs Isaiah's heavenly throne scene (6:3) now commands the armies of history.

verseByVerse.quote: They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his wrath, to destroy the whole land. Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens'—the army comes from beyond the known world: God's judgment is not local but cosmic. 'The LORD and the weapons of his wrath, to destroy the whole land'—the weapons are possessives of the LORD: divine anger expressed through human military means. 'Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come'—the Day of the LORD, announced in ch. 2 against Israel, now comes against Babylon. 'Destruction from the Almighty' (shod mi-shaddai)—the wordplay on Shaddai (Almighty): the all-sufficient one brings all-devastating judgment. Childs: the same structure that threatened Israel (Day of the LORD) now sweeps through the nations; no one is exempt from the covenant-enforcing God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt'—the physical collapse of Babylon's defenders: hands too weak to lift weapons, hearts dissolved in terror. The same language used of Canaan's fear before Israel (Josh. 2:11) now describes Babylon's response to God's army. 'They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor'—the birth-pang metaphor for the uncontrollable onset of divine judgment: it comes in waves, increasingly intense, with no respite until the end. 'They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame'—the horror is total: not one individual's private fear but a corporate, mutual panic. Young: the description is designed to strip Babylon of its terrifying mystique—the great empire is as helpless as a woman in labor when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger'—the Day is characterized: not merely severe but cruel, not merely firm but fierce. The Day is the point of maximum intensity of divine wrath against sin. 'To make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it'—the purpose is both geographical (desolation of the land) and moral (destruction of sinners). The land and its inhabitants share the judgment. 'The stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light'—the cosmic darkness. Babylon was the world center of astronomical religion; its gods were the stars. When the stars go dark, Babylon's gods fail. Motyer: the darkening of the celestial bodies is the language of ultimate judgment reaching beyond any historical event to the final day.

verseByVerse.quote: I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pride of the arrogant, and lay low the haughtiness of the ruthless. I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will punish the world for its evil'—the scope expands from Babylon to the world: Babylon's judgment is the paradigmatic judgment of all human evil. 'I will put an end to the pride of the arrogant, and lay low the haughtiness of the ruthless'—the ch. 2 vocabulary returns: pride brought low, haughtiness leveled. Babylon is the supreme embodiment of the arrogance that ch. 2 condemned. 'I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir'—the depopulation of judgment: the scarcity of survivors will be more remarkable than the scarcity of the rarest gold. Ophir was the source of the finest gold in the ancient world. Oswalt: the reversal of Genesis 1's abundance (people filling the earth) in judgment produces terrible scarcity.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger. And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place'—the cosmic framework of creation destabilized by the intensity of divine wrath. The Day of the LORD is not merely historical but ontological: creation itself responds to God's wrath. 'At the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger'—the triple intensity: wrath, LORD of hosts, fierce anger. 'Like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land'—the diaspora panics: those who came to Babylon from many nations scatter back to their homelands. The gazelle hunted and the sheep without shepherd are images of total vulnerability and aimless flight. Childs: the cosmopolitan empire dissolves into its ethnic components under the pressure of divine judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword'—the mercilessness of ancient conquest: no one is spared. The language is deliberately brutal; Isaiah does not soften the reality of what divine judgment through human armies looks like on the ground. 'Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished'—the extreme horror of ancient warfare cataloged without flinching. Babylon did this to others (cf. Ps. 137:8–9); now it comes to Babylon. Motyer: the law of sowing and reaping operates at the level of empires: Babylon's own methods of conquest become the means of its judgment. The text is morally harrowing precisely because war is morally harrowing.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold. Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I am stirring up the Medes against them'—the Medes named as God's instrument, over a century before Cyrus the Mede overthrows Babylon (539 BC). The prophecy is specific enough to name the people-group. 'Who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold'—the Medes are portrayed as incorruptible: they cannot be bribed to stop. Unlike some conquerors who can be bought off, God's instrument against Babylon pursues its commission to completion. 'Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children'—the mercilessness that Babylon inflicted is the mercilessness it receives. Young: the age-categories (young men, womb-fruit, children) cover all of Babylon's future generations—the empire has no survivors.

verseByVerse.quote: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans'—the grandeur that makes Babylon's fall so dramatic. It is not a minor city but the glory of kingdoms: the most impressive human civilization of its era. 'Will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them'—the comparison is to the paradigmatic total destruction: not merely conquered but erased. 'It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations'—the permanence of the judgment. Historically, after 539 BC Babylon never regained its former glory; by the Roman period it was desolate. 'No Arab will pitch his tent there'—even temporary habitation is excluded. Oswalt: the text reaches its eschatological fulfillment in Revelation 18, where Babylon represents all anti-God empire finally consumed.

verseByVerse.quote: But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures'—the complete reversal of civilization: where human commerce and culture thrived, the wilderness reclaims. 'Ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance'—the inhabitants of desolate wilderness take possession of Babylon's palaces. The dance of the wild goats is a grotesque parody of the celebrations once held in the royal courts. 'Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces'—towers and pleasant palaces—the heights of human pride—echo with the cries of unclean animals. 'Its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged'—from God's perspective, the judgment is imminent, even if a century separates Isaiah from its fulfillment. Motyer: God's sense of time is not ours; what is certain is as good as accomplished.

14.subtitle: The Taunt Against the King of Babylon
14.intro: Overview. Chapter 14 continues the Babylon oracle with a taunt song addressed to the king of Babylon — one of the most dramatically vivid passages in all of Isaiah. The king who exalted himself to the heavens is brought down to Sheol; those who once cowered before him now mock him in death. The famous passage in verses 12–15 has been interpreted from the earliest centuries as a description of the fall of Satan, behind the earthly king. The chapter also contains brief oracles against Assyria and Philistia.

sections.title: The LORD Restores Israel
sections.commentary: Before the taunt song begins, Isaiah establishes its context: it is sung by a people who have been restored. The LORD will have compassion on Jacob, will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land (v. 1). The taunt song is not triumphalism arising from bitterness; it is the song of those who have been through the furnace of exile and have come out the other side. God's judgment on Babylon is inseparable from his restoration of his people. The fall of the oppressor and the freedom of the captives are the same event viewed from two directions.

sections.title: The Taunt Song: How You Are Fallen
sections.commentary:
The taunt song is a masterpiece of irony. The king who “made the world like a desert” (v. 17) now lies without a grave, trodden underfoot, while even the rulers of the nations receive honourable burial. The contrast between his living power and his dead helplessness is the point: all the greatness that seemed permanent and invincible is revealed in death to have been temporary and fragile.

vv. 12–14 — “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!… You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high.’” The imagery here — the shining one (Helel ben Shachar, “Day Star, son of Dawn”) attempting to ascend above God's throne — has been read since the early church as the background to the fall of Satan (Luke 10:18; Rev 12:9). The earthly king of Babylon becomes a type of the spiritual power of pride itself: the will to self-exaltation that is the essence of all rebellion against God.

The five “I will” statements of verses 13–14 are the grammar of pride: I will ascend, I will set my throne, I will sit, I will ascend above the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High. Each one is the assertion of the self against the sovereignty of God. The verdict is verse 15: “But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit.” The higher the ascent claimed, the deeper the fall.

sections.title: Assyria and Philistia
sections.commentary: The chapter closes with brief oracles confirming that Assyria will be broken in God's land, and that Philistia should not rejoice too quickly at Judah's troubles. The oracle against Philistia contains a striking promise: “and the afflicted of his people will find refuge” (v. 32). Amid the oracles of judgment on the nations, the promise that God's own afflicted people have a place of refuge is a recurring refrain — the theme of the whole book compressed into a phrase.

keyVerse.quote: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high… I will make myself like the Most High.’”
keyVerse.note: The five “I will” statements are the grammar of pride at its most naked. Behind every act of human arrogance lies this claim: I will be my own ultimate authority. The king of Babylon is the extreme form of what is present in every sinful heart. This is why pride is not just a character flaw but a theological rebellion — it is the assertion of the self in the place of God.

14.reflection: The taunt song of Isaiah 14 is a meditation on the vanity of earthly greatness. The king who made the world tremble lies without a burial, mocked by those he once terrified. The chapter asks a searching question: in what are you tempted to place your ultimate confidence and identity? Because whatever it is, it has the same trajectory as the king of Babylon unless it is anchored in something that cannot fall.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–32 — The Taunt Against Babylon's King, and Oracles Against Assyria and Philistia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 14 contains three distinct sections: the salvation of Israel following Babylon's fall (vv. 1–4a); the great taunt-song against the king of Babylon (vv. 4b–23); and brief oracles against Assyria (vv. 24–27) and Philistia (vv. 28–32). The taunt-song is one of the most remarkable poems in the Old Testament—a mocking lament that traces the fall of the world's greatest king from heaven to Sheol.
verseByVerse.examples: The taunt-song has been read christologically (the fall of Satan, Luke 10:18; cf. Rev. 12:9) and as a permanent comment on all totalitarian pride. Every regime that makes itself ultimate—'I will be like the Most High'—enacts the Babylonian paradigm and inherits Babylonian judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land, and sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob. And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will possess them in the LORD's land as male and female slaves. They will take captive those who were their captors, and rule over those who oppressed them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel'—the divine compassion is the ground of Israel's restoration. The key word is again: election is reaffirmed, not newly established. 'And sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob'—the nations streaming to Zion (2:2–4) is here realized: non-Israelites voluntarily join the covenant community. This is the mission implicit in 11:10 and explicit throughout the servant songs. 'And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place'—the reversal of exile: instead of being taken into captivity, Israel is escorted home. 'They will take captive those who were their captors'—the reversal is complete. Oswalt: this is not vindictiveness but the moral order reasserted—the oppressor-victim relationship inverted by justice.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD has given you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve, you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When the LORD has given you rest from your pain and turmoil'—the taunt is eschatological: it is sung from the position of rest, after the struggle is over. The rest (nuakh) recalls Sabbath-rest and the gift of the land; it is the end of all covenant anxiety. 'You will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon'—the people of God become the taunters: the formerly mocked now mock their former mockers. 'How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased!'—the exclamation of astonishment: the one who seemed permanent and overwhelming has simply stopped. The cessation of the oppressor is more remarkable than any of his acts of oppression. Childs: the taunt-song is the theological counterpart to the song of Moses (Ex. 15)—redemption celebrated in poetry after the enemy is defeated.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of rulers, that struck the peoples in wrath with unceasing blows, that ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of rulers'—God himself is the agent; the breaking is divine, not merely political. The staff (matteh) and scepter (shebet) are the instruments of coercive power; their breaking means the power itself is dissolved. 'That struck the peoples in wrath with unceasing blows'—the characterization of Babylonian imperial rule: not occasional cruelty but systematic, unceasing violence. 'That ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution'—the double intensity: anger and unrelenting—nothing softens the imperial will to dominate. Motyer: the description identifies why Babylon deserves what it gets; the punishment fits the crime of sustained, systematic brutality.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing. The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, “Since you were laid low, no woodsman comes up against us.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing'—the rest of the whole earth: Babylon's imperial appetite consumed everything; its fall allows rest to spread universally. The singing is spontaneous and universal—even nature sings. 'The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, “Since you were laid low, no woodsman comes up against us.”'—a remarkable moment: the trees speak. Babylon's imperial building projects required vast quantities of cedar and cypress; the forests of Lebanon were harvested for Babylon's palaces. Now that Babylon has fallen, the forests are safe. Young: the speaking trees personify creation's relief at the removal of the exploiting empire—even the natural world participates in the joy of judgment executed.

verseByVerse.quote: Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations. All of them will speak and say to you: “You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come'—the underworld personified as a host awakening to greet the new arrival. The king who shook the earth on his way down finds an ironic reception in death. 'It rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations'—the previous rulers of history, now in Sheol, are roused from their seats of death to receive Babylon's king. They rise not in honor but in mock-ceremony. 'You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!'—the taunt from the already-dead: the great leveler of death has equalized the mightiest of the mighty with all who went before. Motyer: the scene is darkly comic—the king who claimed to be above all other kings receives the same welcome as all of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers. How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps'—all the trappings of royal celebration (pomp, harps) follow the king to Sheol. They cannot be left behind; they are as dead as he is. 'Maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers'—the grotesque reversal: the king who reclined on gold-inlaid beds now lies on a bed of maggots, covered by worms. The body itself becomes the throne room of corruption. 'How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!'—the Hebrew helel ben-shachar (shining one, son of the dawn) was a Canaanite mythological figure. Isaiah uses the image to describe the king's claimed divine status. The Latin Vulgate translated helel as Lucifer; the Christian tradition applied this to Satan's primordial fall. Oswalt: the figure reaches beyond Babylon to the archetypal pride that lies behind all human empire.

verseByVerse.quote: You said in your heart, “I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You said in your heart, “I will ascend to heaven”'—five 'I will' statements expose the nature of the sin: it is not merely ambition but the aspiration to divine status. The king speaks only in his heart; the aspiration is interior before it is acted upon—but God hears hearts. 'Above the stars of God I will set my throne on high'—in ancient cosmology, the stars were divine beings; to be above them is to claim supremacy over all divinity. 'I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north'—the divine mountain where the gods assemble; the king claims the divine council's seat. 'I will make myself like the Most High'—the culminating aspiration, which is the sin of Eden (Gen. 3:5: 'you will be like God'). Young: the five 'I wills' are the anatomy of pride at its theological core.
