verseByVerse.quote: But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit. Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you: “Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit'—the five 'I wills' of ascent are answered by the single 'but you are brought down.' The descent is as absolute as the aspiration was extreme: from above the stars to the far reaches of the pit. 'Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you'—the onlookers in Sheol (v. 9–10) now stare in bewilderment. The king who was too great to be stared at is now an object of perplexed contemplation. 'Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms'—the mocking question: is this the same person? The contrast between the terror he inspired and the pathetic figure before them is the measure of the fall. Childs: the question 'is this the man?' is the taunt's most devastating line—the gap between reputation and reality exposed by death.

verseByVerse.quote: who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?“ All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?'—the three charges against Babylon's king: ecological devastation (the world like a desert), urban destruction (overthrew cities), and the refusal to release prisoners. These are not metaphorical sins but the literal practices of imperial conquest. 'Who did not let his prisoners go home?'—the specific charge that will be answered by Cyrus, who did let the prisoners go home (44:28; 45:1). 'All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb'—the irony: even the conquered kings received honorable burial in their tombs. Motyer: the king of Babylon, who conquered them all, will receive no tomb at all—the final indignity.

verseByVerse.quote: but you are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch, clothed with the slain, those pierced by the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit, like a trampled corpse. You will not be joined with them in burial, because you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. “May the offspring of evildoers nevermore be named! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch'—denied burial: the greatest dishonor in the ancient world. To lie unburied was to have no rest, no dignity, no memorial. 'Clothed with the slain, those pierced by the sword'—not in royal robes but covered with the corpses of his own slaughtered armies. 'Like a trampled corpse'—battlefield dead, walked over and ignored. 'You will not be joined with them in burial, because you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people'—the two crimes that merit the denial of burial: self-destruction (destroyed your own land) and fratricide (slain your own people). Imperial ambition is ultimately self-consuming. 'May the offspring of evildoers nevermore be named!'—the curse closes the taunt: the name extinguished along with the dynasty. Oswalt: denial of burial and denial of name are the two forms of ultimate humiliation in ancient culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers, lest they rise and possess the earth, and fill the face of the world with cities.“ ”I will rise up against them,“ declares the LORD of hosts, ”and will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, descendants and posterity,“ declares the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers'—the dynasty's sin is multigenerational; the judgment falls on the whole line. 'Lest they rise and possess the earth, and fill the face of the world with cities'—the fear is dynastic revival: if the sons survive, they will rebuild the empire. The city-building impulse (cf. Gen. 11: Babel) must be stopped. 'I will rise up against them, declares the LORD of hosts, and will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, descendants and posterity'—the four terms of elimination: name (reputation), remnant (survivors), descendants (next generation), posterity (all future generations). God's edict is comprehensive: Babylon has no future. Motyer: the four terms echo Genesis 12's four terms of blessing—Babylon receives the inverse of Abraham's promise.

verseByVerse.quote: “I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water, and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction,” declares the LORD of hosts. The LORD of hosts has sworn: “As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water, and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction'—three images of Babylon's fate: hedgehog possession (wilderness reclaimed by animals), pools (swampy desolation), and sweeping (total cleansing). The broom of destruction is decisive: no remnant left. 'The LORD of hosts has sworn'—the divine oath: the most solemn form of commitment. God binds himself to his word with an oath. 'As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand'—the divine plan is the guarantee of the divine outcome. There is no gap between God's intention and its realization. Childs: the oath of the LORD of hosts over Babylon is also the security of Israel's restoration—the same God who decrees Babylon's fall decrees Israel's return.

verseByVerse.quote: that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains trample him underfoot; and his yoke shall depart from them, and his burden from their shoulder.“ This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'That I will break the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains trample him underfoot'—a transition: the destruction of Assyria (ch. 10) is now subsumed under the same divine plan as Babylon's fall. God's purpose does not merely target one empire but has a universal scope. 'His yoke shall depart from them, and his burden from their shoulder'—the liberation promised in 9:4 (break the yoke) and 10:27 (burden removed) is here declared as God's sworn purpose. 'This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations'—the universal reach of the divine plan. The hand stretched out against Israel (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4) is now the hand stretched out over all nations. Motyer: God's purposes are not narrowly national but cosmically comprehensive.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?'—the rhetorical challenge: no power in heaven or earth can cancel or redirect God's decree. The question is unanswerable; the sovereignty is absolute. Keller: these two questions are the most comforting words in Isaiah for those who wonder whether God's plan can be thwarted by human wickedness or historical accident—it cannot. 'In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle'—a new superscription introducing the Philistia oracle. The date-stamp anchors the prophecy in history while the content reaches beyond it. Young: the historical grounding is itself theological—God's word enters specific historical moments precisely because he governs history.

verseByVerse.quote: “Do not rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken, for from the serpent's root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent. And the firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy will lie down in safety; but I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant it will slay. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken'—Philistia's celebration of Uzziah's or some other Judean king's death is premature. The rod that struck is broken, but a worse power replaces it. 'From the serpent's root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent'—three intensifying images of the coming Davidic king: serpent, adder, flying fiery serpent (seraph-serpent). Each is more fearsome than the previous; the replacement for the broken rod is far more dangerous. 'The firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy will lie down in safety'—while Philistia suffers, the poor of Judah are tended. The poor are always the sign of covenant faithfulness: when the king rules rightly, the poor flourish. Childs: the contrast between Philistia's destruction and Judah's poor lying down safely encapsulates the eschatological reversal.

verseByVerse.quote: Wail, O gate; cry out, O city; melt in fear, O Philistia, all of you! For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks. What will one answer the messengers of the nation? “The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wail, O gate; cry out, O city; melt in fear, O Philistia'—the three imperatives of lamentation addressed to the three components of the city: the gate (entrance/defense), the city itself, and the whole region. 'For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks'—the invader from the north is perfectly organized: no stragglers means no weak links in the military formation. The smoke of approaching armies (from campfires, burning villages) signals the advance. 'The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge'—the concluding answer to the nations: Zion's foundation is the LORD himself. What the nations call on for security (military strength, alliances, walls) is secondary; Zion's security is the LORD's founding. Webb: the oracle closes where Isaiah's theology always returns—to Zion and the LORD who dwells there.

15.subtitle: The Oracle Against Moab
15.intro: Overview. Chapters 15–16 form a single oracle against Moab, the nation east of the Dead Sea descended from Lot. The oracle is unusual in its tone: there is genuine mourning over Moab's destruction (15:5 — “My heart cries out for Moab”), and a remarkable invitation in 16:3–5 for Moab's fugitives to find shelter under Judah's king. Even in the oracles against the nations, Isaiah's God is not without compassion for the perishing.

sections.title: Moab Laid Waste
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with sudden destruction: “In a night Ar of Moab is laid waste and destroyed.” Town after town is named as the destruction spreads — Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh — a litany of places that had been centres of Moabite life now reduced to weeping and ruin. The people cut off their beards and shave their heads (signs of mourning) as the disaster rolls through the land.

v. 5 — “My heart cries out for Moab.” The speaker here is most naturally God himself (or Isaiah speaking for God). The God who judges Moab also mourns over Moab. This is not inconsistent — the same God who must deal with sin in justice also grieves over those who perish under that judgment. This theme reaches its fullest expression in Lamentations and in Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

keyVerse.quote: “My heart cries out for Moab.”
keyVerse.note: The brevity of this verse is part of its power. In the middle of an oracle announcing destruction, God's own heart cries out. Judgment and compassion are not mutually exclusive in God's character — they are simultaneously present. This is why the cross is simultaneously the most severe expression of divine justice and the most profound expression of divine love.

15.reflection: The oracles against the nations are often read only for their political and historical content. But Isaiah 15:5 breaks through that register entirely: God's heart cries out for the people he is judging. This should shape how God's people relate to those under judgment — not with triumph or indifference, but with the same broken compassion their God displays.
15.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone. <sup>2</sup>He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn; <sup>3</sup>in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears. <sup>4</sup>Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. <sup>5</sup>My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction; <sup>6</sup>the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more. <sup>7</sup>Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows. <sup>8</sup>For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim. <sup>9</sup>For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 15–16 form a unit: the oracle against Moab, one of Israel's oldest neighbors and relatives (descendants of Lot, Gen. 19:37). The oracle is notable for its pathos: Isaiah mourns over Moab even as he announces its judgment. The tone of lament distinguishes this from the Babylon oracle's triumphalism—Moab's destruction evokes grief, not celebration.
verseByVerse.examples: The pattern of prophetic lament over an enemy nation appears throughout the prophets (cf. Ezek. 32 over Egypt; Jer. 48 over Moab). It resists the comfortable division between 'our people God loves' and 'their people God hates.' The God who judges Moab also mourns over it.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Moab. Because in a night Ar of Moab is laid waste and destroyed, because in a night Kir of Moab is laid waste and destroyed, he has gone up to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Because in a night Ar of Moab is laid waste'—the sudden quality of the judgment: overnight. Ar was Moab's chief city; Kir was its fortified capital. Both destroyed in a night: no preparation, no resistance, no warning. 'He has gone up to Dibon, to the high places to weep'—the Moabites flee to their religious sanctuaries (high places) in grief. The high places that were sites of pagan worship now become sites of national mourning. 'On every head is baldness; every beard is cut off'—the two signs of mourning in the ancient Near East: shaved head and cut beard. The entire nation is in the posture of grief. Oswalt: the speed and comprehensiveness of the judgment, combined with the mourning, sets the tone of the entire oracle: Moab suffers and the prophet suffers with it.

verseByVerse.quote: In their streets they put on sackcloth; on their housetops and in their squares everyone wails and melts in tears. Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In their streets they put on sackcloth; on their housetops and in their squares everyone wails'—the mourning pervades every space: streets, housetops, squares. Public grief fills the landscape. 'And melts in tears'—the Hebrew is vivid: the people dissolve in weeping. 'Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz'—the cry of grief is so loud it carries across the landscape from city to city. Heshbon and Elealeh were important cities on the Moabite plateau; Jahaz was a significant distance away. The volume of grief is proportionate to the scale of loss. 'His soul trembles'—the individual Moabite in terror: the whole nation, from city to city, from the public square to the private soul, is undone by the judgment. Childs: the geographic detail gives the disaster a human geography—real places, real people, real grief.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction. For the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My heart cries out for Moab'—the prophet's personal lament, identifying himself with Moab's suffering. This is the voice of prophetic compassion: Isaiah does not merely deliver God's judgment but grieves over those who receive it. 'Her fugitives flee to Zoar'—Zoar was at the southern tip of the Dead Sea; it was the city to which Lot fled from Sodom (Gen. 19:22)—an evocative connection. Moab's refugees flee along the same route. 'For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping'—the pilgrimage of grief: even the road is a place of tears. 'The waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered'—the land itself is affected: the waters that sustained the vegetation are gone. Young: the ecological destruction accompanies the social dissolution—nature and society suffer together under judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows. For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows'—the refugees flee carrying whatever they can take: accumulated wealth that cannot save them but is too precious to leave. The brook of willows is probably the Zered, marking Moab's southern border—the refugees cross out of their land forever. 'For a cry has gone around the land of Moab'—the cry of mourning encircles the entire territory; no corner of Moab is untouched. 'Her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim'—two locations probably at opposite ends of Moab: north and south. The wailing covers the whole country from end to end. Motyer: the geography of mourning maps the geography of the nation—every part weeps.

verseByVerse.quote: For the waters of Dimon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dimon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, and for the remnant of the land. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The waters of Dimon are full of blood'—Dimon is probably Dibon, Moab's capital; the name is altered slightly, perhaps to suggest dam (blood). The waters red with blood: the massacred lie in the waterways. 'For I will bring upon Dimon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, and for the remnant of the land'—even the survivors are not safe: a lion (divine judgment in animal form) awaits those who escaped the initial assault. The remnant is not preserved; it too will be consumed. Oswalt: the chapter ends without hope for Moab—ch. 16 will offer the possibility of finding refuge in Zion, but only for those who humble themselves. The lion awaiting the remnant is the alternative to Zion's refuge.

16.subtitle: Moab's Pride and the Promise of the Throne
16.intro: Overview. Chapter 16 concludes the Moab oracle, moving from a remarkable offer of shelter for Moab's fugitives (vv. 1–5) through the description of Moab's pride (vv. 6–12) to the announcement of Moab's judgment within three years (vv. 13–14). The passage in verses 4–5 — describing a king who will judge in faithfulness and seek justice — is another of Isaiah's quiet Messianic insertions, pointing beyond any immediate political solution to the one king who will fully embody these qualities.

sections.title: Shelter for the Fugitives — A Messianic Glimpse
sections.commentary:
The opening verses offer something remarkable: an invitation for Moab's refugees to find shelter in Judah, and a call to Judah to hide the outcasts and not betray the fugitives (v. 3). In the middle of a judgment oracle, there is an offer of refuge. The fugitives fleeing destruction can find a hiding place under the wing of the Davidic king.

vv. 4–5 — “Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.” This description — a throne of steadfast love, faithfulness, justice, righteousness — cannot be fully satisfied by any historical Davidic king. It points to the one whose throne will be established for ever (9:7). Even in an oracle about Moab, Isaiah cannot help gesturing toward the king who will make everything right.

sections.title: Moab's Pride and Its Consequence
sections.commentary:
The reason Moab does not accept the offer of shelter is named plainly: “We have heard of the pride of Moab — how proud he is! — of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right” (v. 6). The offer of grace is refused because pride will not stoop to accept it. The specific sin of Moab is the same sin that brought down Babylon in chapter 14 — the refusal to acknowledge dependence and the insistence on self-sufficiency.

The mourning of verses 9–11 returns to the note struck in 15:5: genuine grief over Moab's harvest destroyed and its people desolate. The three-year timeline of verses 13–14 gives the oracle a deliberate specificity — this is not vague prophecy but a dated announcement that would soon be verifiable.

keyVerse.quote: “Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.”
keyVerse.note: The four qualities named — steadfast love, faithfulness, justice, righteousness — are the covenant attributes of God himself applied to the coming king. Every good king in Israel's history embodied them partially; the Messiah will embody them fully. This is the throne that will have no end (9:7).

16.reflection: Moab's refusal of the shelter offered in verse 3 is a parable of the pride that refuses grace. The offer is genuine; the shelter is real; the king on the throne of steadfast love is ready to receive. What prevents the fugitive from entering is not the absence of welcome but the presence of pride. This is always the obstacle.
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion. <sup>2</sup>Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon. <sup>3</sup>"Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; <sup>4</sup>let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land, <sup>5</sup>then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness." <sup>6</sup>We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right. <sup>7</sup>Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth. <sup>8</sup>For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea. <sup>9</sup>Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased. <sup>10</sup>And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting. <sup>11</sup>Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth. <sup>12</sup>And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail. <sup>13</sup>This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. <sup>14</sup>But now the LORD says, "In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Moab's Appeal and Its Rejection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 16 continues the Moab oracle with a remarkable inversion: Moab is counseled to send tribute to Zion and find refuge there (vv. 1–5). The counsel is grounded in the promise of the messianic throne of David (v. 5). But the counsel is refused because of Moab's pride (v. 6). The rest of the chapter describes Moab's weeping over its agricultural losses and the prophet's renewed lament.
verseByVerse.examples: The pattern of ch. 16 recurs whenever the gospel meets human pride: the throne of the Son of David is available; the refuge of Zion is open; the requirement is humility. Every human heart that finds Moab's pride in itself confronts the same choice Moab faced.

verseByVerse.quote: Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion. Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion'—a counsel to Moab: send tribute (lamb—perhaps a tax payment in kind) to the Davidic king in Jerusalem. 'The ruler of the land' may be the Davidic king or an anticipation of the messianic king (v. 5). Sela is Petra, Moab's southern stronghold; the route goes through the Arabah desert to Jerusalem. 'Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon'—the fugitive image: birds frightened from a nest, flying in every direction. The Moabite women at the Arnon (their northern border) are trying to cross to safety. Young: the simile captures both the panic and the pathos—scattered, directionless, vulnerable as nestlings.

verseByVerse.quote: “Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon'—the appeal to Judah or to the Davidic king for specific actions: counsel (guidance), justice (legal protection), and shade (physical shelter in the noon heat—a vivid image of relief). 'Shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive'—asylum for the displaced: not handing over refugees to their pursuers. This is the ancient law of asylum applied to Moab's displaced people. 'Let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer'—the destroyer may be Assyria or the internal agent of judgment. Motyer: the counsel to shelter Moab's outcasts is grounded in Israel's own experience as refugee and sojourner (Ex. 22:21; Lev. 19:34); the nation that was sheltered by Egypt is to shelter others.

verseByVerse.quote: When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land, then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.“ We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness'—the messianic throne described in the most beautiful terms: steadfast love (khesed), faithfulness (emet), justice (mishpat), righteousness (tsedaqah). The king who sits on this throne is the righteous judge of 11:4. This throne is the destination toward which all the oracles against the nations are pointing: the one place of true shelter and justice. 'We have heard of the pride of Moab—how proud he is!'—the counsel is refused; pride makes Moab unwilling to come as a refugee seeking shelter. Oswalt: the contrast is stark—the throne is established in steadfast love; Moab's response is arrogance and pride. The way of life is available; pride makes it impossible to take.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth. For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah— its clusters struck down by the lords of the nations, reached to Jazer, wandered into the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail'—because pride has refused the path of refuge, the consequence is confirmed: let the mourning of ch. 15 continue and intensify. 'Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth'—raisin cakes were delicacies associated with Moabite festivals (and sometimes with pagan worship). Their loss epitomizes the loss of all Moab's prosperity. 'For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah'—Moab's agricultural wealth was renowned; its vineyards produced grapes whose vines stretched far and wide. 'Its clusters struck down by the lords of the nations'—the conquerors destroy the viticulture, the most labor-intensive and valuable agricultural investment. Young: the vine of Sibmah functions as the Moabite counterpart to Israel's vineyard in ch. 5—in both cases God is removing the fruit that his people refused to produce righteously.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased. And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh'—the prophet's personal tears, again identifying himself with Moab's suffering. The weeping is specific and personal: Isaiah grieves over named cities and named vineyards. 'For over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased'—the harvest shout (a joyful cry raised during treading) is silent. The silence of the winepress is the silence of death. 'Joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised'—three paired losses: joy and gladness, songs and cheers, treading and shouting. All the expressions of harvest celebration are extinguished. Motyer: the removal of harvest joy is the removal of the blessing God gave; Moab, like Israel, has forfeited the covenant gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth. And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth'—the bodily language of grief: the inner parts (me'im, the bowels as the seat of emotion) moaning like a harp string. Isaiah's grief is visceral, not merely intellectual. 'And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail'—the futility of Moabite religion in the moment of crisis: the high places and sanctuaries that Chemosh was supposed to protect produce nothing. The god does not answer. Childs: the silence of the sanctuary in the moment of need is the proof of the idol's impotence—the false god is revealed precisely when divine help is most desperately needed.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. But now the LORD has spoken, saying, “In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past'—a distinction between the older oracle (perhaps from an earlier source) and the new word that follows. The new word gives a specific timetable. 'In three years, like the years of a hireling'—a hireling works for exactly the contracted period, no more, no less. Three years: a precise and immovable deadline. 'The glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude'—the glory (gaon) of Moab, which was also its pride, will be turned to contempt. The same word used of Moab's pride (v. 6: gaon) describes what will be humiliated. 'Those who remain will be very few and feeble'—the remnant that survives is negligible: few in number, weak in strength. Oswalt: the precision of 'three years' marks this as prophetic speech that will be verified by events, grounding the oracle in accountability to history.

17.subtitle: The Oracle Against Damascus — and a Remnant Who Returns
17.intro: Overview. Chapter 17 contains an oracle against Damascus (the capital of Syria) and its ally Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel), who together formed the anti-Assyrian coalition of chapter 7. Their destruction is announced with the stark brevity of verses 1 and 3. But within the oracle of judgment, Isaiah inserts one of his characteristic remnant promises: a few survivors will look to their Maker, and those survivors will be like gleaned olives, like the stalk left after a harvest. The judgment produces a purified people.

sections.title: Damascus and Ephraim Fall
sections.commentary:
“Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins.” The oracle against Damascus is fulfilled in 732 BC when Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria destroys the city. Ephraim's alliance with Syria brings it the same fate: the northern kingdom falls to Assyria in 722 BC. The two powers that had made Ahaz's heart shake like trees in the wind (ch. 7) are themselves shown to have no more permanence than cities built on sand.

vv. 5–6 — “And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten — two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree.” The remnant is not impressive in number. Two or three berries at the top of the highest bough. But they are there. The harvest of judgment does not leave the tree entirely bare.

sections.title: The Remnant Looks to Their Maker
sections.commentary:
“In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel. He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands.” This is precisely the conversion that judgment is meant to produce. The people who in prosperity turned to their own idols and gardens (v. 10) will, in the fire of affliction, turn back to the one they had abandoned. Judgment is not the end of the story; it is the means by which the remnant is purified and restored to its true object.

Verse 10 names the cause of the disaster plainly: “you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge.” Forgetting God is not an intellectual failure but a moral and relational one — the deliberate neglect of the one who was always present and always sufficient.

keyVerse.quote: “In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: This is the goal of all of Isaiah's prophecy compressed into one verse. The point of every judgment oracle is not destruction but redirection — turning eyes that have been fixed on everything else back to the only one worth looking at. The Holy One of Israel is the beginning and end of all genuine recovery.

17.reflection: Chapter 17 sets the pattern that runs through all of Isaiah's national oracles: judgment that aims at restoration. The stripping of idols from the remnant is not punishment for its own sake but the loving removal of everything that was substituting for God. Where in your own life have you experienced the stripping of something you relied on — and found, on the other side, that your eyes were clearer for it?
17.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. <sup>2</sup>The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid. <sup>3</sup>The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts. <sup>4</sup>And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean. <sup>5</sup>And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. <sup>6</sup>Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten— two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel. <sup>7</sup>In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel. <sup>8</sup>He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense. <sup>9</sup>In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. <sup>10</sup>For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger, <sup>11</sup>though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain. <sup>12</sup>Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! <sup>13</sup>The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. <sup>14</sup>At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Oracle Against Damascus and Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 17 is a paired oracle against Damascus (Syria) and Ephraim (northern Israel), reflecting the Syro-Ephraimite coalition of ch. 7. The chapter begins with the fall of Damascus and moves to the dim glory of Israel, before describing Israel's turn from God and the nations' attempt on Zion (and its failure). The chapter closes with the image of judgment passing as quickly as the morning.
verseByVerse.examples: The pattern of ch. 17 is pastoral: prosperity enables spiritual forgetfulness; calamity restores focus. The instruction is not to wait for calamity to restore our gaze to God but to maintain that gaze in prosperity. Every garden planted (v. 10) that replaces trust in God is a smaller version of Israel's idolatry.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. Her cities will be deserted forever; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and no one will make them afraid. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins'—the most radical prediction about Damascus: total urban erasure. Damascus was one of the oldest continually inhabited cities in the world; its destruction is almost unthinkable. Historically, Tiglath-pileser III destroyed Damascus in 732 BC. 'Her cities will be deserted forever'—the plural cities refers to Damascus's surrounding towns. 'They will be for flocks, which will lie down, and no one will make them afraid'—the pastoral aftermath: the city that made the nations afraid becomes a place of undisturbed animal grazing. The flocks lying down in peace (the image of Psalm 23's protection) is here ironic: peace comes only because the human population has been removed by judgment. Motyer: the oracle fulfills the taunt of 2:11–17 applied to Damascus specifically.

verseByVerse.quote: The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts. And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus'—both partners of the Syro-Ephraimite coalition lose their defining characteristics: Ephraim loses its military fortress; Damascus loses its political kingdom. 'The remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel'—a dark comparison: the remaining Syrians will be as diminished as Israel will be. Both are equally brought low. 'And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean'—the glory (kabod) of Jacob, his historic weight and significance as God's covenant people, diminished. The fat of flesh (prosperity) wasting to leanness: the covenant curses of Deuteronomy (lean instead of fat, little instead of much). Oswalt: the glory that belongs to God alone (6:3) cannot be retained by a people who have rejected the glorious One.

verseByVerse.quote: And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten— two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears'—the harvest metaphor for judgment: the nations are reaped. The reaper takes everything. 'As when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim'—after the main harvest, the gleaner picks what remains. The Valley of Rephaim was a fertile agricultural valley near Jerusalem; to glean there was to be the last to arrive after abundance had been taken. 'Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten'—the olive tree image: after the main harvest (by shaking), a second beating knocks loose a few more olives. 'Two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches'—the remnant is as few as post-harvest gleanings: almost nothing, but not nothing. Motyer: the few berries at the top are precisely the remnant theology of 6:13—a remnant survives, not by luck but by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look to what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel'—the positive purpose of all the preceding judgment: the restoration of the basic human orientation toward God. 'Look to' (sha'ah) means to gaze in trust and dependence. The man who looks to the Maker has been stripped of every other source of security. 'He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look to what his own fingers have made'—the double negation: not to altars, not to the handiwork of fingers. The idols of 2:8 are abandoned not because they were destroyed by the enemy but because the worshipper has turned back to the true God. 'The Asherim or the altars of incense'—the two forms of Canaanite religious apparatus most associated with syncretism: the wooden poles for Asherah (fertility goddess) and the incense altars. Both disavowed. Oswalt: the refusal to look to idols is the positive face of looking to the Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine branch of a stranger, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights'—the fortified cities abandoned: the same cities that the people trusted for security become as empty as the forests the Canaanites fled at Israel's conquest. The historical reversal: Israel became like the Canaanites, and now their cities are abandoned as Canaanite cities once were. 'For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge'—the root cause of the desolation: forgetting (shakhakh) and not remembering. Spiritual amnesia produces moral collapse. 'The God of your salvation' and 'the Rock of your refuge'—two covenant-names: God as deliverer and God as protection. Both forgotten. 'Though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine branch of a stranger'—religious horticulture: planting foreign religious plants (worship-gardens for pagan deities) in place of relationship with the Rock. Childs: the garden metaphor inverts creation—instead of tending God's garden, they plant their own in honor of other gods.

verseByVerse.quote: though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain. Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow'—the frantic pace of pagan religion: even the agricultural metaphor is accelerated. The plants grow the same day they are planted; the blossoms appear the same morning. But this unnatural haste is the sign of its falseness—genuine growth takes time. 'Yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain'—what was produced by religious effort cannot be kept; the harvest of idolatry vanishes under divine judgment. 'Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea'—the next scene: nations gathering against Zion, their noise like ocean waves. The thunder of the nations is impressive and terrifying but, like the sea, bounded. Motyer: the sea-image recalls creation where God bounded the sea—the nations are no more capable of overflowing their limits than the sea is.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away'—God's rebuke is sufficient: a single word dissolves the gathered nations. 'Chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm'—two images of effortless dispersal: chaff (weightless, at the wind's mercy) and dust (insubstantial, formless). The great nations are as light as chaff before God's rebuke. 'At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more!'—the sudden dissolution: the terror of evening gone by morning. The same structure as 10:28–34 (the Assyrian advance that halts at Nob) applied universally. 'This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us'—the closing line makes the lesson explicit: this is what happens to every nation that sets itself against God's people. Webb: the oracle ends as a promise: the nations that thunder against Zion are chaff before the LORD who created and bounded the sea.

18.subtitle: The Oracle Against Cush
18.intro: Overview. Chapter 18 is a brief oracle addressed to the land of Cush (ancient Ethiopia/Sudan), the nation from which Judah might have been tempted to seek military help against Assyria. The oracle is unusual in that it contains no explicit condemnation — it is more of a description of events, addressed to the distant Cushites, announcing that God is watching events unfold from his heavenly throne and will act at the right moment. The chapter ends with the remarkable promise that Cush will one day bring gifts to the LORD on Mount Zion.

sections.title: The LORD Watches from His Dwelling
sections.commentary:
The envoys from Cush — who apparently came to seek an alliance with Judah against Assyria — are sent back home with a message: go and wait. The imagery of verse 4 is striking: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” God is not inactive; he is watching with the quiet intensity of a farmer watching the sky in harvest season. The decisive moment will come, but not yet.

v. 4 — “I will quietly look from my dwelling.” The word quietly is the key. God does not need to be agitated or reactive. He watches with sovereign calm from his throne, knowing precisely when and how he will act. This is the posture of the God who “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph 1:11) — not hurried, not uncertain, not surprised.

Verse 7 closes with an eschatological promise: a people tall and smooth, from a land divided by rivers, will bring gifts to the LORD of hosts on Mount Zion. The oracle that begins with Cush being sent home ends with Cush making a pilgrimage. The rejected envoys become, in the end, worshippers. This anticipates Psalm 68:31 (“Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God”) and the Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.”
keyVerse.note: The image of God watching quietly from his dwelling is one of the most calming pictures of divine sovereignty in Scripture. It is not passivity — the harvest is coming and the pruning shears are ready (v. 5). It is the quiet confidence of one who is never caught off guard, never reactive, always working toward his own purposes at exactly the right pace.

18.reflection: Chapter 18 is a reminder that God's apparent silence is not absence. He is watching — quietly, intently, from his dwelling — and he will act at exactly the right moment. The temptation in every crisis is to rush ahead of God, to seek the Cushite alliance when God has told us to wait. The chapter invites trust in the God who watches before he acts.
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, <sup>2</sup>which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. <sup>3</sup>All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear! <sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest." <sup>5</sup>For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. <sup>6</sup>They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. <sup>7</sup>At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 18 is one of the shorter oracles against the nations—a word to Cush (ancient Ethiopia/Sudan), the great African power of the 25th dynasty that briefly controlled Egypt. The oracle is remarkable for its restraint: God watches quietly while Cush sends its swift messengers (vv. 1–2), then at the appointed harvest time acts (vv. 5–6), and finally receives the tribute of Cush's gifts at Zion (v. 7).
verseByVerse.examples: The church in every age faces the temptation to interpret God's silence as indifference. Isaiah 18 counters this: God sees clearly from his dwelling, knows the season, and will act at the right time. The 'tall and smooth' people of Cush who come to Zion with gifts (v. 7) prefigure the Gentile ingathering of ch. 11 and 60.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush'—the wings may be the buzzing of insects (locust swarms characteristic of the region), or the metaphor of swift ambassadors dispatched like birds. Cush was modern-day Sudan, a powerful empire in Isaiah's day (25th dynasty of Egypt). 'Which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters'—the Cushite diplomatic network: papyrus boats navigating the Nile's tributaries. 'Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far'—the description of Cush: tall, smooth (perhaps smooth-skinned), feared internationally. 'A nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide'—the Nile and its branches divide the Cushite territory. Oswalt: the vivid description of Cush's power and activity sets the stage for the contrast with God's quiet watching in vv. 3–4.

verseByVerse.quote: All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear! For thus the LORD said to me: “I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!'—the universal summons: when God acts, the signal will be unmistakable. 'For thus the LORD said to me: “I will quietly look from my dwelling”'—the surprising word: quietly. Amid all the activity of Cush's ambassadors and the world's nations, God is silently watching. His watching is not passive: it is attentive, purposeful, and prelude to decisive action. 'Like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest'—two images of the quietly relentless. The clear heat of sunshine is invisible yet scorching; the dew-cloud in harvest heat is delicate yet nourishing. Both describe God's presence as powerful without being noisy. Childs: the silence of God is a theological statement—he does not need to be active at every moment; his timing is perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: For before the harvest, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For before the harvest, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks'—God the vinedresser acts at the precise moment: not too early (before the fruit is set) and not too late (after harvest). The timing is agricultural precision applied to divine judgment. Cush's power is cut precisely when it reaches its maximum—not before, not after. 'The spreading branches he lops off and clears away'—what was spreading and expansive is cut back to nothing; the ambition of the empire is pruned. 'They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth'—the army left unburied: the ultimate dishonor and the sign of total defeat. 'The birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them'—summer and winter: the carcasses lie through all seasons, a permanent monument to the empire's fall. Motyer: the harvested vine-shoots are the people of the empire; the parallel with Israel (5:1–7) is intentional.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth'—the description of Cush from v. 2 is repeated: the same people who sent ambassadors to Zion now bring tribute. The transformation is from political diplomacy to covenant submission: they come not as equals negotiating but as those who acknowledge the LORD of hosts as supreme. 'To Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts'—Zion as the destination of all nations' tribute (cf. 2:2–4; 60:1–9). The oracle that began with Cush's impressive diplomatic activity ends with Cush's voluntary pilgrimage to Zion. Oswalt: the chapter encapsulates the movement of the nations from self-sufficiency through judgment to the acknowledgment of God—a movement that the whole of Isaiah envisions for all nations. Young: the tribute of Cush to Zion is the beginning of the Gentile ingathering that the servant songs will develop fully.

19.subtitle: The Oracle Against Egypt — and Egypt's Redemption
19.intro: Overview. Chapter 19 is one of the most astonishing chapters in all of Isaiah. It opens with a severe oracle against Egypt — civil war, failed Nile, economic collapse, foolish counsellors — and then pivots, in its second half, to one of the most remarkable promises in the Old Testament: Egypt will know the LORD, worship him, and be called “my people.” The chapter that begins with God riding on a swift cloud against Egypt ends with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel forming a threefold blessing in the earth.

sections.title: Judgment on Egypt
sections.commentary:
“Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them.” The God who dried up the Red Sea for Israel now comes against Egypt in its own land. The judgment is comprehensive: civil strife (v. 2), failed Nile (v. 5), dried-up canals, economic devastation, and — most cutting of all — counsellors made foolish. Egypt prided itself on its ancient wisdom; the princes of Zoan, sons of ancient kings, are made “utterly foolish” (v. 13).

v. 3 — “And the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers.” When divine wisdom is rejected, the vacuum is filled with the counterfeits — idols, sorcerers, mediums. The pattern is the same as in chapter 8:19. A nation that turns from God's word ends up consulting the dead for guidance.

sections.title: Egypt Will Know the LORD
sections.commentary:
The second half of the chapter is a series of “in that day” oracles that move from judgment to transformation. Five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan (Hebrew) and swear allegiance to the LORD. An altar to the LORD in the heart of Egypt and a pillar at its border will be signs and witnesses to the LORD of hosts. And when Egyptians cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, he will send them a saviour and defend them — exactly as he did for Israel in Egypt.

v. 25 — “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.” These three nations — Egypt, the ancient enslaver of Israel; Assyria, the current oppressor; Israel, the covenant people — are placed side by side in a single blessing. The terms used of Israel throughout Scripture (“my people,” “the work of my hands,” “my heritage”) are distributed equally among all three. This is the most explicit anticipation of Gentile inclusion in the covenant in all of the Old Testament. Paul's mission to the nations is the fulfilment of this verse.

keyVerse.quote: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.”
keyVerse.note: The terms “my people” and “my heritage” are covenant terms used exclusively of Israel throughout the Old Testament. Here they are extended to Egypt and Assyria. This is not the abolition of Israel's election but its expansion — the covenant blessings flowing outward to the nations, exactly as God promised Abraham: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen 12:3).

19.theology: The universal scope of salvation. Isaiah 19:18–25 is the Old Testament's most explicit preview of what the New Testament calls the inclusion of the Gentiles. The nations that were Israel's greatest enemies — Egypt, Assyria — are called by the same covenant names as Israel herself. This does not mean that national identity is erased but that the covenant community is expanded. Paul's entire theology of Jew and Gentile in Ephesians 2–3 is the New Testament commentary on Isaiah 19.
19.reflection: Chapter 19 moves from “the LORD is coming against Egypt” to “blessed be Egypt my people” — from judgment to adoption, from terror to worship. This is the arc of the gospel for every human soul. The God who rides on a swift cloud against his enemies is the same God who says to those same enemies, “You are mine.” The distance between those two verses is the cross.
19.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them. <sup>2</sup>And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; <sup>3</sup>and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers; <sup>4</sup>and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts. <sup>5</sup>And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched, <sup>6</sup>and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. <sup>7</sup>There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more. <sup>8</sup>The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. <sup>9</sup>The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. <sup>10</sup>Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved. <sup>11</sup>The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, "I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings"? <sup>12</sup>Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt. <sup>13</sup>The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have led Egypt astray. <sup>14</sup>The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit. <sup>15</sup>And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do. <sup>16</sup>In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them. <sup>17</sup>And the land of Judah will become a terror to the Egyptians. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against them. <sup>18</sup>In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction. <sup>19</sup>In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. <sup>20</sup>It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them. <sup>21</sup>And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them. <sup>22</sup>And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them. <sup>23</sup>In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. <sup>24</sup>In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth, <sup>25</sup>whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Oracle Against Egypt and Its Remarkable Ending
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 19 is one of the most remarkable chapters in the prophetic corpus. It begins with God riding into Egypt on a swift cloud to judge it (vv. 1–15), but ends with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel forming a holy triad—'my people Egypt, my handiwork Assyria, my inheritance Israel' (v. 25). This eschatological ending is without parallel: the two great superpowers that threatened Israel become God's own people.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah 19:24–25 is one of the most extraordinary texts in the Bible for Christian missiology: the Gentile nations included in Israel's covenant vocabulary ('my people,' 'my inheritance'). The highway between Egypt and Assyria through Israel (v. 23) prefigures the new humanity in Christ where dividing walls are broken down (Eph. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them. And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against his brother and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt'—the theophanic entry: God on a cloud (a mode of divine transportation in the ancient Near East; cf. Ps. 104:3). He comes to Egypt; Egypt is not irrelevant to him. 'The idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence'—the gods of Egypt (the most elaborate polytheism of the ancient world) shudder at the approach of the true God. What terrified the nations (God's presence) unmasks the impotence of Egypt's religious apparatus. 'The heart of the Egyptians will melt within them'—the same response as Babylon's (13:7): all human confidence dissolved at the divine approach. 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against his brother'—civil war: God's instrument of judgment against Egypt is Egypt itself. The internal conflicts that characterized Egypt's late period (the breakdown into competing dynasties) are the fulfillment. Oswalt: God need not bring an external army; he can dissolve a society from within.

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers. And I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out'—the Egyptian spirit (ruakh) of wisdom and confidence vacated. Egypt was famous for its wisdom (Gen. 41; Acts 7:22); God empties that too. 'I will confound their counsel'—Egypt was known for its counselors and advisors; God confuses the very faculty Egypt trusted most. 'They will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers'—in desperation, Egypt consults every available alternative to genuine divine wisdom, all of which are condemned (8:19). 'I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them'—the ultimate judgment: Egyptian sovereignty ends. The hard master may be Assyria (Esarhaddon) or later Babylon or Persia. Childs: Egypt, which was the hard master of Israel (Ex. 1:11–14), now receives its own hard master—the covenantal principle of measure-for-measure applied at the imperial level.

verseByVerse.quote: And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be parched and dry; and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be parched and dry'—the Nile is Egypt: its flooding and retreat governed all agricultural life. To dry up the Nile is to end Egypt. 'Its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up'—the irrigation system (the canals and channels that distributed the Nile's water to the fields) becomes foul and then empty. 'Reeds and rushes will rot away'—the papyrus and reed plants that grew along the Nile's banks—the raw material of Egyptian writing, boat-building, and basket-weaving—disappear. The entire ecological foundation of Egyptian civilization is removed. Young: the judgment against the Nile reverses the plagues of Moses (Ex. 7:14–25 turned the Nile to blood); now the river simply fails. The God who controls the Nile controls Egypt's fate entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will dry up, be driven away, and be no more. The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will dry up'—the agricultural catastrophe: the fields that depended on Nile flooding and irrigation produce nothing. The Egyptian agricultural cycle—plant at the Nile's recession, harvest before the flood—breaks down entirely. 'Be driven away, and be no more'—absolute erasure: what was once productive is completely gone. 'The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water'—the fishing industry collapse: hook-fishermen and net-fishermen alike become unemployed. Fishing was a major Egyptian industry; its failure compounds the agricultural catastrophe. Motyer: the two losses (agricultural and fishing) represent the two primary food sources of Egypt—both cut off simultaneously.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who work in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Those who work in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton'—Egypt's textile industry: flax (for linen) and cotton were Egyptian specialties exported throughout the Mediterranean. The craftsmen of these industries—from raw fiber to finished cloth—face total economic collapse. 'Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed'—the 'pillars' are Egypt's foundations: its elite workers, its ruling class, those who constitute the social structure. When the pillars are crushed, the whole building falls. 'All who work for pay will be grieved'—the wage economy: everyone who depended on employment loses their livelihood. Oswalt: the judgment is socially comprehensive—it touches every economic class, from artisan to elite, from fisherfolk to linen-weavers.

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”? Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel'—Zoan (Tanis) was a Delta city that served as a royal seat; its princes represented Egypt's political intelligence. They are demolished by divine wisdom. 'How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”?'—the claim of pedigree: Egyptian wisdom was measured by antiquity of lineage. But pedigree without the fear of the LORD produces only 'stupid counsel.' 'Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt'—the challenge: if Egypt's wise men are truly wise, they should be able to read the divine plan. Their inability to read the plan exposes the bankruptcy of their wisdom. Childs: the contest between Egyptian wisdom and divine wisdom is the prophetic counterpart to Moses' confrontation with Pharaoh's magicians (Ex. 7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger. The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded'—Zoan (Delta) and Memphis (the ancient capital, near modern Cairo) represent the two poles of Egyptian political geography. Both poles produce fools and deluded men. 'Those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger'—the very leaders (cornerstones) who should stabilize the nation are the agents of its instability. 'The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion'—God is the source of the confusion: he has poured a spirit of delusion into Egypt's leadership. The divine passive reversal of wisdom. 'As a drunken man staggers in his vomit'—the most undignified image: Egypt's leadership is as incapacitated as a drunk man who cannot stand in his own mess. Young: the image deliberately humiliates the world's most sophisticated political culture.

verseByVerse.quote: And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do. In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do'—the vocabulary from 9:14–15 (head/tail, palm/reed) now applied to Egypt: all levels of leadership are equally impotent. No Egyptian—high or low, lofty or humble—can do anything to reverse the divine judgment. 'In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear'—the gender comparison is ancient military idiom for extreme demoralization: the warrior who trembles like a woman in battle has lost all fighting capacity. 'Before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them'—the shaking hand of God: not the stretched-out hand of judgment (9:12 etc.) but the menacing shake of warning. Even the threat of God's hand is enough to make Egypt a trembling mass. Motyer: the contrast with v. 1 (God on the swift cloud coming to Egypt) is the beginning of the chapter; its effect on Egypt is the middle; the surprising conclusion begins at v. 17.

verseByVerse.quote: And the land of Judah will become a terror to Egypt. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against it. In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The land of Judah will become a terror to Egypt'—a remarkable reversal: tiny Judah, which Egypt despised, becomes the source of Egypt's fear. Because God's word comes through Judah, Judah is more powerful than Egypt. 'Because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against it'—the fear is theological, not military: Egypt fears what God has said about Egypt through Judah's prophets. 'In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts'—the beginning of the conversion: Egyptian cities adopting Hebrew (the language of the covenant community) and swearing loyalty to the LORD. This is covenant language applied to Gentile cities. 'One of these will be called the City of Destruction'—possibly heliopolis (City of the Sun, altered to City of Destruction); or a city of judgment that becomes a city of conversion. Childs: five cities—a representative number—of Egypt publicly aligned with the LORD of hosts is an extraordinary sign of the nations' turning.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border.
