It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border'—two covenant signs planted in Egypt: an altar (the place of sacrifice and worship) at the center, a pillar (a memorial monument to God's covenant) at the border. Egypt becomes a place of legitimate Yahweh-worship. This is extraordinary given Deuteronomy's restriction of the altar to the central sanctuary. 'It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt'—the theological function: the altar and pillar testify to the LORD's reality and presence in Egypt. 'When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them'—Egypt's cry to the LORD and the LORD's response mirrors Exodus: the oppressed cry, God delivers (Ex. 3:7–9). Egypt, once the oppressor, now experiences what Israel experienced—and receives the same response. Oswalt: the covenant structure (cry, hear, send savior) is extended to Egypt—they become recipients of covenant grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them. And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day'—the covenantal knowledge that defines Israel's relationship with God ('know the LORD') is now extended to Egypt. 'And worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them'—the full range of covenant worship: sacrifice, offering, and vows. Egypt becomes a worshipping community indistinguishable from Israel in its posture toward God. 'The LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD'—the divine pedagogy: the judgment (striking) produces the return (healing). The striking is purposive: not destruction but the pain that leads to repentance and healing. 'He will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them'—the divine ear opens to Egypt's prayer as it opens to Israel's. Motyer: the healing of Egypt is the healing of the covenant relationship—the same grace that healed Israel is extended to Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria'—the road of enmity (the invasion route Egypt and Assyria used against each other for centuries) becomes a highway of peace. 'Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians'—not trade or diplomacy but worship: the two former enemies worship together. The shared worship of the LORD transforms political enmity into spiritual kinship. 'In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth'—the three nations form a holy triad: Egypt (south), Assyria (north-east), Israel (in the midst). Israel, long the weakest of the three militarily, is in the center—not because it is the most powerful but because it is the mediating bearer of covenant knowledge to the nations. Childs: the highway between ancient enemies is the prototype of the new humanity in Christ (Eph. 2:14–16).

verseByVerse.quote: whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance'—the most astonishing verse in the oracle against Egypt. 'My people' (ammi) was Israel's exclusive covenant designation (cf. Ex. 3:7; 6:7); now it is applied to Egypt. 'The work of my hands' (ma'aseh yadai) was Israel's description of itself as God's creation; now it applies to Assyria. 'My inheritance' (nakhalati) was Israel's title; it remains Israel's but in a context where Egypt and Assyria have been included. The three covenant-titles redistribute without diminishing Israel: Egypt and Assyria receive designations that were Israel's, and Israel still retains its own. Oswalt: this verse is the furthest reach of Isaiah's universalism—the nations not merely subdued or converted but adopted into the covenant family with Israel's own covenant names. It anticipates Romans 9–11 and the mystery of Gentile inclusion in the one people of God.

20.subtitle: The Sign of Isaiah's Nakedness
20.intro: Overview. Chapter 20 is a brief but vivid narrative. For three years, at God's command, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot as a living sign — a prophecy enacted in the prophet's own body. The sign had a specific target: Judah's temptation to rely on an Egyptian-Cushite military coalition against Assyria. Isaiah's three-year acted parable announced that Egypt and Cush would be led away by Assyria as naked prisoners, and therefore they were no foundation to build on.

sections.title: Three Years Naked and Barefoot
sections.commentary:
The chapter is anchored by the historical detail of Sargon II of Assyria's campaign against Ashdod (711 BC), confirming the oracle's specific context. Isaiah's three-year walking sign was a sustained, public, costly demonstration — not a brief prophetic gesture but a years-long embodiment of the message. The prophet's body became the sermon.

v. 3 — “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush.” The word servant here connects Isaiah to the Servant figure of chapters 40–55. Isaiah's willingness to suffer public shame to deliver God's message is itself a foreshadowing of the greater Servant who would bear far greater shame for a far greater purpose.

The practical point of the sign is verse 6: those who were looking to Egypt and Cush for help will be horrified when those powers are themselves led away as prisoners. “And we, how shall we escape?” The question is the point. If your source of security has been captured, what are you left with? Isaiah's answer, consistent throughout the book, is that the only reliable refuge has always been the LORD himself.

keyVerse.quote: “And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?’”
keyVerse.note: The question “how shall we escape?” is the exact question every misplaced confidence eventually produces. When the thing we trusted — whether Egypt, an alliance, a financial plan, a relationship — fails, we are left with the question Isaiah has been asking from chapter 1: to whom are you actually looking? The answer the book provides is always the same: “Look to the rock from which you were hewn” (51:1).

20.reflection: Isaiah's three-year acted sign is a reminder that God sometimes calls his servants to costly, public, apparently undignified forms of witness. The prophet did not get to choose a more respectable way to deliver this message. The question the chapter poses is both historical and personal: what is the Egypt or Cush in your own life — the security that looks impressive but will one day be led away in chains?
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it— <sup>2</sup>at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. <sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, <sup>4</sup>so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt. <sup>5</sup>Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. <sup>6</sup>And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Sign-Act Against Egypt and Cush
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 20 records one of the most dramatic sign-acts in prophecy: Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot for three years as a living parable of what Assyria would do to Egypt and Cush. The sign-act was directed not at Egypt but at Judah's political leaders who were counseling trust in Egypt as a counter-balance to Assyria.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign-act challenges the church's tendency to seek security in human alliances when those alliances require trust in what God has condemned. Every generation finds its Egypt—the powerful alternative to trusting God that seems safer but leads to captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it— at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, “Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet,” and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the year that the commander in chief... came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it'—the historical anchor: 711 BC, the Assyrian capture of Ashdod (a Philistine city allied with Egypt). Ashdod had looked to Egypt for help; Egypt did not come. This is the historical context that makes Isaiah's sign-act intelligible. 'Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet'—God commands a state of public humiliation: stripped of the garments of mourning (sackcloth) and removed from footwear. 'And he did so, walking naked and barefoot'—Isaiah obeyed without recorded protest. The nakedness was probably not total nudity but the minimal undergarment of a slave or captive. Motyer: the sign-act is costly obedience—Isaiah bears in his body the indignity of what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush'—the three years establishes the duration and the authenticating audience. 'My servant Isaiah'—the first use of the servant title in Isaiah for a human figure; it anticipates the Servant Songs of ch. 40–53. 'So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered'—what Isaiah did voluntarily, the Egyptian and Cushite captives will do involuntarily. The humiliation Isaiah adopted symbolically, they will experience actually. 'The nakedness of Egypt'—the exposure of Egypt's shame: the great power that Judah was tempted to trust will itself be stripped and paraded. Oswalt: the sign-act functions as merciful warning to Judah before the disaster becomes inevitable.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, “Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast'—two emotional states: dismayed (khathar, shattered) and ashamed (boshu, humiliated). The source of each is the object of false trust: Cush was the hope, Egypt was the boast. 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped'—the confession of failed expectation: what we relied on has been destroyed. The hope in Egypt and Cush was not merely political but quasi-religious—the kind of trust that belongs only to God. 'And we, how shall we escape?'—the coastland peoples' terrified question. If Egypt fell, they have no alternative refuge. Childs: the question exposes the theological vacuum created by misplaced trust—when the false refuge fails, there is nothing. Isaiah's answer to 'how shall we escape' is the entire remaining book: only through trust in the Holy One of Israel.

21.subtitle: Oracles Against Babylon, Edom, and Arabia
21.intro: Overview. Chapter 21 contains three short oracles, each addressed to a different nation. The first and longest (vv. 1–10) is a vision of Babylon’s fall, delivered with such physical intensity that the prophet reels under it. The second (vv. 11–12) is a night-watchman exchange with Edom — poetic, cryptic, unresolved. The third (vv. 13–17) turns to the desert caravans of Arabia, where the commerce of the ancient world will be silenced within a year. Together they form a triptych: the great empire, its anxious neighbor, and the ordinary trader — all subject to the same sovereign word.

sections.title: The Fall of Babylon
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with a locust-like storm sweeping in from the wilderness — the image of an invading army in Isaiah’s symbolic vocabulary. God commands the Medes and Elamites to besiege, and Isaiah, caught up in the vision, reacts with physical anguish: his body shakes, his mind is dismayed, the twilight he longed for has become terror. The prophet is not a detached analyst but a participant in what he sees. He watches a banqueting table become a battlefield.

v. 3 — “My loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor.” The image of labor pains for divine judgment runs throughout Isaiah (13:8; 26:17; 66:7) and into the New Testament (Matt. 24:8). It conveys both inevitability and agony: what is coming cannot be stopped, and it will not be painless.

The watchman’s announcement — “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” — is laconic and precise. Revelation 18:2 quotes it exactly, applying it to the final fall of the city that represents human empire in all ages. Isaiah sees it as already done; the prophetic perfect collapses the distance between announcement and event. The chapter closes with a word of suffering comfort to “my threshed one, son of my threshing floor” — Israel, ground down but not destroyed, told that this vision is for them.

sections.title: The Watchman of Edom
sections.commentary: Someone calls from Seir (Edom): “Watchman, what time of the night?” The question has an anxious edge — is the darkness nearly over? The watchman’s reply is the most enigmatic in Isaiah: “Morning comes, and also the night. If you would inquire, inquire; come back again.” There is light coming, but darkness too. Not a promise of dawn without night, but a summons to keep inquiring. Edom is told it may return with its question — which is itself a mercy: the door is not closed.

sections.title: Arabia
sections.commentary: The final oracle addresses the caravans of Dedan and the people of Tema, who are called to bring water and bread to the fleeing refugees of Kedar. The judgment on Kedar — the Arabian tribes whose archers and warriors were renowned — is precise: within one year, “all the glory of Kedar will come to an end.” The timeframe is specific, and God underwrites it with his own name. Even the edges of the ancient world are within the scope of his word.

keyVerse.quote: “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night? The watchman says: ‘Morning comes, and also the night.’”
keyVerse.note: The exchange is one of the strangest moments in prophetic literature. But its strangeness is the point: history does not move in simple arcs from darkness to light. Morning and night come together. The right response is not resignation but inquiry — keep asking, keep returning.

21.reflection: Isaiah reeled physically under the vision of Babylon’s fall. The prophets were not spectators of history but participants in God’s grief over it. Is there a situation in the world right now that you have allowed yourself to feel — not just analyze? And what does it mean to keep “inquiring” in the darkness when the watchman can only say that morning and night will both come?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land. <sup>2</sup>A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end. <sup>3</sup>Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see. <sup>4</sup>My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling. <sup>5</sup>They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield! <sup>6</sup>For thus the Lord said to me: "Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees. <sup>7</sup>When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently." <sup>8</sup>Then he who saw cried out: "Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights. <sup>9</sup>And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground." <sup>10</sup>O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you. <sup>11</sup>The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, "Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?" <sup>12</sup>The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again." <sup>13</sup>The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. <sup>14</sup>To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema. <sup>15</sup>For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle. <sup>16</sup>For thus the Lord said to me, "Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end. <sup>17</sup>And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Oracles Against Babylon, Dumah, and Arabia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 21 contains three brief oracles: the oracle of the desert sea (Babylon's fall, vv. 1–10), the oracle of Dumah (Edom, vv. 11–12), and the oracle against Arabia (vv. 13–17). The Babylon oracle is one of the most dramatic in the book: a watchman standing on the wall reports what he sees, and what he sees is the fall of Babylon to Medo-Persian forces.
verseByVerse.examples: Revelation 18:2 quotes Isaiah 21:9 ('Fallen, fallen is Babylon') as a description of the final fall of the anti-God empire. The church's watchman role is to announce what God has declared—including the certainty of judgment and the certainty of salvation—regardless of whether the audience wants to hear it.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land. A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea'—a cryptic title: the wilderness of the sea probably refers to Babylon, surrounded by the Euphrates flood-marshes. The 'wilderness' quality may emphasize desolation to come. 'As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on'—the Negeb's desert storms are sudden, violent, and unstoppable: the image of judgment approaching. 'A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys'—the vision's character: stern, not gentle. The traitor and destroyer are probably Media and Persia, who will end Babylon. 'Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media'—the divine commission to the Medo-Persian forces. 'All the sighing she has caused I bring to an end'—the sighing of Babylon's victims (including Israel) is the grounds for judgment: God has heard the groaning and is acting. Oswalt: the oracle is dense and vivid, like the watchman's breathless report of what he sees approaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see. My heart staggers; horror has overwhelmed me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor'—the prophet's visceral response to the vision. Isaiah does not receive divine judgment as welcome news but as physical torment. The birth-pang metaphor recurs: the onset of judgment is like labor—overwhelming, involuntary, building to a climax. 'I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see'—the prophetic senses overloaded: unable to hear the vision clearly, unable to see it steadily. The intensity of divine revelation produces physical prostration. 'The twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling'—the evening rest (twilight) that the prophet anticipated as respite has become the time of trembling. Childs: the prophet's suffering is not incidental but participatory—he enters into the pain of what he announces, particularly when it involves the suffering of peoples, even enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield! For thus the Lord said to me: “Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink'—the scene of Babylon's feast: the empire at its most comfortable and self-assured. The historical parallel is Belshazzar's feast (Dan. 5), when Babylon was taken while the king feasted. 'Arise, O princes; oil the shield!'—the sudden alarm: from feasting to emergency. The shields were oiled to maintain their leather facing for combat; the command to oil them is a last-minute call to arms. 'Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees'—God commands the appointment of a watchman. The watchman is the ancient equivalent of a surveillance system: stationed on the city wall to report approaching developments. The LORD uses human observation as the medium of prophetic announcement. Motyer: the watchman motif is Isaiah's self-description—he watches, he reports, he does not determine the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently.“ Then he who saw cried out: ”Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently'—the watchman's commission to observe every category of messenger or army approaching: equestrian warriors, donkey-borne traders, camel-mounted messengers. The double 'diligently' stresses the watchman's attention: he must not miss the signal. 'Then he who saw cried out: “Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights”'—the prophet identifies himself as the watchman: stationed, faithful, day and night. 'O Lord, continually'—the continuousness of the prophetic watch. Young: the watchman who prays 'O Lord' turns his post into a prayer station; watching and praying are inseparable in the prophetic calling.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!“ And he answered, ”Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground.“ O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground'—the watchman's report: the doubled 'fallen' is the announcement of total and irreversible collapse. The doubling signals certainty: not 'perhaps will fall' but definitively fallen. 'All the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground'—the gods of Babylon destroyed along with the city: Marduk, Bel, Nabu. The Medo-Persian conquest in 539 BC was the historical fulfillment; Revelation 18:2 applies this to the eschatological Babylon. 'O my threshed and winnowed one'—Isaiah addresses Israel as grain that has been threshed and winnowed: the painful process that separates wheat from chaff. Israel has suffered at Babylon's hand; the announcement of Babylon's fall is addressed specifically to Israel's suffering. 'What I have heard from the LORD of hosts... I announce to you'—the source: not the watchman's own assessment but the word of the LORD of hosts. Oswalt: the prophetic word is authorized precisely because it derives from the LORD of hosts, not from human observation.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?” The watchman says: “Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The oracle concerning Dumah'—Dumah may be a place in Edom or a wordplay on Edom (Edom/Dumah) with the meaning 'silence.' 'One is calling to me from Seir, “Watchman, what time of the night?”'—Seir is Edom's mountain range; the Edomites call out to the watchman (perhaps Isaiah) asking about the duration of the night of judgment. The question is urgent: how much longer? 'Morning comes, and also the night'—the watchman's cryptic answer: morning and night come together. There is both a morning (some relief, some possibility) and also night (judgment persists). 'If you will inquire, inquire; come back again'—the answer is not final; it requires further inquiry. Motyer: the Edom oracle is perhaps the most enigmatic in the book—the ambiguity of the answer matches the ambiguity of Edom's position: not completely under judgment, not yet in the light of dawn. The invitation to come back suggests the door is not permanently closed.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites'—the Dedanites were Arabian traders whose caravan routes ran through the Hejaz. They are lodging in thickets (hiding places) instead of caravanserais—fleeing something. 'To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema'—Tema was an oasis town in northwestern Arabia. The inhabitants are commanded to extend hospitality to the fleeing Dedanite refugees. The commands recall the law of the sabbath-year (Deut. 23:24–25) and the hospitality ethic of the wilderness. Childs: even in the oracles of judgment, the ethic of compassion for the vulnerable continues—the refugees fleeing Assyrian or Babylonian pressure deserve the same care as any other displaced person.

verseByVerse.quote: For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle. For thus the Lord said to me, “Within a year, according to the years of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle'—the reason for the flight: Assyrian military advance into Arabia. The three instruments of war (drawn sword, bent bow, press of battle) catalog the full engagement of military force. 'Within a year, according to the years of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end'—Kedar was a major Arab tribal confederation, famous for its flocks and its archers (v. 17). 'According to the years of a hireling'—the precision of the prophetic timetable; the year is contractually exact, as in 16:14. The glory (kabod) of Kedar—its power, wealth, and reputation—will be annihilated within this precise time. Young: the exact timeframe is a challenge to faith and a test of prophecy: the prophet stakes his credibility on the deadline.

verseByVerse.quote: and the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few'—Kedar was famous for its archers (49:28–29; Ps. 120:5). The warriors who defined Kedar's military reputation are reduced to a remnant. 'For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken'—the oracle's ground and authority: the LORD, God of Israel. Not a god of Arabia, not a Mesopotamian deity, but the LORD of Israel—who governs all nations, including the Arab tribal confederations of the distant desert. Motyer: the closing formula is the prophetic seal: these words are not human political analysis but divine declaration. The specificity of the prophecy (within a year, few archers) makes its fulfillment verifiable and its source unmistakable.

22.subtitle: The Valley of Vision
22.intro: Overview. Chapter 22 is unique in the oracles-against-the-nations sequence: it is addressed not to a foreign power but to Jerusalem itself, here called “the valley of vision.” The city that has received more revelation than any other is judged precisely for what it did with it. The occasion appears to be a near-miss — perhaps Sennacherib’s siege in 701 BC, when the city was threatened and then inexplicably spared. But instead of weeping and repentance, Jerusalem breaks out in celebration. The chapter also contains a striking personal oracle against the arrogant royal steward Shebna, and a promise about a better servant, Eliakim.

sections.title: The Unrepentant City
sections.commentary:
The rooftops of Jerusalem are full of noise and celebration. The prophet asks: what has happened that everyone has gone up to the housetops? The answer comes with heavy irony: your slain were not killed by the sword or in battle — they fled and were taken. The city’s leaders ran, its defenders scattered. Yet now they celebrate as if they had won.

Isaiah weeps, and asks to be left alone in his grief. He refuses to be comforted. This is not performance but prophetic solidarity with what God sees: a day of tumult, of trampling, of confusion. The Assyrian (or Babylonian) army has assembled; the siege equipment is in place; the city’s own water system has been inspected and prepared. Everything is ready for judgment — and Jerusalem parties.

v. 13 — “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Paul quotes this exact phrase in 1 Cor. 15:32 as the logical conclusion of a life with no resurrection. Isaiah identifies it not as honest hedonism but as hardened unresponsiveness — the refusal to hear what God is saying in the events of the day.

The verdict in verse 14 is solemn: “This iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die.” Some sins have a point of no return — not because forgiveness is impossible in principle, but because the heart has crossed a threshold of deliberate, celebratory rejection of what is plainly true.

sections.title: Shebna and Eliakim
sections.commentary:
The oracle pivots from the city to one man: Shebna, the steward (literally “the one over the house”), who has been cutting himself a grand tomb on the heights. He is building his memorial while the city burns. God will take him up like a ball and hurl him into a wide land, and he will die there far from home. His grand tomb will be empty.

In his place God will call Eliakim, on whom he will hang “the key of the house of David” — authority to open and shut, to admit and exclude. Revelation 3:7 applies this language directly to Christ: “the words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens.” Eliakim is a type whose antitype fills the office perfectly.

v. 22 — “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David.” A key on the shoulder was a mark of stewardship over the royal household — physical, weighty, impossible to overlook. The image passes through Isaiah into Revelation as the defining picture of Christ’s absolute authority over access to God.

keyVerse.quote: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.”
keyVerse.note: What begins as a personnel change in Hezekiah’s court becomes one of the richest Christological images in the Old Testament. Rev. 3:7 places this language on the lips of the risen Christ. No one approaches the Father except through him; no one is excluded who comes through him.

22.reflection: Jerusalem celebrated survival without repentance. The near-miss became a party rather than a turning point. Is there a situation in your life where God has been merciful and you have responded with relief rather than return? What would true repentance look like in that situation now?
22.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning the valley of vision. What do you mean that you have gone up, all of you, to the housetops, <sup>2</sup>you who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town? Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle. <sup>3</sup>All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured. All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away. <sup>4</sup>Therefore I said: "Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people." <sup>5</sup>For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains. <sup>6</sup>And Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. <sup>7</sup>Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates. <sup>8</sup>He has taken away the covering of Judah. In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest, <sup>9</sup>and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many. You collected the waters of the lower pool, <sup>10</sup>and you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. <sup>11</sup>You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago. <sup>12</sup>In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth; <sup>13</sup>and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine. "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." <sup>14</sup>The LORD of hosts has revealed himself in my ears: "Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die," says the Lord GOD of hosts. <sup>15</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD of hosts, "Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household, and say to him: <sup>16</sup>What have you to do here, and whom have you here, that you have cut out here a tomb for yourself, you who cut out a tomb on the height and carve a dwelling for yourself in the rock? <sup>17</sup>Behold, the LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man. He will seize firm hold on you <sup>18</sup>and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land. There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house. <sup>19</sup>I will thrust you from your office, and you will be pulled down from your station. <sup>20</sup>In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, <sup>21</sup>and I will clothe him with your robe, and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand. And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. <sup>22</sup>And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. <sup>23</sup>And I will fasten him like a peg in a secure place, and he will become a throne of honor to his father's house. <sup>24</sup>And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons. <sup>25</sup>In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off, for the LORD has spoken."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Oracle About the Valley of Vision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 22 is directed not against a foreign nation but against Jerusalem itself—the 'valley of vision' (the hollow between the hills of Jerusalem). The chapter describes the city's response to imminent siege: not repentance and trust in God but reckless celebration ('let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,' v. 13). The oracle ends with the displacement of Shebna (a royal steward) by Eliakim, who bears the key of David.
verseByVerse.examples: The key of David (v. 22) became a central image in Christian eschatology (Rev. 3:7). The peg in a sure place (vv. 23–25) and its subsequent pulling out warns against placing ultimate trust in any human administrator, however faithful. Christ alone is the peg that never gives way.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the valley of vision. What is wrong with you now, that you have all gone up to the housetops, you who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town? Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The oracle concerning the valley of vision'—Jerusalem is described by two names: valley (geographically accurate—Jerusalem sits in a valley surrounded by hills) and vision (because it is the place where prophetic vision is given). 'What is wrong with you now, that you have all gone up to the housetops'—the prophet confronts the mood of celebration he sees: the whole city on its rooftops, shouting and exulting. 'You who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town'—three descriptions of unwarranted celebration. 'Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle'—those who died in the crisis were not killed in battle but fled or died of other causes; their deaths are still dishonoring even if not heroic. Oswalt: the city celebrates a deliverance without acknowledging the Deliverer—the theological diagnosis begins immediately.

verseByVerse.quote: All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured. All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away. Therefore I said: “Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured'—the leaders who should have stood their ground fled, and were captured anyway—without even fighting. The double shame: cowardice and futility. 'All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away'—flight accomplished nothing; the fugitives were caught at the far end of their flight. 'Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears'—the prophet's grief for Jerusalem. Unlike the Babylon oracle's astonishment or the Moab oracle's lament, here Isaiah mourns for his own people. 'Concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people'—the most intimate grief: 'my people.' This is not the distant mourning of an observer but the personal grief of one who belongs to the community being judged. Childs: the prophet weeps for Jerusalem as Jeremiah will weep—from within the community, not above it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains. And Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision'—the Day of the LORD inverted: instead of coming to Jerusalem's defense, the Day falls on Jerusalem. 'A battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains'—the siege: walls battered, voices echoing off the surrounding hills. 'Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield'—the foreign soldiers in Assyria's multinational army: Elam (ancient Persia) with arrows; Kir (probably in Mesopotamia) with shields. The city is surrounded by the gathered armies of nations. Young: the specific nations named indicate the coalition character of Assyrian forces—Israel's God allows the nations to serve as his instrument against his own city.

verseByVerse.quote: Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates. He has taken away the covering of Judah. In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates'—the Assyrian army occupies Jerusalem's surrounding valleys and blocks its gates. The beautiful valleys of Judah—once sites of agriculture and pastoral life—are filled with enemy military hardware. 'He has taken away the covering of Judah'—the protective covering (masekh): God's providential protection that sheltered Judah from the full force of enemy attack is removed. 'In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest'—the House of the Forest of Lebanon was Solomon's armory (1 Kings 7:2–5), storing shields and weapons. The city turns to its arsenal rather than to its God. Motyer: looking to the armory instead of to the Maker is the precise spiritual failure Isaiah has been diagnosing throughout the book.

verseByVerse.quote: and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many. You collected the waters of the lower pool, and you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You saw that the breaches of the city of David were many'—the multiple gaps in Jerusalem's walls created by the siege. The city's defenders responded with emergency fortification. 'You collected the waters of the lower pool'—the famous Siloam tunnel of Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chron. 32:30): cutting a tunnel through solid rock to secure Jerusalem's water supply. An extraordinary engineering achievement. 'You counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall'—the drastic measure: demolishing houses to use their stones for emergency wall repairs. Oswalt: the emergency measures are not wrong in themselves—Hezekiah's tunnel is praised in 2 Kings—but vv. 11–12 will reveal what was not done alongside these practical preparations: looking to God.

verseByVerse.quote: You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago. In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool'—another hydraulic engineering reference: the reservoir between the city walls for water storage. 'But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago'—the decisive failure: the crisis was God's doing (he planned it long ago), and the appropriate response was to look to him. Instead Jerusalem looked to its engineering. 'In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth'—God's own reading of the moment: this is a moment for national repentance, for the full outward expression of grief. The city responded with celebration; God called for mourning. Childs: the inversion of appropriate response is Isaiah's core critique—the city knew how to cry out to God in crisis (cf. Hezekiah's prayer in ch. 37) but chose not to.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine. “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” The LORD of hosts has revealed himself in my ears: “Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die,” says the Lord GOD of hosts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'And behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine'—instead of repentance, a feast. The city celebrated the lifting of the siege with a party. 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'—the philosophy of hedonism in the face of death: since judgment may come, seize pleasure now. Paul quotes this phrase in 1 Cor. 15:32 as the logical conclusion of a worldview without resurrection. 'Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die'—the gravest word in the chapter: atonement withheld. The sin of unrepentant celebration in God's judgment has reached the point where no atoning offering will cover it. Motyer: this is the declaration that mercy has been irrevocably refused—not because God withdrew it arbitrarily but because the people's deliberate choice of pleasure over repentance made atonement inapplicable.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD of hosts, “Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household, and say to him: What have you to do here, and whom have you here, that you have cut out here a tomb for yourself, you who cut out a tomb on the height and carve a dwelling for yourself in the rock? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household'—the oracle shifts to an individual judgment: Shebna, the royal steward (perhaps prime minister). His name and office are given precisely. 'What have you to do here, and whom have you here'—the double question exposes his presumption: by what authority does he act, and what connections justify his position? 'That you have cut out here a tomb for yourself, you who cut out a tomb on the height and carve a dwelling for yourself in the rock?'—Shebna's sin: cutting an elaborate rock-cut tomb in the aristocratic area (probably the Kidron Valley). He is securing his legacy in Jerusalem's prestigious burial ground while his administrative failures contributed to the crisis. Oswalt: the tomb represents the misalignment between Shebna's self-perception (important enough for a prominent tomb) and his actual service to God and country.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man. He will seize firm hold on you and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land. There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man'—the divine action against Shebna: hurled (talpelekha), whirled (atol), thrown like a ball. The threefold action of expulsion is the opposite of his elaborate self-establishment. 'He will seize firm hold on you and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land'—the image of God as a sling or catapult: Shebna is the projectile hurled out of Jerusalem into exile. 'There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house'—he dies in exile, far from his carefully prepared tomb. His chariots—the sign of status—lie with him in a foreign land. 'You shame of your master's house'—his administration has been an embarrassment to the Davidic house he served. Young: the shame of the steward is the shame of the dynasty he misrepresented.

verseByVerse.quote: I will thrust you from your office, and you will be pulled down from your station. In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will thrust you from your office, and you will be pulled down from your station'—the divine displacement: the same God who elevated Shebna removes him. Office (matzab) and station (ma'amad) are taken from him; others will fill them. 'In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah'—the replacement named. Eliakim (meaning 'God raises up') will succeed Shebna. 'My servant'—the same title used of Isaiah in 20:3 and anticipating the Servant songs. Eliakim is summoned by God's personal calling (I will call), not by political maneuver. Motyer: the contrast between Shebna's self-aggrandizement and Eliakim's divine calling captures the difference between self-appointed ministry and God-appointed service.

verseByVerse.quote: and I will clothe him with your robe and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand. And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will clothe him with your robe and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand'—the transfer of office through the transfer of garments and authority: the robe, sash, and governmental power are moved from Shebna to Eliakim. 'He shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah'—the pastoral dimension of political office: the good steward is a father figure. 'I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David'—the key of David: the symbol of authority over the royal household. 'He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open'—absolute authority in his domain: what he opens stands open, what he closes remains closed. Revelation 3:7 applies this text to Christ—he holds the key of David eternally. Childs: the Eliakim passage points beyond its immediate reference to the one administrator who perfectly fulfills the servant-father role.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will fasten him like a peg in a sure place, and he will become a throne of honor to his father's house. And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will fasten him like a peg in a sure place, and he will become a throne of honor to his father's house'—the peg hammered into the wall for hanging items: secure, functional, honorable. Eliakim as peg is the center of support for the entire family. 'And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons'—the danger of a peg's success: everything gets hung on it. The honor, the family's reputation, the various relatives and clients—all attached to Eliakim's position. Motyer: the peg metaphor warns that even good appointments can be overwhelmed by excessive dependence—when a peg bears too much, it gives way.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, the peg that was fastened in a sure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off, for the LORD has spoken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The peg that was fastened in a sure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall'—the shocking reversal: even the sure-placed peg eventually gives way. Whether this refers to Eliakim's own eventual failure or to Shebna (whose peg will fall), the theological point is clear: no human administrator—however faithful—is the final solution. 'And the load that was on it will be cut off, for the LORD has spoken'—everything hung on the peg falls with it. Webb: the warning that even the best peg gives way is the book's reminder that no human figure can bear the weight of the key of David permanently. Only Christ, to whom Revelation 3:7 applies this text without the caveat of failure, is the peg that never gives way.

23.subtitle: The Oracle Against Tyre
23.intro: Overview. Tyre was the commercial capital of the ancient world — the great Phoenician port whose ships connected Egypt, Canaan, Spain, and the Greek islands. Its fall would be like the collapse of a global financial center. Isaiah’s oracle against it (the last of the series begun in chapter 13) is not merely a military prediction but a theological meditation: what happens when the city that made itself indispensable is removed? The chapter ends with a surprising note: after seventy years, Tyre’s commerce will resume — and its profits will be consecrated to the LORD.

sections.title: The Fall of the Merchant City
sections.commentary:
Ships returning to Tyre from Tarshish (likely Spain, the far western edge of the known world) will find no harbor, no house, no city. The news reaches Cyprus; it reaches Egypt; the sea itself mourns. Tyre is called “the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes” — a city so wealthy it made kings. Now its makers of purple cloth are silent.

The agent of judgment is Babylon (v. 13), whose armies will lay siege and bring it down. The theological point is pressed in verse 9: the LORD of hosts has planned it, “to defile the pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth.” Tyre is not judged for being a trading city but for the pride that made commerce an end in itself — the assumption that prosperity is self-generated and self-sustaining.

v. 9 — “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pride of all glory.” This phrase gathers the entire oracles-against-the-nations sequence into one sentence. The common thread in Babylon, Assyria, Moab, and Tyre is pride — the assumption that human achievement is the ultimate story. God’s purpose, running through all these judgments, is to defile that assumption.

sections.title: Seventy Years and Restoration
sections.commentary:
After seventy years — an echo of Jeremiah’s number for Babylon’s dominion — Tyre will be forgotten and then restored. Isaiah uses a striking metaphor: Tyre will be like a forgotten prostitute, taking up her harp and singing to attract customers again, going back to her trade. The image is deliberately undignified: commerce for its own sake is not ennobled by its resumption.

But the oracle ends with an unexpected consecration: Tyre’s profits will not be stored for itself but will be “holy to the LORD” and used to feed those who dwell before him. Commerce redeemed becomes service. The wealth of the nations, purged of its pride, flows at last toward God. It is a small seed of the larger vision in Isaiah 60–62.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth.”
keyVerse.note: The oracles against the nations are not vindictive but clarifying. God is not against cities or commerce; he is against the pride that refuses to acknowledge him as the source of all prosperity. Every judgment in chapters 13–23 is a reorientation of glory toward its proper object.

23.reflection: Tyre’s commerce was eventually consecrated rather than abolished. God’s goal is not the destruction of human achievement but its reorientation. What gifts, skills, or resources in your life are currently operating for self-glorification — and what would it look like to consecrate them?

From the land of Cyprus it is revealed to them. <sup>2</sup>Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you. <sup>3</sup>And on many waters your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile; you were the merchant of the nations. <sup>4</sup>Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea, saying: "I have neither labored nor given birth, I have neither reared young men nor brought up young women." <sup>5</sup>When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre. <sup>6</sup>Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coast! <sup>7</sup>Is this your exultant city whose origin is from days of old, whose feet carried her to settle far away? <sup>8</sup>Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth? <sup>9</sup>The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth. <sup>10</sup>Cross over your land like the Nile, O daughter of Tarshish; there is no restraint anymore. <sup>11</sup>He has stretched out his hand over the sea; he has shaken the kingdoms; the LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds. <sup>12</sup>And he said: "You will no more exult, O oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon; arise, cross over to Cyprus, even there you will have no rest." <sup>13</sup>Behold the land of the Chaldeans! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered." <sup>17</sup>At the end of seventy years, the LORD will visit Tyre, and she will return to her wages and will prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth. <sup>18</sup>Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD. It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 23 closes the oracles against the nations section (ch. 13–23) with the oracle against Tyre, the great Phoenician commercial city. Tyre was the center of Mediterranean trade—the New York or London of the ancient world. Its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar (and later Alexander the Great) demonstrated that commercial empire is no more exempt from divine judgment than military empire.
verseByVerse.examples: The church must navigate the Tyre oracle carefully: commercial activity is not inherently sinful, but commercial empire that makes itself ultimate and feeds only itself is under judgment. The transformation of Tyre's gain into gift to the LORD (v. 18) pictures the transformation of all human activity in the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor! From the land of Cyprus it is revealed to them. Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor!'—the ships of Tarshish (the great commercial vessels of the western Mediterranean) are called to mourn because their home port is destroyed. No harbor means no trade; no trade means the ships are purposeless. 'From the land of Cyprus it is revealed to them'—the news reaches the ships while they are at sea, off Cyprus: they learn en route that their destination no longer exists. 'Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you'—Sidon was Tyre's sister city; together the Phoenician cities dominated Mediterranean trade. 'Have filled you' means Sidon filled the coastland with commercial activity. Oswalt: the oracle opens with the viewpoint of those dependent on Tyre's commercial infrastructure—the sailors learning mid-voyage that their world has ended.

verseByVerse.quote: and on many waters your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile; you were the merchant of the nations. Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea, saying: “I have neither labored nor given birth, I have neither reared young men nor brought up young women.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile'—Tyre was the commercial intermediary for Egyptian grain traded across the Mediterranean. Shihor is a branch of the Nile; its grain was Tyre's major commodity. 'You were the merchant of the nations'—the supreme commercial title: not a local market but the global trader. 'Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea'—Sidon mourns because Tyre (the stronghold of the sea) announces its own desolation in personification: 'I have neither labored nor given birth, I have neither reared young men nor brought up young women'—the sea, Tyre's mother, laments her childlessness. The city that once produced sailors and merchants produces nothing. Childs: the anthropomorphization of the sea announcing childlessness captures the emptiness of Tyre's commercial collapse—the mother of trade produces no more offspring.

verseByVerse.quote: When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre. Pass over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coast! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre'—Egypt depended on Tyre as its commercial intermediary; Tyre's fall disrupts the Egyptian export trade in grain and luxury goods. 'Pass over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coast!'—the coastland inhabitants are commanded to emigrate: with Tyre gone, the Mediterranean coast has no commercial center. They must go all the way to Tarshish (Spain) to find what was available in Tyre. 'Wail, O inhabitants of the coast!'—the double address: first commanded to flee, then commanded to mourn. The mourning is appropriate; the flight may be necessary. Motyer: the command to flee and wail simultaneously captures the double response to catastrophe—escape the immediate danger while mourning the permanent loss.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this your exultant city whose origin is from days of old, whose feet carried her to settle far away? Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Is this your exultant city whose origin is from days of old'—the shocked question: is this the city of ancient pride? The contrast between Tyre's glorious antiquity and its present desolation is the measure of the fall. 'Whose feet carried her to settle far away'—Tyre's colonial expansion: she planted trading colonies throughout the Mediterranean (Carthage, the most famous, was a Tyrian foundation). 'Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns?'—another shocked question: who could plan this? 'The bestower of crowns' captures Tyre's commercial supremacy: she crowned kings through the economic power of trade. 'Whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth'—commercial honorifics: merchants with the status of princes, traders with the honor of nobility. Young: the catalog of Tyre's former greatness makes the judgment more complete—everything that made Tyre great is taken.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth. Cross over to your own land, O daughter of Tarshish; there is no restraint anymore. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth'—the answer to v. 8's question: the LORD of hosts is the one who planned Tyre's fall. The purpose is theological: to defile (challel, profane) the pride of glory. Commercial pride—like military pride—falls under the same divine judgment of ch. 2. 'To dishonor all the honored of the earth'—what human commerce honored (the merchants who were princes), God dishonors. 'Cross over to your own land, O daughter of Tarshish; there is no restraint anymore'—the direction reverses: instead of ships from Tarshish going to Tyre, ships from Tyre go to Tarshish. The commercial flow has inverted. Oswalt: God's purpose against Tyre is not commercial but theological—the same leveling of pride that applies to every form of human self-exaltation.

verseByVerse.quote: He has stretched out his hand over the sea; he has shaken the kingdoms; the LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds. And he said: “You will no more exult, O oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon; arise, cross over to Cyprus; even there you will have no rest.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He has stretched out his hand over the sea; he has shaken the kingdoms'—the outstretched hand of God (9:12 etc.) extended now to the sea, Tyre's domain. The sea-kingdom is shaken as land-kingdoms are shaken. 'The LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds'—Tyre and Sidon are the Canaanite cities par excellence; the command against Canaan (long delayed since the conquest) now includes the Phoenician coast. 'You will no more exult, O oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon'—the address to Sidon as a virgin daughter: Sidon, which thought itself beyond judgment (a virgin never conquered), is now oppressed. 'Arise, cross over to Cyprus; even there you will have no rest'—flight to Cyprus provides no permanent refuge. The judgment follows. Motyer: no commercial alternative to Jerusalem exists; the sea-empire and its refuges all fail.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold the land of the Chaldeans! This is the people that was not; Assyria destined it for wild beasts. They erected their siege towers, they stripped her palaces bare, they made her a ruin. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Behold the land of the Chaldeans! This is the people that was not'—the Chaldeans (Babylonians) were originally not a great people but became the instrument of Tyre's destruction. 'Assyria destined it for wild beasts'—perhaps referring to Sennacherib's earlier devastation of Babylon (689 BC), which was later restored: a people that was once nothing became great enough to destroy Tyre. 'They erected their siege towers, they stripped her palaces bare, they made her a ruin'—the methodical siege: towers, stripping, ruination. 'Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste'—the refrain from v. 1 returns, bracketing the oracle's middle section. The ships still wail; the stronghold is still ruined. Childs: the refrain creates a frame that traps the ships in perpetual mourning—the loss is not temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king. At the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute: “Take a harp; go about the city, O forgotten prostitute! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king'—the seventy years matches the seventy years of Babylon's dominance (Jer. 25:11; 29:10). 'Like the days of one king'—a human lifetime, or the span of one dynasty. During this period Tyre is forgotten: the bustling commercial center silent and invisible. 'It will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute'—Tyre is compared to a prostitute: not because of sexual immorality but because she has sold herself commercially, trading her services to every nation. 'Take a harp; go about the city, O forgotten prostitute! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered'—the prostitute's strategy for restoring her clientele: music to attract attention. Tyre will use commercial re-engagement to rebuild her commercial reputation. Oswalt: the comparison is uncomfortable but precise—commerce that makes itself available to any buyer for profit has the structure of prostitution.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of seventy years, the LORD will visit Tyre, and she will return to her wages and will prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth. Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD. It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'At the end of seventy years, the LORD will visit Tyre, and she will return to her wages and will prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world'—the restoration of commercial activity, described with the same unflattering metaphor: prostitution. Trade resumes; the commercial impulse survives judgment. 'Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD'—the most surprising line of the oracle: what was 'wages of prostitution' (trade driven by self-interest) becomes holy to the LORD. The transformation is total: the same commercial activity now directed to God's purposes. 'It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD'—the commercial wealth not accumulated (Tyre's old pattern) but distributed to those who serve God. Motyer: the eschatological conversion of Tyre's commerce into holy provision for God's worshippers is the final statement about the purpose of economic activity—it exists to serve the community of faith, not to accumulate private wealth.

24.subtitle: The LORD’s Devastation of the Earth
24.intro: Overview. With chapter 24 the focus widens dramatically from individual nations to the whole earth. Sometimes called the “Isaiah Apocalypse,” chapters 24–27 form a distinct unit dealing with universal judgment and ultimate renewal. Chapter 24 describes the desolation of the earth in terms that deliberately echo the flood narrative — a covenant broken, creation undone — before closing with a vision of the LORD reigning on Mount Zion. It is not primarily about a specific historical event but about the logic of history itself: what happens when human civilization persistently violates the terms of its existence.

sections.title: The Earth Laid Waste
sections.commentary:
The opening is sweeping and egalitarian in the worst possible way: God will empty the earth and twist its surface, and it will be the same for everyone — priest and people, master and servant, buyer and seller, lender and borrower. All social distinctions collapse under universal judgment. The reason is given in verse 5: the earth is defiled under its inhabitants “because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant.” The language draws on Noahic covenant categories: the earth’s desolation is the consequence of civilization’s persistent rejection of its creaturely status.

v. 5 — “The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant.” The “everlasting covenant” here is almost certainly the Noahic covenant (Gen. 9:1–17), which bound all humanity, not just Israel. The judgment is universal because the violation is universal — not ethnic but human.

The joy of the city has ceased, the wine dries up, the music stops. In the middle of chapter 24 there is a haunting image: in the city of chaos, the gates are battered into desolation. “For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done” — the remnant image again. Something is left, but barely.

sections.title: Songs in the Midst of Judgment
sections.commentary:
From the west, voices lift up. From the east, they glorify the LORD. From the coastlands: “Glory to the Righteous One.” Isaiah hears these and collapses: “But I say, I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me!” The contrast is jarring — songs of praise interrupted by the prophet’s grief at the ongoing treachery of those still on the earth. The praises are real and deserved; the grief is also real and warranted. The two exist together until the judgment is complete.

The chapter ends with cosmic upheaval — the host of heaven and the kings of the earth gathered, imprisoned, punished. Then: “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.” The chapter that began with universal desolation ends with God on his throne. The devastation is not the last word; the reign is.

v. 23 — “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem.” This anticipates the great vision of chapters 65–66 and the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21–22. All the oracles against the nations — all the demolition of human pride — have been in service of this: the earth cleared for God’s unchallenged reign.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders, for the LORD of hosts will reign.”
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of comprehensive devastation, this sentence arrives like a foundation stone. The point of all the undoing is not nihilism but preparation — the clearing of the earth for the reign that cannot be shaken. It is the same movement John sees in Revelation: the bowls of wrath followed by the marriage supper of the Lamb.

24.theology: Creation, Covenant, and Judgment. Chapter 24 ties judgment to covenant violation in creation terms, not merely national terms. The “everlasting covenant” of verse 5 reaches back to Noah and forward to all humanity. This is not Israel’s judgment but the world’s judgment — grounded in the creational order that God established and humanity persistently subverts. Reformed theology has always insisted that general revelation leaves all people without excuse (Rom. 1:20), and Isaiah 24 shows what that accountability looks like at scale.
24.reflection: Isaiah hears songs of praise and immediately collapses in grief — both responses are appropriate to the same reality. How do you hold together genuine worship with honest lament over the state of the world? Which comes more naturally to you, and which do you need to cultivate?
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants. <sup>2</sup>And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor. <sup>3</sup>The earth shall be utterly empty and utterly plundered; for the LORD has spoken this word. <sup>4</sup>The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and withers; the highest people of the earth languish. <sup>5</sup>The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant. <sup>6</sup>Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt; therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched, and few men are left. <sup>7</sup>The wine mourns, the vine languishes, all the merry-hearted sigh. <sup>8</sup>The mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled. <sup>9</sup>No more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it. <sup>10</sup>The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter. <sup>11</sup>There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished. <sup>12</sup>Desolation is left in the city; the gates are battered into ruins. <sup>13</sup>For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done. <sup>14</sup>They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west. <sup>15</sup>Therefore in the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. <sup>16</sup>From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One. But I say, "I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed." <sup>17</sup>Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth! <sup>18</sup>He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble. <sup>19</sup>The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken. <sup>20</sup>The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again. <sup>21</sup>On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth. <sup>22</sup>They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished. <sup>23</sup>Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — The Isaiah Apocalypse (Part 1): The Devastated Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 24–27 are often called 'the Isaiah Apocalypse'—a sustained vision of cosmic judgment and cosmic renewal that exceeds any single historical event. Chapter 24 describes the undoing of the created order: the earth desolate, the population scattered, the covenant violated, the joy of creation silenced, the foundations of earth shaking. It ends with the LORD reigning on Mount Zion, shaming the sun and moon with his glory.
verseByVerse.examples: The church reads ch. 24 as both warning and promise: this is where history is heading—not endless progress but divine judgment of the earth's covenant-violation. The few survivors who lift up their voice from 'the west' and the 'islands of the sea' are the scattered, singing church of every age.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants. And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants'—three divine actions: empty, make desolate, twist (scatter or distort). The emptying of the earth reverses the filling of creation (Gen. 1:28).
