'And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master'—the six pairs that follow cover every social category: religious (people/priest), economic (slave/master, buyer/seller, lender/borrower, creditor/debtor), and gender (maid/mistress). The judgment is leveling: no category, no relationship, no social structure is exempt. Childs: the pairs are a complete sociology of the human world—the judgment erases every distinction built by civilization, leaving all equally under the Creator's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth shall be utterly empty and utterly plundered; for the LORD has spoken this word. The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and withers; the highest people of the earth languish. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The earth shall be utterly empty and utterly plundered; for the LORD has spoken this word'—the doubled 'utterly' intensifies the totality: nothing left, nothing retained. The ground for this certainty: the LORD has spoken. 'The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and withers; the highest people of the earth languish'—three subjects of withering: the earth (eretz, the specific land), the world (tebel, the inhabited world), and the highest people (meron ha-aretz, the exalted ones of the earth). The highest people—those most invested in the world's structures—languish most visibly. Motyer: the withering of the exalted mirrors the withering of the earth—what is lifted up in the human order falls with the natural order under judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt; therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched, and few men are left. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant'—the theological diagnosis: the earth is defiled (khaniph: profaned) by covenant-violation. 'The everlasting covenant' (berit olam) is probably the Noahic covenant (Gen. 9:16), which bound all humanity (not just Israel) to basic moral law. The earth's desolation is the consequence of universal covenant violation, not merely Israel's particular failures. 'Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt'—the curse-consequence of covenant violation (Deut. 27–28 applied universally). 'Therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched, and few men are left'—the depopulation of judgment: scorched (by drought, war, famine) until few remain. Young: the 'few' recalls the remnant theology throughout Isaiah—judgment is total but never annihilates the last remnant.

verseByVerse.quote: The wine mourns, the vine languishes, all the merry-hearted sigh. The mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The wine mourns, the vine languishes'—the personification of wine as a mourner: the joy-giver mourns the loss of joy. The vine that produces wine is the vine of creation-order; its languishing is the languishing of created blessing. 'All the merry-hearted sigh'—those who were characterized by gladness can only sigh now. The reversal from celebration to grief runs through the social fabric. 'The mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled'—three instruments of celebration silenced: tambourine (percussion), joyful noise (vocal), lyre (strings). The complete musical vocabulary of celebration is absent. Oswalt: the silencing of music is the silencing of human culture at its most festive; the judgment attacks joy itself at its most innocent expression.

verseByVerse.quote: No more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it. The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'No more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it'—the transformation of wine from joy to bitterness. The same drink that was the accompaniment of celebration has become repugnant. 'The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter'—the city (tohu, chaos/wasteland—the same word as Gen. 1:2 'without form and void') has become what the earth was before creation. The shut houses are houses of death: no community, no coming and going, no hospitality. Childs: the city of chaos (ir tohu) is the reversal of the city of righteousness promised in 1:26—the judgment deconstructs what the creation and covenant built.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished. Desolation is left in the city; the gates are battered into ruins. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished'—the grief for the absence of joy: people cry out for what is gone, not merely for physical necessities but for gladness itself. 'All joy has grown dark'—joy is a light that has been extinguished; darkness is the absence of joy as well as the absence of light. 'The gladness of the earth is banished'—sent into exile like the population: joy has been deported. 'Desolation is left in the city; the gates are battered into ruins'—the city's entry-points (gates) destroyed: what was open to commerce and community is broken. Young: the ruins of the gate signal the end of the city as a functioning social organism—gates are where justice, commerce, and community life were transacted.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done. They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done'—the olive-tree image from 17:6 and the gleaning image from 17:5–6: the remnant as the few remaining after thorough harvesting. The few berries left after the olive-beating are the remnant who survive. 'They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west'—the sudden reversal: from mourning to singing. The scattered remnant (from the west and the sea-islands, v. 15) sings over the Lord's majesty. 'The majesty of the LORD'—the glory that was hidden in the judgment now becomes the content of the remnant's praise. Motyer: the singing remnant in the midst of desolation is Isaiah's recurring eschatological hope—the few who survive become the first-fruits of the new creation's song.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore in the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One. But I say, “I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD'—east and west (coastlands), north and south implicit: the four directions of the earth summoned to praise. 'From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One'—the Righteous One (tsaddiq) is a divine title: the songs are addressed to the righteous God. 'But I say, “I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me!”'—the prophet's sudden intrusion of grief amid the praise. He hears the distant songs but also sees the immediate reality: the traitors are still at work. 'For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed'—the triple use of the treachery root (bagged): relentless human faithlessness. Childs: the prophet oscillates between the eschatological hope (the distant song) and the present reality (the traitors)—both are simultaneously true in prophetic vision.

verseByVerse.quote: Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth! He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth!'—the triple trap of judgment: terror (pahad), pit (pahat), snare (pakh). The wordplay in Hebrew is phonetically intense: pahad-pahat-pakh. No direction of escape: flight from terror leads to the pit; climbing out of the pit leads to the snare. 'For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble'—the cosmic dimensions of the judgment: the windows of heaven (the source of the flood in Gen. 7:11) opened again; the earth's foundations trembling. The judgment deconstructs both the upper waters and the lower earth—creation is being undone. Young: the judgment of ch. 24 is the maximum possible expression of divine wrath against creation's covenant-violation—not a local event but a cosmic undoing.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken. The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken'—the triple earthquake description: broken (ra'ah), split (pororah), shaken (mot titmoteth). The repetition of earth (eretz) three times drives the cosmic scope home. 'The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut'—two images of instability: the drunkard who cannot walk straight, the temporary shelter (sukkah) that sways in the wind. The solid earth becomes as unreliable as a drunk and as flimsy as a tent. 'Its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again'—the earth itself bears the weight of human sin; the cumulative burden of cosmic covenant-violation brings it down. 'It falls, and will not rise again'—a finality: this fall is permanent, not temporary. Oswalt: the earth falling and not rising again anticipates the new heaven and new earth of ch. 65–66 and Rev. 21.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth. They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth'—the two-level judgment: the spiritual powers ('host of heaven'—perhaps angelic or demonic powers behind the nations, cf. Dan. 10) and the earthly rulers. Both levels of authority that opposed God's purposes are judged simultaneously. 'They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison'—the imprisonment: not immediate execution but confinement. The pit and prison recall the Abyss of Revelation 20:1–3. 'After many days they will be punished'—the delay between imprisonment and final punishment: history continues while the prisoners wait. Motyer: the two-level judgment (heaven and earth) ensures that no power that resisted God's purposes escapes—neither the visible (kings) nor the invisible (host of heaven).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed'—the luminaries that were darkened at the judgment (13:10) are here not merely darkened but ashamed: their own light is eclipsed by something greater. 'For the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem'—the reason for the celestial shame: the LORD himself reigns visibly on Zion. His glory outshines the sun and moon. 'And his glory will be before his elders'—the elders (probably the covenant representatives of the new community, recalling Ex. 24:9–11 where the elders saw God) witness the divine glory directly. Childs: the chapter that began with cosmic desolation ends with cosmic coronation—the same LORD who emptied the earth now fills Zion with his glory. The arc from ch. 24's opening devastation to its closing enthronement is the arc of the entire book: judgment preceding and producing the reign of God.

25.subtitle: A Feast on the Mountain
25.intro: Overview. Chapter 25 is one of the high points of Isaiah — a psalm of praise for what God has done and will do, including two of the most stunning promises in the Old Testament: the abolition of death and the wiping away of every tear. After the cosmic devastation of chapter 24, God throws a banquet. The chapter also contains a compact oracle against Moab (vv. 10–12), which serves as a foil to highlight the contrast between those who trust in the LORD and those who trust in their own strength.

sections.title: Praise for the Faithful God
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with first-person praise: “O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you.” It is notable that individual praise comes here, after the widest-angle vision of chapters 13–24. The movement is not from personal piety to cosmic concern but the reverse: having seen what God will do to the whole earth, the prophet responds personally. The grounds for praise are specific: God has done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. The destroyed city (the fortified city of the nations, v. 2) becomes a heap; the strong peoples glorify him; the ruthless nations fear him.

Verses 4–5 describe what God has been to the poor and needy: a stronghold, a shelter from the storm, shade from the heat. When the ruthless come like a winter rainstorm, God is the wall that deflects them. The theology of divine protection is always concrete in Isaiah: not abstract comfort but a specific interposition between the vulnerable and the force bearing down on them.

sections.title: The Feast, the Veil, and the Death of Death
sections.commentary:
On this mountain — Zion, the place of God’s reign — God will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine. The universality is emphatic: for all peoples, for all nations. The banquet that was only available to Israel in its fullest form is opened to everyone. John’s vision of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9) is the New Testament realization of this promise.

v. 7 — “He will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations.” The veil is interpretive: it is the darkness of ignorance and spiritual blindness that prevents people from seeing reality as it is. Paul picks up this language in 2 Cor. 3:14–16, speaking of the veil over the heart that is removed in Christ. The feast and the lifting of the veil belong together: to eat at God’s table is to see clearly.

Verse 8 stands among the most important sentences in the Old Testament: “He will swallow up death forever.” Paul quotes it directly in 1 Corinthians 15:54 as the word that is fulfilled in the resurrection of Christ. And then: “The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces.” John echoes it in Revelation 21:4. These are not figures of speech; they are the literal program of what God intends to do. Death will not be managed or mitigated but swallowed — consumed by something greater than itself.

sections.title: Moab as Foil
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with a brief, harsh oracle against Moab, who is described as a swimmer flailing in a dunghill. The contrast with the feast is deliberate: those who feast on the mountain are those who trusted the LORD; Moab, representing self-sufficient pride, finds its fortifications brought low and trampled. The joy of verses 6–9 and the judgment of verses 10–12 are two sides of the same reality: the same God who prepares the feast also brings down the proud.

keyVerse.quote: “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth.”
keyVerse.note: This is one of the clearest resurrection promises in the entire Old Testament. “Swallow up death forever” is the language of total, permanent defeat — not death postponed but death ended. Paul places it at the climax of his resurrection argument (1 Cor. 15:54), and John plants it at the center of the new creation (Rev. 21:4). The whole trajectory of redemptive history bends toward this sentence.

25.theology: The Death of Death. Isaiah 25:8 stands at the foundation of the biblical doctrine of resurrection and new creation. It is not a metaphor for spiritual renewal but a literal promise about the fate of death itself. Reformed theology has always held that bodily resurrection is not an add-on to salvation but its culmination — the restoration of the whole person in a redeemed creation. The feast of verse 6 is the eschatological Eucharist, the wedding supper of the Lamb, the culmination of all that the covenant has been building toward. Timothy Keller often noted that Christianity is unique in offering not escape from the material world but its transformation — Isaiah 25 is one of the oldest and clearest biblical grounds for that claim.
25.reflection: God’s response to the devastation of chapter 24 is a banquet. Not a repair program or a recovery plan — a feast. What does it tell you about God that his ultimate answer to the brokenness of the world is abundance and celebration? And which promise from this chapter do you most need to hold onto right now: the feast, the lifted veil, or the end of death and tears?
25.text: <sup>1</sup>O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. <sup>2</sup>For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin; the foreigners' palace is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. <sup>3</sup>Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you. <sup>4</sup>For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat; for the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall, <sup>5</sup>like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down. <sup>6</sup>On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined. <sup>7</sup>And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations. <sup>8</sup>He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken. <sup>9</sup>It will be said on that day, "Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation." <sup>10</sup>For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill. <sup>11</sup>And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands. <sup>12</sup>And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Song of Salvation: Death Swallowed Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 25 is a song of praise celebrating the completion of ch. 24's judgment and anticipating the eschatological salvation. It contains one of the most celebrated promises in all of Scripture: 'He will swallow up death forever' (v. 8). The chapter also includes the great banquet on the mountain (vv. 6–8), which Jesus used as the template for the messianic feast, and a somber conclusion about Moab's pride (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah 25:8 is the mountain-top text of Christian eschatology: death conquered, tears wiped, shame removed. The church confesses this as accomplished in Christ's resurrection and awaiting its final manifestation at the general resurrection. Every funeral and every tear is held in the light of this promise.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin; the foreigners' palace is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things'—the personal declaration of faith: 'my God.' The praise is grounded in specific divine acts ('wonderful things') not in general religious sentiment. 'Plans formed of old, faithful and sure'—the works of God are the execution of his eternal plans: nothing surprised him, nothing deviated from his intention. 'For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin'—the specific act of praise: Babylon's destruction (the paradigm city of judgment, ch. 13–14; 21). The city that was the center of imperial pride is a heap. 'It will never be rebuilt'—the permanence of the judgment echoes the prophecy of 13:19–22. Motyer: the song begins with the personal ('my God') before expanding to the universal—praise is always personal before it is cosmic.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you. For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat; for the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you'—the paradox: the very nations that seemed most beyond God's reach (strong peoples, ruthless nations) become his worshippers. The judgment of the proud city (vv. 1–2) produces the glorification of God among the nations. 'For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress'—the reason the nations glorify God is the same reason throughout Isaiah: his advocacy for the poor and needy. 'A shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat'—the shelter imagery of 4:6 returns: God as protection from every kind of hostile pressure. 'For the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall'—the ruthless attack like a stormwind; God is the wall that deflects it. Childs: the contrast between the strong/ruthless (who are conquered) and the poor/needy (who are protected) is the great reversal at the heart of Isaiah's theology.

verseByVerse.quote: like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down. On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down'—God subdues the nations as a cloud subdues the desert heat: not by violent confrontation but by providing overwhelming covering. The song of the ruthless (their triumphant boasting) is silenced. 'On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined'—the eschatological banquet on Mount Zion. 'All peoples'—the universal guest list; no nation excluded. 'Rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined'—the best possible food: marrow (the richest part of the animal) and refined wine (the clearest, most aged). Jesus' parable of the great banquet (Luke 14:15–24) draws on this text. Oswalt: the feast is not merely an upgrade of earthly luxury but the covenant meal of the new creation—the communion of all peoples with God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations. He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations'—the covering (masekh, also 'the shroud') that has darkened all human perception of God: removed. The nations have been veiled from the truth; the veil is taken away. Paul may echo this in 2 Cor. 3:14–18. 'He will swallow up death forever'—the great promise. The verb is the same as Sheol swallowing (5:14): now God swallows death. Death is consumed by life. 'Forever' (lanetsakh): permanently, to the uttermost, without reversal. 'The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces'—the divine tenderness: the Creator of the universe wiping each face personally. 'The reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth'—the shame of suffering, exile, and apparent abandonment removed. Paul quotes 25:8 in 1 Cor. 15:54; Revelation 21:4 echoes the tear-wiping. Motyer: this is the summit of Old Testament eschatology—and the ground of Christian hope.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be said on that day, “Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation.” For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us'—the confession of patient faith vindicated: the waiting is over. The God they waited for has appeared and acted. 'Let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation'—the joy of the saved: not merely relief but active gladness. The Hebrew yashenu (his salvation) plays on yeshua (Jesus/salvation)—the name of the one in whom this promise is fulfilled. 'For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain'—the protective, resting hand: God's power settled on Zion. 'And Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill'—the sudden, jarring contrast: Moab trampled in a dunghill. The representative of proud nations that refused the invitation (cf. 16:6) is treated with contempt. Childs: the juxtaposition of salvation's joy and Moab's trampling shows that the eschatological salvation is not universal in the sense of automatic—it requires the faith that the saved people exercised ('we have waited').

verseByVerse.quote: And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands. And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands to swim'—Moab swimming (struggling to survive) in the dunghill of v. 10: flailing to escape. The image is grotesque and deliberate: the proud nation reduced to a person drowning in its own mess. 'But the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands'—Moab's two resources: pride (the sin named in 16:6) and the skill of his hands (practical human capability). Both are laid low simultaneously—neither arrogance nor competence can resist divine judgment. 'The high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust'—the same vocabulary as ch. 2:11–17 (high things brought down, lofty things laid low). Motyer: Moab's end is the end of every human project that relies on fortification against God—the wall that seemed impregnable lies in dust.

26.subtitle: The Song of the Strong City
26.intro: Overview. Chapter 26 is a sustained song — partly communal, partly prophetic — celebrating the security of those who trust in the LORD while the lofty city of the nations lies in the dust. It includes one of the clearest Old Testament anticipations of bodily resurrection (v. 19), framed within a meditation on the contrast between God’s reliable character and human weakness. The chapter invites Israel to enter her chambers and wait while God’s judgment passes — an echo of Passover, a foretaste of the final hiding.

sections.title: The City That Trusts
sections.commentary:
The strong city of Israel is contrasted with the lofty city of the nations brought down in chapter 25. What makes the strong city strong is not its walls but its trust: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.” The Hebrew is shalom shalom — doubled peace, complete peace — for the mind (yetser, inclination or imagination) that is stayed on God.

v. 3 — “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.” John MacArthur noted that the word stayed implies something leaning on God for support — not passive acceptance but active, sustained reliance. The peace is not the absence of trouble but a stability that the trouble cannot reach.

Verses 7–9 are among the most honest statements of desire in the entire Bible: “My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you.” The desire for God is itself the fruit of God’s character becoming visible through judgment — when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.

sections.title: Human Weakness and God’s Power
sections.commentary:
The middle section is brutally honest about Israel’s limitations. The wicked do not learn righteousness even when shown grace; they do not see God’s majesty. And Israel itself has accomplished nothing: “We have not achieved any deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen.” The labor-pain image returns: like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out but bears only wind. All of Israel’s effort at self-salvation has produced nothing.

This is not despair but preparation — the emptying that precedes the divine act. God does not share the rescue with a secondary agent; the deliverance must come entirely from him, precisely because human strength has exhausted itself trying.

sections.title: Your Dead Shall Live
sections.commentary:
Into the confession of human futility God speaks: “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!” The resurrection here is explicitly bodily — bodies, dust, awakening. It is addressed to those who have died in covenant with the LORD. The dew of God will fall on the land of the dead and give life. This is not mere national restoration but the earliest clear promise of individual bodily resurrection in Isaiah.

v. 19 — “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise.” The passage is directly in line with Daniel 12:2 (“many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake”) and forms the Old Testament ground for what Paul will develop fully in 1 Corinthians 15. Those who died having produced only wind (v. 18) will be raised by God’s dew (v. 19) — the reversal is total.

The chapter closes with a call to hide: “Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by.” The Passover echo is unmistakable — blood on the doorpost, God passing through to judge, the hidden people emerging into the morning of salvation.

keyVerse.quote: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.”
keyVerse.note: The doubled shalom — peace-peace — is not accidental. It indicates completeness: there is no dimension of a person’s life that this peace does not reach. And it is entirely relational — it belongs to the one whose imagination is anchored in God, not in circumstances. Philippians 4:7 is the New Testament cognate: the peace of God that guards heart and mind in Christ Jesus.

26.reflection: The people in this chapter are told to enter their chambers and hide “for a little while.” There is a season of patient waiting in the darkness that belongs to the life of faith. Where are you right now — in a waiting season, a labor season, or a morning-after season? And what does “staying your mind on God” actually look like in the middle of it?
26.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: "We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. <sup>2</sup>Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in. <sup>3</sup>You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. <sup>4</sup>Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock. <sup>5</sup>For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust. <sup>6</sup>The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy." <sup>7</sup>The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous. <sup>8</sup>In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul. <sup>9</sup>My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness. <sup>10</sup>If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD. <sup>11</sup>O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them. <sup>12</sup>O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works. <sup>13</sup>O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance. <sup>14</sup>They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them. <sup>15</sup>But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land. <sup>16</sup>O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them. <sup>17</sup>Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD; <sup>18</sup>we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. <sup>19</sup>Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead. <sup>20</sup>Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by. <sup>21</sup>For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Song of Trust and the Hope of Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 26 is a song of trust for the redeemed community in the new Jerusalem. It moves from confidence in God's strong city (vv. 1–6) to meditation on walking in the ways of God (vv. 7–11) to lament over past failure (vv. 12–18) to the extraordinary promise of resurrection (v. 19) and the summons to wait out judgment in the safety of God's presence (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah 26:3–4 has anchored the church's spirituality of trust across two millennia: the mind fixed on God receives peace beyond circumstances. Isaiah 26:19 is foundational for resurrection faith. Every funeral liturgy and every Christian statement about eternal life is grounded in promises like this.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah'—the song is eschatological: in that day of God's final victory. It is a communal song—'we'—the redeemed community singing together. 'We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks'—the new Jerusalem: not fortified by stone but by salvation itself. The walls are God's saving acts; the bulwarks are his covenant faithfulness. The city of Babylon that was strong in ch. 13 is now contrasted with the city that is strong in salvation. 'Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in'—the opened gates of the eschatological city: who may enter? The righteous nation that keeps faith (emunim, literally faithfulnesses—the consistently faithful). Childs: the contrast with the shut houses of 24:10 is deliberate—what was closed in judgment is opened in salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you'—shalom shalom: the doubled shalom indicates fullness and completeness of peace. 'Whose mind is stayed on you'—literally whose imagination (yetser) is stayed/supported/leaned (samukh) on you: the inner life oriented toward God. Trust is the condition; peace is the consequence. 'Because he trusts in you'—the causal connection: trust produces peace, not as a psychological technique but as the proper response of a creature to its Creator. 'Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock'—the ground of perpetual trust: the everlasting rock (tsur olamim) does not shift. Motyer: the doubled shalom is the double completeness—peace in circumstances and peace at the deepest level of being. Keller: the 'stayed mind' is not the mind that has stopped thinking but the mind that has anchored its thinking in God's reality.

verseByVerse.quote: For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust. The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city'—the ground for trust: God has already demonstrated his power by humbling the proud city. The vocabulary of ch. 2 (height, lofty) and ch. 24–25 (brought down, cast to dust) is consolidated here. 'He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust'—the threefold laying low emphasizes completeness. 'The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy'—the great reversal: the city that once trampled the poor is now trampled by the poor. The poor who were ground into the face of the millstone (3:15) now walk over the ruins of the grinding empire. Oswalt: the feet of the poor treading on the ruins of the proud city is Isaiah's most concentrated image of the covenantal reversal—the last are first, the trampled trample.

verseByVerse.quote: The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous. In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous'—the level (yashar: straight/upright/level) path of the one who follows God: God actively levels the road for those who walk faithfully with him. 'In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you'—the waiting is not passive resignation but active orientation toward God's revealed way (judgments). The community walks in the path of God's will and waits for his timing. 'Your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul'—the deepest desire is not blessing but God himself: his name (identity and character) and his remembrance (the memorial of his acts). Young: the desire for God's name rather than God's gifts distinguishes mature faith from merely transactional religion—knowing God for himself, not merely for what he provides.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness. If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you'—the night-seeking: the time of darkness (both literal night and the darkness of judgment) is the time of intense spiritual seeking. 'For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness'—the purpose of divine judgment: moral education. Judgment teaches what grace alone may not: the seriousness of righteousness. 'If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness'—a disturbing theological observation: unrestrained grace toward the wicked does not produce righteousness. The wicked require judgment to learn. 'In the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD'—placed in the best possible environment, the wicked still corrupt it. They lack the perception to see God's majesty. Motyer: this verse is the most direct biblical statement about the pedagogical function of judgment—and the limits of grace without discipline.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them. O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it'—the blindness of the wicked to divine activity: the hand of God visible in history is invisible to those who refuse to acknowledge him. 'Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed'—the prayer that the zeal of God becomes undeniably visible to those who now ignore it. 'Let the fire for your adversaries consume them'—not vindictiveness but the recognition that divine justice requires the enemies of God to receive what they have given. 'O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works'—the closing confession: all our works are God's doing. The community has nothing to boast of in itself. Childs: the phrase 'you have done for us all our works' is the most complete statement of divine sovereignty over human action in the book—it is the ground of peace, not of passivity.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance. They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance'—the confession of past idolatry (other lords—Assyria, Babylon, the false gods): but in the new song, only God's name is remembered. 'They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction'—the dead lords in contrast with the living God: Assyria, Babylon, the gods—all dead, all incapable of revival. 'You have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them'—the permanence of the judgment on false lords: they are destroyed and forgotten. Young: the contrast with v. 19 is intentional—the dead lords will not rise; the dead of God's people will. The resurrection is selective: it applies to those who belong to the Resurrector.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land. O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land'—the reversal of the depopulation of judgment: the nation increased again, the borders expanded. 'You have increased the nation' is doubled for emphasis; God's expanding of the covenant community is inseparable from his own glorification. 'O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them'—the confession of what it took to produce prayer: distress and discipline. The people prayed only when under pressure. 'Whispered prayer' (lahash)—the quiet, desperate murmuring of people who have nowhere else to turn. Motyer: even inadequate prayer—the whisper of the distressed—God receives. The discipline that produced the prayer was worth the pain if it resulted in seeking God.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD; we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD'—the birth-pang metaphor applied to Israel's own experience: all the pain and labor of suffering under judgment. 'We were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind'—the devastating admission: all the labor produced nothing. Wind (ruakh) here means nothing of substance—the effort and pain did not produce the desired child (national restoration). 'We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen'—the confession of human inability: Israel's own efforts at self-deliverance and judgment of the nations produced nothing. Childs: the admission of total human incapacity prepares for the divine act of v. 19—since we produced only wind, God must produce the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead. Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!'—the resurrection promise: the dead of God's people will live again. The 'bodies' (nebhelah, corpses) will rise. This is the most explicit resurrection text in Isaiah and one of the clearest in the Old Testament. 'For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead'—the dew of light: life-giving moisture from God's own radiance. The earth, which received the dead, will give birth to them again. 'Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by'—the instruction for the interim: shelter in God's protection while judgment completes its course. The chambers (khadarim) are God's own protection—a hiding-place within his presence. Motyer: the movement from human failure (v. 18) to divine resurrection (v. 19) to divine protection (v. 20) is the movement of grace: where human effort ends, divine act begins.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the LORD is coming out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD is coming out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity'—the theophanic exit: God coming out of the heavenly sanctuary to act in history. His 'place' (maqom) is the holy dwelling; his exit is an event. 'The earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain'—the earth as the repository of unpunished violence: blood has been absorbed, bodies have been buried, injustice has been covered. But in the day of judgment the earth disgorges what it has absorbed. All the violence done to the innocent comes to light. Oswalt: the image of the earth refusing to cover its dead connects to Abel's blood crying from the ground (Gen. 4:10)—every unpunished wrong is recorded and will be disclosed. The shelter of vv. 20–21 is shelter from the judgment that falls on the earth's violence, not from God's presence.

27.subtitle: The Great Harvest
27.intro: Overview. Chapter 27 concludes the Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24–27) with three movements: the defeat of the serpentine powers (v. 1), the song of the vineyard revisited (vv. 2–6), and the ingathering of scattered Israel (vv. 12–13). It stands in deliberate contrast with chapter 5’s vineyard song — the same vineyard, but now God tends it with care and there is fruit. The chapter is eschatological: it looks to the final outcome of history.

sections.title: Leviathan Defeated
sections.commentary: A single verse, but a thunderclap: on that day, the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and will slay the dragon that is in the sea. Three designations for the same chaos-monster — the ancient Near Eastern symbol of cosmic disorder, rebellion against creation, the power behind human empires. In Revelation 12–13, John identifies this figure as the dragon who is the Devil and Satan. The sword of the LORD ends what began in the garden.

sections.title: The Vineyard Song Reversed
sections.commentary:
Chapter 5 opened with a vineyard song that ended in destruction: the wall torn down, the vineyard given to thorns. Here the song begins again, but God’s posture has changed: “I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day.” God is now the attentive gardener, not the disappointed owner. His anger has gone; he longs to make peace.

v. 4 — “I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me.” The urgency of the repeated “make peace with me” is striking. God is not waiting to be asked; he is pressing the offer. The thorn-and-brier threat has no target if the people will only turn and accept the peace.

Israel, by contrast, will send out its roots and fill the whole world with fruit (v. 6) — the vine that was to fill the land now fills the earth. This is the mission vision of Isaiah 19 and 60 in compressed form.

sections.title: The Ingathering
sections.commentary: The section closes with an image of harvest and return. God will thresh from the River to the Brook of Egypt, and the scattered ones will be gathered “one by one” — not in masses but individually, personally known and retrieved. A great trumpet will sound, and those lost in Assyria and Egypt will come and worship on the holy mountain. The apocalypse ends not in cosmic wreckage but in pilgrimage and praise.

keyVerse.quote: “In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.”
keyVerse.note: The vine that was stripped in chapter 5 becomes the vine that fills the earth. This is the covenantal logic of Isaiah in miniature: judgment clears the way for new growth, and the new growth exceeds the old. It is also a Christological verse: Jesus declares himself the true vine (John 15:1), and his fruitfulness fills the world through those who abide in him.

27.reflection: God says “I have no wrath” and doubles the invitation: “let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me.” There is urgency in the repetition — not threat, but longing. In what area of your life have you been treating God’s patience as distance rather than invitation?
27.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. <sup>2</sup>In that day, "A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! <sup>3</sup>I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day; <sup>4</sup>I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. <sup>5</sup>Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me." <sup>6</sup>In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit. <sup>7</sup>Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain? <sup>8</sup>Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind. <sup>9</sup>Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing. <sup>10</sup>For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches. <sup>11</sup>When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor. <sup>12</sup>In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel. <sup>13</sup>And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Final Victory and the Return of the Scattered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 27 closes the Isaiah Apocalypse (ch. 24–27) with the defeat of Leviathan, the song of the true vineyard, and the gathering of the scattered people of God. The chapter moves from cosmic battle (v. 1) to pastoral tending (vv. 2–6) to the measured discipline of Jacob (vv. 7–11) to the final trumpet and return (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.examples: The defeat of Leviathan (v. 1) opens the chapter as the final confrontation with the chaos-power that underlies all anti-God empire. The great trumpet (v. 13) closes it as the call home for the dispersed—the second Exodus from Egypt and Assyria is enacted. Every Christian reading of ch. 27 hears the last trumpet of 1 Cor. 15:52 and the gathering of the elect in Matt. 24:31.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. In that day, “A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea'—the final battle: God's sword against the mythological chaos-monster. Leviathan appears three times (fleeing, twisting, in the sea) in three descriptions of the same cosmic opposition to God. The Canaanite myth used Leviathan to represent the primordial chaos-water; Isaiah uses it as a symbol of all anti-God empire and power. 'He will slay the dragon that is in the sea'—Revelation 12:9 identifies the dragon as Satan. The final defeat of chaos is the overthrow of the ultimate enemy. 'In that day, “A pleasant vineyard, sing of it!”'—the abrupt transition: from the cosmic battle to a pastoral song. The defeat of chaos produces the conditions for the pleasant vineyard. Oswalt: the contrast is radical and deliberate—from God's sword against Leviathan to God's song over his vineyard.

verseByVerse.quote: “I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day; I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it'—the direct contrast with ch. 5: God's abandoned vineyard now has God as its constant keeper. 'Every moment' is the most intensive possible care: not occasionally, not when convenient, but ceaselessly. 'Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day'—the protective keeping: no enemy can harm the vineyard while God guards it. 'I have no wrath'—toward his vineyard: the wrath directed against Leviathan and the nations is not directed at the renewed covenant community. 'Would that I had thorns and briers to battle!'—the conditional hypothetical: if there were thorns and briers (the sign of the abandoned vineyard in ch. 5:6), God would deal with them decisively. 'I would march against them, I would burn them up together'—the divine readiness: no enemy is beyond God's capacity to handle. Childs: the 'no wrath' toward the vineyard is the ground of the community's peace—the God who tends it has directed his wrath elsewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me.“ In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me'—the alternative to being burned: taking hold of God's protection (ma'uz, his stronghold). The doubled 'let them make peace with me' is both invitation and condition: those who grab hold of God's strength find that strength is their protection. 'In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit'—the eschatological vine: taking root (stability), blossoming (life), putting forth shoots (expansion), filling the whole world with fruit. The vine of 5:1–7 that produced wild grapes now fills the world with good fruit. Motyer: the contrast with ch. 5 is complete—the vineyard that failed under its own management succeeds under God's direct tending.

verseByVerse.quote: Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been killed as their killers were killed? Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been killed as their killers were killed?'—the question of proportionality: did God judge Israel as severely as he judged Israel's enemies? The answer implied is no: Israel was disciplined, not destroyed. 'Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them'—the measured nature of Israel's judgment: by measure (bissa'on), in proportion. God's judgment of Israel is calibrated rather than absolute. 'He removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind'—the east wind (sirocco) is the desert wind: hot, dry, scorching but not permanently destructive. Israel's exile was like the east wind's blast: fierce but temporary, not like the conflagration of the enemy cities. Oswalt: the distinction between judgment-unto-destruction (enemies) and judgment-unto-purification (Israel) is fundamental to the covenant relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing. For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin'—the atonement of Jacob is the goal of the exile: it produces the purification that sacrifice could not achieve because the people refused repentance. 'When he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing'—the sign of genuine atonement: the total demolition of the pagan religious apparatus. The Asherim (wooden poles for Asherah) and incense altars are the recurring idols of syncretism. When these are gone, the heart-change is real. 'The fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken'—the enemy city in ruins: its fortification and habitation both gone. 'There the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches'—the same pastoral imagery as ch. 5's vineyard abandoned: animals where humans once lived. Young: the contrast is between Israel's purified worship and the enemy's ruined city—atonement produces new life while judgment produces desolation.

verseByVerse.quote: When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor. In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them'—the dead tree of the enemy city: dry branches fit only for firewood, gathered by women (not warriors). 'For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them'—the theological verdict: no discernment (understanding of God's ways) means no compassion. God's compassion requires the capacity to receive it. 'In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain'—the gathering of the scattered Israel: from the Euphrates (east, Babylon) to the Brook of Egypt (southwest, the boundary of the promised land). God as thresher: winnowing the grain of his people from the chaff of the nations. 'And you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel'—the gentle precision of the gathering: one by one, no one left behind. Motyer: the individual gathering ('one by one') contrasts with the mass deportation of exile—God brings each one home personally.

verseByVerse.quote: And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day a great trumpet will be blown'—the eschatological signal: the great trumpet as the call to gather (cf. Matt. 24:31; 1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16). 'Those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt'—the two directions of exile: east (Assyria) and southwest (Egypt). The lost and the driven-out: both categories of the dispersed gathered by the trumpet call. 'Will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem'—the destination is worship: the gathered people go to the mountain of the LORD to worship. Not political restoration primarily but covenantal restoration—the nation reconstituted around the worship of the true God. Childs: the great trumpet closing ch. 27 closes the entire first movement (ch. 1–27): from the arraignment of 1:2 ('Hear, O heavens') to the trumpet of 27:13 that gathers the worshippers home. The story of Israel from unfaithfulness to gathering reaches its resolution in worship on the holy mountain.

28.subtitle: Woe to the Drunkards of Ephraim
28.intro: Overview. With chapter 28, Isaiah moves from the oracles-against-the-nations and the apocalypse into a new section of woes (chs. 28–33), directed primarily against Judah’s leaders for their catastrophic political strategy: seeking alliance with Egypt against Assyria rather than trusting in the LORD. Chapter 28 opens with a woe against the northern kingdom (Ephraim/Samaria), already fallen or falling, then turns to Jerusalem’s leaders — drunk priests and prophets who have made a “covenant with death.” It contains the foundational cornerstone promise (vv. 16–17) and the unforgettable image of a bed too short to stretch out on.

sections.title: The Fading Flower of Ephraim
sections.commentary:
The woe against Ephraim opens with a vivid image: the drunkard’s crown, glorious in its beauty, is like the first ripe fig of summer — whoever sees it swallows it immediately. The northern kingdom is beautiful, conspicuous, and already doomed. Assyria will come and trample it. But through the wreckage God himself will be a crown of glory and a diadem of beauty to the remnant — the contrast between the fading wreath of human pride and the unfading crown of divine presence.

The Judean priests and prophets are then addressed — and they too are drunk: reeling in their visions, stumbling in their judgments, vomiting over their tables. Their response to Isaiah’s preaching is sarcastic mockery: who is he to teach us? Are we children? Line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little, there a little — the kind of rote instruction given to infants. God accepts the characterization: fine, since you won’t listen to clear Hebrew, you will learn through the incomprehensible language of foreign conquerors. The very thing they mocked as elementary becomes the instrument of their undoing.

vv. 9–10 — The priests’ mockery is one of the most poignant moments in Isaiah. They had received more revelation than any generation — and dismissed it as baby talk. Paul reflects on this dynamic in 1 Cor. 14:21, quoting Isaiah 28:11: foreign tongues become a sign, not to believers, but to unbelievers.

sections.title: The Covenant with Death and the Cornerstone
sections.commentary:
Jerusalem’s rulers have made “a covenant with death” and “an agreement with Sheol.” The language is startling — Isaiah is naming their political strategy (the Egyptian alliance) for what it actually is: a bargain with the powers that kill. They believe the overwhelming scourge will pass them by because of this deal. God pronounces their lie exposed.

Against it he sets the cornerstone: “Behold, I am the one who has laid in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: ‘Whoever believes will not be in haste.’” Peter (1 Pet. 2:6) and Paul (Rom. 9:33; 10:11) both quote this verse as fulfilled in Christ — the cornerstone against whom others stumble but in whom believers find the only sure foundation. Justice will be the measuring line; righteousness the plumb line. Everything built on other foundations will be swept away.

v. 20 — “For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in.” A memorable image of Egypt as a security blanket: it cannot actually cover you. Every alliance that substitutes for trust in God will prove too small for the crisis it was supposed to manage.

sections.title: The Parable of the Farmer
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with an unexpected parable from agriculture: the farmer does not plow endlessly, does not thresh every grain the same way, does not run the cartwheel over every crop. He knows that different plants require different tools, and he knows when to stop. This wisdom, Isaiah says, comes from God: “His God instructs him and teaches him the right way.” The point is subversive: if God has the wisdom to vary his means in farming, does he not also vary his means in judgment? The Assyrian invasion is not the end of the story; the threshing is proportioned to the grain, and something will be left.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, I am the one who has laid in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation. Whoever believes will not be in haste.”
keyVerse.note: The stone’s primary characteristic is that it has been tested — proven under pressure. The one who builds on it will not need to run in panic. Peter and Paul both identify the stone as Christ, and the New Testament adds the layer of stumbling: the same stone is a rock of offense to those who reject him. Cornerstone or stumbling-block — the stone is the same; the relationship to it makes all the difference.

28.reflection: The leaders of Jerusalem made a “covenant with death” because they could not bear to trust in something invisible when a visible alliance was available. Where in your life are you reaching for a bed that’s too short rather than resting on the tested cornerstone? What would it look like to believe without being in haste?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Cornerstone and the Scoffers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 28 opens the second great section of the book (ch. 28–35), the 'Woe' oracles. The chapter weaves together a woe against the drunkards of Ephraim (vv. 1–6), a woe against Judah's corrupt leadership (vv. 7–13), a stunning promise of the cornerstone (vv. 14–22), and a concluding parable from agriculture (vv. 23–29). The cornerstone promise is one of the most important messianic texts in Isaiah.
verseByVerse.examples: The cornerstone promise grounds the church's entire existence: built not on human wisdom, political strategy, or religious performance but on the one God himself has laid. Peter applies this to the church as living stones built on the cornerstone (1 Pet. 2:4–8). Every attempt to build on another foundation will be swept away by the overflowing scourge.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley of those overcome with wine! Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest, like a storm of mighty, overflowing waters, he casts down to the earth with his hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim'—the woe-particle (hoy) opens against the northern kingdom's capital, Samaria (the head of the rich valley, v. 1, probably referring to Samaria's hill). The crown of pride is the city's self-perception: glorious, adorned. 'The fading flower of its glorious beauty'—the flower image: beauty that was real but is already fading. Ephraim's glory was genuine once; now it is wilting. 'The Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest'—God's instrument against the drunkards: Assyria, described as hail, tempest, and overflowing water. 'He casts down to the earth with his hand'—the casting down: the crown of pride is knocked from the head. Oswalt: the fading flower cast to earth by a hailstorm is the image of all human glory before the force of divine judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot; and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot'—the crown-as-garland: a wreath of flowers worn at a banquet, trampled on the ground when the party ends in chaos. The thing that displayed honor is now the thing dishonored underfoot. 'The fading flower of its glorious beauty... will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer'—the fig metaphor: early figs (before the main harvest) were considered delicacies, eagerly grabbed and eaten immediately. Ephraim is like that fig: something desirable that will be consumed the moment it is within reach. 'When someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand'—Assyria sees Ephraim and immediately consumes it. No resistance, no delay: the moment of contact is the moment of consumption. Childs: the fig metaphor establishes the contrast with the cornerstone—what the nations grab and consume without a thought is the opposite of what God lays with care.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people'—the reversal of vv. 1–4: instead of the pride-crown of Ephraim (which is fading and being trampled), the LORD himself becomes the crown. The crown is not a city or wealth but a person—God himself as the adornment of the faithful remnant. 'A spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment'—the just judge receives the gift of the Spirit for justice: the capacity to judge rightly is given by God. 'Strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate'—the warriors who defend the city receive strength not from military training alone but from God. Motyer: the fourfold gift (glory-crown, beauty-diadem, spirit of justice, battle-strength) replaces the fourfold false glory of Ephraim's drunkards—God is the better version of everything they sought in wine and pride.

verseByVerse.quote: These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed by wine, they stagger with strong drink, they reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment. For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink'—the condemnation shifts from Ephraim to Judah: 'these also.' Judah's priests and prophets—the religious leaders who should provide sober guidance—are as drunk as Ephraim's drunkards. 'They are swallowed by wine'—the verb swallowed echoes v. 4 (the fig swallowed by the hand): the leaders are consumed by alcohol as Israel will be consumed by Assyria. 'They reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment'—the specific professional failures: prophetic vision distorted, judicial judgment impaired. 'For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left'—the state of the feasting hall: not celebration but degradation. The tables that should host covenantal meals are covered in vomit. Young: the degradation of religious leadership produces the degradation of the spaces where that leadership is exercised.

verseByVerse.quote: “To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast? For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message?'—the mocking question from the drunken priests: who does Isaiah think his audience is? Children? Babies? 'Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast'—the scoffers accuse Isaiah of lecturing them like infants. 'For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little'—they mock the prophet's method as childish repetition: tsav latsav, tsav latsav, qav laqav, qav laqav. The sounds may be childlike babble in the scoffers' ears. Oswalt: the scoffers are right about the method but wrong about their own readiness—they need the elementary instruction they despise, because they have refused the deeper teaching and now can only receive the basic. Childs: Paul cites this passage (1 Cor. 14:21) in his discussion of tongues as a sign of judgment for unbelievers.

verseByVerse.quote: For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people, to whom he has said, “This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose”; yet they would not hear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people'—the judgment: if they mock the prophet's elementary Hebrew, they will hear something far worse—Assyrian. The foreign tongue they despised will become the language of their judgment. Paul quotes this in 1 Cor. 14:21 to explain tongues as a sign of judgment for unbelievers. 'To whom he has said, “This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose”'—God had already offered rest: the Sabbath-rest, the covenant-rest, the dwelling of trust (cf. 30:15). The offer of rest had been extended before the mocking. 'Yet they would not hear'—the root cause: hearing-refusal. The precept-upon-precept method was not Isaiah's fault; it was the only form of communication available to those who refused to hear the message in its fullness. Motyer: the mocking of elementary instruction reveals the hearer's unwillingness to receive any instruction at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little, that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken. Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept... that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken'—the devastating irony: the very thing they mocked (precept-upon-precept instruction) becomes the instrument of their judgment. They stumbled over elementary teaching; they will be broken by it. 'That they may go, and fall backward'—falling backward is the position of a person who has refused to go forward: stubborn resistance produces the fall. 'Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem!'—the direct address to the ruling class in Jerusalem. The scoffers are not peripheral cynics but the ruling leadership. Their scoffing at prophetic instruction is a political and social crisis, not merely a theological one. Oswalt: those who lead while mocking God's word lead their followers into the pit they themselves are falling into.
