verseByVerse.quote: Because you have said, “We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement; when the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter”; therefore thus says the Lord GOD, “Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement'—the political leaders' self-description of their Egypt alliance: they have secured a pact with the powers of death and underworld. The covenant with death is probably the alliance with Egypt, which Isaiah consistently treats as a dead-end. 'When the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter'—the self-deception is precise: they have built a shelter out of deception (probably the deceptive counsel that Egypt will protect them). 'Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation'—the divine response to the covenant with death: I have already laid a foundation that cannot be shaken. The cornerstone is tested (proven reliable), precious, sure. 'Whoever believes will not be in haste'—will not panic, will not flee. Faith in the cornerstone produces stability. Peter applies this to Christ in 1 Pet. 2:6. Childs: the cornerstone is the answer to the covenant with death—only one foundation survives the overflowing scourge.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter.“ Then your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand; when the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line'—God is the master builder using the proper instruments: justice and righteousness as the measuring tools. What is not built to these standards will be demolished. 'Hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter'—the instruments of judgment here are the same hail and overflowing waters used against Ephraim (v. 2). What they imagined was a shelter (falsehood, Egypt) will be swept away by the very forces they thought it would protect them from. 'Your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand'—God unilaterally cancels the false covenant: it had no binding force in heaven. 'When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it'—what they thought would pass over them becomes the thing that beats them down. Motyer: the shelter built from lies falls precisely when tested by the storm; only the cornerstone of v. 16 stands.

verseByVerse.quote: As often as it passes through, it will take you; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night; and it will be sheer terror to understand the message. For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As often as it passes through, it will take you; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night'—the overwhelming scourge is relentless: not once but repeatedly. Morning and night, unceasing. 'It will be sheer terror to understand the message'—the final awakening: when the people finally understand what the prophet was saying, the realization will be terrorizing. Understanding arrives too late. 'The bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in'—a proverb about inadequate provision: the false refuge (Egypt) is like a bed too short for comfort and a blanket too small for warmth. It cannot provide what it promised. Young: the bed-and-blanket proverb captures the inadequacy of every human refuge not built on the cornerstone—it always turns out too small, too short, insufficient for the crisis it faces.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused; to do his deed—strange is his deed! and to work his work—alien is his work! Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of hosts against the whole land. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused'—historical precedents: at Perazim (2 Sam. 5:20) and Gibeon (Josh. 10:12) God fought for Israel against its enemies. Now God fights the same way but against his own people. 'To do his deed—strange is his deed! and to work his work—alien is his work!'—the strangeness of God judging his own people is acknowledged: it is strange, alien, unlike his normal pattern. But it is necessary. 'Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong'—the pastoral application: the information about the coming judgment is a warning, not entertainment. Scoffing intensifies the bonds. 'For I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of hosts against the whole land'—the prophet has heard the divine council's decree: certain, authorized, and all-encompassing. Childs: the prophet's role is to warn before the decree is executed.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech. Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech'—the summons to hear: the agricultural parable requires careful attention. 'Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground?'—the rhetorical question expects 'no': the farmer does not plow endlessly. Plowing is preparation for sowing; once the soil is ready, plowing stops. The farmer's actions are purposive and seasonal. Motyer: the parable defends the wisdom of divine pedagogy—each stage of judgment or cultivation is appropriate to its purpose and limited by its function. God is the master farmer who knows when to plow and when to stop, when to thresh and when to harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cummin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border? For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cummin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border?'—the variety of crops sown in their proper places: dill, cummin (small seeds scattered broadcast), wheat (in rows), barley (in its proper place), and emmer wheat as border planting. Each crop has its method, its location, its purpose. 'For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him'—the farmer's wisdom is not self-generated: God teaches him the agricultural knowledge he uses. The farmer who knows when to plow and what to sow learned from the divine Teacher. Oswalt: the farmer's wisdom is an analogy for the prophet's proclamation—Isaiah is also taught by God what to say and when, how much judgment and when to offer comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cummin, but dill is beaten out with a stick, and cummin with a rod. Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever; when he drives his cart wheel over it with his horses, he does not crush it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cummin'—the delicate spices (dill, cummin) require delicate handling: a threshing sledge would crush them to powder. 'But dill is beaten out with a stick, and cummin with a rod'—each crop receives appropriate treatment: not excessive force but calibrated handling. 'Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever'—even grain (sturdier than spices) is not threshed endlessly. The threshing has a limit: enough to release the grain from the husk, not so much as to crush the grain itself. Motyer: the agricultural precision pictures God's judgment: each nation, each person, each situation receives the appropriate instrument of divine dealing—not the same treatment indiscriminately applied, but wisely calibrated. God does not thresh his people with the same force he uses on his enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'This also comes from the LORD of hosts'—the agricultural wisdom the farmer practices was given by God (v. 26); now the parable is completed: 'this also'—all of the wisdom in the parable, the judgment and the calibration and the harvest, is from the LORD of hosts. 'He is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom'—Wonderful Counselor (pele' yoets) echoes the throne-name of 9:6: the child whose name includes Wonderful Counselor. God's counsel, which the scoffers mocked and the drunkards ignored, is wonderful—beyond ordinary human comprehension. Childs: the closing ascription of wisdom ties the chapter to its cornerstone promise: the God who lays the cornerstone is the same God who teaches the farmer, and his dealings with his people are as wisely ordered as a master farmer's seasonal work.

29.subtitle: Ariel in Distress
29.intro: Overview. Chapter 29 continues the woes with an oracle against Jerusalem, here called Ariel — a word meaning either “lion of God” or “altar hearth,” both rich with associations. The chapter moves through three great movements: the distress and siege of Jerusalem (vv. 1–8), the spiritual blindness of prophets and people (vv. 9–16), and then a surprising turn to hope (vv. 17–24). It contains two of the most-quoted passages in the New Testament from Isaiah: the lip-service condemnation (v. 13) and the potter-clay image (vv. 15–16).

sections.title: Siege and Deliverance
sections.commentary: Ariel adds year to year and celebrates feasts — and yet God himself will besiege it. The city that trusts in its rituals will find God on the side of those who attack it. This is not because God hates Zion but because he is using the siege to bring his people low, to make them speak from the dust in a whisper. And then — suddenly — he will intervene. The attacking nations will become like a dream, like a night vision. Their armies will vanish like a hungry man who dreams of food and wakes still hungry.

sections.title: Spiritual Blindness
sections.commentary:
Astonish yourselves, be astonished; blind yourselves, and be blind. The command is ironic: you have already done this to yourselves. God has poured upon them a spirit of deep sleep; the prophets have become the eyes of the vision, the seers have become the heads of what they see, and it is all covered and sealed. When they hand the sealed book to the literate man he says he cannot read it because it is sealed; when they hand it to the illiterate man he says he cannot read at all. The revelation is present but inaccessible because the heart is closed.

v. 13 — “This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.” Jesus quotes this verse directly against the Pharisees in Matt. 15:8–9, identifying their tradition-keeping as the precise dynamic Isaiah diagnosed. The form of religion has survived while the heart of it has been evacuated.

Verses 15–16 address those who “dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD.” The potter-clay image: does the clay say to the potter, “He did not make me”? Paul develops this image extensively in Romans 9:20–21 in his argument about divine sovereignty. The absurdity of the creature questioning the Creator’s right is the point.

sections.title: The Turn to Hope
sections.commentary: Lebanon will become a fruitful field; the deaf will hear; the blind will see. The meek will obtain fresh joy; the poor will exult in the Holy One of Israel. The tyrant will vanish; the scoffer will be gone; all who watch for evil will be cut off. Jacob will no longer be ashamed. His children will see the work of God’s hands — and those who wandered in spirit will come to understanding. The chapter that began in siege ends in sight and comprehension. The blindness is real and severe, but it is not the final word.

keyVerse.quote: “This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.”
keyVerse.note: Jesus’ application of this verse to the Pharisees makes it timelessly diagnostic. The Pharisees were the most religiously serious people of their generation — and the most thoroughly described by Isaiah’s warning. The danger is not irreligion but religion that has become self-referential: honoring God with forms that protect the heart from actual encounter with him.

29.reflection: Isaiah describes a form of blindness that is self-inflicted: “blind yourselves, and be blind.” The spiritual numbness he diagnoses is not simply ignorance but the accumulated result of not wanting to see clearly. Is there something God has been trying to show you that you have been sealing and covering? What would it cost to open the book?
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round. <sup>2</sup>Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be moaning and lamentation, and she shall be to me like an Ariel. <sup>3</sup>And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you. <sup>4</sup>And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper. <sup>5</sup>But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly, <sup>6</sup>you will be visited by the LORD of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire. <sup>7</sup>And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, all that fight against her and her stronghold and distress her, shall be like a dream, a vision of the night. <sup>8</sup>As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched, so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion. <sup>9</sup>Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink! <sup>10</sup>For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers). <sup>11</sup>And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot, for it is sealed." <sup>12</sup>And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot read." <sup>13</sup>And the Lord said: "Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men, <sup>14</sup>therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden." <sup>15</sup>Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, "Who sees us? Who knows us?" <sup>16</sup>You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, "He has no understanding"? <sup>17</sup>Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest? <sup>18</sup>In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see. <sup>19</sup>The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel. <sup>20</sup>For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off, <sup>21</sup>who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right. <sup>22</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: "Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale. <sup>23</sup>For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 29 addresses Jerusalem as Ariel ('hearth of God' or 'lion of God'), the city of David's encampment. God will besiege his own city, reduce it to whispers from the dust—and then, suddenly, deliver it by direct divine intervention. The chapter then exposes the people's spiritual blindness (vv. 9–14) and the arrogance of those who try to hide their counsel from God (vv. 15–16), before ending with the promise of reversal: the deaf will hear, the blind will see, the humble will rejoice.
verseByVerse.examples: The church reads Ariel as itself: the city of God that sometimes faces siege from outside and deadness within. The promise that God will suddenly intervene—by thunder and earthquake and great noise—sustains faith when all outward circumstances suggest God has forgotten his city.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round. Yet I will distress Ariel, and there will be moaning and lamentation, and she shall be to me like an Ariel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped!'—the double address creates both intimacy and pathos. Jerusalem is called by its alternative name: Ariel (possibly 'altar hearth of God' or 'lion of God'), evoking both the sacred fire and the strength of the covenant city. 'Add year to year; let the feasts run their round'—the unbroken liturgical calendar: feast following feast, year after year. But the religious routine is not spiritually nourishing. 'Yet I will distress Ariel, and there will be moaning and lamentation'—God will distress his own city. The very name (Ariel as altar hearth) becomes the image of judgment: she will be like an altar hearth consuming itself. 'She shall be to me like an Ariel'—a city burning like an altar. Oswalt: the transformation of the city's name from honor (lion of God) to judgment (burning hearth) is one of Isaiah's most concentrated ironies.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you. And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers'—God as the besieger of his own city. This reverses the Exodus: God protected Israel from Egypt's siege; now he lays siege to Jerusalem himself. 'You will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak'—the depth of the humbling: brought so low that speech comes from the earth level, from the dust. 'Your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost'—the ghost (ob) was the spirit consulted by mediums (8:19); Jerusalem's voice will be as faint and eerie as a spirit speaking from underground. 'From the dust your speech shall whisper'—the lavish, confident city reduced to a whisper from the dust. Childs: the city that was full of shoutings (22:2) now whispers from the ground—the trajectory of all pride brought low by divine siege.

verseByVerse.quote: But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly, you will be visited by the LORD of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff'—the sudden reversal: the besieging armies that seemed overwhelming are reduced to dust and chaff—as light and insubstantial as the defeated Gideonites before God's power. 'And in an instant, suddenly, you will be visited by the LORD of hosts'—the suddenness of divine intervention: 'in an instant, suddenly.' There is no gradual buildup; God acts without warning. 'With thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire'—five instruments of theophanic intervention: thunder, earthquake, noise, whirlwind, fire. These are the phenomena of Sinai (Ex. 19:16–18) applied to military deliverance. Motyer: Sennacherib's retreat in ch. 37 is the historical fulfillment, but the theological pattern recurs whenever God intervenes for his besieged people.

verseByVerse.quote: And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, all that fight against her and her stronghold and distress her, shall be like a dream, a vision of the night. As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched, so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All the nations that fight against Ariel... shall be like a dream, a vision of the night'—the nations that confidently besieged Jerusalem will find their campaign was like a dream: it seemed real, it was powerfully felt, and then it simply vanished. 'As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied'—the dream of eating satisfies nothing; the hunger remains when waking. 'As when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched'—the dream of drinking leaves the thirst intact. 'So shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion'—the nations' campaign against Zion will produce nothing: they will wake from their assault with nothing gained. Young: the dream-imagery is one of Isaiah's most beautiful illustrations of the vanity of opposition to God's city—it seems real, it feels real, and then it is simply not there.

verseByVerse.quote: Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink! For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers). (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind!'—the bitter irony: the people are invited to observe their own stupefaction. Their blindness is self-induced before it is divinely confirmed. 'Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink!'—the spiritual drunkenness: incapacitated by something other than alcohol. The intoxication of religious formalism without spiritual reality. 'For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep'—the judicial blinding: God confirms what the people have chosen. The deep sleep (tardemah) is the sleep of spiritual insensibility, the same word as Adam's sleep (Gen. 2:21). 'He has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers)'—the specific closure: the prophets' eyes shut, the seers' heads covered. The very people appointed to see for the community have been given the spirit of blindness. Childs: the judicial hardening of 6:9–10 is here applied directly to the prophets themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, “Read this,” he says, “I cannot, for it is sealed.” And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, “Read this,” he says, “I cannot read.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed'—prophetic revelation has become inaccessible: the words are present but cannot be opened. 'When men give it to one who can read, saying, “Read this,” he says, “I cannot, for it is sealed”'—the literate person's excuse: ability is not the problem; the seal is. The one who can read is stopped by external closure. 'And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, “Read this,” he says, “I cannot read”'—the illiterate person's limitation: ability is the problem. Between these two—the sealed book and the illiterate reader—the entire population is covered. No one can access the vision. Motyer: the sealed book is a metaphor for the spiritual condition of a people who have lost both the ability and the opportunity to receive divine revelation through their own hardness of heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said: “Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men, therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me'—the diagnosis of religious formalism: external proximity (mouth and lips) with internal distance (heart far away). 'Their fear of me is a commandment taught by men'—religion as cultural performance rather than covenantal relationship: they learned piety as a social skill, not as the response of a heart met by the living God. 'Therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder'—the reversal of wisdom: God's response to human wisdom's failure is the demonstration of divine wisdom. 'The wisdom of their wise men shall perish'—the very resource they trusted (human wisdom) is confiscated. Paul quotes this text in 1 Cor. 1:19 as the basis for the wisdom of the cross confounding human wisdom. Jesus cites vv. 13–14 in Matt. 15:8–9 against Pharisaic tradition. Oswalt: lip-service religion produces the divine confiscation of the very tools it relied upon.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, “Who sees us? Who knows us?” You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, “He did not make me”; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, “He has no understanding”? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, “Who sees us? Who knows us?”'—the arrogance of secret political counsel: the leaders who plotted their Egyptian alliance in private (the anti-prophetic counsel of 30:1) imagined God did not see. 'You turn things upside down!'—the moral universe inverted: they have reversed creator and creature. 'Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, “He did not make me”'—the absurdity of the inversion: the clay claiming independence from the potter who formed it. 'Or the thing formed say of him who formed it, “He has no understanding”?'—the clay critiquing the potter's competence. Paul develops this image extensively in Romans 9:19–21 to defend divine sovereignty. Motyer: the potter-clay illustration is not cold logic but intimate theology—the God who made you knows what he's doing with you.

verseByVerse.quote: Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest? In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest?'—the reversal of the natural order: the barren becomes fruitful, the fruitful becomes forested. The transformation signals the eschatological reversal of all judgment. 'In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book'—the sealed book of v. 11 is now opened to those who could not hear. The judicial deafness of vv. 9–10 is reversed. 'Out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see'—the darkness of spiritual blindness lifted. The transformation is not gradual improvement but sudden reversal. Jesus quotes from this passage in Matt. 11:5 (the blind see, the deaf hear) as evidence that he is the one who accomplishes this reversal. Childs: the signs of the messianic age (deaf hearing, blind seeing) are the precise reversal of the judicial hardening of 6:9–10.

verseByVerse.quote: The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel. For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel'—the reversal of the social order: those who were overlooked by the powerful leaders (the meek and poor who could not access justice in the courts) now obtain the fresh joy of God's direct attention. 'The Holy One of Israel' is their joy: not policy changes or new leadership but God himself. 'For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off'—the threefold removal of the enemies of the poor: the ruthless (powerful oppressors), the scoffers (who mocked God's word), and those who watched for opportunities to do evil. All three categories—named repeatedly in the woe oracles—are simultaneously removed. Motyer: the joy of the meek is inseparable from the cutting off of their oppressors; the one cannot come without the other.

verseByVerse.quote: who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right. Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: “Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right'—three legal abuses: false accusation (making the innocent an offender), trapping the advocate (who reproves at the gate, the place of justice), and using empty legal arguments to deny the just claim. These are the specific corruptions of justice that Isaiah has condemned throughout (1:17, 23; 3:14–15; 5:23; 10:1–2). 'The LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob'—the appeal to the Abrahamic redemption: God who called Abraham out of Ur and redeemed him will not abandon the house of Jacob to permanent shame. 'Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale'—the reversal of shame: the face that has grown pale with humiliation will be restored to the open, unashamed face of the redeemed. Oswalt: the promise to Jacob is grounded in God's faithfulness to Abraham—the original promise guarantees the ultimate restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel. And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name'—the moment of reversal: when Jacob sees his children gathered (the restored covenant community), the response is sanctification of the divine name. 'They will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel'—the Holy One of Israel (the signature title) is sanctified and reverenced by the restored people. 'Those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding'—the spiritually disoriented find their bearings: the deep sleep (v. 10) reversed into understanding. 'And those who murmur will accept instruction'—the murmurers (who criticized and complained against God's word) become learners. Childs: the final promise reverses every indictment of ch. 29—the blind see, the deaf hear, the disoriented find direction, the murmurers accept teaching. The reversal is total and gratuitous.

30.subtitle: The Rebellious Children
30.intro: Overview. Chapter 30 contains the fullest treatment in the woes section of Judah’s Egyptian alliance — the plan to go to Pharaoh for protection against Assyria. God calls them “rebellious children” who carry out a plan but not his, who weave a web but not of his Spirit. The chapter is also one of the richest sources of comfort in Isaiah, closing with a remarkable promise about God’s waiting, his gracious response when his people turn, and the coming day when idols will be thrown away like menstrual rags.

sections.title: The Egyptian Alliance
sections.commentary:
Woe to the rebellious children who go to Egypt without asking God, who take refuge in Pharaoh’s protection and shelter in Egypt’s shadow. Isaiah frames this not merely as a political miscalculation but as a spiritual act of unfaith. They have rejected the Holy One of Israel — and chosen horses and chariots instead.

The procession to Egypt is described in detail: they carry their riches on donkeys, their treasures on camels, through the Negeb desert, a land of trouble and anguish — all this to reach a people who cannot help. Egypt is a broken reed, a people who “profit nothing but shame and disgrace.” The oracle is written down as a witness “forever and ever” precisely because the temptation to substitute visible alliances for invisible trust will recur in every generation.

v. 15 — “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.” This is the counter-strategy to the Egyptian alliance. Not military preparation but repentance (returning), not feverish diplomacy but quiet confidence (rest, quietness, trust). The people’s response in verse 16 — “No! We will flee on horses” — is one of the most heartbreaking lines in the whole book.

sections.title: God Waits to Be Gracious
sections.commentary:
The turn in verse 18 is one of the most beautiful sentences in Isaiah: “Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him.” The word waits is extraordinary: God himself is in suspense, watching for the moment he can pour out grace. He is not reluctantly delayed — he is actively oriented toward the moment of return.

The following verses describe what that day will look like: a teacher who will not hide, a voice behind you saying “This is the way, walk in it,” rain for the seed you sow, oxen and donkeys with good fodder, streams of water. And the idols — the gold and silver images, the Egyptian gods they trusted — will be thrown away like a menstrual cloth: “Away with you!” The contempt is the contempt of someone who can finally see clearly what they were holding.

v. 21 — “And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, ‘This is the way, walk in it,’ when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left.” The image of a voice from behind is a guide who walks with you, not a map you consult in advance. The guidance is personal, immediate, relational — not a system but a shepherd.

keyVerse.quote: “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.”
keyVerse.note: The verse is both a promise and a rebuke, because it was rejected. The strength on offer was completely counterintuitive — not cavalry but quietness, not diplomacy but trust. Alistair Begg often noted that God’s strategy always appears inadequate until it is the only strategy left. The tragedy of verse 16 is that Judah never found out whether it worked, because they refused to try.

30.reflection: God is described as waiting to be gracious — not holding back, but oriented toward the moment of your return. What would returning and resting actually look like in whatever you are currently trying to manage by your own strength? And what are the “horses” you keep reaching for instead?
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"Ah, stubborn children," declares the LORD, "who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin; <sup>2</sup>who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt! <sup>3</sup>Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation. <sup>4</sup>For though his officials are at Zoan and his envoys reach Hanes, <sup>5</sup>everyone comes to shame through a people that cannot profit them, that brings neither help nor profit, but shame and disgrace." <sup>6</sup>An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent, they carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them. <sup>7</sup>Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her "Rahab who sits still." <sup>8</sup>And now, go, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever. <sup>9</sup>For they are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD; <sup>10</sup>who say to the seers, "Do not see," and to the prophets, "Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions, <sup>11</sup>leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel." <sup>12</sup>Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel, "Because you despise this word and trust in oppression and perverseness and rely on them, <sup>13</sup>therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse, whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant; <sup>14</sup>and its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern." <sup>15</sup>For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, "In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling, <sup>16</sup>and you said, "No! We will flee upon horses"; therefore you shall flee away; and, "We will ride upon swift steeds"; therefore your pursuers shall be swift. <sup>17</sup>A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain, like a signal on a hill. <sup>18</sup>Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him. <sup>19</sup>For a people shall dwell in Zion, in Jerusalem; you shall weep no more. He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you. <sup>20</sup>And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher. <sup>21</sup>And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, "This is the way, walk in it," when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left. <sup>22</sup>Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver and your gold-plated metal images. You will scatter them as unclean things. You will say to them, "Be gone!" <sup>23</sup>And he will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous. In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures, <sup>24</sup>and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork. <sup>25</sup>And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks running with water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. <sup>26</sup>Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow. <sup>27</sup>Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire; <sup>28</sup>his breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck; to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads astray. <sup>29</sup>You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel. <sup>30</sup>And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones. <sup>31</sup>The Assyrians will be terror-stricken at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod. <sup>32</sup>And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres. Battering them in battle he will fight with them. <sup>33</sup>For a burning place has long been prepared; indeed, for the king it is made ready, its pyre made deep and wide, with fire and wood in abundance; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–33 — The Egyptian Folly and the Grace That Waits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 30 is one of the most pastorally rich chapters in the book. It opens with the sharpest condemnation of the Egypt alliance (vv. 1–7), then delivers the shattering rebuke of the people who told the prophets to stop prophesying (vv. 8–14), then offers one of the book's greatest invitations to repentance (vv. 15–17), then an extraordinary promise of divine grace waiting to be poured out (vv. 18–26), culminating in the defeat of Assyria and the final song of salvation (vv. 27–33).
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction of ch. 30 is permanently relevant: the temptation to replace the prophetic word with 'smooth things' is the temptation of every congregation and every age. The promise that 'your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, “This is the way, walk in it”' (v. 21) sustains every believer navigating uncertainty.

verseByVerse.quote: “Ah, stubborn children,” declares the LORD, “who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin; who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ah, stubborn children,' declares the LORD'—the divine parental grief: the double indictment of stubbornness and being children (who should know better). 'Who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit'—the double failure of their political strategy: the plan is real but unauthorized; the alliance is real but not Spirit-directed. 'That they may add sin to sin'—every unauthorized plan compounds the original apostasy. 'Who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh'—the specific sin: going to Egypt for shelter without consulting God. 'The protection of Pharaoh' (tsel pharaoh, the shadow of Pharaoh)—the shadow (tsel) normally refers to God's protection (Ps. 91:1); seeking Pharaoh's shadow instead of God's shadow is the precise spiritual displacement. Oswalt: the chapter opens with the diagnosis before the prognosis—the sin must be named before the grace can be offered.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the protection of Pharaoh shall turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation. For though his officials are at Zoan and his envoys reach Hanes, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Therefore the protection of Pharaoh shall turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation'—the consequence matches the sin: what was sought as protection produces shame; what was sought as shelter produces humiliation. The false refuge fails at the moment of testing. 'Though his officials are at Zoan and his envoys reach Hanes'—the Egyptian diplomatic apparatus is impressive: Zoan (Tanis) in the Delta, Hanes (Heracleopolis) further south. The envoys have penetrated deep into Egypt. But impressiveness of diplomatic effort does not equal effectiveness of protection. Young: the geographical depth of the Egyptian diplomatic engagement is noted precisely to underline the depth of the disappointment when Egypt fails to deliver.

verseByVerse.quote: everyone comes to shame through a people that cannot profit them, that brings neither help nor profit, but shame and disgrace. An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent, they carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Everyone comes to shame through a people that cannot profit them'—Egypt as the great disappointment: unable to deliver help, its only product is shame and disgrace. 'An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb'—a title for the following scene: the journey through the southern wilderness. 'Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent'—the Negeb desert route to Egypt is dangerous: wild animals, scorpions, heat. The embassy to Egypt must traverse a perilous landscape. 'They carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them'—the tribute-caravan: costly gifts sent to purchase Egyptian military protection. The wealth is real; the protection bought with it is worthless. Motyer: the irony is double—they risk life and wealth traveling through dangerous desert to purchase useless help from a country that will only shame them.

verseByVerse.quote: Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her “Rahab who sits still.” A prophecy of rebuke and shame. Go now, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her “Rahab who sits still”'—Rahab was a mythological sea-monster (cf. Ps. 89:10), a symbol of chaotic power. 'Rahab who sits still' (rahab hem shabet) means a Rahab that just sits there—all fearsome appearance, no actual power. Egypt looks like the ancient chaos-monster but does nothing. 'A prophecy of rebuke and shame'—the oracle's double character: rebuking the decision and predicting the shame. 'Go now, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever'—the command to preserve the oracle: written on a tablet (for immediate public display) and in a book (for permanent record). The testimony will outlast the generation that refused it. Childs: the written word is God's recourse when the spoken word is rejected—what cannot be heard now will be read later as testimony of God's faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: For they are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD; who say to the seers, “Do not see,” and to the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD'—the triple description: rebellious (mori, defiant), lying (kazab, false), unwilling to hear (lo avu shmo'a). The connection between lying and rebelliousness: the people who reject the prophetic word replace it with what they prefer to hear. 'Who say to the seers, “Do not see,” and to the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us what is right”'—the explicit rejection of prophetic truth: the seers are commanded not to see, the prophets not to speak what is right. 'Speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions'—the demand for flattering prophecy and comfortable visions. This is perhaps the most direct description of the false-prophecy dynamic in the Old Testament. Oswalt: the demand for smooth things is the death-wish of any community—it produces the very disaster it was trying to avoid by refusing to hear about it.

verseByVerse.quote: leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel.“ Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel, ”Because you despise this word and trust in oppression and perverseness and rely on them, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel'—the ultimatum of the people against the prophets: stop mentioning the Holy One. The name they want removed from their vocabulary is the signature title of the entire book. 'Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel'—the divine response begins with the very title they wanted silenced. God does not honor the request to be forgotten. 'Because you despise this word and trust in oppression and perverseness and rely on them'—the specific sin: despising the prophetic word and replacing it with trust in oppression and perverseness (probably the deceptive diplomacy of the Egypt alliance). Childs: the Holy One refuses to be dismissed—his title opens the indictment of those who tried to silence it, and his reality guarantees the judgment they tried to avoid by ignoring him.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse, whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant; and its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern.“ (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'This iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse'—the bulging wall: it looks solid but has been undermined. The structural failure is internal and invisible until the moment of collapse. 'Whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant'—the collapse is not gradual: a moment of apparent stability, then total failure without warning. 'Its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found'—complete pulverization. A broken pot normally leaves pieces useful for small tasks; this vessel is ground to powder. 'Not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern'—not even the most basic utility remains. Motyer: the imagery deliberately recalls the cornerstone of 28:16—what is not built on the tested stone cannot survive any test; it fails catastrophically and produces nothing useful.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.” But you were unwilling, and you said, “No! We will flee upon horses”; therefore you shall flee away; and, “We will ride upon swift steeds”; therefore your pursuers shall be swift. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength'—one of the great pastoral promises of the book. Four words define the way of salvation: returning (teshuvah—repentance and turning to God), rest (nuakh—the Sabbath-rest of trust), quietness (shalvah—the stillness that comes from leaving outcomes to God), and trust (bitakhon—confident reliance). 'But you were unwilling, and you said, “No! We will flee upon horses”'—the direct refusal: the four graces of salvation were available; they refused. The alternative: horses. 'Therefore you shall flee away; and “We will ride upon swift steeds”; therefore your pursuers shall be swift'—a bitter wordplay: they wanted swift horses; their pursuers will be swifter. The instrument of their boasted escape becomes the instrument of their pursuit. Oswalt: the refusal of the way of rest forces them into the exhausting panic they chose over stillness.

verseByVerse.quote: A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain, like a signal on a hill. Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain'—the covenant curse of Leviticus 26:8 inverted: instead of five chasing a hundred, one pursues a thousand. The people who refused quietness and trust flee at the smallest provocation, until only a flagstaff remains—a pole without a flag, a signal without an army. 'Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you'—the most patient word in Isaiah. Despite the refusal of rest, the pursuit and flight, the humiliation—the LORD waits. 'For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him'—the ground of patient waiting: God is just, and justice eventually arrives. Those who wait for God share the character of God who waits for them. Motyer: 'the LORD waits to be gracious' is the pastoral center of the entire chapter—and perhaps of the entire book.

verseByVerse.quote: For a people shall dwell in Zion, in Jerusalem; you shall weep no more. He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you. And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For a people shall dwell in Zion, in Jerusalem; you shall weep no more'—the promised reversal of the exile: the scattered people dwelling again in Zion, where weeping has ceased. 'He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you'—the immediacy of divine response: the moment of crying is the moment of hearing; the moment of hearing is the moment of answering. There is no delay between need and response. 'Though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction'—the pathway to restoration may be through hardship. Not comfort first, then repentance—but bread of adversity and water of affliction leading to the Teacher. 'Your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher'—the hidden Teacher of 8:17 (who hid his face from Jacob) now reveals himself. Young: the Teacher who appears to the eyes is God himself—the personal, direct knowledge of God promised in 11:9.

verseByVerse.quote: And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, “This is the way, walk in it,” when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left. Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver and your gold-plated metal images. You will scatter them as unclean things. You will say to them, “Be gone!” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, “This is the way, walk in it,” when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left'—the gentle pastoral guidance: when uncertainty tempts to veer right or left, a voice corrects the direction. The word behind you is not prediction but direction: navigational guidance in the moment of decision. 'Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver and your gold-plated metal images'—when the Teacher is seen and heard, the idols lose their appeal. The same images that were precious become unclean things to be scattered. 'You will say to them, “Be gone!”'—the decisive rejection: the verbal dismissal of what was once worshipped. Oswalt: the voice saying 'this is the way' is the specific guidance that replaces the seers' smooth things—the true word that the people tried to silence becomes the welcome guidance of the restored community.

verseByVerse.quote: And he will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous. In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures, and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous'—the agricultural restoration: the covenant blessings (Deut. 28:12) return. The rain withheld in judgment (1:30; 5:6) is given again. 'In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures'—the expanded pasture: the land can support large flocks. 'The oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork'—even the working animals eat well: not straw and chaff but winnowed, seasoned feed. The prosperity extends to every level of the agricultural economy, including the animals. Motyer: the detail about the working animals is the covenant's generosity extended to its widest scope—even the ox benefits from Zion's restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks and streams of water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'On every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks and streams of water'—the eschatological hydrology: water flowing from the highest places. Normally mountains are dry; in the new creation, water flows from the heights as from Zion itself (cf. Ezek. 47; Rev. 22:1). 'In the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall'—the simultaneous events: cosmic renewal alongside historical judgment (Assyria's defeat). 'The light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold'—the luminaries intensified beyond their current output: sevenfold light (the number of completeness) in the age of healing. 'In the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow'—God both wounds and heals: the judgment was his blow; the healing is also his act. The God who struck is the God who binds up. Childs: the intensified light is the outward sign of what 60:19–20 will describe: the LORD himself becomes the everlasting light.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire; his breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads them astray. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke'—the theophanic approach: the divine name (not merely a concept but a reality approaching from heaven) comes with burning anger and smoke. The name is active: the character and authority of the LORD in motion toward judgment. 'His lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire'—divine speech as fire: the word of God literally burns. 'His breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck'—the same overflowing-to-the-neck imagery as 8:8 and 28:17, now applied to the judgment of Assyria. 'To sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads them astray'—God sifting (winnowing) the nations and bridling them. The imagery combines the agricultural (sieve) and equestrian (bridle): God controls the nations as a farmer controls grain and a rider controls a horse. Oswalt: the judgment of Assyria is the vindication of all God's pastoral promises in vv. 19–26—the Teacher who appeared leads his people safely while destroying their enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel. And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept'—the Passover night: the night of salvation that was also the night of judgment. The pilgrims who went up to Jerusalem for the feasts traveled by night with songs. 'Gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel'—the pilgrimage joy: music, movement, anticipation of God's presence on the mountain. 'The LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard'—the thunder of divine speech: simultaneously the song of the pilgrims and the voice of their God. 'The descending blow of his arm... in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones'—the instruments of theophanic judgment against Assyria. What is song for the rescued is destruction for the enemy. Motyer: the same divine event—the appearance of God—is simultaneously the song of the redeemed and the terror of the judged.

verseByVerse.quote: The Assyrians will be terror-struck at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod. And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres. Battling with brandished arm, he will fight against them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Assyrians will be terror-struck at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod'—the reversal: Assyria was God's rod against Israel (10:5); now God's rod strikes Assyria. The instrument of judgment becomes the object of judgment. 'Every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres'—the battle against Assyria is accompanied by music: each blow of God's staff is celebrated by the tambourines and lyres of Israel's worship. The battle and the praise are simultaneous. 'Battling with brandished arm, he will fight against them'—God personally fights: the divine warrior with his arm raised. The imagery recalls the Red Sea crossing (Ex. 14:30: 'the LORD saved Israel'). Young: the coincidence of music and divine warfare is the liturgical imagination at full stretch—all of reality, including the destruction of the oppressor, is worship.

verseByVerse.quote: For a burning place has long been prepared; indeed, for the king it is made ready, its pyre made deep and wide, with fire and wood in abundance; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A burning place has long been prepared'—Topheth, the valley south of Jerusalem where child sacrifice was practiced (2 Kings 23:10) and later became a symbol of final judgment. The burning place was prepared long ago: the judgment of Assyria was not improvised but planned from eternity. 'Indeed, for the king it is made ready'—the king of Assyria is the specific target: the burning place awaits him. 'Its pyre made deep and wide, with fire and wood in abundance'—the scale is massive: deep enough to hold the king and his army; wide enough for all of them. 'The breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it'—the breath of God is the match: the same breath that spoke creation now ignites judgment. Childs: the chapter that opened with God's patient waiting (v. 18) closes with the burning prepared for the unrepentant oppressor—grace and judgment are both attributes of the same God who is 'a God of justice' (v. 18).

31.subtitle: Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt
31.intro: Overview. Chapter 31 is the sharpest, most compressed of the Egyptian-alliance woes. It drives the contrast between horses and the Holy One to a single question: do you not look to him? But it closes with a promise — Assyria will fall, and not by a human sword — and an image of God as a lion and a mother bird over Jerusalem. The chapter is brief but theologically dense.

sections.title: The Folly of Horses
sections.commentary:
Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD. The critique is not that horses are worthless — they are magnificent military assets. The critique is that Egypt is flesh and not spirit, and God will stretch out his hand and both Egypt and those seeking Egypt’s help will stumble together. The helper and the helped will fall together.

v. 3 — “The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit.” This verse draws the sharpest possible line between trusting in visible power and trusting in the invisible God. The horses are real; the power is real; the military logic is sound. But flesh and spirit operate in different registers, and in a contest between them, flesh will fall.

sections.title: The Lion and the Bird
sections.commentary:
Two images of divine protection, very different in character. First, God as a lion growling over its prey: no noise of shepherds disturbs him; he comes down to fight for Mount Zion. Second, God as birds hovering over Jerusalem: protecting and delivering, passing over and rescuing. The two images together — fierce predator and protective parent — cover the full range of divine care. No threat from below (Assyrian army) and no threat from above (sky) can reach those under his wings.

Assyria’s fall is then announced: he will fall by a sword, not of man; and his officers will be in panic. The army that no human force can stop will be brought down by God alone, without any help from Egypt. This is the practical consequence of God’s sovereignty over military outcomes: the Egyptian alliance was not just wrong theologically but useless strategically.

keyVerse.quote: “The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.”
keyVerse.note: The verse does not disparage military preparation as such but exposes the category error of treating flesh as if it were spirit — of giving to Egypt the trust that belongs only to God. This is the idol-structure in practical form: not a carved image but a military alliance functioning as ultimate security.

31.reflection: The leaders of Judah were not irreligious people — they went to the temple, kept the feasts, consulted prophets. They simply also went to Egypt. The problem was not the absence of religion but its compartmentalization. In what area of your life do you practice religion in one compartment while making practical decisions in another, as if God were not involved?
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD! <sup>2</sup>And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. <sup>3</sup>The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together. <sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me, "As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill. <sup>5</sup>Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it." <sup>6</sup>Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel. <sup>7</sup>For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you. <sup>8</sup>"And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor. <sup>9</sup>His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic," declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah 31 continues the theme of ch. 30: the Egypt alliance condemned, and the alternative of trusting the LORD offered. The chapter is compact but powerful, contrasting the human (Egypt: horse, chariot, flesh) with the divine (the LORD: lion, bird, fire). The decisive theological statement is v. 3: 'The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit.'
verseByVerse.examples: The call to 'turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted' (v. 6) is the pastoral heart of the chapter. The Assyrian defeat (v. 8) is accomplished not by Egypt's horses but by a sword 'not of man'—God acts directly, without human instrument. Every generation must confront the same choice: Egypt's horses or God's sword.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD! And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong'—the two qualities of Egypt's military that impressed: quantity (many chariots) and quality (very strong cavalry). 'But do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD!'—the defining failure: every military calculation was made without reference to God. 'And yet he is wise and brings disaster'—the irony: God, whom they did not consult, is wiser than all their calculations and brings the very disaster they tried to avoid through their planning. 'He does not call back his words'—prophetic word is not retracted; what God has decreed through Isaiah stands. 'He will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity'—Judah is the evildoer; Egypt is the helper of evildoers. Both are judged. Oswalt: the indictment falls on both parties: the nation that sought help and the nation that provided it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together. For thus the LORD said to me, “As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit'—the decisive theological statement. Two contrasts: man/God and flesh/spirit. Egypt has the wrong category of power. Man and flesh are real but limited; God and spirit are real and unlimited. 'When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall'—the simultaneous collapse: Egypt (the helper) and Judah (the helped) both go down together when God acts. 'As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise'—the lion-God: unmoved by organized human opposition. The shepherds (Egypt's army) can shout and make noise, but the lion (God) does not retreat. 'So the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill'—God fights for Zion with the same unyielding determination as a lion over its prey. Motyer: the lion that fights for Zion is the same lion whose roar in 5:29 signaled judgment; now the lion is on Zion's side.

verseByVerse.quote: Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it.“ Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it'—the four verbs of protection: protect, deliver, spare, rescue. The bird-hovering image is tender and total: a mother bird hovering over her nest to protect it from harm. God's protection of Jerusalem is this comprehensive and instinctive. 'Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel'—the pastoral call in the middle of the oracle: the protection is available; the revolution must be reversed. 'Deeply revolted' (he'emiqu sora): the revolt is deep, not superficial—embedded in the culture and the choices of generations. But the call is given anyway. Childs: the call to turn follows the promise of protection—the grace of God's hovering birds is the context within which repentance is called for, not the reward for repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you. “And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you'—the result of turning to God: the idols are abandoned. As in 2:20 and 30:22, the repentance that turns to the LORD automatically produces rejection of what competed with him. 'The Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him'—the decisive statement about how Assyria falls: not Egypt's cavalry, not Judah's army, not any human sword. A non-human sword—divine action. The historical fulfillment: 185,000 Assyrians die overnight (37:36), with no human hand raised. 'He shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor'—the survivors flee and become labor-conscripts: the proud Assyrian army reduced to slave-work. Motyer: the 'sword not of man' is the chapter's answer to the 'horses that are flesh'—human weapons fail; divine action succeeds.

verseByVerse.quote: His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic,“ declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'His rock shall pass away in terror'—the Assyrian king's foundational security (his rock, perhaps Nineveh or his throne) passes away in terror. The rock of Assyria crumbles; only the Rock of Israel (26:4) remains. 'His officers desert the standard in panic'—military collapse from the top: the officers who should organize resistance flee the battle standard in terror. The organized army of ch. 30:31 dissolves. 'Declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem'—God's own fire and furnace are in Zion: the burning that judged Israel (30:27–28 in judgment) is the burning that refines Zion. The same divine fire that is threat to the enemy is the purifying presence of God for his city. Young: 'whose fire is in Zion' is the eschatological counterpart to the coal from the altar (6:6–7)—the fire that cleansed the prophet now dwells permanently in the city.

32.subtitle: A King Who Reigns in Righteousness
32.intro: Overview. Chapter 32 pivots from the woes to a vision of what good leadership looks like — a king who reigns in righteousness and princes who rule in justice. It is partly a description of Hezekiah as a contrast to the current failed leaders, and partly a messianic vision of the coming king whose reign will be characterized by true sight, true hearing, and true speech. The chapter also includes a striking oracle to the complacent women of Jerusalem, and closes with a vision of the Spirit poured out.

sections.title: The Righteous King
sections.commentary: In this king’s reign, each person will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, streams of water in a dry place, the shade of a great rock in a weary land. Good governance, Isaiah suggests, creates conditions in which people can actually live and flourish. The eyes of those who see will not be closed; the ears of those who hear will give attention. The social pathology of chapter 29 — blindness, deafness, confusion of moral categories — will be reversed. The fool will no longer be called noble; the scoundrel will no longer be honored. Social recognition will track reality rather than distort it.

sections.title: The Complacent Women
