Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth? <sup>22</sup>It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in; <sup>23</sup>who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness. <sup>24</sup>Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble. <sup>25</sup>To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One. <sup>26</sup>Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable. <sup>29</sup>He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. <sup>30</sup>Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted; <sup>31</sup>but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great opening of Isaiah's second major movement. Comfort is proclaimed to a people who have served their sentence of exile. A voice cries in the wilderness to prepare the way. All flesh is grass, but the word of God stands forever. The LORD comes as a mighty warrior and tender shepherd. The incomparable greatness of God is celebrated against all idols. And those who wait on the LORD will mount up with wings like eagles.
verseByVerse.theology: Motyer calls ch40 one of the greatest chapters in Scripture. Its opening word — 'Comfort' — is spoken twice for emphasis and sets the tone for all that follows. Keller uses vv.28-31 repeatedly in pastoral ministry: the promise that God gives strength to the weary is not a cliché but a covenant commitment from the Creator of the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The double imperative — comfort, comfort — signals urgency and emphasis. The exile has been a sentence justly served; now it is over. Three declarations: warfare ended, iniquity pardoned, penalty paid. Double for all her sins does not mean God was unjust but that the full penalty has been absorbed — the debt is cleared. Motyer notes that the prophetic announcement anticipates the ultimate comfort: the atonement of Christ, who bears the double weight of sin so that God can speak tenderly to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice cries: “In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain. And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The New Testament applies vv.3-5 to John the Baptist (Matt 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, John 1:23). The highway preparation is for the LORD himself to come in the new exodus — as he led Israel through the wilderness, so now he comes through all obstacles. The leveling of mountains and filling of valleys is the reversal of every barrier between God and his people. Young: the ultimate fulfillment is in the incarnation — the glory of the LORD revealed in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise toward which all preparation points: the glory of the LORD shall be revealed. Not merely the glory of a military victory or a political restoration, but the very radiance of God's presence unveiled for all flesh to see. All flesh shall see it together — universal and simultaneous. John 1:14 identifies Jesus as the fulfillment: we have seen his glory. Young: this verse is the eschatological climax of the comfort announcement — the return from exile is a foretaste of the ultimate revelation of God to the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice says, “Cry!” And I said, “What shall I cry?” All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass. The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast is the most basic in existence: human transience versus divine permanence. All human glory — physical beauty, political power, cultural achievement — is grass that withers. Peter quotes this in 1 Peter 1:24-25 to ground the gospel: the word that abides forever is the good news preached to you. The comfort of ch40 is not built on human resilience but on the word of God that outlasts every empire, every crisis, and every human life.

verseByVerse.quote: The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological anchor of all gospel proclamation: the word of God stands forever. Everything else withers — human beauty, human wisdom, human empires. But God's word, once spoken, cannot be unmade. Peter quotes this verse (1 Pet 1:24-25) and identifies the abiding word as the good news preached to you. The gospel is not a temporary arrangement; it is the eternal word of the eternal God, which means those who receive it receive a standing that outlasts all created things. Motyer: this is the foundation of Christian assurance.

verseByVerse.quote: Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, “Behold your God!” Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The herald is Zion herself — Jerusalem becomes the proclaimer of good news to the other cities of Judah. The announcement is the simplest and most powerful: Behold your God! The LORD comes as a mighty warrior, his reward in his hand — the returning exiles, their rescue, their vindication. Oswalt: Behold your God is the essence of all gospel proclamation. Every sermon, every witness, every act of Christian care is ultimately pointing to this: look — here is your God.

verseByVerse.quote: He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Immediately after the warrior image comes the shepherd. The same God who comes with might gathers lambs in his arms. This is the paradox of divine love: omnipotence in the service of tenderness. The lambs and nursing ewes receive special care — the weakest and most vulnerable are not left behind. Motyer: this verse, directly applied to Christ in John 10 and implicitly in Luke 15, shows that the gentleness of Jesus is not a departure from divine power but its most perfect expression.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance? Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A series of rhetorical questions celebrating God's incomparability. The creation imagery is staggering in scale: the oceans in his palm, the heavens measured by his handspan, the mountains on his scales. Paul quotes v.13 in Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16 to marvel at the unsearchable depths of God's wisdom. No one taught God; no one counseled him; no one showed him the way of justice. He is the source, not the student. Every human wisdom project eventually runs into the limits of creaturely knowledge; God has none.

verseByVerse.quote: Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: No one taught God wisdom; no counselor directed his path; no teacher showed him the way of understanding. God is the source of all wisdom, not a student of it. This matters practically for the exiles in Babylon: the God who directs their history needs no guidance from Babylon's wise men, her astrologers, or her kings. He has been governing wisely from eternity past. Childs: the rhetorical questions of vv.13-14 establish that God's counsel is self-generated, self-sufficient, and incapable of being improved upon by human advice.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the coastlands like fine dust. Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its animals enough for a burnt offering. All the nations are as nothing before him; they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The nations that seemed so threatening — Assyria, Babylon, Egypt — are a drop in the bucket, dust on the scales. Even Lebanon's cedar forests and all its animals are insufficient for a worthy offering to this God. The cumulative effect of vv.12-17 is to make every earthly power feel small. Childs: this is deliberate pastoral theology — the exiles feel overwhelmed by Babylon's might, and Isaiah insists they view all nations through the lens of God's incomparable greatness. Babylon is dust before the Holy One of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: All the nations are as nothing before him; they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The cumulative verdict on the nations: before God they are less than nothing — emptiness (tohu, the same word used for the formless void in Gen 1:2). The creation imagery is deliberate: just as the formless void was entirely shaped by God's creative word, so the nations have whatever existence they have only within God's ordering. Motyer: this is not political contempt but theological precision — apart from God, nothing has independent standing. The exiles' confidence in God is therefore not irrational but the most realistic position possible.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him? An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains. He who is too poor for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The idol polemic begins: after describing the incomparable God, Isaiah turns to the alternative — handmade images. The sequence is devastating in its logic: a craftsman makes it, a goldsmith gilts it, a poor man chooses rot-resistant wood. The idol that results cannot move on its own. Contrast the God who measures oceans in his palm, who moves nations like dust. Oswalt: idolatry is not merely foolish aesthetically; it is a categorical confusion — treating the made thing as if it were the Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: He who is too poor for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The poor man's idol: choosing rot-resistant wood (a practical consideration) and commissioning a skilled craftsman — all to produce an image that cannot move. The investment of skill, care, and craft into something fundamentally powerless is the tragedy of idolatry. Oswalt: Isaiah is not mocking simple people but exposing the fundamental absurdity of substituting the made thing for the Maker. The craftsman's skill is genuine; the project is futile. Every era has its version of this: replacing the living God with impressive human constructions that cannot act.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth? It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Four rhetorical questions that expose willful ignorance. Creation itself testifies to God's greatness — this is general revelation. The God who sits above the circle of the earth and stretches the heavens like a tent is not hidden; he is the most obvious reality in creation. Human beings appear as grasshoppers from his perspective — not to demean us but to calibrate the scale. Motyer: the tragedy of idolatry is not ignorance of the truth but suppression of it (Rom 1:18-20).

verseByVerse.quote: who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness. Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Political power is equally subject to God's breath. Princes and rulers are planted and uprooted in a single breath — the same imagery as the grass of v.7. Babylon's Nebuchadnezzar, Persia's Cyrus, Rome's Caesar — all are stubble before God's wind. This is not political nihilism but political realism: human governance exists within God's sovereign ordering, and no empire is permanent. The exiles in Babylon are not in the grip of an unconquerable power — they are watched over by the one who reduces all rulers to stubble.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The stars become evidence of God's personal knowledge and power. He brings them out by number and calls each by name. The ancient world worshipped stars as deities; Isaiah says they are God's attendants, called into existence and maintained by him. And not one is missing — his power does not falter in sustaining even the greatest of his works. Oswalt: not one is missing is a pastoral word to the exiles who feel forgotten. The God who keeps every star keeps every one of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God”? Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The pastoral application: the exiles feel forgotten and their cause ignored. God answers with a series of attributes — he is everlasting, Creator, inexhaustible, and unsearchably wise. He does not faint or grow weary — the very thing the exiles do (v.30). The God who measures heavens in a handspan does not run out of strength or lose track of his people. Keller: the answer to feeling forgotten by God is not better feelings but deeper theology — knowing who God actually is.

verseByVerse.quote: He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The paradox: even the strongest humans — young men at the peak of physical vitality — eventually fail. This is not pessimism but realism that sets up the divine promise. If human strength at its peak is insufficient, then the only adequate power must come from outside. The God who does not faint gives power to the faint. His strength flows toward human weakness. Motyer: the entire economy of grace operates on this principle — God's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Wait for the LORD — active, expectant, trusting patience. The Hebrew word suggests hoping, expecting, remaining oriented toward God. The result is strength that exceeds human capacity: eagle wings, tireless running, unwearied walking. Oswalt notes the progression from spectacular to ordinary: first eagle wings (the dramatic), then running (vigorous activity), then walking (daily life) — suggesting that sustained faithfulness in the ordinary is the greatest gift of waiting on the LORD. Calvin: this promise encompasses the whole Christian life.

41.subtitle: Fear Not, I Am with You
41.intro: Overview. Chapter 41 opens the great courtroom sequence of Isaiah 40–48, in which God puts the nations and their gods on trial. The charge: who can declare what is coming? Who has roused the conqueror from the east (Cyrus, though unnamed until chapter 44)? The answer is God alone. Against the silence of the idols — “they are all a delusion” — God speaks the most repeated promise in all of Isaiah: Fear not, I am with you.

sections.title: The Courtroom of History
sections.commentary:
God summons the coastlands to renew their strength and bring their case: who has stirred up the one from the east, delivering nations before him? He pursues them, passes safely, comes swiftly. The coastlands tremble; the craftsmen make idols to encourage each other. The contrast is deliberate: the nations’ response to historical turbulence is to make better gods. God’s response is to announce that he himself is the cause of the turbulence.

Then the address to Israel pivots entirely: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend — I took you from the ends of the earth, called you from its corners, and said to you, you are my servant; I have chosen you and not cast you off. Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God. The theological grounding of the promise is the servant-calling itself: the basis for “fear not” is not the circumstances but the identity God has declared over his people.

v. 10 — “Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.” The three verbs — strengthen, help, uphold — move from the inside out: inner fortification, active assistance, sustained support. The hand is described as “righteous” — the help is not merely powerful but morally aligned, committed to what is true and good.

sections.title: The Silence of the Idols
sections.commentary: God challenges the gods of the nations: set forth your case, bring your proofs. Tell us what is to come hereafter; tell us what is coming. Do good, or do harm. Nothing. They are nothing; their works are nothing; to choose them is an abomination. The silence of the idols in the divine courtroom is their condemnation. They cannot speak because they are not real. The God of Israel is the only one who has been speaking throughout history — announcing, then doing — and his record stands uncontested.

keyVerse.quote: “Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.”
keyVerse.note: The command “fear not” appears more often in Isaiah 40–55 than anywhere else in the Bible. It is not a rebuke of honest fear but a reorientation: you are looking at the wrong thing. The antidote to fear is not courage but the presence of God — I am with you is the reason, not an afterthought.

41.reflection: God says “fear not” immediately after describing himself as the one who roused a conqueror to destabilize the world. The same God who orchestrates the turbulence is the one who says “I am with you.” What would it change about your current fears if you believed that the same God who governs what frightens you is personally committed to upholding you?
41.text: <sup>1</sup>Listen to me in silence, O coastlands; let the peoples renew their strength; let them approach, then let them speak; let us together draw near for judgment. <sup>2</sup>Who stirred up one from the east whom victory meets at every step? He gives up nations before him, so that he tramples kings underfoot; he makes them like dust with his sword, like driven stubble with his bow. <sup>3</sup>He pursues them and passes on safely, by paths his feet have not trod. <sup>4</sup>Who has performed and done this, calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he. <sup>5</sup>The coastlands have seen and are afraid; the ends of the earth tremble; they have drawn near and come. <sup>6</sup>Everyone helps his neighbor and says to his brother, "Be strong!" <sup>7</sup>The craftsman strengthens the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer him who strikes the anvil, saying of the soldering, "It is good"; and they strengthen it with nails so that it cannot be moved. <sup>8</sup>But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend; <sup>9</sup>you whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, "You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off"; <sup>10</sup>fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. <sup>11</sup>Behold, all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded; those who strive against you shall be as nothing and shall perish. <sup>12</sup>You shall seek those who contend with you, but you shall not find them; those who war against you shall be as nothing at all. <sup>13</sup>For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, "Fear not, I am the one who helps you." <sup>14</sup>Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. <sup>15</sup>Behold, I make of you a threshing sledge, new, sharp, and having teeth; you shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and you shall make the hills like chaff; <sup>16</sup>you shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the tempest shall scatter them. And you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory. <sup>17</sup>When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. <sup>18</sup>I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys. I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. <sup>19</sup>I will put in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive. I will set in the desert the cypress, the plane and the pine together, <sup>20</sup>that they may see and know, may consider and understand together, that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it. <sup>21</sup>Set forth your case, says the LORD; bring your proofs, says the King of Jacob. <sup>22</sup>Let them bring them, and tell us what is to happen. Tell us the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, that we may know their outcome; or declare to us the things to come. <sup>23</sup>Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; do good, or do harm, that we may be dismayed and terrified. <sup>24</sup>Behold, you are nothing, and your work is less than nothing; an abomination is he who chooses you. <sup>25</sup>I stirred up one from the north, and he has come, from the rising of the sun, and he shall call upon my name; he shall trample on rulers as on mortar, as the potter treads clay. <sup>26</sup>Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know, and beforehand, that we might say, "He is right"? There was none who declared it, none who proclaimed it, none who heard your words. <sup>27</sup>I was the first to say to Zion, "Behold, here they are!" and I give to Jerusalem a herald of good news. <sup>28</sup>But when I look, there is no one; among these there is no counselor who, when I ask, gives an answer. <sup>29</sup>Behold, they are all a delusion; their works are nothing; their metal images are empty wind.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Fear Not, I Am with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the nations to a courtroom and presents the evidence of his control of history, specifically the rise of Cyrus (the one from the east, v.2). Then he turns to his servant Israel with the most tender assurance: 'Fear not, for I am with you.' The chapter is a courtroom drama demonstrating the LORD's unique sovereignty over history against the utter impotence of idols.
verseByVerse.theology: Motyer sees vv.8-16 as one of the warmest passages of divine comfort in Scripture. The term 'Israel my servant' is introduced here for the first time — a title that will climax in the servant songs. Young notes that 'Fear not, I am with you' (v.10) echoes the covenant formula throughout Scripture from Abraham to the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me in silence, O coastlands; let the peoples renew their strength; let them approach, then let them speak; let us together draw near for judgment. Who stirred up one from the east whom victory meets at every step? He gives up nations before him, so that he tramples kings underfoot; he makes them like dust with his sword, like driven stubble with his bow. He pursues them and passes on safely, by paths his feet have not trodden. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God opens a courtroom hearing: the nations are invited to present their case. Then he immediately presents his own evidence — a conqueror from the east whom victory follows at every step. Most commentators identify this as Cyrus of Persia, though the word 'Cyrus' does not appear until 44:28 and 45:1. The advance announcement of Cyrus's victories, written in the eighth century BC, is a central example of predictive prophecy. Oswalt: God's control of history is demonstrated by his ability to announce it in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: He pursues them and passes on safely, by paths his feet have not trodden. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Cyrus's advance is so rapid that his feet hardly seem to touch the paths he travels — paths he has never trodden before (the conquests are unprecedented). The image conveys both speed and divine momentum: this conqueror moves at God's pace, not his own. Motyer: the historical fulfillment in Cyrus's remarkably swift campaigns (546-539 BC) vindicates the oracle spoken 150+ years before. God's advance announcement and history's fulfillment are the double testimony to the LORD's uniqueness as the only God who controls the future.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has performed and done this, calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he. The coastlands have seen and are afraid; the ends of the earth tremble; they have drawn near and come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God answers his own courtroom question: I, the LORD, the first and with the last. The title 'first and last' — repeated in 44:6 and 48:12 — declares God's existence before all things and beyond all things, the Alpha and Omega (Rev 1:8, 17; 22:13). The nations tremble at what they see but rush toward idols for reassurance rather than toward the God who actually controls history. Childs: this is the irony of unbelief — the evidence of God's sovereignty produces fear but not faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone helps his neighbor and says to his brother, “Be strong!” The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer him who strikes the anvil, saying of the soldering, “It is good”; and they fasten it with nails so that it cannot be moved. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The nations' response to their terror is communal idol-making — they encourage each other in the production of images that cannot move. The irony is savage: human cooperation and skill go into manufacturing a god that then cannot move on its own. Contrast the LORD who moves Cyrus like a chess piece across the geopolitical board. Motyer: the idol-making scene is deliberately comic in its futility — 'it is good,' they say (echoing Genesis), about a piece of metal nailed to the floor.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend; you whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, “You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off”; fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The pivot from nations to Israel is marked by but you. Three bases of Israel's security: servant status, divine choice, Abrahamic descent. Abraham is called God's friend (2 Chron 20:7, James 2:23) — a remarkable intimacy. Then the great promise: fear not, for I am with you. Three future pledges follow: strengthen, help, uphold. The righteous right hand is the hand of covenant faithfulness and power. Young: this is one of the great pastoral texts in all Scripture — applicable to every believer in every moment of fear.

verseByVerse.quote: fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The three pledges of divine faithfulness climax in the most vivid image: I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. The right hand is the hand of covenant faithfulness and power; the grip is God's, not Israel's. This is the pastoral core of election theology: not that God chooses and then leaves us to manage, but that God chooses, strengthens, helps, and holds. Keller: fear not, I am with you is not a feeling to be worked up but a fact to be believed — the presence of the God who created the ends of the earth is pledged to every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded; those who strive against you shall be as nothing and shall perish. You shall seek those who contend with you, but you shall not find them; those who war against you shall be as nothing at all. For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, “Fear not, I am the one who helps you.” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise reverses Israel's position: the ones who shame and threaten Israel will themselves be shamed and will vanish. The repeated as nothing echoes the earlier description of nations before God (40:17). The tenderest image: I hold your right hand. God is not just a distant sovereign who has declared victory; he is the One who reaches down to take the hand of his frightened child and says: I am the one who helps you. Motyer: the grip is on God's side — Israel cannot hold on, but God holds them.

verseByVerse.quote: For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, Fear not, I am the one who helps you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God takes Israel by the right hand — the hand of covenant relationship and personal intimacy. This is the image of a parent taking a frightened child's hand in the dark. The God who created the universe stoops to take the hand of his trembling people. Fear not, I am the one who helps you — not 'help is available' but 'I personally am your helper.' Motyer: every 'fear not' in Isaiah is addressed to weakness; God's help is not distributed to the strong but given to those who know they cannot manage alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I will make of you a threshing sledge, new, sharp, and having teeth; you shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and you shall make the hills like chaff. You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the tempest shall scatter them. And you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Worm Jacob — not an insult but an acknowledgment of real weakness: small, soft, easily crushed. Yet God will transform this worm into a threshing sledge that pulverizes mountains. The transformation is entirely God's work — not self-improvement but divine empowerment. The result: joy and glory in the LORD, not in oneself. Childs: this is consistently the pattern of divine election — God chooses the weak to shame the strong (1 Cor 1:27-29) so that all glory returns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the tempest shall scatter them. And you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The worm Jacob, transformed into a threshing sledge, now winnows the mountains — and the result is joy in the LORD and glory in the Holy One of Israel. The triumph belongs entirely to God; the joy is a response to his action, not human achievement. This is the eschatological pattern of all God's saving work: he reverses the situation of the weak and poor so completely that joy and worship are the only possible response. Childs: Israel's glorying in the Holy One of Israel is the culmination of the servant's mission — a redeemed people who know where their salvation came from.

verseByVerse.quote: When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys. I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The desert transformation is both literal (the new exodus through the wilderness) and spiritual (the quenching of deepest thirst). God answers those whose tongue is parched — the desperately thirsty who have no recourse. Rivers on barren heights and fountains in valleys reverse the natural order: water appears where it cannot naturally be. Oswalt: this anticipates Jesus's offer of living water (John 4:10-14; 7:37-38) — the ultimate satisfaction of the soul's thirst that only God can provide.

verseByVerse.quote: I will put in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive. I will set in the desert the cypress, the plane and the pine together, that they may see and know, may consider and understand together, that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Seven trees planted in the wilderness form a picture of paradise restored — the reversal of curse and desolation. The purpose is explicitly missional: so that all may see and know, consider and understand that the LORD has done this. Even the transformation of creation is evangelistic. Motyer: the new creation is the sign by which the nations recognize that the God of Israel is the LORD. The wilderness is not just beautified; it becomes testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: Set forth your case, says the LORD; bring your proofs, says the King of Jacob. Let them bring them, and tell us what is to happen. Tell us the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, that we may know their outcome; or declare to us the things to come. Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; do good, or do harm, that we may be afraid and terrified. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The courtroom resumes: the idols are challenged to present evidence. The test is simple: tell us what has happened and what will happen. This is the unique mark of the true God — predictive prophecy. Idols can do neither. The final challenge — do good, or do harm, that we may fear you — is darkly ironic: even if the idols could produce some effect, that would establish only power, not the trustworthiness of a covenant God. Young: the challenge exposes the fundamental bankruptcy of false religion.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; do good, or do harm, that we may be afraid and terrified. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The courtroom challenge reaches its most direct demand: if you are gods, produce evidence — do something, even something harmful, that we might fear you. The willingness to accept even a demonstration of destructive power shows how low the bar is. But the idols cannot meet even this minimal test. They are not merely good-neutral; they are actively nothing. Oswalt: the deepest problem with idols is not that they are powerless to do good — it is that they are unable to act at all. The living God, by contrast, does both good and harm, always in justice and covenant faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are nothing, and your work is less than nothing; an abomination is he who chooses you. I stirred up one from the north, and he has come, from the rising of the sun, and he shall call upon my name; he shall trample on rulers as on mortar, as the potter treads clay. Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know, and beforehand, that we might say, “He is right”? There was none who declared it, none who proclaimed it, none who heard your utterance. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The verdict: idols are nothing, and choosing them is an abomination. Then God renews his claim: he announced Cyrus in advance. The double geographic marker — north and east — describes Persia's approach. He shall call upon my name — Cyrus will acknowledge the LORD (44:28-45:6). The rhetorical question drives home the uniqueness: no idol, no other deity said any of this. The silence of false gods at this point is its own verdict. Oswalt: true deity is proven by the ability to speak history before it happens.

verseByVerse.quote: Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know, and beforehand, that we might say, He is right? There was none who declared it, none who proclaimed it, none who heard your utterance. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rhetorical question exposes the idols' silence: no one declared Cyrus in advance, no one said beforehand 'He is right,' no voice was heard from any idol affirming that this was the plan. The LORD alone spoke — through Isaiah — and the plan is unfolding. This is the decisive proof of divine uniqueness: the ability to announce history before it happens is not shared by any other claimant to deity. Young: all of Isaiah 40-48 is structured around this argument — the LORD's predictions come true; the idols make no predictions that come true.

verseByVerse.quote: I was the first to say to Zion, “Behold, here they are!” and I give to Jerusalem a herald of good news. But when I look, there is no one; among these there is no counselor who, when I ask, gives an answer. Behold, they are all a delusion; their works are nothing; their metal images are empty wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God was the first to announce good news to Zion — he spoke it before it happened. Idols, searched for a response, produce silence. Their works are nothing; they are empty wind. The chapter ends with a triple verdict on idolatry: delusion, nothing, empty wind. Motyer: the contrast could not be starker — the God who fills history with his announced purposes versus the idols who produce only silence and emptiness. The chapter's pastoral purpose is to free the exiles from any residual fear of Babylon's gods.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, they are all a delusion; their works are nothing; their metal images are empty wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The triple verdict on idols closes the courtroom scene: delusion, nothing, empty wind. Delusion (aven — vanity, trouble), nothing, empty wind — each term denotes a different dimension of futility. They deceive (delusion), they lack substance (nothing), and they lack power (wind). Motyer: the progression is complete — the God who spoke history is contrasted with the gods who cannot speak at all. The exiles need to hear this verdict so that Babylon's intimidating religious apparatus does not capture their imagination. Babylon's gods are empty wind; the LORD of hosts fills the universe.

42.subtitle: The First Servant Song
42.intro: Overview. Chapter 42 contains the first of the four Servant Songs (vv. 1–9), the most extended and theologically rich of them. The Servant is introduced by God himself, with echoes that Jesus will hear at his baptism (Matt. 3:17). What follows the Song is a portrait of Israel as a blind and deaf servant — the contrast making the Servant’s obedience all the more striking. The chapter ends with a vision of God who has held his peace for a long time and will now act.

sections.title: Behold My Servant
sections.commentary:
“Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights.” These are the words that will be spoken over Jesus at his baptism and transfiguration. The Servant will bring justice to the nations — but not with the tools of power: he will not cry aloud, will not lift up his voice, will not make it heard in the street. The bruised reed he will not break; the faintly burning wick he will not quench. He will faithfully bring forth justice. He will not fail or be discouraged.

v. 3 — “A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice.” Matthew 12:20 quotes this as the explanation of why Jesus withdrew rather than making himself known. His gentleness is not weakness but chosen method — the same power that will establish justice in the earth is the power that refuses to extinguish the last flickering of faith.

The Servant is given as a covenant for the people, a light for the nations — to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon. Three specific tasks: sight, freedom, light. They will recur throughout Isaiah 40–55 as the shape of the Servant’s mission.

sections.title: Israel: the Blind Servant
sections.commentary: The contrast is stark. God calls: hear, you deaf; look, you blind. Who is blind but my servant, deaf as my messenger whom I send? The very nation called to be a light to the nations cannot see; the people who have God’s law in their possession do not hear him. It is a diagnostic of the failure that makes the individual Servant’s obedience necessary: Israel as a whole has been unable to fulfill its calling, so the Servant will fulfill it instead, and in doing so will fulfill it for Israel.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.”
keyVerse.note: The divine introduction of the Servant is the same language used at Jesus’ baptism (Matt. 3:17). The Spirit on the Servant and the justice for the nations are both explicitly taken up in Jesus’ ministry: Luke 4:18 (Spirit upon me) and the Gentile mission of Acts. The Servant Song is not merely predictive but constructive — it defines what the mission will look like before it happens.

42.reflection: The Servant brings justice without a raised voice, without breaking what is already bruised. This describes both Jesus’ method and the method he calls his followers to. Where in your life are you trying to bring about what is right through pressure, volume, or force — rather than the Servant’s patient, gentle faithfulness?

<sup>3</sup>a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice. <sup>4</sup>He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice in the earth; I will gasp and pant. <sup>15</sup>I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their vegetation; I will turn the rivers into islands, and dry up the pools. <sup>16</sup>And I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Servant of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first servant song (vv.1-4) introduces the mysterious figure who will accomplish what Israel could not — bringing justice to the nations with gentleness rather than force. The servant is upheld by God, endowed with the Spirit, and committed to not breaking the bruised reed or quenching the smoldering wick. The rest of the chapter celebrates the new exodus and laments Israel's blindness and deafness to its calling as servant.
verseByVerse.theology: Oswalt sees the servant songs (42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12) as progressively revealing a figure who cannot be identified with historical Israel — the servant succeeds where Israel fails and atones for Israel's sin. The songs anticipate Christ with extraordinary precision.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations. He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice, or make it heard in the street; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God introduces the servant with pride and delight: in whom my soul delights — the same words spoken at Jesus's baptism (Matt 3:17). The Spirit rests on him (cf. Isa 11:2), equipping him for his global mission: justice for the nations. Yet his method is deliberately quiet — no public shouting, no strident political campaigns. The Messiah does not come the way empires come. Motyer: the servant's power is not the power of coercion but the power of the Spirit, and his mission is accomplished not by force but by faithful, quiet obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice. He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands wait for his law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The bruised reed and dimly burning wick are the broken and barely-alive — those the world discards. The servant's care for them is gentleness to the point of protecting what barely exists. This is the heart of the gospel: Christ came for the bruised and barely-burning. Matthew 12:20 applies this to Jesus's healing ministry. And the servant will not himself grow faint — he perseveres until justice is established globally. The coastlands (distant nations) wait for his instruction: this mission is universal from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says God, the LORD, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and what comes from it, who gives breath to the people on it and spirit to those who walk in it: “I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness; I will take you by the hand and keep you; I will give you as a covenant for the people, a light for the nations, to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Creator of all now commissions the servant with a cosmic mandate: a covenant for the people, a light for the nations. The servant is not just a messenger of the covenant — he embodies it. The mission is threefold: open blind eyes, free prisoners, bring light to darkness. Luke 4:18-19 records Jesus reading a parallel passage (Isa 61:1-2) and saying Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing. Young: every aspect of the servant's mission becomes the ministry of Jesus — physical healing as sign of spiritual liberation.

verseByVerse.quote: to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's liberating mission reaches its most concrete expression: open blind eyes, release prisoners from the dungeon, bring light to those sitting in darkness. This is both literal (Jesus heals the blind, Matt 11:5) and spiritual (the great liberation of the new creation). Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus read the parallel passage from Isa 61 and claim its fulfillment. Young: the servant's work is the reversal of every consequence of sin — darkness, bondage, blindness — replaced with light, freedom, and sight. This is the gospel in miniature.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols. Behold, the former things have come to pass, and new things I now declare; before they spring forth I tell you of them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the LORD; that is my name — the absolute self-identification of the God who will share his glory with no idol, no human rival, no false deity. The servant's mission is inseparable from God's own glory: to give the servant his Spirit and his commission is not to share glory but to accomplish it through him. The new things declared before they happen prove that this God — and not the idols — is the genuine LORD of history. Childs: the servant song is framed by proof of divine sovereignty, grounding the servant's mission in God's control of all things.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise from the end of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and all that fills it, the coastlands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its cities lift up their voice, the villages that Kedar inhabits; let the habitants of Sela sing for joy, let them shout from the top of the mountains. Let them give glory to the LORD, and declare his praise in the coastlands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's mission produces a new song — the same language as Psalms 96 and 98, anticipating the new creation praise. The geography is universal: sea and coastlands, desert and Kedar (Arab nomads), Sela (Petra in Edom). Every corner of creation joins the praise. Motyer notes that the new song is not simply the old song in a new key — it is the song of those who have seen the new thing God has done, the redemption accomplished by the servant. This is the worship of the redeemed world.

verseByVerse.quote: Let them give glory to the LORD, and declare his praise in the coastlands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The praise commanded in vv.10-12 climaxes in the coastlands — the most remote and previously unreached peoples — giving glory to the LORD. Declare his praise in the coastlands is a missionary mandate embedded in a song of praise. The new song that the redeemed sing is not for their own benefit alone but as testimony to the world. Oswalt: every act of genuine worship is implicitly evangelistic — when the redeemed glorify the LORD, the watching world receives testimony about who he is and what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD goes out like a mighty man, like a man of war he stirs up his zeal; he cries out, he shouts aloud, he shows himself mighty against his foes. For a long time I have held my peace; I have kept still and restrained myself; now I will cry out like a woman in labor; I will gasp and pant. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God presents two images of himself: the Divine Warrior who roars into battle, and a woman in labor who has waited long and now cries out. The labor image is striking — the long delay of God's action was not indifference but restraint, like a woman holding in the intensity of labor. When God acts, it is with all the pent-up energy of what has been held back. Oswalt: the contrast between the servant's quietness (vv.1-4) and God's battle-cry suggests that the servant's gentle mission is followed by God's decisive judgment of all that opposes it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their vegetation; I will turn the rivers into islands, and dry up the pools. And I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not trodden I will guide them. I will turn the darkness before them into light, the rough places into level ground. These are the things I do, and I do not forsake them. But those who trust in carved idols, who say to metal images, “You are our gods,” shall be turned back and utterly put to shame. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine warrior's advance transforms landscape: mountains leveled, rivers dried, darkness turned to light — all for the sake of leading blind exiles home. I will not forsake them — a covenant promise in the midst of cosmic action. The parallel fate of idol-worshippers is shame and reversal. Motyer: the contrast is the two destinies — the blind led home by the LORD, and the idol-trusters driven back in shame. Faith in the living God leads forward; trust in idols leads backward.

verseByVerse.quote: But those who trust in carved idols, who say to metal images, You are our gods, shall be turned back and utterly put to shame. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast closes the section: those who trust carved idols — saying you are our gods to metal images — shall be turned back and utterly shamed. The same word used for Israel's shame in the earlier chapters (the shame of trusting Egypt) is now applied to idol-worshippers universally. Motyer: the servant's mission to bring light to the nations is met by resistance from those who prefer darkness (idols). Their shame is not vindictive but natural — when the light comes, the darkness is exposed for what it is.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see! Who is blind but my servant, or deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is blind as my dedicated one, or blind as the servant of the LORD? He sees many things, but does not observe them; his ears are open, but he does not hear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A jarring reversal: the servant of vv.1-9 (the ideal servant who opens blind eyes) is now contrasted with Israel, who is blind and deaf despite being God's servant. The nation called to be God's witness cannot see or hear what God is doing. Oswalt: Isaiah distinguishes between the ideal servant (the coming Messiah) and the empirical servant (Israel), who has failed its calling. The servant songs reveal that Israel's failure necessitates a servant who will do perfectly what Israel could not.

verseByVerse.quote: He sees many things, but does not observe them; his ears are open, but he does not hear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel's failure as servant is summarized with painful irony: eyes open but not seeing, ears open but not hearing. The nation that received the greatest revelation in history — the Torah, the prophets, the temple — failed to attend to any of it. This is the mystery of spiritual blindness that Paul will wrestle with in Romans 9-11. Oswalt: the difference between the ideal servant (vv.1-9) and the actual servant (Israel, vv.18-20) is the gap that requires the new covenant and the Spirit — only transformed people can truly see and hear what God reveals.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious. But this is a people plundered and looted; they are all of them trapped in holes and hidden in prisons; they have become plunder with none to rescue, spoil with none to say, “Restore them!” (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's purpose in the law was glorious — to display his righteousness. Israel's situation is precisely the opposite of that glory: plundered, looted, trapped, imprisoned, with no rescuer. The gap between God's glorious intention and Israel's actual condition is the measure of their failure. Childs: this is the theological problem the servant must solve — how can God's glorious purposes be accomplished through a people who have utterly failed? The answer comes in the servant songs, culminating in ch53.

verseByVerse.quote: Who among you will give ear to this, who will attend and listen for the time to come? Who gave up Jacob to the looter, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned, in whose ways they were not willing to walk, and whose law they would not obey? So he poured out on him the heat of his anger and the might of battle; it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him, but he did not take it to heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with a searching question: will anyone learn from this? The exile was the LORD's own doing — judgment for sin, willful refusal to walk in God's ways. And even the fire of judgment did not produce understanding. Israel burned but did not learn. Oswalt: this is the tragedy of unbelief — even the severest providential warnings do not produce repentance without the Spirit's work. The chapter that opened with the servant who opens blind eyes closes with a people still blind. The servant's mission becomes all the more urgent.

verseByVerse.quote: So he poured out on him the heat of his anger and the might of battle; it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him, but he did not take it to heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the fire of judgment — the exile itself — did not produce understanding or repentance. Israel burned but did not learn. This sobering observation explains why the comfort of ch40 is so urgently needed: not because Israel has earned it by repentance but because God, in grace, will act even for people who have not yet understood. Childs: the chapter ends in the darkness of spiritual failure, which makes the opening of ch43 — 'But now thus says the LORD, he who created you, O Jacob… Fear not, for I have redeemed you' — all the more glorious as unmerited grace.

43.subtitle: I Have Called You by Name
43.intro: Overview. Chapter 43 is one of the most personally intimate chapters in Isaiah. After the cosmic sweep of chapters 40–42, God addresses Israel with singular directness: you are mine. The chapter contains the extraordinary promise that when they pass through waters and fire, God will be with them — and then the declaration that Israel is his witness, the one group in all the world called to testify that he alone is God.

sections.title: When You Pass Through the Waters
sections.commentary:
But now — the pivot after chapter 42’s indictment of Israel’s blindness. God created Jacob; he formed Israel. Fear not: I have redeemed you; I have called you by name; you are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned. The promise is not that there will be no waters or fire but that they will not overwhelm or burn.

v. 2 — “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned.” The preposition is through, not around. The promise does not reroute the suffering; it accompanies through it. This is what the three friends of Daniel discovered in the furnace (Dan. 3:25): not rescue from fire but presence in it.

God gives nations as ransom for Israel because Israel is precious in his eyes and honored and he loves them. The language is almost embarrassing in its tenderness: precious, honored, loved. The same God who measures the oceans in his hand names each of his people and counts them worth the world.

sections.title: You Are My Witnesses
sections.commentary:
Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, deaf, yet have ears. Let them assemble: who among the gods can declare this and show the former things? Let them bring their witnesses to justify them. “You are my witnesses,” declares the LORD, “and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he. Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me. I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior.”

The witness is to the absolute uniqueness of God — no savior besides him, no former things he did not announce, no new things he cannot declare. The exodus is evoked as the paradigm of saving power: I made a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters. And now: behold, I am doing a new thing; it springs up; do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.

sections.title: Blotted Out Transgressions
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with a startling reversal: Israel has not called on God or wearied herself with offerings — the worship God is owed has not been given. But God says: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. The motivation for forgiveness is divine — not Israel’s repentance or merit but God’s own name and purposes. The grace is more radical than the sin: the people have exhausted God with their sins, and God responds by blotting out the debt entirely.

keyVerse.quote: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.”
keyVerse.note: Three ground-level declarations: redeemed, named, owned. Each one is a complete answer to a different fear — the fear of condemnation (redeemed), the fear of anonymity (named), the fear of abandonment (mine). The chapter builds everything else on these three. Knowing you are named and owned is the prerequisite for walking through waters and fire without being overwhelmed.

43.reflection: God says “I am doing a new thing; do you not perceive it?” The question implies that the new thing is already present but not yet seen. Where might God be doing something new in your situation that you are too focused on the wilderness to perceive? What would it take to look up from the desert and see the river he is making there?

I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you. <sup>4</sup>Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life. <sup>5</sup>Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you. <sup>6</sup>I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth, <sup>7</sup>everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made." <sup>8</sup>Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears! <sup>9</sup>All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble.
