verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — Fear Not, I Have Redeemed You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens with one of Scripture's most tender assurances: 'Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.' God promises to be with his people through fire and water, identifies himself as the only Savior, announces a new exodus surpassing the old, and then pivots to rebuke Israel's failure to bring him offerings — before declaring the incomparable grace of forgiveness for his own name's sake.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption and name: the word 'redeemed' (go'el) evokes the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth — the one who takes personal responsibility for the restoration of a family member. God presents himself as Israel's kinsman-Redeemer, with a prior claim ('you are mine') that precedes and grounds the rescue. The personal knowledge — 'I have called you by name' — connects to John 10:3 and 20:16, where the risen Christ calls Mary by name. This is covenant intimacy.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller calls Isaiah 43:1-4 one of the great pastoral texts in Scripture, used repeatedly in his ministry with people facing death or loss. The promise 'when you pass through the waters… they shall not overwhelm you' does not promise freedom from suffering but presence through it — which is the deeper gift.

verseByVerse.quote: But now thus says the LORD, he who created you, O Jacob, he who formed you, O Israel: Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: But now — cutting across the lament of ch42's ending. The God who just described Israel's blindness now speaks the most intimate assurance imaginable. Created and formed (bara and yatsar, the words of Gen 1-2) ground the relationship in origination: God made Israel, so Israel is his. I have called you by name — not category ('one of the Israelites') but personal identity. The promises of vv.2 do not exempt from fire and flood but guarantee divine accompaniment through them. Motyer: the comfort is not the removal of the trial but the presence of the Redeemer in it.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you. Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The ransom language is striking: God values Israel so highly he exchanges nations for them. Egypt, Cush, and Seba may refer to Cyrus's subsequent Persian campaigns in Africa. But the theological weight is in the middle verse: you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you. These words — spoken to the exiles in Babylon, a people who had failed, sinned, and suffered — are among the most stunning in Scripture. Oswalt: the love of God for his people is not based on their merit but on his sovereign choice and delight.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The ingathering is universal — east, west, north, south — covering every direction from which the scattered exiles can come. God commands the geographic regions as if they were servants: give up, do not withhold. The language of sons and daughters anticipates the adoption imagery of the New Covenant (2 Cor 6:18; Rev 21:7). Childs: the regathering of Israel from all nations foreshadows the eschatological gathering of God's people from every tribe and tongue (Rev 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made. Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The gathered people are defined by divine calling and purpose: created for my glory. Human existence has a telos beyond itself — the display of God's character and grace. Then the paradox of v.8: those gathered are blind and deaf, yet have eyes and ears — the spiritually impaired servant-people who nonetheless possess the faculties for perception. Young: God gathers his people not because they have seen and heard correctly, but to restore their sight and hearing. Grace precedes reformation.

verseByVerse.quote: All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and show us the former things? Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right, and let them hear and say, It is true. You are my witnesses, declares the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he. Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The courtroom scene from ch41 reconvenes. The nations are challenged to produce witnesses who can declare past and future events. Then God designates Israel as his witness: you are my witnesses. The purpose of witness is transformative: that you may know and believe me and understand. Witnessing to God's acts produces knowledge of God. And the knowledge is absolute: before him no god was formed; after him none shall exist. Motyer: this is pure monotheism — not 'our god is better' but 'there is only one.'

verseByVerse.quote: I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior. I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you; and you are my witnesses, declares the LORD, and I am God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The doubled I, I am is emphatic self-declaration — the divine name itself spoken with urgency. Besides me there is no savior — in the ancient world, gods were frequently divided into creator-gods and savior-gods; Isaiah insists the LORD is both. You are my witnesses — Israel's existence is itself evidence of God's unique saving power. Oswalt: the history of Israel, from exodus to exile to return, is the most sustained empirical argument for monotheism in history.

verseByVerse.quote: Also henceforth I am he; there is none who can deliver from my hand; I work, and who can turn it back? Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I send to Babylon and bring them all down as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's action is irreversible: when he works, no one can turn it back. The oracle against Babylon is remarkable — God will bring down the Chaldeans as fugitives, turning the ships of Babylonian pride into vessels of defeat. This oracle is spoken before the exile is over, before Cyrus has risen — pure predictive prophecy. Young: the One who cannot be stopped in his purposes turns Babylon's boastful power into the occasion of his own glory.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King. Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The titles multiply — Holy One, Creator, King — before the pivot to the exodus. The one who makes a way in the sea is the God of the Red Sea crossing (Ex 14). The new exodus will recapitulate the old. Motyer: every title connects Israel's history to the coming rescue — Creator implies ownership and care; King implies authority over all obstacles; Holy One implies that purity and power are on their side.

verseByVerse.quote: who brings forth chariot and horse, army and warrior; they lie down, they cannot rise, they are extinguished, quenched like a wick: Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Egypt's army swallowed by the sea — extinguished like a wick — is the paradigm of God's saving power. But then comes the stunning command: remember not the former things. The exodus was magnificent, but what God is about to do exceeds it. Childs: this is one of the most astonishing statements in Isaiah. The paradigm event of redemption is being relativized by a promise of something greater. The first exodus is preparation; the new exodus is the reality it foreshadowed.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. The wild beasts will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches, for I give water in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my chosen people, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Behold, I am doing a new thing — present tense, already beginning. The wilderness road and desert rivers invert the old exodus geography: instead of a way through water (Red Sea), now water through the wilderness. Even wild animals (jackals, ostriches — creatures of desolation) will honor God because the desert becomes a paradise. Keller: do you not perceive it? is an invitation to spiritual perception — God is already moving, already at work; faith is the faculty that sees what has not yet appeared.

verseByVerse.quote: the people whom I formed for myself that they might declare my praise. Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The pivot is jarring. Israel was formed to declare God's praise — but instead they grew weary of him. The indictment is not active rebellion but passive neglect: you have been weary of me. Prayer dried up; worship became burdensome; the relationship atrophied. Oswalt: the greatest danger to faith is not violent persecution but spiritual fatigue — the slow drift away from God not through dramatic apostasy but through boredom and neglect.

verseByVerse.quote: You have not brought me your sheep for burnt offerings, or honored me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense. You have not bought me sweet cane with money, or satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God reverses the charge of weariness: you have wearied me with your iniquities. The sacrificial system God gave was not burdensome — he did not demand crushing labor. But Israel substituted sin for sacrifice, burdening God rather than honoring him. Young: the indictment reaches its sharpest point here — God himself is wearied by his people's sin. The anthropomorphism reveals the relational reality: sin grieves God, dishonors him, and makes demands on his patience.

verseByVerse.quote: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Put me in remembrance; let us argue together; set forth your case, that you may be proved right. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions. After the indictment, the most startling grace: God forgives entirely and for his own sake — not because Israel deserves it but because his name and character are expressed in mercy. The invitation to argue one's case (v.26) is ironic — no argument from Israel can succeed; the only ground of forgiveness is God's own initiative. Motyer: for my own sake is the foundation of all gospel assurance. Our forgiveness is secured not by our merit but by the honor of God's own character as Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me. Therefore I will profane the princes of the sanctuary, and deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The judgment is rooted in history: from the first father (perhaps Adam, or Abraham, or Jacob himself — commentators differ) through the priests and mediators, Israel has been a people of persistent sin. The profaning of the sanctuary's princes and the deliver to destruction is the exile itself. But this dark conclusion (the chapter ending in judgment) makes the grace of v.25 all the more vivid — God forgives knowing the full extent of the transgression. Childs: the canonical juxtaposition of condemnation and pardon in this chapter is the shape of all gospel preaching.

44.subtitle: I Have Blotted Out Your Transgressions
44.intro: Overview. Chapter 44 continues the sustained anti-idol polemic of chapters 40–48, but bookends it with two of the most tender promises in Isaiah. God pours out his Spirit on the offspring of his people like water on a thirsty land; the idolater’s absurdity is exposed in devastating detail; and Cyrus is named for the first time as the agent of Israel’s release. It ends with a call to sing — because the LORD has redeemed Jacob.

sections.title: Water on Thirsty Ground
sections.commentary:
“Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen.” Jeshurun — the upright one — is a term of affection, almost a nickname. God will pour water on the thirsty land and streams on the dry ground; he will pour his Spirit upon Israel’s offspring. They will spring up like grass and like willows by flowing streams. The Spirit’s outpouring in the new creation (32:15; Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17) is promised here in terms of fertility and growth.

v. 6 — “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.” Revelation 1:17 and 22:13 place these words on the lips of Christ: “I am the first and the last.” The title is a claim to absolute sovereignty over the whole of history — nothing before him, nothing after him, nothing alongside him.

sections.title: The Absurdity of Idols
sections.commentary:
The idol-maker passage is Isaiah’s longest and most detailed. The craftsman shapes iron with tongs, weakened by hunger and thirst. The carpenter stretches a line, marks with a pencil, shapes it into a human form, a beautiful human figure. He cuts down a tree: half he burns to warm himself and bake bread, saying “Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire.” With the other half he makes a god and bows down to it and says, “Deliver me, for you are my god.”

“No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, ‘Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?’” He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray. The tragedy is not stupidity but a specific spiritual incapacity: he cannot see that he is holding a lie.

sections.title: Cyrus and the Command to Return
sections.commentary:
Remember these things, O Jacob. I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you. Sing, O heavens; shout, O depths of the earth. For the LORD has redeemed Jacob.

Then the astonishing: God “who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose,’ saying of Jerusalem, ‘She shall be built,’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation shall be laid.’” A pagan king is named as God’s shepherd — the very title used of Israel’s ideal king. God has no rivals; even pagan history runs on his lines.

keyVerse.quote: “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you.”
keyVerse.note: The metaphor is precisely chosen: a cloud dissipates without leaving a trace. God does not file Israel’s sins for later reference; he makes them as though they had never been. The motivation for returning is not fear of punishment — the sins are gone — but gratitude: for I have redeemed you. The imperative follows the indicative.

44.reflection: The idol-maker cannot see that half the log is warming his house and the other half is being worshiped as his god. Isaiah says a “deluded heart” blocks the perception. What are the things in your life that you are using half for legitimate comfort and half as ultimate security? What would it take to see clearly enough to say “shall I fall down before a block of wood?”
44.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen! <sup>2</sup>Thus says the LORD who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen. <sup>3</sup>For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants. <sup>4</sup>They shall spring up among the grass like willows by flowing streams. <sup>5</sup>This one will say, 'I am the LORD's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The LORD's,' and name himself by the name of Israel." <sup>6</sup>Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the LORD of hosts: "I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god. <sup>7</sup>Who is like me? Let him proclaim it. Let him declare and set it before me, since I appointed an ancient people. Let them declare what is to come, and what will happen. <sup>8</sup>Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any." <sup>9</sup>All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame. <sup>10</sup>Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? <sup>11</sup>Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together. <sup>12</sup>The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint. <sup>13</sup>The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house. <sup>14</sup>He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it. <sup>15</sup>Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it. <sup>16</sup>Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, "Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!" <sup>17</sup>And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, "Deliver me, for you are my god!" <sup>18</sup>They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand. <sup>19</sup>No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, "Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?" <sup>20</sup>He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, "Is there not a lie in my right hand?" <sup>21</sup>Remember these things, O Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant; I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me. <sup>22</sup>I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you. <sup>23</sup>Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it; shout, O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forest, and every tree in it! For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and will be glorified in Israel. <sup>24</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb: "I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by myself, <sup>25</sup>who frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners, who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish, <sup>26</sup>who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers, who says of Jerusalem, 'She shall be inhabited,' and of the cities of Judah, 'They shall be built, and I will raise up their ruins'; <sup>27</sup>who says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers'; <sup>28</sup>who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'; saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The Spirit Poured Out and the Idol-Maker's Folly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God reassures his servant Jacob with the promise of the Spirit poured out on descendants, then delivers the most sustained and devastating critique of idol-making in Scripture (vv.9-20). The chapter ends with a lyrical declaration of forgiveness and, for the first time, the naming of Cyrus as God's shepherd who will commission the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology: Spirit and salvation: the promise in vv.3-5 that the Spirit will be poured out 'on your offspring' anticipates Pentecost (Joel 2:28-29; Acts 2:17-18). The idol polemic (vv.9-20) is structured as an extended narrative of self-deception: the craftsman uses half his wood for warmth and food, then worships the other half. The conclusion — 'a deluded heart has led him astray' — is Isaiah's diagnosis of all idolatry: a cognitive and spiritual malfunction, not merely a cultural habit.
verseByVerse.examples: Oswalt sees vv.9-20 as one of the Bible's great pieces of satirical theology. The craftsman's logic is internally consistent but catastrophically wrong at the foundational level: he treats wood (created material) as if it could be Creator. The application extends to every age: we worship the work of our hands — achievements, relationships, ideologies — rather than the Maker of all things.

verseByVerse.quote: But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen! Thus says the LORD who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with the same pastoral assurances as ch43 — chosen, made, formed from the womb. Jeshurun (the upright one) is a poetic name for Israel (Deut 32:15; 33:5, 26) that carries affection. God's help is pledged to the servant he has chosen. Motyer: the repeated titles (servant, chosen, made, formed) are not empty repetition but pastoral accumulation — each grounds Israel's security in a different dimension of God's prior action and commitment.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring and my blessing on your descendants. They shall spring up among the grass like willows by flowing streams. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The physical imagery (water, streams) becomes transparent to spiritual reality: the Spirit poured on offspring. The parallel structure makes the equation explicit — water : dry ground :: Spirit : offspring. The result is flourishing, like willows by streams. Joel 2:28-32 (quoted in Acts 2:17-21) picks up this promise and applies it to Pentecost. Childs: the pouring of the Spirit is not merely for Israel's children but foreshadows the universal outpouring that will characterize the new age begun at Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: This one will say, 'I am the LORD's,' and another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The LORD's,' and name himself by the name of Israel. Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the LORD of hosts: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit-filled community will be marked by glad self-identification with the LORD — voluntary, public, personal. Writing on the hand (The LORD's) inverts the slave-mark of the ancient world: these people brand themselves as God's servants out of love, not compulsion. Then God declares himself: First and Last — Alpha and Omega — the title repeated in Rev 1:8, 17; 22:13 applied to Jesus. Young: the First and Last encompasses all of time within God's being; nothing precedes him, nothing outlasts him.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is like me? Let him proclaim it. Let him declare and set it before me, since I appointed an ancient people. Let them declare what is to come, and what will happen. Fear not, nor be afraid; have you not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The challenge to all rival deities: declare the future. God has announced events from ancient times and Israel has witnessed their fulfillment. Is there a God besides me? — the question is rhetorical but real. The answer: I know not any. God's self-knowledge is the final court of appeal. If there were another God, he would know. The Rock image (Israel's ancient metaphor for God's stability and solidity) is claimed exclusively. Oswalt: every other would-be rock proves sandy; God alone provides the foundation that does not shift.

verseByVerse.quote: All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit; their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame. Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The idol polemic opens. The craftsmen are nothing; their products do not profit; their witnesses cannot see or know. Three dimensions of futility: the maker, the made thing, and the witnesses are all impotent. The rhetorical question — who fashions a god? — exposes the category error: fashioning a god is a contradiction in terms. A god that can be fashioned is by definition not God. Motyer: this is the foundational irony of all idolatry — the very act of making a god demonstrates that the maker has more power than the made.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together. The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The craftsmen are only human — a devastating qualifier. The ironsmith who forges a god grows hungry, grows faint. His god is limited by his own human limitations: the deity is as strong as the tired arm that beat it into shape. Isaiah's satire is not dismissive of the skill involved but devastating about the pretensions of the product. Young: the craftsman's very weakness refutes the deity of what he makes. A god fashioned by a hungry, thirsty, fainting human being shares its maker's creaturely limitations.

verseByVerse.quote: The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house. He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a holm tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The carpenter's craft is described with precision — lines, pencils, planes, compass. Genuine skill goes into idol-making. The tree itself grew by God's rain; God's water nourished the material that becomes a rival to God. Childs: Isaiah does not deny the beauty of the idol-image; the problem is not aesthetic but ontological. The human form is chosen for the idol because it is the most beautiful and complex thing the craftsman knows — yet it is still a creature, not the Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it. Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, 'Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic is exposed: the same piece of wood serves for heat, cooking, and worship. Half in the fire, half made a god. The absurdity is complete: the man decides which half is divine. Oswalt: the satire lands on the arbitrariness of idolatry — there is no principled distinction between the fuel-half and the god-half. The person who made the decision has exercised more power over the 'god' than the god could ever exercise over the person.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, 'Deliver me, for you are my god!' They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Deliver me, for you are my god! — the prayer is moving in its pathos: genuine religious need, but misdirected at a piece of wood. Then the explanation of the blindness: God has shut their eyes. This is not an excuse but a judgment — the willful suppression of truth (Rom 1:18-21) has resulted in a judicial hardening. Motyer: idolatry begins in deliberate rejection of the known truth about God; the resulting blindness is not accidental but the consequence of that rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, 'Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?' He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray; he cannot deliver himself or say, 'Is there not a lie in my right hand?' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The diagnostic conclusion: a deluded heart has led him astray. The blindness is not primarily intellectual but cardiac — a disordered affection that distorts reasoning. The final image is devastating: he feeds on ashes — the most nutritionally worthless substance imaginable. He holds a lie in his right hand and cannot perceive it. Childs: this is Isaiah's deepest analysis of sin — not ignorance alone but the self-deception that makes correction impossible from within. Only God can open these eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember these things, O Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant; I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me. I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After the idol polemic, the contrast is glorious: Israel's God knows them, formed them, will not forget them. And the forgiveness announced in 43:25 is repeated: I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud. Clouds disperse; the sins are gone. Return to me, for I have redeemed you — the redemption precedes and grounds the call to return. This is grace: the invitation to come back is based on a completed act, not a conditional promise. Young: the God who blots out sins is not waiting for repentance to decide to forgive; he has already redeemed and now calls the redeemed to walk accordingly.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it; shout, O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forest, and every tree in it! For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and will be glorified in Israel. Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb: I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by myself, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Creation erupts in praise — heavens, earth's depths, mountains, forests. The redemption of Jacob is a cosmic event warranting cosmic celebration. Then God identifies himself as the solitary Creator: who alone stretched out the heavens… by myself. No assistant, no co-creator, no divine council shared in the making. The solitary Creator is the solitary Redeemer. Oswalt: the connection between creation and redemption is essential to Isaiah — the God who made everything can do anything, including bringing his exiled people home through the hand of a Persian king.

verseByVerse.quote: who frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners, who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish, who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers, who says of Jerusalem, 'She shall be inhabited,' and of the cities of Judah, 'They shall be built, and I will raise up their ruins'; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God frustrates Babylon's religious experts (diviners, astrologers, wise men) and confirms his own servants' words. The contrast is between human wisdom that God makes foolish and prophetic counsel that God fulfills. Motyer: every prophetic system that tries to read the future without God ends in frustration — God's word alone stands. The specific oracle about Jerusalem being inhabited and Judah's cities rebuilt was given before the Babylonian destruction. Its fulfillment under Cyrus/Nehemiah is the historical vindication of prophetic truth.

verseByVerse.quote: who says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers'; who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'; saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: For the first time, Cyrus is named — a specific individual identified in prophecy 150+ years before his birth (c. 559-530 BC). He is called God's shepherd — the same term used of God himself in 40:11. God gives his own title to a pagan king to describe the pastoral care Cyrus will exercise toward God's people. Young: the naming of Cyrus is Isaiah's most specific predictive prophecy and is one of the strongest evidences for the prophetic nature of the book. The fulfillment (Ezra 1:1-4) is historical and documented.

45.subtitle: The Creator’s Sovereign Freedom
45.intro: Overview. Chapter 45 is the fullest development of the Cyrus oracle and the theological argument behind it: God is the creator of all things, including darkness and disaster, and he can therefore use whomever he chooses — even an uncircumcised Persian king — as his instrument. The chapter culminates in the most universal call to salvation in all of Isaiah: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.”

sections.title: Cyrus: My Anointed
sections.commentary:
God addresses Cyrus directly — a pagan king, called by name, called “my anointed” (mashiach), the only non-Israelite in Scripture given this title. God will go before him, level mountains, open doors, give him treasures of darkness. And why? “For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen.” Cyrus does not know God — this is stated twice. His ignorance does not diminish his commission.

vv. 6–7 — “I am the LORD, and there is no other. I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things.” The claim is absolute: God creates both poles of every binary — light and darkness, peace and disaster. This is not a statement about the origin of moral evil but about the scope of divine sovereignty over all creaturely reality. Nothing exists outside his governance.

Those who dispute with God are rebuked in the potter-clay language of chapter 29: does the clay question the potter? “Woe to him who strives with his Maker.” The theological point is not that God owes no explanation — Isaiah has given extensive explanations — but that the explanation he gives is not subject to human veto.

sections.title: Turn and Be Saved
sections.commentary:
The nations will come and say: only in you is God, and there is no other. But God hides himself — the God of Israel is truly a God who hides himself — and yet he did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; he did not say to Jacob’s offspring, seek me in vain. The hiddenness and the revelation coexist.

Then the universal call: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other. By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: ‘To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.’” Paul quotes verse 23 in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10–11, applying it to the universal lordship of Christ. Isaiah’s universal call becomes the shape of the new covenant mission.

keyVerse.quote: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.”
keyVerse.note: Spurgeon heard this verse preached at age fifteen and was converted. He later called it the simplest and greatest verse in the Bible: nothing required of the one turning except the turn itself. The universal scope — all the ends of the earth — is not a prediction of universalism but an unlimited offer. The chapter that began with an uncircumcised Persian king ends with an uncircumcised invitation.

45.reflection: God says he is a God who hides himself — and then immediately says he did not speak in secret or in vain. The hiddenness and the revelation are both real. Where in your life does God feel hidden? And what has he already spoken clearly that you can hold onto while waiting for more light?

Does the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' or 'Your work has no handles'? <sup>10</sup>Woe to him who says to a father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'With what are you in labor?'" <sup>11</sup>Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: "Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands? <sup>12</sup>I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. <sup>13</sup>I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward," says the LORD of hosts. <sup>14</sup>Thus says the LORD: "The wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and be yours; they shall follow you; they shall come over in chains and bow down to you. They will plead with you, saying: 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other, no god besides him.'" <sup>15</sup>Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior. <sup>16</sup>All of them are put to shame and confounded; the makers of idols go in confusion together. <sup>17</sup>But Israel is saved by the LORD with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity. <sup>18</sup>For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens (he is God!), who formed the earth and made it (he established it; he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!): "I am the LORD, and there is no other. <sup>19</sup>I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, 'Seek me in vain.' I the LORD speak the truth; I declare what is right. <sup>20</sup>Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, you survivors of the nations! They have no knowledge who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save. <sup>21</sup>Declare and present your case; let them take counsel together! verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Cyrus, the Potter, and Salvation to the Ends of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter addresses Cyrus as God's anointed, uniquely — the only non-Israelite called 'messiah' in Scripture. God declares he will go before Cyrus to open doors and give him treasures. Then follows a challenge to those who question God's methods, using the potter-clay image. The chapter climaxes with the great declaration that 'every knee shall bow and every tongue swear' — the text Paul applies to Christ in Romans 14 and Philippians 2.
verseByVerse.theology: Sovereignty and salvation: God's anointing of Cyrus demonstrates that his saving purposes are not limited to covenant insiders. He can use whoever he chooses. The potter-clay argument (vv.9-10) responds to those who question God's methods: the clay cannot interrogate the potter. Paul deploys this argument in Romans 9:20-21. The universal bow and confession (v.23) is the final vision of Philippians 2:9-11.
verseByVerse.examples: Oswalt notes that calling Cyrus 'anointed' (mashiach) must have shocked original hearers. The term reserved for Israel's kings, priests, and the coming deliverer is applied to a pagan king — showing that God's sovereignty over history is not parochial. This prepares the ground for the universal scope of salvation in v.22: 'Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.'

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed: I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God takes Cyrus by the right hand — the same gesture used of Israel in 41:13. The title anointed (mashiach) given to a pagan Persian king is deliberate and arresting. God will personally go before Cyrus — divine advance preparation for historical conquest. The bronze doors and iron bars refer to ancient Babylon's fortifications; historically, Cyrus's army entered through the city's waterway. Motyer: the God who governs all history uses the most powerful king of the age as his instrument of grace toward his people.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God gives Cyrus treasures — the accumulated wealth of conquered nations — for a purpose: that you may know that it is I, the LORD. God's goal even in secular history is the knowledge of himself. The phrase though you do not know me is remarkable: Cyrus serves God's purposes without personal faith. Childs: this is not universalism (Cyrus is not saved by serving God's purposes) but it is a demonstration that God's sovereignty extends far beyond the covenant community.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the LORD, and there is no other — the monotheistic declaration is made three times in this passage (vv.5, 6, 18). Every action in history — including the rise of Cyrus — is oriented toward this knowledge: from east to west, all people should know there is only one God. Young: global monotheism is Isaiah's missional vision. The goal of redemption is not merely Israel's restoration but the universal recognition of the one true God.

verseByVerse.quote: I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things. Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God claims sovereignty over light and darkness, well-being and calamity — a direct rebuttal to Persian dualism (Zoroastrianism's good god Ahura Mazda vs. evil god Ahriman). There is no rival divine power behind evil; God's sovereignty is total. Then the lyrical invitation: let the heavens rain righteousness, let the earth sprout salvation. Oswalt: the image of salvation sprouting from the earth like vegetation anticipates the new creation, where righteousness is the soil and atmosphere of existence.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' or 'Your work has no handles'? Woe to him who says to a father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'With what are you in labor?' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The potter-clay argument silences those who question God's choice of Cyrus as his instrument. Clay does not interrogate the potter; children do not interrogate parents about the manner of their conception. Paul applies exactly this logic in Romans 9:20-21 to address the question of divine election. Motyer: the argument is not that God is arbitrary but that God's wisdom exceeds creaturely comprehension. The creature who demands to understand every divine decision has misunderstood the relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands? I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rhetorical inversion: instead of the creature questioning the Creator, God invites questions about the future — ask me of things to come. God is not closed to inquiry but to insubordination. Then the credentials: he made the earth, created man, stretched out the heavens. The Creator of the cosmos needs no instructions about how to run history. Young: the challenge is to question God's purposes respectfully in prayer (as in 40:31) rather than rebelliously demanding that his methods conform to our expectations.

verseByVerse.quote: I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward, says the LORD of hosts. Thus says the LORD: The wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and be yours; they shall follow you; they shall come over in chains and bow down to you. They will plead with you, saying, 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other, no god besides him.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Cyrus's mission is defined: build God's city, free the exiles, at no cost to Israel. Then a vision of nations bringing tribute and confessing: surely God is in you. The nations acknowledge Israel's God through Israel's restoration. Childs: this anticipates the eschatological pilgrimage of nations to Zion that appears throughout Isaiah (2:2-4; 60:3-7). The restoration of exiles is not merely a political event but a missional statement to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior. All of them are put to shame and confounded; the makers of idols go away in confusion together. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A God who hides himself — one of the most honest theological statements in Isaiah. God's saving purposes are not always visible; he works through unexpected instruments (Cyrus), through suffering (the exile), through a path not yet apparent. Yet the same verse names him Savior — hidden but not absent, concealed but not defeated. Motyer: the hiddenness of God is the crucible of faith. To believe in a hidden Savior requires trusting his character when we cannot trace his hand. This prepares for the hidden suffering of the Servant in ch53.

verseByVerse.quote: But Israel is saved by the LORD with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity. For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens (he is God!), who formed the earth and made it (he established it; he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!): I am the LORD, and there is no other. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Everlasting salvation — not a temporary arrangement but an eternal state. The idol-makers are confounded; Israel is saved forever. The Creator who formed the earth to be inhabited (not empty, tohu) is making that same intention explicit for his people: the earth is for human flourishing, and so is Israel's redemption — for permanent, lasting habitation in God's presence. Oswalt: the salvation offered in Isaiah is not a rescue from the earth but a rescue to the life the Creator intended for his image-bearers.

verseByVerse.quote: I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, 'Seek me in vain.' I the LORD speak the truth; I declare what is right. Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, you survivors of the nations! They have no knowledge who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's revelation has been public, not hidden in mystery cults or esoteric chambers. Seek me in vain — the LORD has never issued such a call. He speaks truth and declares what is right; his word can be trusted. Then the evangelistic summons to the nations: come, draw near. Those who carry wooden idols are without knowledge, praying to non-saving gods. Young: the invitation to all nations in v.20 is the first explicit universal evangelistic call in the chapter, preparing for the stunning universalism of vv.22-23.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare and present your case; let them take counsel together! Who told this long ago? Who declared it of old? Was it not I, the LORD? And there is no other god besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! — the universal gospel invitation in the Old Testament. No qualifier, no ethnic boundary: all the ends of the earth. The basis: God alone is righteous and Savior. This text grounded Charles Spurgeon's conversion (he heard a lay preacher quote it in a snowstorm when he was fifteen) and has anchored evangelical missions ever since. Childs: this is the climax of the monotheistic argument — if there is only one God, then salvation through him is available to all, and the offer must go to all.

verseByVerse.quote: By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: 'To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.' Only in the LORD, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength; to him shall come and be ashamed all who were incensed against him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God swears by himself — there is no higher oath. The decree is irrevocable: every knee will bow, every tongue confess. Paul applies this directly to Jesus in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10-11, identifying the homage due to the LORD as the homage owed to the exalted Christ. Motyer: this is the most explicit Old Testament anticipation of the universal lordship of Christ. The swearing of allegiance will come either in worship or in judgment; none will escape the encounter with the sovereign God.

verseByVerse.quote: In the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The final verse resolves the chapter's universal scope back to the covenant people: all the offspring of Israel shall be justified. Paul's use of Isaiah throughout Romans includes this inclusive-exclusive dynamic: Israel's covenant privileges culminate in a justification by the LORD that all the nations are invited to share. Young: to be justified in the LORD is to receive the verdict of right-standing before God on the basis of his righteousness, not one's own — the Pauline gospel in seed form.

46.subtitle: Bel Bows Down
46.intro: Overview. Chapter 46 is one of the sharpest contrast-passages in Isaiah: the gods of Babylon are carried on the backs of weary animals, unable to save their worshipers; the God of Israel carries his people from birth to old age. The chapter also contains a pointed challenge to the stubbornly resistant: “remember this and stand firm.”

sections.title: The Gods That Must Be Carried
sections.commentary:
Bel and Nebo — the chief gods of Babylon — bow down and stoop; their idols are on beasts and livestock. The things that were supposed to carry the people are being carried — a burden on weary animals. They cannot save the burden-bearer; they go into captivity themselves. Against this God contrasts himself: even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save. The God who carries has no carrier; the god carried cannot carry.

vv. 3–4 — “You who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.” The carrying runs the full length of a life: from before birth to gray hair. This is the most tender parental image in Isaiah — God as the one who has never set the child down.

sections.title: Remember This
sections.commentary:
Remember this and stand firm; recall it to mind. I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning, from ancient times things not yet done, saying, ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.’ I call a bird of prey from the east — Cyrus — to accomplish my purpose.

I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay. The chapter closes with urgency and finality. The stubborn in heart who are far from righteousness are addressed: I will put salvation in Zion, my glory in Israel. The chapter ends not on judgment but on the arrival of what was promised.

keyVerse.quote: “Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.”
keyVerse.note: The contrast with Bel and Nebo is precise: they were carried to exile; God carries his people to salvation. The idol is the god you must transport; the LORD is the God who transports you. The whole life — from womb to gray hair — is held in arms that have never grown tired.

46.reflection: At what stage of life do you most easily forget that you are being carried? Youth tends to feel self-sufficient; success amplifies it; weariness in old age sometimes makes the carrying visible again. What would it mean, today, to let yourself be carried rather than carrying the weight yourself?
46.text: <sup>1</sup>Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts. <sup>2</sup>They stoop; they bow down together; they cannot save the burden, but themselves go into captivity. <sup>3</sup>"Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; <sup>4</sup>even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save. <sup>5</sup>To whom will you liken me and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be alike? <sup>6</sup>Those who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver in the scales, hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a god; then they fall down and worship! <sup>7</sup>They lift it to their shoulders, they carry it, they set it in its place, and it stands there; it cannot move from its place. If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble. <sup>8</sup>Remember this and stand firm, recall it to mind, you transgressors, <sup>9</sup>remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, <sup>10</sup>declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' <sup>11</sup>calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it. <sup>12</sup>Listen to me, you stubborn of heart, you who are far from righteousness: <sup>13</sup>I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Bel Falls; the LORD Carries
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon's gods Bel and Nebo are carried off by beasts — they are a burden to their worshippers. In contrast, the LORD has carried Israel from birth and will carry them to old age. God alone can declare the end from the beginning. He calls his purpose from afar and will not turn back. The chapter climaxes with a call to remember this and come to salvation.
verseByVerse.theology: Burden vs. carrier: the controlling contrast of the chapter is posture. Idols are carried (they are dead weight); the LORD carries his people (he bears their burden). This reversal illuminates the nature of true religion: does our god need us to sustain him, or does our God sustain us? The idol requires processions, feeding, maintenance, protection. The LORD requires nothing and gives everything.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller uses this contrast in pastoral ministry: every false god ultimately demands more than it gives. We spend ourselves maintaining our idols — reputation, success, approval — and they cannot carry us when we most need carrying. The God who bore Israel from the womb carries them to gray hair. This is the rest that the gospel offers.

verseByVerse.quote: Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts. They stoop; they bow down together; they cannot save the burden, but themselves go into captivity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Bel (Marduk) and Nebo (Nabu), Babylon's chief deities, are depicted in defeat — carried out of the city as its defenses collapse. The very processions intended to honor them (carrying the idol-images in festival) become the image of defeat. Oswalt: the gods who were supposed to protect Babylon cannot even protect themselves; they go into captivity with their worshippers. The same beasts that carried the gods of Babylon in triumph carry them in flight.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast is complete: Babylon carries its gods; the LORD carries his people. From womb to old age — the full arc of human life — the LORD bears his people. I have made, and I will bear — creation and redemption are the same divine commitment. The God who made Israel assumes responsibility for what he made. Motyer: the image of being carried from the womb to gray hair is one of the tenderest in Scripture, depicting God not as a sovereign demanding service but as a parent sustaining the life he gave.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom will you liken me and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be alike? Those who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver in the scales, hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a god; then they fall down and worship! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The incomparability challenge — to whom will you liken me? — introduces another idol-making description. This time the emphasis is on economic cost: gold lavished, silver weighed, goldsmith hired. Idolatry is expensive. People pour their wealth into making gods that then require prostration. The economics of idolatry are perverse: spend everything to get nothing that can help. Young: the contrast with v.3-4 is pointed — the idol costs money; the LORD costs nothing and gives everything.

verseByVerse.quote: They lift it to their shoulders, they carry it, they set it in its place, and it stands there; it cannot move from its place. If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble. Remember this and stand firm, decide, you transgressors, take it to heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The idol's passivity is catalogued: carried on shoulders, set in place, stands immovably, cannot answer, cannot save. The statue-god's stability (it cannot move) is its weakness — it is stuck, unable to act. Contrast the LORD who moves in history, who stirs up Cyrus, who acts in Babylon. Motyer: remember this and stand firm — the call to remembrance grounds the call to repentance. Transgressors who remember the difference between Bel and the LORD will see the absurdity of their ways.

verseByVerse.quote: remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Declaring the end from the beginning — this is God's unique attribute: comprehensive foreknowledge expressed in advance announcement. From ancient times he has said what will happen; what he says stands; his purpose will be accomplished. Childs: this is not merely omniscience (knowing the future) but sovereign determination (ensuring it). God is not a spectator of history but its architect. No Babylonian astrologer or Greek oracle could speak this way with verified accuracy.

verseByVerse.quote: calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it. Listen to me, you stubborn of heart, you who are far from righteousness: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The bird of prey from the east is Cyrus — swift, decisive, hunting down his prey. God calls him from afar; he comes. The principle is universal: what God speaks, he brings to pass; what he purposes, he does. Then the pastoral turn: listen, you stubborn of heart. The stubbornness is not just Babylon's but Israel's — those who resist this God's purposes by their hardness. Young: the sovereignty of God is addressed to the discouraged and the stubborn alike — the discouraged need to know God will act; the stubborn need to know resistance is futile.

verseByVerse.quote: I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter's final word is imminent grace: my righteousness is not far off, my salvation will not delay. After all the polemic against idols and all the demonstration of divine sovereignty, the summary is: salvation is coming, and coming soon. Salvation in Zion — the return of the exiles, the rebuilding, the restoration. Israel my glory — the people through whom God's splendor is displayed to the world. Oswalt: the chapter that began with fallen gods ends with standing salvation — the one sure thing in a world of collapsing idols.

47.subtitle: The Fall of Babylon
47.intro: Overview. Chapter 47 is a taunt song against Babylon — the personified city addressed as a proud queen brought low. It is one of Isaiah’s most sustained pieces of rhetorical art: every claim Babylon made about herself is systematically dismantled. The proud city said “I shall be mistress forever” and “I am, and there is no one besides me.” These are divine prerogatives stolen by a creature. The judgment follows inevitably from the theft.

sections.title: Come Down from Your Throne
sections.commentary:
Virgin Daughter Babylon must come down and sit in the dust — no more called tender and delicate. The queen who sat on a throne will now grind at the mill, cross rivers, have her skirt stripped, her nakedness uncovered. God will take vengeance for the way Babylon treated his people: she showed them no mercy, laid a very heavy yoke on the aged. She did not consider that her power was derivative — that God had given his people into her hand, not into her throne.

v. 8 — “Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no one besides me.’” “I am, and there is no one besides me” is God’s own claim (45:6, 18, 21–22) placed in the mouth of a city. This is the essence of idolatry at the civic scale: a human system claiming divine uniqueness. Revelation 18:7 quotes it directly in the lament over fallen Babylon.

sections.title: Your Wisdom Has Failed You
sections.commentary: Babylon trusted in her evil, saying “no one sees me.” Her wisdom and knowledge have led her astray. Her enchanters, her astrologers, the monthly prognosticators who predict from the stars — let them stand up and save you. They will be like stubble; the fire will consume them. They are of no use, unable to save themselves — much less Babylon. The chapter closes: “there is no one to save you.” The city whose wisdom was sought by all nations has nothing left to offer.

keyVerse.quote: “I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children.”
keyVerse.note: Babylon takes for herself the language of divine uniqueness — the exact words God uses of himself. The claim is both audacious and suicidal: to speak what belongs only to God is to put yourself in the place where only God can stand. The widow-and-loss of the next verse is the precise reversal of the claim: both things you said would never happen will happen in a single day.

47.reflection: The chapter shows what happens when a system — political, economic, cultural — begins to claim divine attributes: self-sufficiency, uniqueness, the guarantee of its own continuation. Where do you see that dynamic in the world today? And where might it be present, more subtly, in your own heart?
47.text: <sup>1</sup>Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate. <sup>2</sup>Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers. <sup>3</sup>Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. <sup>4</sup>Our Redeemer— the LORD of hosts is his name— is the Holy One of Israel. <sup>5</sup>Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms. <sup>6</sup>I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. <sup>7</sup>You said, "I shall be mistress forever," so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end. <sup>8</sup>Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children": <sup>9</sup>These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments. <sup>10</sup>You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, "No one sees me"; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me." <sup>11</sup>But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing. <sup>12</sup>Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror. <sup>13</sup>You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you. <sup>14</sup>Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before! <sup>15</sup>Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A taunt-song against Babylon, addressed as a proud queen brought low. Babylon sat as an eternal queen, never imagining widowhood or loss. She added cruelty to her role as God's instrument of judgment against Israel. Her sorceries and astrologers — her religion — will fail utterly when disaster comes. None of them will be able to save her from the fire.
verseByVerse.theology: Pride and its reversal: Babylon's sin is the claim of eternity — 'I shall be mistress forever' (v.7), 'I am, and there is no one besides me' (v.8, 10). The exact language of divine self-declaration is appropriated by Babylon to claim divine status. This is the ultimate idolatry: self-divinization. The reversal is exact — she who sat enthroned sits on the ground; she who clothed herself in luxury bares herself in shame.
verseByVerse.examples: Childs and Oswalt both note that Babylon's language ('I am, and there is no one besides me') deliberately echoes God's own self-declaration in 45:5-6. Babylon has committed the ultimate sin of claiming to be God. Her fall is therefore not merely political but theological — the cosmos itself must correct the confusion between Creator and creature.

verseByVerse.quote: Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate. Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Babylon is addressed as a pampered virgin daughter now dethroned. The commands are degrading: grind at the mill (a slave's task), strip the veil (a protected woman's covering), wade through rivers (undignified exposure). The reversal from luxury to labor, from queenly dignity to slave's shame, is deliberately humiliating. Motyer: the nation that enslaved others now performs slave labor. The measuring rod used on Israel is applied to Babylon — God is not finished with justice when Israel is punished.

verseByVerse.quote: Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. Our Redeemer — the LORD of hosts is his name — is the Holy One of Israel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Babylon's shame will be fully exposed — no diplomatic cover, no partial concealment. God declares: I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. This is not vindictiveness but justice — the same impartiality that judged Israel judges her oppressor. The interruption of v.4 — Our Redeemer — the LORD of hosts — is a congregational affirmation embedded in the oracle. Israel's worship breaks through: this Avenger is our Kinsman-Redeemer. Young: the community of faith celebrates God's justice on their behalf even in the midst of the judgment oracle.

verseByVerse.quote: Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The indictment of Babylon: she was God's instrument for judging Israel but exceeded her mandate. God was angry with his people and gave them to Babylon — but Babylon showed no mercy, crushed the elderly, exercised gratuitous cruelty. Being used by God does not legitimize all actions. Oswalt: Babylon made the theological error of thinking that because God gave Israel into her hand, her treatment of Israel was therefore approved. But God's use of an instrument does not justify the instrument's excess.

verseByVerse.quote: You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end. Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children': (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: I shall be mistress forever… I am, and there is no one besides me — the exact language of divine self-declaration (45:5-6; 46:9) claimed by Babylon for itself. This is the apex of pride: the creature claiming to be the Creator. The two denials — I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children — will both be false within a generation. Childs: Babylon's sin is not merely pride but theological usurpation — claiming the divine prerogative of eternal self-existence.

verseByVerse.quote: These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments. You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, 'No one sees me'; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The judgment comes in a moment, in one day — the sudden overthrow that historically occurred when Cyrus's forces entered Babylon in 539 BC with virtually no resistance. Sorceries, enchantments, wisdom, knowledge — Babylon's entire religious and intellectual apparatus — will not avert disaster. No one sees me is the delusion of secrecy; I am, and there is no one besides me is repeated, now clearly as the root sin. Young: Babylon's self-sufficiency and self-divinization are the model sins — what began with the serpent in Eden reaches its corporate political expression in Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing. Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sarcasm is withering: stand fast in your enchantments — go ahead, try everything you have. Perhaps it will work. The three disasters (evil, disaster, ruin) are uncharmable, unatonable, and unexpected. All three religious and magical resources fail: the charmer cannot deflect it, there is no ritual that atones for it, and no oracle predicted it. Motyer: the gods and religious systems of Babylon — sophisticated, ancient, elaborate — are helpless before the word of the LORD. What they cannot explain, they cannot prevent.

verseByVerse.quote: You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you. Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Babylon's astrologers — star-gazers, new-moon predictors — are summoned to save her. They fail. They are stubble consumed by the very fire they were supposed to predict and prevent. The dark irony: the specialists in fire-signs (astrology used fire-omens) are consumed by fire. They cannot even warm themselves, let alone save a city. Oswalt: this is the final reductio ad absurdum of divination. When the fire of judgment comes, all the fire-reading experts are fuel for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Such to you are those you have labored with, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction. There is no one to save you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The final verdict on Babylon's allies: they scatter, each fleeing in a different direction. The trading partners, the spiritual advisors, the power-brokers — none stays; none can save. There is no one to save you — the echo of the anti-idol refrain (44:17; 45:20; 46:7). What Babylon said of herself (there is no one besides me) God now says of her situation (there is no one to save you). The woman who claimed to need no one is abandoned by everyone. Young: Babylon's final isolation is the natural consequence of the pride that refused community, accountability, and the LORD.

48.subtitle: Refined in the Furnace of Affliction
48.intro: Overview. Chapter 48 closes the first movement of Isaiah 40–55 with a complex word to Israel — a mixture of rebuke and promise. Israel calls itself by the name of the LORD but not in truth; it has been obstinate and stubborn. God has refined them in the furnace of affliction for his own name’s sake. And then the call: go out from Babylon with singing — and the lament that if only they had listened, their peace would have been like a river.

sections.title: Obstinate Israel
sections.commentary:
Israel swears by the name of the LORD and evokes the God of Israel but not in truth or right. God has long announced former things; they were declared before they sprang forth, lest Israel claim it was its own idol that did them. Because Israel is obstinate — stubborn as iron, hard as bronze — God tells new things that were previously hidden, so Israel cannot say it already knew them.

“Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction. For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned?” The motive for preservation is not Israel’s merit but God’s name. The refining is not primarily punitive but purifying: something is being extracted that was not precious.

v. 10 — “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction.” “Not as silver” means the affliction was not primarily to produce refined material but to prevent a harder outcome. Peter uses the same furnace-of-refining image in 1 Pet. 1:7 for the testing of faith. The furnace belongs to God; nothing enters it without his permission, and nothing leaves it without his purpose served.

sections.title: Go Out from Babylon
sections.commentary:
Listen to me, O Jacob, Israel whom I called: I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. Cyrus will carry out God’s purpose — and then: go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, with a shout of joy, proclaim it. God redeems his servant Jacob.

The chapter closes with one of the great “if only” statements of Scripture: “If only you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.” This is not recrimination but lament — the grief of God over what could have been. The river-peace was available; Israel chose differently. And then the last verse of the chapter: “There is no peace, says the LORD, for the wicked.” The section closes on both the promise and the condition.

keyVerse.quote: “Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.”
keyVerse.note: The “oh that” is a divine wish — God grieving over the peace his people did not take hold of. River-peace suggests both depth and continuity: not a burst of feeling but a sustained, flowing shalom. It was always available; obedience was always the channel. The lament is an invitation dressed as regret.
