48.reflection: God says he refined Israel “for my own sake” — not primarily for their growth but for his name’s vindication. How does it feel to know that God’s purposes in your suffering may have more to do with his name than your comfort? And what does the promise of river-peace say to you about the connection between obedience and the peace you most want?
48.text: <sup>1</sup>Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel, and who came from the waters of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right. <sup>2</sup>For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name. <sup>3</sup>"The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass. <sup>4</sup>Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass, <sup>5</sup>I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.' <sup>6</sup>You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? From this time forth I announce to you new things, hidden things that you have not known. <sup>7</sup>They are created now, not long ago; before today you have never heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.' <sup>8</sup>You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel. <sup>9</sup>For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off. <sup>10</sup>Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction. <sup>11</sup>For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another. <sup>12</sup>Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. <sup>13</sup>My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together. <sup>14</sup>Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans. <sup>15</sup>I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way. <sup>16</sup>Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it came to be I have been there." And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit. <sup>17</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go. <sup>18</sup>Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; <sup>19</sup>your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me." <sup>20</sup>Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, "The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!" <sup>21</sup>They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out. <sup>22</sup>"There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Refined but Not Consumed; Come Out of Babylon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter rebukes Israel's stubbornness and hypocrisy — swearing by God's name without truth or right — while declaring that God announced events in advance so Israel could not credit idols. God refined Israel in the furnace of affliction for his own name's sake. The chapter closes with the great invitation: 'Go out from Babylon!' — the new exodus, the declaration that there is no peace for the wicked.
verseByVerse.theology: Stubbornness and grace: the tension in the chapter is between Israel's persistent hardness (vv.4, 8 — 'I know that you are obstinate') and God's persistent grace ('for my name's sake I defer my anger,' v.9). God's purpose in the exile was refining (v.10), not destroying. He acts for his own name's sake — which is the surest foundation for his people's hope, because God's name cannot fail even when his people are faithless.
verseByVerse.examples: Childs notes that chapter 48 closes the first major section of Isaiah 40-55. The closing verse — 'there is no peace for the wicked' — creates a hinge. It appears again in 57:21 to close the middle section and points forward to the work of the Servant (53:5, 'upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace').

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel, and who came from the waters of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right. For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The indictment is subtle and devastating: Israel uses all the right language — swearing by the LORD, confessing the God of Israel, calling themselves after the holy city — but not in truth or right. Formal religious identity without genuine commitment. Oswalt: this is the perennial danger of covenant religion — inheriting the vocabulary of faith without the reality. The people who claim God's name most loudly may be most insulated from actually knowing him.

verseByVerse.quote: The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass. Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God declared events in advance and fulfilled them — so Israel could not claim the idols did it. But the reason for this advance declaration is Israel's stubbornness: the obstinate, brass-forehead people needed extra evidence. Motyer: God's predictive prophecy is not merely an apologetic tool but a pastoral accommodation to human hardness of heart. He builds the evidential case for those who would otherwise refuse to believe. The hardness is real and God knows it; the grace works around and through it.

verseByVerse.quote: I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.' You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? I announce to you new things from this time, things hidden and you have not known. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of advance prophecy: to deny idols any credit for fulfilled events. Now new things are announced — things hidden, not previously revealed. The new exodus, Cyrus, the servant — things unprecedented. Childs: the distinction between former things (announced and fulfilled) and new things (now being announced) structures the entire argument of Isaiah 40-48. The former things prove God's prophetic power; the new things are the substance of the gospel announcement.

verseByVerse.quote: They are created now, not long ago; before today you have not heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.' You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The new things are genuinely new — not extensions of old patterns but unprecedented acts. God withheld them precisely so Israel could not claim prior knowledge and thereby dismiss the grace. The accusation intensifies: from before birth you were called a rebel. The stubbornness is not circumstantial but constitutional — Israel's rebellion is original, not acquired. Young: this is not pessimism about human nature but realism — the grace that works with such deep obstinacy must be all the more powerful and sovereign.

verseByVerse.quote: For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: For my name's sake I defer my anger — the foundation of grace is God's own character, not Israel's merit. The restraint of judgment is for his praise — God's reputation as Redeemer requires that he not abandon the people he has called. The furnace of affliction (exile) is a refining process, but not as silver: silver is refined to purity; Israel's refining produces survivors who know their dependence on God. Motyer: the exile is simultaneously judgment and grace — God judges Israel's sin but preserves the remnant for his purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another. Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The doubled for my own sake is emphatic: God's action in redemption is self-motivated. This is not cold or selfish — it means redemption is grounded in the most reliable foundation possible, God's own honor. My glory I will not give to another — the covenant commitment that makes rescue certain. Then: I am the first and I am the last — the Alpha and Omega declaration that encompasses all time within God's being. Childs: the First and Last encompasses every moment of Israel's history within God's sovereign care.

verseByVerse.quote: My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together. Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Creator who spoke creation into being by name — stars obeying his call — is the same God who speaks Cyrus into action. The personification is striking: creation has a worshipper's response to God's voice (they stand forth together). Then the court is reconvened: who among the idol-worshippers predicted Cyrus? None. The LORD loves him — Cyrus is an object of divine affection in the sense of divine purpose. Young: God's love for Cyrus is instrumental, purposive love — he loves him for what he will accomplish for Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way. Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it was, there I was. And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: V.16b is one of the most remarkable statements in Isaiah: the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit — a three-person dynamic: the LORD (Father), the speaker (the servant/prophet), and the Spirit. Many commentators (Childs, Motyer, Young) see this as a transition from prophetic speech to servant speech, with trinitarian overtones. Motyer: whether referring to the prophet or the Servant, the three-person formula anticipates the NT revelation of Trinity and the Spirit-anointed mission of the Servant.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go. Oh that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The lament is one of Scripture's great what ifs: Oh that you had listened! Peace like a river, righteousness like ocean waves — these are what obedience would have produced. The images convey abundance, persistence, and irresistible flow. But Israel did not listen. The lament is not resignation but passion: God is grieved by the peace his people forfeited. Oswalt: the oh that of v.18 is the divine ache — God who could not be forced to feel anything feels the loss of what might have been.

verseByVerse.quote: your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me. Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, 'The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After the lament comes the command: Go out from Babylon! The new exodus begins with a shout rather than a flight. Declare this… proclaim it… send it to the end of the earth — the redemption of Jacob is news for all nations. The scope of the announcement makes the return from exile the prototype of the universal gospel proclamation. Childs: the command to go out from Babylon is echoed in Rev 18:4 (Come out of her, my people) — the spiritual Babylon of any age is to be abandoned by God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out. There is no peace, says the LORD, for the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The water-from-the-rock miracle (Ex 17:1-7; Num 20:7-11) is recalled as promise: the God who provided in the first wilderness will provide in the new wilderness of the return journey. Then the jarring close: there is no peace for the wicked. This refrain (repeated in 57:21) closes the section with a warning: the comfort and the new exodus are for those who come out of Babylon — the wicked who remain outside the covenant of grace have no access to the peace that the LORD gives. Young: the hinge verse points forward to ch53, where the servant's suffering produces the peace that the wicked cannot have.

49.subtitle: The Second Servant Song
49.intro: Overview. Chapter 49 contains the second Servant Song (vv. 1–6), in which the Servant speaks of his calling from the womb, his discouragement, and the breathtaking expansion of his mission: not just to restore Israel, but to be a light to the nations, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth. The remainder of the chapter addresses Israel’s complaint that God has forsaken her, with one of the most intimate motherhood images in the Bible.

sections.title: Light to the Nations
sections.commentary:
The Servant addresses the coastlands and distant peoples. He was called from the womb, his name named before his birth. God made his mouth like a sharp sword, his hand a polished arrow. And then a confession: I said, I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity. Yet my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God. The Servant experiences what every faithful minister experiences: the apparent futility of the work.

v. 6 — “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.” Paul quotes this verse in Acts 13:47 as the mandate for the Gentile mission. The Servant’s calling to restore Israel turns out to be too small — God’s purposes are always larger than even the faithful servant imagines. The mission expands to fill the earth.

sections.title: The Mother Who Cannot Forget
sections.commentary:
Zion says: the LORD has forsaken me; the LORD has forgotten me. The divine answer is one of the most intimate passages in Isaiah: Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.

The image of engraving on palms is permanent and personal: this is not a note filed away but a mark on the body that cannot be removed without injury to God himself. The walls of Zion are not ruins to God but a living concern he holds before himself constantly. The chapter ends with the restoration of the scattered: kings will be nursing fathers, queens nursing mothers; and all flesh will know that the LORD is the Savior, the Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.

keyVerse.quote: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.”
keyVerse.note: The argument moves from the most reliable human attachment — mother to nursing infant — to something more reliable still. God does not merely match maternal love; he exceeds it. The engraving-on-palms image anticipates the wounds in the hands of Christ — the permanent bodily record of what it cost to keep the promise.

49.reflection: The Servant confessed that he had labored in vain — and God immediately expanded his commission. The experience of apparent futility preceded the revelation of greater purpose. Where in your life have you been most tempted to conclude that your faithfulness has been wasted? And what would it mean to respond with the Servant’s posture: “yet my right is with the LORD”?
49.text: <sup>1</sup>Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name. <sup>2</sup>He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away. <sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified." <sup>4</sup>But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God." <sup>5</sup>And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength— <sup>6</sup>he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth." <sup>7</sup>Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you." <sup>8</sup>Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages, <sup>9</sup>saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture; <sup>10</sup>they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. <sup>11</sup>And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up. <sup>12</sup>Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene." <sup>13</sup>Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted. <sup>14</sup>But Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me." <sup>15</sup>"Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. <sup>16</sup>Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me. <sup>17</sup>Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you. <sup>18</sup>Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does. <sup>19</sup>Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land— surely now you will be too cramped for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away. <sup>20</sup>The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too cramped for me; make room for me to dwell in.' <sup>21</sup>Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'" <sup>22</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders. <sup>23</sup>Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame." <sup>24</sup>Can the prey be taken from the mighty man, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued? <sup>25</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children. <sup>26</sup>I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Servant's Mission and Zion Comforted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second servant song (vv.1-6) introduces the servant speaking in first person about his hidden preparation and his commission to restore Israel and be a light to the nations. The servant is discouraged (v.4) but God enlarges his mission globally. Zion then voices the fear of abandonment; God answers with one of Scripture's most tender speeches — 'Can a woman forget her nursing child? Even if she could, I will not forget you.'
verseByVerse.theology: The servant and Israel: in the second servant song the servant is distinguished from Israel (v.5 — 'to bring Jacob back to him, and that Israel might be gathered to him'). The servant has a mission TO Israel, which means he cannot simply be identified with Israel. He is the true Servant who does what Israel failed to do — bringing both Israel and the nations to God. This distinction is crucial for understanding Isaiah 53.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller notes that vv.14-16 ('I have engraved you on the palms of my hands') are among the most comforting in all Scripture. The image of engraved palms (permanent inscription, unlike writing that fades) means God's people are literally written on his hands — impossible to forget, impossible to remove.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named me. He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant speaks to the nations — not to Israel alone but to the farthest coastlands. Called from the womb (like Jeremiah, Jer 1:5; like Paul, Gal 1:15; and supremely like Jesus, Luke 1:31), the servant's vocation precedes his birth. The weapons — sharp sword, polished arrow — are instruments of the word, not of violence. Both are hidden before deployment: in the shadow of God's hand, in his quiver. Motyer: hiddenness is the preparation for the appointed time of revelation. The Servant who suffers in obscurity is being sharpened for his ultimate mission.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified.' But I said, 'I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant is addressed as Israel — he embodies and represents the true Israel. But v.4 reveals genuine discouragement: the work seems fruitless, strength spent in vain. This is the dark night of the prophetic soul. Yet the servant's faith holds: my right is with the LORD. He entrusts the verdict and the reward to God. Oswalt: the servant's combination of human discouragement and divine trust is the portrait of faithful ministry — persisting without visible results because God has promised vindication.

verseByVerse.quote: And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength— he says: 'It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's answer to the servant's discouragement is an enlarged commission. Restoring Israel is too light a thing — the servant's mission is extended to all nations, that God's salvation may reach earth's farthest boundary. Paul and Barnabas quote v.6 in Acts 13:47 as the mandate for Gentile mission: I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth. Childs: the universality of the Servant's mission means that what begins with Israel's restoration is destined to encompass the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: 'Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.' Thus says the LORD: 'In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant for the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's present state — deeply despised, abhorred, subject to rulers — will be reversed when kings prostrate themselves before him. The reversal is grounded in God's faithfulness, not the servant's current status. Paul quotes in a time of favor… in a day of salvation from v.8 in 2 Cor 6:2: now is the favorable time; now is the day of salvation. Motyer: the servant given as a covenant for the people means he embodies the covenant relationship — he is not merely a covenant messenger but its personal guarantor.

verseByVerse.quote: saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture; they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's liberating proclamation — come out, appear — echoes the jubilee trumpet (Lev 25) and foreshadows Jesus's reading of Isa 61 in Luke 4. The released prisoners enjoy the care of a shepherd: food on bare heights (where shepherds lead), freedom from thirst and scorching heat, guidance to springs. Revelation 7:16-17 applies exactly this imagery to the great multitude before the throne. Young: the servant's release of prisoners becomes the pattern for all gospel proclamation — to announce liberty to captives is the very definition of the good news.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up. Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Sinim. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The geography of return is universal: mountains become roads, every terrain obstacle is engineered for the homecoming. People come from every direction — north, west, and Sinim (perhaps the far east, possibly China). The ingathering exceeds the original exodus in geographic scope. Childs: the return from Babylon is the type; its antitype is the eschatological gathering of all God's people from every nation. The servant's mission that began in obscurity (vv.1-2) ends in a universal homecoming.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted. But Zion said, 'The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Heaven and earth erupt in praise at God's comfort — but Zion's voice interrupts with the darkest lament: forsaken, forgotten. The juxtaposition is pastoral genius: even when cosmic forces celebrate God's salvation, the suffering community cannot yet perceive it. The lament is real, not wrong. It expresses the experience of desolation. Motyer: God does not rebuke Zion for the lament. He answers it. The cry of abandonment is met not with correction but with the most tender possible response.

verseByVerse.quote: Can a woman forget her nursing infant, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The answer to Zion's lament is the tenderest image in Isaiah. A nursing mother's bond is the strongest natural human attachment imaginable — and even this may theoretically be broken. But God's bond with his people cannot be. I have engraved you on the palms of my hands — permanent inscription, like a tattoo on skin. You are written on the very hands God uses to act in history. Oswalt: the engraving imagery suggests that every act of God's hand in history is performed by hands that bear our names. We are literally carried in his action.

verseByVerse.quote: Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you. Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The destroyed city will be rebuilt faster than it was ruined; the destroyers leave while the builders arrive. The returning exiles are pictured as jewels, as bridal ornaments — what was loss becomes adornment. The oath as I live (God swearing by his own existence) is the strongest possible pledge. Young: Zion's fear of being forgotten is answered not merely by promise but by divine oath. The God who cannot die guarantees by his own undying life the restoration he has promised.

verseByVerse.quote: Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land — surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away. The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The desolate city will be overpopulated — more children than space can contain. The children born in exile and bereavement will fill Jerusalem beyond capacity. This reversal of desolation is so complete that the city complains of crowding rather than emptiness. Motyer: the imagery deliberately echoes the barren woman who bears more children than the married woman (54:1). God's creative power turns the most devastating loss into the most extravagant abundance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?' Thus says the Lord GOD: 'Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Zion's bewildered question — who has borne me these? — is the voice of grace received beyond expectation. The children appear from nowhere; the bereaved mother cannot account for them. God's answer: the nations will carry them home, sons in arms, daughters on shoulders. The nations who were instruments of judgment become the couriers of restoration. Childs: the reversal is complete — those who carried Israel off in exile will carry Israel's children home with care.

verseByVerse.quote: Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame. Can the prey be taken from the mighty man, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Kings as foster-fathers, queens as nursing-mothers — the political reversal is complete. Those who once oppressed Israel now nurture her. The prostration and dust-licking is the ancient Near Eastern gesture of complete submission. Then the rhetorical question sets up the final promise: can prey be taken from the mighty? Can captives escape a tyrant? Humanly, no. But God says yes — he will contend with the contender and rescue the captives.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD: 'Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children. I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God answers his own rhetorical question with total commitment: he will personally contend with the contenders. The graphic judgment on oppressors — eating their own flesh, drunk on their own blood — is covenant language for complete self-destruction (the oppressor's violence turns back on itself). The purpose is universal knowledge: all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior. Young: the Mighty One of Jacob is the One who proved his might at the Exodus and now proves it again. The title carries every previous act of divine rescue into this new promise.

54.subtitle: Sing, O Barren One
54.intro: Overview. Chapter 54 is the song of the covenant renewed after the Servant’s work in chapter 53. The barren woman who is called to sing is Israel, and the grounds for the singing are the husband’s return. God was angry for a moment but will have everlasting love. The chapter closes with a promise that no weapon formed against God’s people shall prosper — not because they are invincible but because God is their champion.

sections.title: The Barren Woman Sings
sections.commentary:
Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! Paul quotes verse 1 in Galatians 4:27, applying it to the new covenant community — the children of the free woman, born not through natural descent but through promise. Enlarge your tent; lengthen your cords; strengthen your stakes. You will spread abroad to the right and to the left.

vv. 7–8 — “For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you.” The proportion is startling: a brief moment of anger against everlasting love. The exile felt like eternity; God sees it as a moment. The everlasting love is not the same quantity as the anger; it is categorically different in kind and duration.

The covenant of peace — berith shalom — will not be removed. As God swore to Noah that the waters would never again cover the earth, so he swears that his steadfast love will not depart from his people. The Noah comparison is deliberate: this is a covenant with creation-level permanence.

sections.title: The City of Righteousness
sections.commentary:
O afflicted city, storm-tossed and not comforted: I will set your stones in antimony, your foundations in sapphires, your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles. All your children will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their peace. This is the city of chapter 35 and the new Jerusalem of Revelation 21 — the same precious stones, the same divine instruction, the same peace.

And the climax: “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me.” The promise is specific: not that no weapons will be fashioned — they will be — but that none will succeed. God guarantees the outcome without removing the conflict.

keyVerse.quote: “For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you.”
keyVerse.note: The geological stability of mountains is the benchmark for everything we consider permanent — and God places his love above it. Mountains will move before his love departs. This is the answer to chapter 39’s shadow and every experience of divine absence: the absence was a moment; the love is permanent.

54.reflection: God describes the exile as a “brief moment” of anger against which he sets “everlasting love.” What season of God’s apparent absence are you in or have you been in? What would it mean to let God re-proportion your experience — to see the moment in the light of the everlasting, rather than letting the moment obscure the everlasting?
54.text: <sup>1</sup>"Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married," says the LORD. <sup>2</sup>"Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. <sup>3</sup>For you will spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations and will people the desolate cities. <sup>4</sup>Fear not, for you will not be ashamed; be not confounded, for you will not be disgraced; for you will forget the shame of your youth, and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more. <sup>5</sup>For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name; and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer, the God of the whole earth he is called. <sup>6</sup>For the LORD has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off," says your God. <sup>7</sup>"For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. <sup>8</sup>In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you," says the LORD, your Redeemer. <sup>9</sup>"This is like the days of Noah to me: as I swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you and will not rebuke you. <sup>10</sup>For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed," says the LORD, who has compassion on you. <sup>11</sup>"O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires. <sup>12</sup>I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones. <sup>13</sup>All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children. <sup>14</sup>In righteousness you shall be established; you shall be far from oppression, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. <sup>15</sup>If anyone stirs up strife, it is not from me; whoever stirs up strife with you shall fall because of you. <sup>16</sup>Behold, I have created the smith who blows the fire of coals and produces a weapon for its purpose. I have also created the ravager to destroy; <sup>17</sup>no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me, declares the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Sing, Barren Woman: the Everlasting Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Following the servant's atoning work, the barren woman (Zion) is called to sing, for she will have more children than the married woman. The husband who seemed to abandon her returns with everlasting love and great compassion. The covenant of peace is as sure as the covenant with Noah. God will build Jerusalem with precious stones, and no weapon formed against her will prosper.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace through the servant's work: ch54 flows directly from the servant's sacrifice in ch53. The barren woman who is suddenly fruitful, the forsaken wife who is reclaimed — these are pictures of the community that benefits from the servant's atoning death. Paul quotes v.1 in Galatians 4:27 as describing the freedom of the gospel over against the bondage of the law: the barren (Gentile) church has more children than the established synagogue.
verseByVerse.examples: The everlasting covenant of peace (v.10) is one of Isaiah's terms for the new covenant (also 55:3; 61:8). Unlike the Mosaic covenant which could be broken (Jer 31:32), this covenant of peace will never be removed. It rests on God's love and compassion, not human faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married, says the LORD. Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The barren woman — Zion in exile, desolate and childless — is commanded to sing before the children arrive. Faith anticipates the gift. Enlarge the tent — expect overflow, not merely a modest restoration. Sarah was the original barren woman (51:2); Zion now receives the same promise in an expanded key. Paul quotes v.1 in Gal 4:27 to show that the barren church (Gentiles, outside the covenant) is becoming more populous than the established covenant community. Motyer: the command to enlarge before seeing the children is the posture of faith — acting on the promise before the evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: For you will spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations and will people the desolate cities. Fear not, for you will not be ashamed; be not confounded, for you will not be disgraced; for you will forget the shame of your youth, and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The expansion is geographic and missiological: left, right, possessing nations, repopulating desolate cities. The community formed by the servant's work is inherently outward-moving. Shame and disgrace — the marks of the exile — will be forgotten: the shame of Egypt (Israel's youth), the disgrace of Babylon (the widowhood). Oswalt: the complete forgetting of shame is one of the most distinctive promises of Isaiah. God does not merely reduce shame; he eliminates its power over the community's identity. New identity in redemption requires the release of old shame.

verseByVerse.quote: For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name; and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer, the God of the whole earth he is called. For the LORD has called you like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit, like a wife of youth when she is cast off, says your God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Your Maker is your husband — the intimacy of the Creator-Redeemer relationship expressed in marital language. The God of the whole earth stoops to be the husband of a deserted, grieving community. Wife of youth when she is cast off — the most vulnerable, most painful marital situation. This is the condition God addresses: not the proud or the established but the abandoned. Young: the marriage metaphor throughout Isaiah (and Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea) grounds the covenant relationship in the most intimate human bond, showing that God's commitment is relational, not merely contractual.

verseByVerse.quote: For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you, but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you, says the LORD, your Redeemer. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The exile is placed in perspective: a brief moment of desertion, a moment of overflowing anger. But the other side is disproportionate: great compassion, everlasting love. The contrast of brief versus everlasting is the key. Oswalt: God is not equating his anger and his love as equal forces; the anger was momentary, the love is eternal. The exile reveals the temporary consequence of sin; the return reveals the permanent priority of grace. Paul's logic in Romans 8:18 is parallel: present suffering is not worth comparing to coming glory.

verseByVerse.quote: This is like the days of Noah to me: as I swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you and will not rebuke you. For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant of peace is as permanent as the Noahic covenant. The rainbow promise — no more flood — stands as the analogy: just as certain as God's promise to Noah (which has held for all of human history) is his promise to never again be angry with his people. Mountains may depart and hills be removed — geological catastrophe — but the steadfast love (hesed) will not depart. The new covenant is unconditional and eternal: not based on Israel's faithfulness but God's character. Childs: the everlasting covenant of peace is the new covenant in Jeremiah 31:31-34, grounded in the servant's atoning work.

verseByVerse.quote: O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires. I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The storm-tossed, uncomforted city will be rebuilt in precious stones — antimony, sapphires, agate, carbuncles. This is the New Jerusalem vision that Revelation 21:18-21 develops explicitly, with its twelve foundations adorned with every jewel. The desolate exile who had rubble for walls receives gem-studded walls instead. Motyer: the architectural extravagance is not literal urban planning but the language of incomparable beauty — the restored community will be visibly, unmistakably glorious. What was shamed will be splendid.

verseByVerse.quote: All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children. In righteousness you shall be established; you shall be far from oppression, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: All your children shall be taught by the LORD — the new covenant community will be characterized by direct divine instruction (Jer 31:34: they shall all know me). Jesus quotes this in John 6:45 as evidence that those who come to him are the fulfillment of this promise: everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. The stability of this community — established in righteousness, far from oppression, free from terror — is the social expression of the servant's atoning work. Young: peace is the fruit of righteousness (32:17), which is the fruit of the servant's suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone stirs up strife, it is not from me; whoever stirs up strife with you shall fall because of you. Behold, I have created the smith who blows the fire of coals and produces a weapon for its purpose. I have also created the ravager to destroy; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God asserts sovereignty even over the makers of weapons and the agents of destruction. The smith who forges weapons exists within God's creative order. The ravager is not an independent power; God created him. This is not divine approval of destruction but assertion of divine control over it: what appears to be random violence or organized oppression is within the scope of God's sovereign ordering. Oswalt: the assurance to Zion is grounded not in the absence of threats but in the truth that no threat originates outside God's awareness and control.

verseByVerse.quote: no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD and their vindication from me, declares the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: No weapon formed against you shall succeed — the covenant protection of the servant's community is total. This is not a promise of the absence of attack but of the failure of every attack. The tongue that rises in accusation will be refuted. Then the glorious designation: the servants of the LORD — plural, the community formed by the servant's work. Their vindication comes not from their own strength but from God. Motyer: the heritage of the servants is the inheritance won by the one Servant — what he purchased, they receive as their permanent possession.

55.subtitle: Come, Everyone Who Thirsts
55.intro: Overview. Chapter 55 is the great invitation — the open call that closes the central movement of Isaiah (chs. 40–55). It begins at a marketplace, shouting to everyone who is thirsty, hungry, and poor. It ends with one of the most profound statements about the relationship between God’s word and human history: my word shall not return to me empty. The whole of chapters 40–55 is captured in the final image of the mountains and hills breaking into singing as the exiles return home.

sections.title: The Free Feast
sections.commentary:
Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. The marketplace imagery is deliberate: the things on offer at this stall cost nothing, which means the only people who miss out are those who insist on paying. Why do you spend your money for what is not bread, and your labor for what does not satisfy? The indictment is of misplaced economic energy — working hard for emptiness while refusing the feast that is free.

Incline your ear and come to me; hear, that your soul may live. The call to hear is the call to be made alive. God offers an everlasting covenant — the sure mercies of David — and David is given as a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander. Nations that did not know Israel will run to her because of the LORD.

sections.title: Seek the LORD While He May Be Found
sections.commentary:
Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked forsake his way; let the unrighteous man his thoughts. Return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him; to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. The urgency is grounded in an implicit limit: “while he may be found,” “while he is near.” The invitation has a horizon.

vv. 8–9 — “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.” This verse is often quoted to explain divine mystery — why God acts in ways we cannot understand. But the context is pardon: God will abundantly pardon in ways that exceed our calculations. The higher thoughts are thoughts of grace that outrun our capacity to imagine forgiveness. The gap between his ways and ours is not primarily about inscrutable providence but inexhaustible mercy.

For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout — so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it. The word is not merely information; it is power — it does what it says.

keyVerse.quote: “So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.”
keyVerse.note: This is Isaiah’s doctrine of the word: it is not contingent on human reception. It goes, it works, it returns with the harvest of its purpose. The whole of chapters 40–55 has been one extended word-act — comfort, promise, prediction, invitation — and this verse stands at the end of it as the guarantee of everything that was spoken.

55.reflection: God asks: why do you spend your money for what is not bread? This is one of the most diagnostic questions in Scripture. What are you currently investing time, money, or emotional energy in that does not satisfy — while the free feast sits unattended? What would it actually cost you to “come to the waters” today?
55.text: <sup>1</sup>"Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. <sup>2</sup>Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food. <sup>3</sup>Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David. <sup>4</sup>Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples. <sup>5</sup>Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you. <sup>6</sup>Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near; <sup>7</sup>let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. <sup>8</sup>For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. <sup>9</sup>For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts. <sup>10</sup>For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, <sup>11</sup>so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it. <sup>12</sup>For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands. <sup>13</sup>Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Ho! Come to the Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great gospel invitation of the Old Testament. Come without money, without price — buy wine and milk freely. Listen, that your soul may live. Seek the LORD while he may be found. God's thoughts and ways are higher than ours as the heavens are higher than the earth. The word of God will not return empty. The mountains and trees will break forth in singing at the new creation.
verseByVerse.theology: Free grace and divine sovereignty: the free invitation ('come without money') and the sovereign effectiveness of God's word ('it shall not return empty') are two sides of the same grace. The gospel is genuinely free — no precondition, no purchase price. Yet it is also sovereignly effective — God's word accomplishes what he sends it to do. These are not contradictory but complementary: the free offer is backed by divine power.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller frequently uses Isaiah 55 to explain the paradox of grace: the water, wine, and milk are free to us because they were purchased at infinite cost by the servant of ch53. The call to 'seek the LORD while he may be found' (v.6) carries both urgency (there is a limited time of availability) and assurance (he is near to those who call).

verseByVerse.quote: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The invitation is universal (everyone who thirsts) and unconditional (without money, without price). The paradox of buying without price — the commercial language used for a transaction that requires nothing — is the paradox of grace. What cannot be earned is freely given. The rhetorical question of v.2 exposes the futility of human self-provision: money spent on non-bread, labor producing no satisfaction. Augustine's famous opening of the Confessions echoes this: our heart is restless until it rests in God. Motyer: the waters, wine, and milk represent every dimension of nourishment — physical, celebratory, basic. God offers comprehensive flourishing, not merely spiritual comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast love for David. Behold, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hear, that your soul may live — eternal life flows from hearing God's word. The everlasting covenant is the Davidic covenant extended to the community: my steadfast love for David. The sure mercies pledged to David (hesed in the plural of intensity) are now offered to all who come to God's feast. David was a witness and commander to peoples; now the community of the servant will fulfill this role globally. Childs: the democratization of the Davidic covenant — applying its privileges to all God's people — is the shape of the new covenant community.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you shall call a nation that you do not know, and a nation that did not know you shall run to you, because of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you. Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Nations previously unknown will run to the community that carries God's invitation — the gospel's attractive power exceeds all human marketing. The running of the nations echoes the pilgrimage passages of chs 2, 60, 66. Then the urgency: seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. The window of availability is real; urgency is appropriate. Oswalt: the pairing of free invitation (vv.1-2) with urgent seeking (v.6) is the rhythm of gospel preaching — grace is freely offered but not permanently available to the person who perpetually delays.

verseByVerse.quote: let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The call to repentance is concrete: forsake way, forsake thoughts, return to the LORD. The motivation for return is overwhelming: he will abundantly pardon. The Hebrew is literal: multiply to pardon — God's forgiveness is not grudging or minimal but extravagant. Then the theological grounding: God's thoughts and ways are categorically higher than human thoughts and ways. Our calculation of what forgiveness costs, what is forgivable, what mercy requires — all are too small. Young: the abundant pardon of v.7 requires the categorical difference of v.8 — we can receive grace beyond what we can calculate because God's ways exceed ours.

verseByVerse.quote: For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts. For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The height of God's ways above human ways is illustrated by the distance between heaven and earth — spatial infinity as a picture of qualitative incomprehensibility. Then the analogy shifts to agriculture: rain and snow descend purposively, doing their work before returning to the cycle. The word of God will be similarly effective. Motyer: the agricultural image is beautifully apt — rain does not ask for permission, does not negotiate its effectiveness, does not return unused. It simply does what it is sent to do, and the earth responds. God's word is like this.

verseByVerse.quote: so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it. For you shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and the hills before you shall break out into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: My word shall not return to me empty — the divine guarantee of gospel effectiveness. Not every individual responds, but God's word always achieves its purpose — either the salvation of those who receive it or the judgment of those who reject it. The return with joy and peace, mountains and hills singing, trees clapping — creation celebrates the homecoming. Childs: the new exodus is so transformative that it re-orders the natural world, reversing the curse. Creation was made to sing God's praises; the return of the redeemed restores creation's song.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress; instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle; and it shall make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The curse of thorns and briars (Gen 3:18) is reversed: cypress and myrtle replace them — beauty and fragrance replacing thorns. This is new creation language — the undoing of the curse, the restoration of the garden. And the purpose: to make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign. The transformation of creation is itself a witness — the watching world will see the landscape change and know that the LORD has acted. Young: the everlasting sign that shall not be cut off connects to the new covenant that shall never be removed (54:10). Both are permanent expressions of the same grace.

56.subtitle: My House Shall Be a House of Prayer for All Peoples
56.intro: Overview. Chapter 56 opens the final section of Isaiah (chs. 56–66), which applies the great promises of chapters 40–55 to the community returning from exile. Two groups who were excluded from the assembly under the Mosaic law — eunuchs and foreigners — are explicitly included in God’s coming house. The chapter is the Old Testament ground for Jesus’ cleansing of the temple: “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”

sections.title: The Included Outsiders
sections.commentary:
Keep justice and do righteousness, for my salvation is about to come. Blessed is the man who does this — who keeps the Sabbath, who keeps his hand from evil. And then two expansions that must have been startling to the original hearers.

Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, “The LORD will surely separate me from his people.” And let not the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” The eunuch who keeps the Sabbath and holds fast to the covenant will be given “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; an everlasting name that shall not be cut off.” The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD — to serve him, to love his name, to be his servants — these God will bring to his holy mountain. Their offerings will be accepted on his altar.

v. 7 — “For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” Jesus quotes this verse in Matt. 21:13 when he overturns the money changers’ tables. His point is not merely about commerce but about access: the outer courts — the only place Gentiles were permitted — had been taken over by the very commerce that made worship transactional and excluded the outsiders Isaiah said God had already included.

sections.title: Blind Watchmen
sections.commentary: The chapter pivots to a biting critique of Israel’s own leaders: the watchmen are blind, knowing nothing, silent dogs who cannot bark. They dream, lie down, love to slumber. They are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain. The contrast is severe: God is expanding his house to include all nations while the leaders of the house are asleep. The ones most responsible for keeping watch are the ones least alert.

keyVerse.quote: “For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
keyVerse.note: The text Jesus quotes when he cleanses the temple. The inclusivity is the point: God’s house was always designed for all peoples, not just Israel. The commerce that Jesus disrupted was not incidental but structural — it was physically occupying the only space available to outsiders. To clear it out was to enact Isaiah 56.

56.reflection: The two groups God explicitly includes — eunuchs and foreigners — were both defined by what they lacked or what they were not. God offers them something better than biological legacy or ethnic membership: an everlasting name. Who in your community occupies the place of the “excluded outsider”? And what does God’s explicit inclusion of the eunuch and the foreigner say about the shape of his house?
56.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed. <sup>2</sup>Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil." <sup>3</sup>Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, "The LORD will surely separate me from his people"; and let not the eunuch say, "Behold, I am a dry tree." <sup>4</sup>For thus says the LORD: "To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, <sup>5</sup>I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off. <sup>6</sup>And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to minister to him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath and does not profane it, and holds fast my covenant— <sup>7</sup>these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples." <sup>8</sup>The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, declares, "I will gather yet others to him besides those already gathered." <sup>9</sup>All you beasts of the field, come to devour— all you beasts in the forest. <sup>10</sup>His watchmen are blind; they are all without knowledge; they are all silent dogs; they cannot bark, dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber. <sup>11</sup>The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain, one and all. <sup>12</sup>"Come," they say, "let me get wine; let us fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be like this day, great beyond measure."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The House of Prayer for All Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third major section of Isaiah begins (chs 56-66). God declares his salvation is near and calls for justice and righteousness. Foreigners and eunuchs — those excluded from the Mosaic assembly (Deut 23:1-8) — are explicitly included in the new covenant community. God's house will be a house of prayer for all nations. But the chapter ends with a harsh rebuke of Israel's blind and greedy leaders.
verseByVerse.theology: Inclusion and the eschatological community: Isaiah 56 is one of the most explicit inclusivity texts in the Old Testament. Those who were excluded by the Mosaic law's purity codes are included in the new covenant based on one criterion: holding fast to the covenant, loving the LORD's name, keeping the sabbath. Jesus quotes v.7 ('a house of prayer for all nations') when cleansing the temple (Mark 11:17), identifying his action as the beginning of the fulfillment of this promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer sees chs 56-66 as the application of the servant's atoning work to the life of the community. The servant suffers in 52:13-53:12; the community reaps the benefits in chs 54-66. The inclusion of foreigners and eunuchs in ch56 is the direct consequence: the servant's sacrifice breaks down every wall of separation.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: 'Keep justice, and do righteousness, for soon my salvation will come, and my righteousness be revealed. Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath, not profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with ethical imperatives grounded in eschatological imminence: keep justice and do righteousness because salvation is coming soon. The ethical life is not the basis of salvation but its anticipatory response. The sabbath-keeper is blessed — the sabbath becomes a synecdoche for covenantal faithfulness generally. Oswalt: the call to justice in light of coming salvation is the structure of NT ethics as well — in view of God's mercies, present your bodies (Rom 12:1). Eschatology energizes ethics.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, 'The LORD will surely separate me from his people'; and let not the eunuch say, 'Behold, I am a dry tree.' For thus says the LORD: 'To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two groups who feared exclusion are explicitly addressed. The foreigner joined to the LORD fears second-class status; the eunuch (excluded from the assembly in Deut 23:1) fears permanent exclusion (a dry tree = no descendants, no future). God speaks directly to each fear. The criterion for full inclusion is not ethnicity or physical wholeness but covenant faithfulness: keeping sabbath, choosing what pleases God, holding fast the covenant. Childs: the eschatological community is defined not by biological or ethnic identity but by covenant loyalty.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off. And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD, to minister to him, to love the name of the LORD, and to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath and does not profane it, and holds fast my covenant— (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: To the eunuch who feared a dry tree: an everlasting name better than sons and daughters. The monument within the walls of God's house is permanent memorial — a name that cannot be cut off, unlike biological lineage that ends with childlessness. For the foreigner: full membership, ministry, love of God's name, servant status. Three criteria for the foreigner (v.6): keeping sabbath, not profaning it, holding fast the covenant. Motyer: the three criteria are intensive and complementary — active observance, avoidance of violation, and covenantal commitment — covering the whole of covenant life.

verseByVerse.quote: these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, declares, I will gather yet others to them besides those already gathered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A house of prayer for all peoples — the climax of the inclusion promise. The temple, which had become an exclusively Israelite space, is declared God's universal place of access. Jesus quotes this in Mark 11:17 when cleansing the temple — the money-changers had turned it from a house of prayer into a commercial zone, reversing the inclusivity God intended. Young: God gathers not only the outcasts of Israel but also the Gentile others — the already-gathered plus more to be gathered. The community of grace is always expanding outward.

verseByVerse.quote: All you beasts of the field, come to devour — all you beasts in the forest. His watchmen are blind; they are all without knowledge; they are all silent dogs; they cannot bark, sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A dramatic tonal shift: the watchmen (prophets, priests, leaders) are blind dogs who cannot bark. The beasts of prey are invited to devour — God himself opens the gate to destruction because the shepherds have failed. The silence of watchmen who should warn is the church's perennial failure in every age. Childs: the contrast between the coming global community (vv.1-8) and the corrupt present leadership (vv.9-12) reveals the gap that only the servant's renewal can bridge.

verseByVerse.quote: The dogs have a mighty appetite; they never have enough. But they are shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain, one and all. 'Come,' they say, 'let me get wine; let us fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be like this day, great beyond measure.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The corrupt shepherds: insatiable appetite, no understanding, self-serving, greedy, given to drunken complacency. Tomorrow will be like today — the willful blindness to coming judgment. This is the pastoral failure that precedes every national disaster in Scripture — leaders who look after themselves rather than the flock. Oswalt: the rebuke of corrupt shepherds in vv.9-12 is the shadow side of the inclusion promise in vv.1-8. Until the servants of God are transformed (the work of the Spirit in chs 59-66), the community's leaders will remain the obstacle to the very inclusion God promises.

57.subtitle: The High and Holy One Who Dwells with the Contrite
57.intro: Overview. Chapter 57 contains a scathing critique of Israel’s idolatrous practices — sexual fertility rites, child sacrifice, pagan deal-making — before arriving at one of Isaiah’s most theologically surprising statements: the high and exalted God, who inhabits eternity, chooses to dwell with the lowly and contrite in spirit. The chapter ends with the peace that is for the contrite and the restlessness that awaits the wicked.

sections.title: Idolatry’s Exhausting Program
sections.commentary:
The righteous perish and no one lays it to heart — the devout are taken away while the wicked prosper and no one understands. Then God indicts: you who mock, you offspring of the adulterer and the prostitute. Behind every idol there is a journey: you journeyed far, going to Sheol, wearing yourself out. The idol program is exhausting. You were wearied by the length of your way, but you did not say “It is hopeless.”

v. 10 — “You were wearied by the length of your way, but you did not say ‘It is hopeless.’” This is one of the saddest diagnoses in Isaiah: the people are exhausted by idolatry but refuse to acknowledge it is not working. The energy to keep trying substitutes for the honesty to stop and return. Idolatry is primarily characterized not by blasphemy but by stubbornness in the face of evidence.

sections.title: With the Contrite and Lowly
sections.commentary:
And it shall be said: build up, build up, prepare the way; remove every obstruction. God will revive the heart of the contrite ones. For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.”

The two addresses — the eternal heights and the lowly spirit — are not in tension but in design. God is not condescending when he comes to the lowly; he is fulfilling the same character that makes him exalted. His holiness and his humility are two expressions of the same nature. The chapter closes: “There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked” — the wicked are always in motion (v. 20: like the tossing sea). The contrite are still; the wicked cannot stop.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit.”
keyVerse.note: This verse holds together what would seem like opposites: the infinite God and the broken person. The condition for the divine indwelling is not religious achievement but contrition. Jesus’ first beatitude (“blessed are the poor in spirit”) is the New Testament form of this verse. The throne and the broken heart are the same address.

57.reflection: God inhabits eternity and chooses to dwell with the contrite in spirit. Not with the successful, the together, the impressive — with the contrite. What would it mean for you to stop managing your spiritual life well enough to avoid contrition, and instead to let yourself be small enough for God to actually dwell there?
57.text: <sup>1</sup>The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity; <sup>2</sup>he enters into peace; they rest in their beds who walk in their uprightness. <sup>3</sup>But you, draw near, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the loose woman. <sup>4</sup>Against whom do you sport yourselves? Against whom do you open your mouth wide and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, the offspring of deceit, <sup>5</sup>you who burn with lust among the oaks, under every green tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks? <sup>6</sup>Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion; they, they are your lot; to them you have poured out a drink offering, you have brought a grain offering.
