verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — New Heavens and New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the prayer of chs 63-64. He was found by those who did not seek him; he held out his hands to a rebellious people. But now he will distinguish: servants will eat, rebels will go hungry. Then the great promise — new heavens and new earth. No more infant who lives but a few days; the oldest will die like a youth. They will build and inhabit, plant and eat. The wolf and the lamb will feed together. The former things will not be remembered.
verseByVerse.theology: New creation: Isaiah 65 is the Old Testament foundation for Revelation 21's new heavens and new earth. The promise that the former things will not be remembered (v.17; Rev 21:4) and that creation's violence is reversed (wolf and lamb, lion and ox, v.25) frames the entire vision. Paul quotes v.1-2 in Romans 10:20-21 in the context of Gentile salvation — God found by those who did not seek him (Gentiles) while Israel resisted.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer calls ch65 the answer to the prayer of chs 63-64 — but it answers beyond what was prayed for. The community prayed for restoration; God promises re-creation. This is always the pattern of divine grace: the answer to prayer exceeds the request. We ask for healing; God promises resurrection. We ask for forgiveness; God promises adoption.

verseByVerse.quote: I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name. I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes vv.1-2 in Romans 10:20-21, applying v.1 to the Gentiles (found by those who did not seek) and v.2 to Israel (rebellious people to whom God spread out his hands all day). God's initiative precedes all human seeking — the doctrine of prevenient and effectual grace embedded in the prophet's answer. The spread hands of v.2 are simultaneously an embrace and a gesture of patience — God holding open the offer all day to the very people who reject him. Oswalt: divine persistence in grace toward the rebellious is one of the most stunning claims in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: a people who provoke me to my face continually, who sacrifice in gardens and make offerings on bricks, who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The specific indictments of syncretistic worship: garden shrines (Canaanite practice), brick altars (not the prescribed altar), spending nights among the tombs (consulting the dead — cf. 8:19-20), eating pig's flesh (Levitical prohibition). These are Israel's practices alongside formal temple worship — the syncretism that the prophets consistently condemned. Childs: the catalog is not exhaustive but representative — illustrating a community that has imported every surrounding religion while keeping the forms of covenant worship. Double-minded religion cannot receive undivided grace.

verseByVerse.quote: who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.' These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day. Behold, it is written before me: I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The ultimate irony: the syncretists claim holiness — do not come near me, I am too holy for you. Religious pride coexisting with pagan practice is the most toxic spiritual condition. God's response: smoke in my nostrils, the irritant that will not dissipate. The ledger is kept; repayment will come. Motyer: the claim to superior holiness while practicing idolatry is not merely hypocrisy but inversion — the unholy claiming holiness. This is the spiritual condition that makes grace hardest to receive because it insulates the person from recognizing their need.

verseByVerse.quote: both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together, says the LORD; because they made offerings on the mountains and insulted me on the hills, I will measure into their lap payment for their former deeds. Thus says the LORD: 'As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The judgment is intergenerational — present iniquities compounded by fathers' sins. But then the grace: like the winemaker who spares the whole cluster for the sake of the good grapes in it, God preserves a remnant within the whole. The servants are the believing minority within the covenant community — the all Israel that is saved in Romans 11 is the whole of the elect, not every ethnic descendant. Oswalt: the remnant theology of Isaiah reaches its resolution here — God will not destroy all, because there is a blessing (elect remnant) within the cluster of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah inheritors of my mountains; my chosen shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there. Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The servants and chosen will inherit the mountains and dwell in the land. The geographical specificity — Sharon (the coastal plain), Achor (a valley associated with covenant failure in Josh 7) — grounds the promise in real landscape. What was cursed becomes pastoral; what was associated with failure becomes restful habitation. Hosea 2:15 also uses Achor as a door of hope. Childs: the transformation of specific geographical curses into blessings is part of the new creation's concreteness — this is not merely spiritual reality but renewed physical creation.

verseByVerse.quote: But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny, I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter, because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Fortune (Gad) and Destiny (Meni) are pagan deities of luck — the setting of a table for them is a rite of divination and luck-seeking. The contrast with seeking the LORD is stark. Those who sought luck from idols will find their destined end in the sword. The explanation: when God called, they did not answer; when God spoke, they did not listen. The judgment is the mirror image of the offense — they chose deafness; they receive a silencing. Young: the two-way division of the chapter (servants/rebels) is consistent with all of Isaiah — the community's response to God determines which blessing or judgment they receive.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The four-fold contrast — eat/hungry, drink/thirsty, rejoice/ashamed, sing/wail — is structured as an extended blessing-and-curse pronouncement echoing Deuteronomy 28. The servants receive the covenant blessings; the rebellious receive the covenant curses. Motyer: the contrast does not create two classes arbitrarily but reveals the two trajectories that have always existed within the covenant community — those who respond to God's call and those who ignore it. The judgment is the crystallization of choices already made.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by a different name. So that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rebels' name becomes a byword of curse; the servants receive a new name. The God of truth (literally, the God of Amen — the faithful God) becomes the standard of all blessing and oath. The former troubles are forgotten — the exile and all its suffering will not shadow the new age; they will be hidden from God's own memory. Young: God's forgetting of former troubles is the most radical possible statement of new beginning — not merely forgiven but forgotten, not merely healed but the wound no longer visible to the one who healed it.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in what I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: New heavens and new earth — the most expansive promise in Isaiah, taken up in 66:22 and Revelation 21:1. Not renovation but recreation — the former order passes away entirely. The former things not remembered: the completeness of discontinuity with all previous suffering. The recreation begins with Jerusalem — I create Jerusalem to be a joy — but extends to the entire cosmos. Childs: the new creation is not the recovery of Eden but something beyond it — Eden was the first creation's beginning; this is the second creation's perfect completion.

verseByVerse.quote: I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress. No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's joy in Jerusalem — the divine delight first named in 62:4 (Hephzibah) now expressed as active rejoicing. No more weeping, no more crying — the Revelation 21:4 promise (God will wipe away every tear) is here in seed form. The new age is characterized by fullness of life: infants reach maturity; elders complete their days. Even a hundred-year-old death would be considered premature — the new creation recalibrates the entire scale of human flourishing. Motyer: the absence of infant mortality and premature death is the new creation's sign that the curse on human life has been fully reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The reversal of Deuteronomy 28:30 (building and another inhabiting, planting and another eating — the covenant curses). In the new creation, the worker enjoys the fruit of their labor — security, stability, uninterrupted flourishing. Like the days of a tree — the longevity of ancient cedars applied to human life. The chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands — not a moment of abundance but sustained, multigenerational flourishing. Young: labor in the new creation is not the curse of Gen 3 but the blessing of meaningful work that produces fruit the worker keeps.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them. Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Futility removed: no vain labor, no children born for tragedy. The blessing of Abraham flows through every generation. Then the astonishing promise about prayer: before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear. The God who seemed silent through all of chs 63-64 is now perpetually attentive — answering before the question is finished. Oswalt: this is the ultimate promise of divine presence — not just response to prayer but anticipation of it. God knows the need before we articulate it and moves to meet it while we are still finding words.

verseByVerse.quote: The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain, says the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The new creation reverses the enmity between predator and prey (11:6-9 — the peaceable kingdom). Wolf and lamb together, lion eating straw — the violence built into the fallen created order is undone. Only the serpent retains its curse (Gen 3:14 — dust shall be your food): the symbol of original rebellion continues to bear the mark of its defeat. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain — the comprehensive peace that is the goal of all redemption. Motyer: the new creation is not the absence of creatures but the removal of their fallen characteristics. It is creation restored and perfected, not annihilated.

66.subtitle: This Is the One to Whom I Will Look
66.intro: Overview. Chapter 66 is Isaiah’s final word, and it holds nothing back. God asks: where is the house you would build for me? Heaven is my throne; the earth is my footstool. The one he looks to is not the grand temple-builder but the one who is humble and contrite and trembles at his word. The chapter moves through birth-like imagery of Zion’s sudden deliverance, the judgment of the rebellious, and closes with the greatest gathering of all nations in Scripture — including some as priests and Levites — and the permanent worship of the redeemed. The final verse is unresolved: the corpses of those who rebelled will be seen; their worm does not die. The book ends holding both eternal life and eternal judgment before the reader.

sections.title: The One Who Trembles at My Word
sections.commentary:
Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me? The question demolishes every project of confining God in human-made spaces. He made everything; everything is already his address. But then: this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. The cosmic vision contracts to a single quality: trembling at the word.

v. 2 — “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.” The enormous God — whose throne is heaven — looks at one specific kind of person. Not the grand, not the theologically sophisticated, not the ritually accomplished: the humble and trembling. This is the New Testament’s “poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3) and the Publican’s prayer (Luke 18:13). The character of the look is not pity but delight.

sections.title: The Birth and the Deliverance
sections.commentary:
A sound of uproar from the city, a sound from the temple, the sound of the LORD rendering recompense to his enemies. Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. The birth metaphor for the restoration is instantaneous and overwhelming: not a long recovery but a sudden arrival.

Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy. As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem. The comforting of chapter 40 is here at the end, in its fullest personal form: God as mother, the comforted as child, Jerusalem as the home where the comfort happens.

sections.title: The Final Gathering
sections.commentary:
For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory. God will send survivors to the nations — to Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, Javan, the coastlands — and they shall declare his glory among the nations. And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD. Some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites.

The inclusion of Gentiles as priests and Levites is breathtaking in context: the offices reserved for a single tribe in Israel will be given to those from the farthest nations. This is the fulfillment of chapter 56’s promise and the ground of 1 Peter 2:9: “you are a royal priesthood, a holy nation.”

And from new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD. The book ends with unending worship — all flesh, every cycle of time, before God. And then, immediately: they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh. The book of Isaiah ends holding eternity open in both directions: unending worship and unending judgment, side by side, without resolution, before the reader.

keyVerse.quote: “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.”
keyVerse.note: The cosmic God — whose throne is heaven and footstool the earth — focuses his gaze on one kind of person. Not the magnificent, not the impressive, not the doctrinally complete: the humble and trembling. This is the first beatitude in Old Testament form. It is also the conclusion Isaiah has been building toward: after 66 chapters about the incomparable God, the question is not what house will satisfy him but what heart — and the answer is the broken, attentive one.

66.theology: Eternal Life and Eternal Judgment. Isaiah 66:24 — “their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched” — is the Old Testament text Jesus quotes three times in Mark 9:44–48 as the description of hell. The book of Isaiah ends with eternal life (all flesh worshiping forever) and eternal judgment (worm and fire that do not die) placed side by side without resolution. Reformed theology has always insisted that both are real and both are permanent: universalism fails on Isaiah 66:24, and despair fails on 66:23. The response the book calls for is the response of verse 2: humility, contrition, and trembling at the word of the God who holds both futures in his hand.
66.reflection: Isaiah ends not with a resolution but with two destinations placed before the reader. The worm and fire of verse 24 are visible from the place of endless worship in verse 23 — the redeemed will forever know what they were saved from. After 66 chapters of the incomparable God — his holiness, his judgment, his grace, his suffering Servant, his new creation — what is your response? Is it trembling at his word? Humble faith? The book leaves the question with you, as every prophet must.
66.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest? <sup>2</sup>All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. <sup>3</sup>He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations; <sup>4</sup>I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in." <sup>5</sup>Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: "Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, 'Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy'; but it is they who shall be put to shame. <sup>6</sup>The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies! <sup>7</sup>Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. <sup>8</sup>Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. <sup>9</sup>Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?" says the LORD; "shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb?" says your God. <sup>10</sup>Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her; <sup>11</sup>that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance." <sup>12</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees. <sup>13</sup>As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies. <sup>15</sup>For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. <sup>16</sup>For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many. <sup>17</sup>Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD. <sup>18</sup>For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory, <sup>19</sup>and I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations. <sup>20</sup>And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and on dromedaries, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the LORD, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD. <sup>21</sup>And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD. <sup>22</sup>For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain. <sup>23</sup>From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD. <sup>24</sup>And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–24 — Heaven Is My Throne: the New Creation Complete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final chapter of Isaiah. God declares that heaven is his throne and earth his footstool — what house can contain him? He looks to the humble and contrite who tremble at his word. Hypocritical worship is rejected. The woman who gives birth before labor is announced — Zion will give birth to a nation in a moment. The comfort of Jerusalem is promised like nursing at a mother's breast. The LORD comes in fire to judge all flesh. Survivors are sent to the nations. New heavens, new earth, new moon and sabbath worship. All flesh will worship before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: The end of the book: ch66 gathers the book's major themes — temple and no-temple, humble versus proud, new creation, universal worship, and the two destinies of the redeemed and the wicked. The final verse is one of the most sobering in Scripture ('and they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me'). Isaiah ends not in unqualified triumph but in the solemn reality of two destinations.
verseByVerse.examples: Childs notes that Isaiah 66 is designed to resonate with Isaiah 1 — the book is framed. Chapter 1 condemned hypocritical worship; ch66 condemns it again. Chapter 1 promised the purging of Jerusalem; ch66 fulfills it. Chapter 1 called the nations to account; ch66 sends witnesses to them. The book's end is its beginning fulfilled.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest? All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Stephen quotes vv.1-2 in Acts 7:49-50 before his martyrdom, challenging the Sanhedrin's idolatry of the temple. No building can contain the God whose throne is the cosmos. Yet this transcendent God has a specific focus: the humble and contrite who tremble at his word. The infinite God looks specifically at the small, broken, word-reverent person. Motyer: the vertical scale (heavens to earth) intensifies rather than diminishes the condescension of v.2 — the One whose throne is heaven stoops to the contrite and lowly (cf. 57:15).

verseByVerse.quote: He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations; I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ritual without obedience is worse than no ritual — it becomes a new kind of abomination. The shocking equivalences (sacrificing a lamb = breaking a dog's neck) are not critiques of the sacrificial system but of hearts that have departed from God while maintaining worship forms. This echoes 1:10-15 and ch58's critique of fasting without justice. Oswalt: God does not reject sacrifice per se but sacrifice offered from a heart that has chosen its own way. The worship that begins in self-will rather than trembling before God's word is not worship at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, 'Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy'; but it is they who shall be put to shame. The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The community of the humble who tremble at God's word has been cast out by their brothers — perhaps a reference to the split between those who returned from exile with pure worship and those who compromised. The mockers say sarcastically: let the LORD be glorified — but they will be shamed. The uproar from the city and temple is the sound of divine judgment on the disobedient. Childs: the division within the covenant community that runs through chs 65-66 mirrors the two responses to the servant of ch53 — those who see and believe, and those who see and reject.

verseByVerse.quote: Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The miraculous birth — labor coming after delivery, not before. The new community of God comes into existence instantaneously, in a moment. This is the logic of Pentecost (Acts 2): 3,000 converted in one day, the church born in a moment. No nine-month gestation for the new creation; God can create a nation in a day. Motyer: the image of birth before labor is the image of pure divine initiative — no human preparation, no gradual development, only the sovereign act of the Creator who speaks new things into existence.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth? says the LORD; shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb? says your God. Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God commits himself to completing what he begins. The divine midwife who brings to the point of birth will not leave the birth incomplete. Oswalt: the argument from divine consistency — God never abandons the work of his hands (64:8) — grounds the confidence that the new creation will be fully realized. The call to rejoice with Jerusalem (v.10) echoes 65:18-19 — God rejoices and calls his people to rejoice with him. The joy is communal, not private.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance. For thus says the LORD: Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jerusalem as nursing mother — the most intimate image of communal care. Satisfied, drinking deeply, carried on hips, bounced on knees — the vocabulary of infant care applied to the whole community. Peace extended like a river, the wealth of nations like an overflowing stream — abundance beyond containment. Young: the maternal imagery of vv.11-13 presents God's care through Jerusalem as the most attentive, intimate care possible. The city that was devastated becomes the nursing mother of nations.

verseByVerse.quote: As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem. You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his wrath against his enemies. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: As one whom his mother comforts — the tenderest comparison in the Bible for divine comfort, picking up 49:15's nursing mother. The comfort comes in Jerusalem — the place of meeting with God. Bones flourishing like grass: the dry bones of exile (Ezek 37) come fully to life. The hand of the LORD known to servants and shown in wrath against enemies — the same divine hand that saves and judges is revealed simultaneously to two different groups with two different effects. Motyer: the final chapters of Isaiah consistently present the two destinations without softening either — the comfort of the servants and the wrath against enemies are both real.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine warrior returns — fire, whirlwind, chariots, sword. The judgment of 63:1-6 is here in its universal scope: with all flesh. The slain shall be many — the judgment of God is not a minor adjustment but a comprehensive reckoning. This is the day the servants were sheltered from (57:1); this is the day the wicked could not escape (57:21). Childs: the fire of judgment has purifying and destroying functions simultaneously — for the new creation to emerge, everything resistant to God's holiness must be consumed.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD. For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The syncretists of v.3 and 65:3-5 — the garden-worship, pig-flesh eaters — will come to an end together. But then the universal gathering: all nations and tongues shall come and see God's glory. The judgment on the disobedient within the covenant and the ingathering of the nations are simultaneous events. Motyer: the negative (end of the syncretists) and the positive (all nations seeing glory) are two aspects of the same final act. God's glory is the fire that destroys the resistant and the light that draws the seeking.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations. And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and on swift beasts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the LORD, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The survivors of judgment become missionaries — sent to the farthest nations (Tarshish = Spain, Pul and Lud = Africa, Tubal and Javan = north and Greece) that have never heard. Their message: the glory of the LORD. Then they bring the dispersed people home as an offering — the nations become the instrument of Israel's final ingathering, just as Israel was the instrument of the nations' initial hearing. Oswalt: the missionary structure of vv.19-20 is the ecclesiological shape of the new covenant community — those who have seen glory are sent to those who have not, so that they too may come and see.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD. For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Some of the Gentile converts will be made priests and Levites — the most radical inclusivity possible. The priestly calling is no longer ethnic but spiritual. The permanence of the new creation ensures the permanence of the community: as long as the new heavens and new earth endure — forever — so shall God's people endure. Childs: the extension of priestly status to Gentile believers is the fulfillment of Ex 19:6 (a kingdom of priests, a holy nation) and anticipates 1 Pet 2:9's application of that text to the church of all nations.

verseByVerse.quote: From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD. And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abomination to all flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The book ends on two notes held simultaneously. First, the great worship: all flesh, new moon to new moon, sabbath to sabbath, coming before the LORD. The sabbath cycles of the new creation are pure worship — the eternal sabbath rest anticipated in Heb 4:9-11. Second, the two destinies: the worshippers will see the dead bodies of rebels — those who rejected God's word and ways (v.24). Jesus quotes this verse three times in Mark 9:44-48 in the context of hell: the worm that does not die, the fire not quenched. The book of Isaiah ends not in sentimentality but in the sober reality of two eternal destinations — everlasting worship and everlasting judgment. Motyer: the final image is precisely calibrated. Isaiah does not soften the end; he lets both realities stand, as Jesus himself does.

0.subtitle: Introduction
0.intro:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem through the reigns of four kings — Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah — from around 740 to 700 BC. His call came in the year that King Uzziah died (chapter 6): a vision of the Lord high and lifted up, the seraphim crying Holy, holy, holy, and the commission to speak a word that most would refuse to hear. From that moment Isaiah became the greatest of the writing prophets — and this book became what Luther called “the fifth Gospel.”

The book divides naturally into two great halves. Chapters 1–39 address the Assyrian crisis: God’s judgment on Israel and Judah, the fate of the surrounding nations, and the demand for faith in the Holy One rather than military alliance. Chapters 40–66 address a people in Babylonian exile, not yet experienced but anticipated by prophetic foresight: comfort, homecoming, and the glorious emergence of the Servant who bears the sin of the world. The two halves share the same vocabulary, the same theology, and the same God — against all critical attempts to divide them.

The name of God that defines the book is the Holy One of Israel. It appears twenty-six times in Isaiah and only six times in the rest of the Old Testament. Holiness is not merely moral purity; it is the utter otherness of God, his transcendent glory that both terrifies and draws. Everything in Isaiah — judgment and comfort, wrath and mercy — flows from who this God is. The prophet’s task is to make the Holy One of Israel known.

The four Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) form the theological heartbeat of the second half. They move from the Servant’s gentle justice to his voluntary suffering — despised, crushed, pierced for our transgressions — and his ultimate vindication. The New Testament quotes or alludes to Isaiah more than any other Old Testament book. Jesus opened his ministry with Isaiah 61. Philip expounded Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian on the road. John saw Isaiah 6 as a vision of Christ’s glory.

To preach Isaiah is to preach the whole gospel in its Old Testament register: the holiness that makes sin impossible to ignore, the grace that makes forgiveness inconceivably costly, and the glory of a God who will not rest until his purposes fill the earth as the waters cover the sea. Sproul said that no book of Scripture humbled him more. No book of Scripture delighted him more either. Both responses flow from the same source: the Holy One of Israel, sovereign, saving, and surpassingly glorious.
